Initially created: 2026-03-10T22:34:17.542+09:00 by CH Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: 1.1 The *Qū Lǐ* says:
Let there be no lack of reverence,
let your appearance be as if in deep thought,
and let your speech be calm and certain.
How peaceful the people would be!
1.2 Arrogance should not be allowed to grow;
desires should not be indulged;
the will should not be fully gratified;
and pleasures should not be taken to the extreme.
1.3 Be intimate with the worthy and respect them;
hold them in awe and love them.
Love them, yet recognize their faults;
dislike them, yet recognize their good qualities.
Accumulate wealth and be able to distribute it;
be content in security and yet be able to move.
When facing wealth, do not obtain it improperly;
when facing difficulty, do not escape it improperly.
In contention, do not seek only to win;
in division, do not seek the larger share.
Do not give definitive judgments on doubtful matters;
if you are right, do not be possessive of it.
1.4 Regarding behavior: sit like a sacrificial personator (*shī*),
and stand as if performing a fast (*zhāi*).
Rites follow what is appropriate;
missions follow local customs.
1.5 The Rites
are the means by which one determines closeness or distance,
resolves doubts and suspicions,
distinguishes similarities and differences,
and clarifies right and wrong.
In the Rites,
one does not please others recklessly,
nor does one waste words in speech.
In the Rites,
one does not overstep boundaries,
does not insult or encroach upon others,
and does not favor over-familiarity.
Cultivating oneself and fulfilling one's words
is called virtuous conduct.
When conduct is cultivated and speech follows the Way (*Dào*),
this is the essence of the Rites.
Regarding the Rites, one hears of being taken by others,
but not of taking others.
One hears of people coming to learn,
but not of going to teach.
1.6 The Way (*Dào*), Virtue (*Dé*), Benevolence (*Rén*), and Righteousness (*Yì*)
cannot be fulfilled without the Rites;
instruction and the rectification of customs
cannot be complete without the Rites.
Resolving disputes and lawsuits
cannot be decided without the Rites.
The relations between ruler and minister, superior and inferior, father and son, elder and younger brother
cannot be established without the Rites.
Serving teachers in study or official life
cannot be intimate without the Rites.
Ranking the court, governing the army,
presiding over offices, and executing laws
cannot be majestic or effective without the Rites.
Prayers, sacrifices,
and offerings to ghosts and spirits
cannot be sincere or solemn without the Rites.
Therefore, the superior man (*jūnzǐ*) uses humility,
reverence, restraint,
moderation, withdrawal,
and yielding to manifest the Rites.
A parrot can speak,
but it remains a bird.
An orangutan (*xīngxing*) can speak,
but it remains a beast.
Now, if a human being has no Rites,
even if they can speak,
do they not have the heart of a beast?
It is only because beasts have no Rites
that father and son share the same female deer.
Therefore, the sages arose
and established Rites to teach people.
They caused people to have Rites,
so that they would know how to distinguish themselves from beasts.
1.7 In the highest antiquity, Virtue (*Dé*) was valued;
next, giving and reciprocating were emphasized.
The Rites prize reciprocity;
to give and not receive
is not in accordance with the Rites;
to receive and not give
is also not in accordance with the Rites.
If people have Rites, they are secure;
if they have no Rites, they are in danger.
Therefore it is said:
"The Rites cannot be left unstudied."
For the Rites
consist in humbling oneself and honoring others.
Even for peddlers and porters,
there must be respect,
how much more so for the wealthy and noble?
If the wealthy and noble know how to love the Rites,
they will not be arrogant or dissolute;
if the poor and humble know how to love the Rites,
their will will not be daunted.
1.8 A child of ten is called young (*yòu*),
and begins learning.
At twenty, one is called weak (*ruò*),
and is capped (*guān*).
At thirty, one is called strong (*zhuàng*),
and has a wife.
At forty, one is called vigorous (*qiáng*),
and enters official service.
At fifty, one is called gray-haired (*ài*),
and manages government affairs.
At sixty, one is called elderly (*qí*),
and gives directions.
At seventy, one is called old (*lǎo*),
and passes on duties.
At eighty or ninety, one is called aged (*mào*);
a child of seven is called "object of pity" (*dào*).
Both the *dào* and the *mào*,
even if they commit a crime,
shall not have punishment applied to them.
At a hundred, it is called *qī*, and they are to be nourished (*yí*).
A Great Officer (*Dàfū*) at seventy retires from service.
If he is not allowed to resign,
he must be granted a stool and a staff,
and have a woman attend him on journeys.
When going to the four quarters,
he travels in a carriage with a seat (*ānchē*).
He refers to himself as "the old man" (*lǎofū*);
within his own state, he uses his personal name;
if asked from another state,
he must be answered according to his own state's regulations.
1.9 When consulting with an elder,
one must carry their stool and staff to follow them.
If an elder asks a question,
to answer without a polite refusal
is not in accordance with the Rites.
1.10 The Rites for a son:
Be warm in winter and cool in summer,
settle parents at night and inquire in the morning,
and in the company of equals
or foreigners, do not quarrel.
1.11 For a son,
even after three promotions, his carriage and horses should not match his father's.
Thus the neighborhoods and villages call him filial (*xiào*),
brothers and relatives call him affectionate (*cí*),
colleagues call him brotherly (*tì*),
close friends call him benevolent (*rén*),
and associates call him trustworthy (*xìn*).
When seeing his father’s friend,
if not told to advance, he does not dare advance;
if not told to withdraw, he does not dare withdraw;
if not asked a question,
he does not dare reply.
This is the conduct of a filial son.
1.12 For a son:
When going out, he must inform his parents;
when returning, he must present himself;
his travels must have a regular destination,
and his studies must have a consistent occupation.
In ordinary speech, he does not refer to himself as "old."
If someone is twice his age, he serves them as a father;
if ten years older, he serves them as an elder brother;
if five years older, he walks slightly behind their shoulder.
When in a group of five,
the elder must have a separate mat.
1.13 For a son:
In the house, he does not occupy the southwest corner (*ào*);
in sitting, he does not occupy the middle of the mat;
in walking, he does not use the middle of the path;
in standing, he does not occupy the middle of the doorway.
At feasts, he does not act as the one who sets the standard for food or drink;
at sacrifices, he does not act as the personator (*shī*).
He listens for what has no sound
and looks for what has no form.
He does not climb to great heights
or go near deep waters.
He does not criticize recklessly,
nor does he laugh recklessly.
A filial son does not perform tasks in the dark
and does not climb into danger,
fearing to bring disgrace upon his parents.
While his parents are living,
he does not promise to die for a friend.
He does not have private wealth.
1.14 For a son:
While his parents are living,
the borders of his cap and clothes are not pure white.
An orphaned son in charge of the household
does not have borders of bright colors on his cap and clothes.
1.15 A young child should be constantly observed so they are not deceived;
a child does not wear fur or a lower garment (*shang*).
When standing, they must be upright and square.
They do not lean to listen.
If an elder takes them by the hand,
they hold the elder's hand with both of theirs.
When carrying a burden or a sword, if the elder turns their face away to speak to them, they cover their mouth to answer.
1.16 When following a teacher (*xiānsheng*),
one does not cross the road to speak with others.
If meeting a teacher on the road,
one hurries forward,
stands upright, and clasps the hands.
If the teacher speaks to him, he replies;
if not, he hurries away.
When following an elder up a hill,
one must look in the direction the elder is looking.
When ascending a city wall, do not point;
when atop the wall, do not shout.
When about to stay at a lodging,
do not be insistent in your requests.
When about to enter a hall,
your voice must be raised.
If there are two pairs of shoes outside a door,
enter if voices are heard,
but do not enter if no voices are heard.
When about to enter a door,
the gaze must be lowered.
Upon entering the door, hold the door-bar;
do not let the gaze wander.
If the door was open, leave it open;
if the door was closed, leave it closed.
If there is someone following behind,
close the door but do not shut it completely.
Do not step on others' shoes;
do not step across the mats;
lift the hem of your robe and move quickly to a corner.
One must be careful with every response and assent.
When Dàfū and Shì enter or exit the ruler's gate,
they pass to the right of the central post
and do not step on the threshold.
1.17 Whenever entering with a guest,
yield to the guest at every gate.
When the guest reaches the door of the private chamber,
the host asks to enter first to arrange the mats,
then comes back out to welcome the guest.
If the guest firmly declines,
the host bows to the guest and they enter.
The host enters the gate and stays to the right;
the guest enters the gate and stays to the left.
The host approaches the eastern steps;
the guest approaches the western steps.
If the guest is of a lower rank,
he approaches the host's steps.
The host firmly declines,
after which the guest returns to the western steps.
The host and guest yield to each other in ascending;
the host ascends first,
and the guest follows him.
They pick up their feet and bring them together on each step,
ascending step by step.
When ascending the eastern steps, lead with the right foot;
when ascending the western steps,
lead with the left foot.
1.18 Do not scurry outside the curtains,
do not scurry on the hall,
and do not scurry while holding jade.
In the hall, walk with the heel of one foot meeting the toe of the other;
below the hall, take full steps.
In the room, do not move with arms spread like wings.
When sitting together, do not stretch out the elbows.
When giving something to someone standing, do not kneel;
when giving something to someone sitting, do not stand.
1.19 In the ritual of sweeping for an elder,
the broom must be placed upon the dustpan;
use the sleeve to shield the dust and retreat.
Ensure the dust does not reach the elder,
and hold the dustpan facing oneself while gathering the dust.
Carry the mat as if holding a level crossbeam.
Ask which direction the mat should face;
ask at which end the feet should be.
Regarding mats:
when facing south or north,
the west is the place of honor;
when facing east or west,
the south is the place of honor.
If the guest is not there for a meal,
spread the mats
with a space of ten feet between them.
The host kneels to straighten the mat,
and the guest kneels, touches the mat, and declines.
If the guest tries to remove the extra mat,
the host firmly declines.
Once the guest steps onto the mat,
then they sit.
If the host does not ask,
the guest does not initiate.
When about to take one's seat,
the expression should not be flustered.
Lift the robe with both hands,
keeping them a foot from the hem.
Do not let the robe flap,
and do not let the feet stumble.
If the Xiānshēng's books, tablets, or musical instruments are in front,
kneel to move them,
being careful not to step over them.
When sitting without food, sit as far back as possible;
when sitting to eat, sit as far forward as possible.
One must sit steadily
and maintain one's composure.
If the elder has not yet reached a point,
do not interrupt.
Rectify your appearance
and listen with reverence.
Do not plagiarize others' words
or echo them blindly.
One must take the ancients as a model
and cite the former kings.
When attending a Xiānshēng while sitting:
if the Xiānshēng asks a question,
wait until he finishes, then respond.
When requesting instruction, stand up;
when requesting further clarification, stand up.
When a father calls, do not merely say "nuò";
when a Xiānshēng calls, do not merely say "nuò";
say "wéi" and stand up.
When attending someone highly respected,
leave no empty space on the mat.
Do not stand when seeing an equal.
Stand when the candle arrives,
stand when the food arrives,
and stand when a distinguished guest arrives.
Do not let the candle burn down to its base.
Do not scold a dog in the presence of a respected guest.
When declining food, do not spit.
1.20 When attending a Jūnzǐ:
if the Jūnzǐ yawns and stretches,
reaches for his staff and shoes,
or looks at the time of day,
the attendant should ask to take his leave.
When attending a Jūnzǐ,
if the Jūnzǐ asks about a new topic,
stand up to answer.
When attending a Jūnzǐ,
if someone comes to report, saying:
"In a short while,
I wish to make a report,"
then those to the left and right should withdraw and wait.
1.21 Do not eavesdrop,
do not answer with a shout,
do not stare lewdly,
and do not be negligent.
Do not be arrogant when traveling;
do not stand on one leg;
do not sit with legs splayed;
and do not sleep on your stomach.
Gather the hair and do not use false hair;
do not remove the cap;
do not bare the shoulders when working;
and do not hitch up the skirt in the heat.
1.22 When attending an elder,
shoes are not brought onto the hall.
When taking off shoes, do not do so directly in front of the steps.
When approaching the shoes to put them on,
kneel and lift them,
then move them to the side.
Face the elder while putting on shoes;
kneel to move the shoes
and bend down to step into them.
1.23 If others are sitting apart or standing apart,
do not go and join them.
For those standing apart,
do not pass through the middle.
1.24 Men and women do not sit together.
They do not use the same clothes racks or stands.
They do not share towels or combs,
and they do not hand items directly to each other.
A sister-in-law and her husband's brothers do not exchange greetings.
The father's concubines do not wash the main wife's robes.
Words of the outside world do not enter the inner threshold;
words of the inner quarters do not leave the inner threshold.
When a girl is betrothed,
she wears a ceremonial tassel;
unless there is a major cause,
no one enters her door.
Paternal aunts, elder sisters, younger sisters, and
daughters
who have married and returned home
do not sit on the same mat as their brothers
nor eat from the same vessel.
Father and son do not sit on the same mat.
Unless there is a matchmaker,
men and women do not know each other's names.
Unless the betrothal gifts are received,
they do not associate or become intimate.
Therefore, the date is announced to the ruler,
fasting and purification are used to inform the spirits,
and wine and food are prepared to invite neighbors and colleagues
to emphasize the distinction between them.
When taking a wife, do not take one of the same surname.
If a concubine is purchased and her surname is unknown,
perform divination for it.
The son of a widow,
unless he has shown exceptional merit,
is not to be befriended.
1.25 To congratulate someone on taking a wife,
say:
"So-and-so has sent me,
hearing that you have a guest,
to present these delicacies."
1.26 The poor are not expected to fulfill rituals with goods and wealth;
the elderly are not expected to fulfill rituals with physical strength.
1.27 In naming a son, do not use the name of a state,
nor the names of the sun or moon,
nor the names of hidden diseases,
nor the names of mountains or rivers.
1.28 Males and females are ranked differently.
When a male is twenty,
he is capped and given a style name.
In the presence of his father,
a son refers to himself by his given name;
in the presence of his ruler,
a minister refers to himself by his given name.
When a girl is betrothed,
she is hair-pinned and given a style name.
1.29 Regarding the general rules for serving food:
place meat with bones on the left and sliced meat on the right.
The grain is placed to the left of the person,
and the soup to the right.
Minced and roasted meats are placed further away,
while pickles and sauces are placed closer.
Steamed scallions are placed at the end,
and wine or beverages are on the right.
When placing dried meat or strips,
the bent parts are on the left and the ends on the right.
If a guest is of a lower rank,
he should hold the food and rise to decline it;
the host then rises to decline the guest's courtesy,
and then the guest sits.
The host invites the guest to make the offering:
to offer the grain,
offering first what was served first.
In the sequence of meats,
one makes an offering of each kind.
After three mouthfuls of rice,
the host invites the guest to eat the sliced meat,
and then they partake of all the various meats.
Until the host has finished partaking of everything,
the guest does not rinse his mouth.
When attending a meal with an elder,
if the host personally presents the food,
one bows before eating.
If the host does not personally present it,
one eats without bowing.
When eating with others, do not eat to satiety; when eating from a common bowl of rice, do not moisten your hands.
Do not roll the rice into balls;
do not let leftover rice fall back;
do not slurp the soup;
do not smack your lips;
do not gnaw on bones;
do not put back fish or meat that has been bitten;
do not throw bones to dogs.
Do not grab the best pieces for yourself;
do not fan the rice.
Use fingers, not chopsticks, for eating millet.
Do not gulp down the soup;
do not add seasonings to the soup at the table;
do not pick your teeth;
do not slurp the pickled sauce.
If a guest seasons the soup,
the host apologizes for his poor cooking;
if a guest slurps the pickled sauce,
the host apologizes for his poverty.
Wet meat is bitten through with the teeth;
dry meat is not bitten through with the teeth.
Do not bolt down roasted meat.
When the meal is finished,
the guest kneels forward,
removes the dishes and stands to hand them to the attendants;
the host rises to decline this,
and then the guest sits back down.
When attending an elder at a drink,
when the wine is served, one stands up
and bows to receive it at the place of the wine vessel.
If the elder declines the bow,
the junior returns to his mat to drink.
When the elder raises his cup
but has not yet finished it,
the junior does not dare to drink.
When an elder gives a gift,
a junior or someone of lower status does not dare to decline.
If fruit is given in the presence of a ruler,
those that have pits should have their pits tucked into the bosom.
When serving a ruler at a meal,
if the ruler gives leftovers,
if the vessel is washable, do not transfer the food;
otherwise, all remaining food is transferred to another dish.
Leftovers from a meal are not used for offerings.
A father does not make an offering of his son's leftovers,
nor a husband of his wife's.
When attending an elder,
even if there is a second serving, do not decline;
when sitting in company, do not decline.
Use chopsticks for soup with vegetables;
do not use them for soup without vegetables.
He who peels a melon for the Tiānzǐ slices it into eight pieces,
covering it with a fine linen cloth.
For a Guójūn, it is sliced into four pieces,
covered with a coarse hemp cloth.
For a Dàfū, it is sliced crosswise;
for a Shì, the stem is removed;
for a Shùrén, he bites into it.
When parents are ill,
a son who has been capped does not comb his hair,
does not walk with a rhythmic swing,
does not speak idly,
does not play the Qín or Sè,
eats meat but not until the taste changes,
drinks wine but not until his appearance changes,
laughs without showing his gums,
and expresses anger without cursing.
Once the illness is over, he returns to his usual ways.
One in sorrow sits on a mat placed to the side;
one in mourning sits on a single mat.
1.30 When the floods subside,
one does not present fish or turtles.
He who presents a bird should twist its head;
if it is a pet bird, do not twist its head.
He who presents a carriage and horses holds the whip and the mounting strap.
He who presents armor holds the helmet.
He who presents a staff holds its lower end.
He who presents captives holds them by the right sleeve.
He who presents grain holds the right half of the tally;
he who presents rice holds the measuring vessel.
He who presents cooked food holds the sauces and seasonings.
He who presents land or houses holds the written documents.
Whenever giving a bow to someone:
if it is strung, keep the sinew side upward;
if unstrung, keep the horn side upward.
The right hand holds the end of the bow,
and the left hand supports the grip.
Both superior and inferior allow their sashes to hang down.
If the host bows,
the guest turns aside to avoid it,
declining the bow.
When the host receives it himself,
he moves to the guest's left,
placing his hands below to support the grip;
he stands side-by-side with the guest,
and then receives it.
He who presents a sword does so with the hilt to the left.
He who presents a gē puts its butt-end forward
and the blade behind.
He who presents a spear or halberd puts its ferrule forward.
He who presents a stool or staff brushes it off.
He who presents a horse or sheep leads it with the right hand;
he who presents a dog leads it with the left hand.
He who presents a captured bird holds it with its head to the left.
He who presents a lamb or a wild goose decorates it with colored cloth.
He who receives pearls or jade does so with cupped hands.
He who receives a bow or sword does so with his sleeves.
He who drinks from a jade cup does not wave it about.
Whenever sending someone with a bow, sword, bundle of meat, or baskets to inquire after another,
he holds the object while receiving the command,
assuming the appropriate appearance for the mission.
1.31 Whenever one serves as a messenger for a ruler,
once the command is received,
the ruler's words do not stay overnight in the messenger's house.
When the ruler's command arrives,
the host goes out to bow, acknowledging the honor;
when the messenger departs,
the host must bow to see him off outside the gate.
If sending a messenger to the ruler's place,
one must wear court robes while giving the command;
when the messenger returns,
one must descend from the hall to receive the report.
1.32 To be broad in learning and strong in memory, yet remaining humble,
and to be earnest in good deeds without tiring,
is what is called a Jūnzǐ.
A Jūnzǐ does not exhaust all the pleasures people can provide,
nor does he demand the utmost loyalty from people,
in order to preserve the relationship.
The *Lǐ* says:
"A Jūnzǐ holds his grandson but not his son."
This means a grandson can serve as the Personator for his grandfather,
but a son cannot serve as the Personator for his father.
When someone acts as the Personator for a ruler,
if a Dàfū or Shì see him,
they must descend from their carriages.
If the ruler knows the one acting as the Personator,
the ruler himself descends for him,
and the Personator must lean forward on the carriage crossbar.
When mounting a carriage, the Personator must use a mounting stool.
One who is fasting does not listen to music or offer condolences.
1.33 During the rites of mourning,
though one may be worn thin, it should not reach the point of physical deformity,
and sight and hearing should not be impaired.
Ascending and descending should not be by the eastern steps,
and entering or exiting should not be directly through the center of the gate.
1.34 During the rites of mourning,
if there is a wound on the head, one may wash the hair;
if there are sores on the body, one may bathe;
if there is illness, one may drink wine and eat meat,
returning to the former restrictions when the illness stops.
Not being able to endure the mourning rituals
is considered equivalent to being unkind or unfilial.
At fifty, one does not become excessively thin through mourning;
at sixty, one does not become thin;
at seventy, one only wears the sackcloth on the body,
but drinks wine and eats meat,
and remains in the inner chambers.
Birth is associated with the days to come,
death is associated with the days that have passed.
Those who know the living pay a visit of condolence,
those who know the deceased express grief.
If one knows the living but did not know the deceased,
one pays a visit of condolence but does not express grief;
if one knew the deceased but does not know the living,
one expresses grief but does not pay a visit of condolence.
When paying a visit of condolence, if one cannot contribute to the funeral expenses,
one should not ask about the costs.
When visiting the sick, if one cannot provide a gift,
one should not ask what they desire.
When seeing someone, if one cannot provide lodging,
one should not ask where they are staying.
To bestow something on others, one does not say
"Come and take it."
When giving to others, one does not ask what they desire.
1.35 When going to a grave, one does not climb onto the burial mound;
when assisting at a burial, one must hold the funeral rope.
When attending a funeral service, one does not laugh.
When bowing to others, one must step out of one’s position.
When looking at a coffin, one does not sing.
When entering to pay respects, one does not move with soaring arms.
When at a meal, one does not sigh.
When a neighbor has a funeral,
the pounding of grain is not accompanied by songs.
When there is a coffin in the village,
one does not sing in the lanes.
When going to a grave, one does not sing.
On a day of wailing, one does not sing.
When escorting a funeral procession, one does not take shortcuts;
when escorting a burial, one does not avoid mud or puddles.
When attending a funeral service, one must have a mournful expression;
when holding the funeral rope, one does not laugh;
when attending a musical performance, one does not sigh;
in armor
and helmet, there should be an expression of inviolability.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ is cautious and prudent,
and does not lose his proper composure before others.
When the Guójūn leans on the carriage crossbar to show respect,
the Dàfū descends.
When a Dàfū leans on the crossbar,
the Shì descends.
Propriety does not extend down to the Shùrén;
penal law does not extend up to the Dàfū.
Punished persons are not at the side of the ruler.
1.36 In a war chariot, one does not lean on the crossbar.
In military chariots, the banners are lowered;
in chariots of peace, the banners are tied up.
1.37 The Shǐ carries the writing brush;
the Shì carries the records of words.
If there is water ahead,
then one carries the green banner.
If there is dust ahead,
then one carries the banner with the calling kite.
If there are chariots and horsemen ahead,
then one carries the banner with the wild goose.
If there is an army ahead,
then one carries the tiger-skin banner.
If there are fierce beasts ahead,
then one carries the Píxiū banner.
When marching:
The Zhūquè is in front,
and the Xuánwǔ is behind,
the Qīnglóng is on the left, and the Báihǔ is on the right.
The Zhāoyáo is above,
to sharpen the spirit of the soldiers.
Advancing and retreating have their measure,
left and right have their designated positions,
each attending to their own duty.
1.38 Regarding the killer of one’s father,
one does not live with him under the same heaven.
Regarding the killer of one’s brother,
one does not need to go back for a weapon.
Regarding the killer of one’s friend,
one does not live with him in the same state.
1.39 When there are many fortifications in the four suburbs,
this is the shame of the Qīng and Dàfū.
When the territory is vast,
but it is neglected and not cultivated,
this is also the shame of the Shì.
1.40 When performing a sacrifice, one must not be slothful.
When sacrificial robes are worn out, they should be burned;
when sacrificial vessels are worn out, they should be buried;
when tortoise shells and milfoil stalks are worn out, they should be buried;
when sacrificial animals die, they should be buried.
All who participate in a sacrifice at the ruler’s court
must themselves remove their sacrificial stands.
1.41 Only after the final wailing is the taboo name observed.
In the rites, one does not taboo names that sound similar.
With double names, one does not taboo only one of the components.
If one served one’s parents while they were alive,
then one taboos the names of the grandparents;
if one did not serve one’s parents while they were alive,
then one does not taboo the names of the grandparents.
In the presence of the ruler, there are no private taboos;
in the household of a Dàfū, there are only public taboos.
In the Shī and Shū, names are not tabooed;
in writing a text, names are not tabooed.
In the ancestral temple, names are not tabooed.
The taboo name of a ruler’s wife,
even when mentioned before the ruler,
the subject does not taboo it;
the taboo name of a wife does not go outside the gate.
During the Dàgōng and Xiǎogōng periods of mourning, names are not tabooed.
Entering the borders, one asks about the prohibitions;
entering the capital, one asks about the customs;
entering a gate, one asks about the taboo names.
1.42 External affairs are conducted on Gāngrì,
internal affairs are conducted on Róurì.
Whenever divining by tortoise shell or milfoil for a day:
if it is more than ten days away, it is called "a distant such-and-such day";
if it is within ten days, it is called "a near such-and-such day."
For funeral matters, the distant days are chosen first;
for auspicious matters, the near days are chosen first.
One says:
"For this day,
I borrow from you, Great Tortoise, with your constancy,
I borrow from you, Great Milfoil, with your constancy."
Divination by shell or milfoil should not exceed three times;
one should not repeat the same divination twice.
The tortoise shell is for bǔ,
the stalks are for shì;
shell and milfoil divination
were used by the former Sage Kings to make the people believe in the proper times and days,
respect the spirits and gods,
and stand in awe of the laws and decrees;
they were used to make the people resolve doubts and suspicions,
and settle hesitations.
Therefore it is said:
"When in doubt, use milfoil divination;
then one will not be in the wrong;
when a day is chosen and the task performed,
then it must be followed through."
1.43 When the ruler’s carriage is about to be harnessed,
the Pú holds the whip and stands in front of the horses.
Once it is harnessed,
the Pú inspects the lin-plates and reports that the carriage is ready,
then shakes his robe and mounts from the right,
takes the second mounting-strap,
kneels down in the carriage,
holds the whip and separates the reins,
drives it forward five steps, and stops.
When the ruler comes out to get into the carriage,
the Pú gathers the reins and hands him the mounting-strap.
The attendants on the left and right clear the way,
and the carriage drives off while the runners trot.
Upon reaching the main gate,
the ruler places his hand on the Pú’s hand and looks back
to order the Chēyòu to mount;
at gates, alleys, ditches,
and channels, one must proceed at a walk.
In the general etiquette of a driver,
one must hand the mounting-strap to the person.
If the driver is of lower rank,
then one receives it;
if not,
then one does not.
If the driver is of lower rank,
then one places one’s hand on the driver's hand;
if not,
then one grasps the strap from below the driver's hand.
A guest's carriage does not enter the main gate.
A woman does not stand while riding in a carriage.
Dogs and horses do not go up into the hall.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ leans on the crossbar to show respect to the elderly,
and descends from the carriage when passing the place of a Qīng;
entering the capital, he does not gallop,
entering a village, he must lean on the crossbar.
When there is a summons from the ruler,
even if the messenger is of low rank,
the Dàfū and Shì must drive the carriage themselves.
A person in armor does not bow;
for if he bowed, it would be a squatting bow.
In a funeral carriage, the left side is left empty;
in riding in the ruler's carriage,
one does not dare leave the left side empty;
on the left, one must lean on the crossbar.
When a Pú drives for a woman,
he advances his left hand
and keeps back his right hand;
when driving for a Guójūn,
he advances his right hand
and keeps back his left hand, and bows his head.
A Guójūn does not ride in strange or unusual carriages.
In a carriage, one does not cough loudly,
and does not point about wildly.
Standing, one's gaze extends to the distance of five wheel-rotations;
leaning on the crossbar, one’s gaze is on the horses’ tails;
looking back, one does not look beyond the hub.
In the capital, one uses the brush-end of the whip to touch the horses lightly
and does not drive them fast.
Dust should not rise higher than the wheel-ruts.
The ruler of a state descends from his carriage before the sacrificial ox;
he bows to the crossbar when passing the ancestral temple.
Great Officers (*Dàfū*) and Officers (*Shì*) descend at the palace gate;
they bow to the crossbar when passing the ruler's carriage horses.
When riding in the ruler's carriage,
one must wear court robes.
When carrying the whip and goad,
one does not dare to hand over the mounting strap;
on the left side, one must bow to the crossbar.
When leading the ruler's horses at a walk,
one must keep to the middle of the road.
If one kicks the fodder of the ruler's horses with their foot,
there is a punishment.
If one mentions the age of the ruler's horses,
there is a punishment.
2.1 Whenever carrying an object with both hands, it should be held at the level of the heart;
when carrying it with one hand, it should be at the level of the belt.
When holding a vessel of the Son of Heaven (*Tiānzǐ*), it is held higher than the brow;
for a ruler of a state (*Guójūn*), it is level with the brow;
for a Great Officer (*Dàfū*), it is held at the level of the mounting strap;
for an Officer (*Shì*), it is carried by the handle.
Whenever holding the vessels of one's lord,
even if holding something light, one should act as if unable to sustain the weight.
When holding the lord's vessels,
or handling silks, jade tablets (*guī*), or jade discs (*bì*),
one favors the left hand.
In walking, one does not lift the feet;
the feet should drag like the revolving of carriage wheels.
When standing, one should be bent like a sounding stone, with the girdle pendants hanging down.
When the lord's pendants lean against him,
the minister's pendants should hang straight.
When the lord's pendants hang straight,
the minister's pendants should touch the ground.
When holding jade,
if there is a mat for it, one displays the inner garment;
if there is no mat, one keeps the outer garment closed.
2.2 The ruler of a state does not call the Senior Ministers (*Qīnglǎo*) or the titled wives (*Shìfù*) by their personal names.
A Great Officer does not call hereditary ministers (*Shìchén*), or his nieces (*zhí*), or his younger sisters-in-law (*dì*) by name.
An Officer does not call his household manager (*Jiāxiàng*) or his senior concubine (*Zhǎngqiè*) by name.
The son of a ruler or a Great Officer
does not dare to refer to himself as "I, the little child" (*yú xiǎozǐ*);
the son of a Great Officer or an Officer
does not dare to refer to himself as "The successor-son so-and-so,"
and does not dare to have the same name as the heir apparent (*Shìzǐ*).
2.3 When the ruler commands an Officer to practice archery
and he is unable,
he declines on account of illness;
he says:
"I have the sorrow of carrying firewood."
When waiting upon a superior,
to answer without first looking towards him
is contrary to ritual propriety (*lǐ*).
2.4 When a superior man performs rituals,
he does not seek to change the local customs.
The rituals of sacrifice,
the garments of mourning,
and the positions for wailing
should all be according to the old customs of his state;
he carefully follows its laws
and carries them out with scrutiny.
If he has been away from the state for three generations,
and his rank and emolument are still listed at court,
and his comings and goings are announced to the state;
if brothers and clansmen still remain,
then he returns to report to the head of the lineage (*Zōnghòu*).
If he has been away from the state for three generations,
and his rank and emolument are no longer listed at court,
and his comings and goings are not announced to the state;
then only on the day of his establishment
does he follow the laws of his new state.
2.5 A superior man who has already lost his father does not change his personal name.
If, after being orphaned, he suddenly attains high rank,
he does not confer a posthumous title upon his father.
While in mourning,
before the burial,
one reads the mourning rites;
after the burial,
one reads the sacrificial rites;
when mourning is over and one returns to normalcy,
one reads the musical compositions.
While in mourning, one does not speak of music;
at sacrificial matters, one does not speak of ill-omens;
in the public court, one does not speak of women.
2.6 Shaking out dust from books or straightening books in the presence of the ruler
is subject to punishment.
Reversing the divination stalks or tilting the tortoise shell in the presence of the ruler
is subject to punishment.
Divination shells and stalks,
stools and staffs,
mats and covers,
double-layered plain white garments,
and single thin hempen garments
do not enter the palace gate.
Straw sandals,
garments with the skirts tucked into the belt,
and mourning caps
do not enter the palace gate.
Lists of funeral gifts,
mourning garments, and ill-omened vessels,
if not reported,
do not enter the palace gate.
Public affairs are not discussed in private.
2.7 When a superior man is about to build his palace and chambers:
the ancestral temple comes first,
the stables and granaries come next,
and the residential rooms come last.
2.8 For all household provisions:
sacrificial vessels come first,
the provision for sacrificial victims comes next,
and vessels for daily use come last.
Those without land and emolument
do not set up sacrificial vessels;
those with land and emolument
first prepare sacrificial robes.
Though a superior man be poor,
he does not sell his sacrificial vessels;
though he be cold,
he does not wear his sacrificial robes.
When building his chambers,
he does not cut trees from graveyard mounds.
When Great Officers or Officers leave their state,
their sacrificial vessels do not cross the border.
A Great Officer entrusts his sacrificial vessels to another Great Officer;
an Officer entrusts his sacrificial vessels to another Officer.
When Great Officers or Officers leave their state:
having crossed the border,
they build an altar and wail facing towards their state.
They wear white upper garments,
white lower garments,
and white caps;
they remove the borders of their garments;
they wear leather sandals
and use white carriage mats;
they ride on horses with untrimmed manes;
they do not trim their nails or hair;
they do not offer a portion of their food in sacrifice;
they do not explain to others that they are guiltless;
and their wives do not serve them in the bedchamber.
After three months, they return to their normal dress.
When Great Officers or Officers are received by their ruler,
if the ruler commends their service,
they step aside,
bow twice and touch their heads to the ground (*qǐshǒu*).
If the ruler bows to welcome them,
they step aside,
not daring to return the bow.
When Great Officers and Officers meet each other,
even if their ranks are not equal,
if the host wishes to honor the guest,
he bows first to the guest;
if the guest wishes to honor the host,
he bows first to the host.
Except when offering condolences for mourning
or seeing the ruler of a state,
there are none who do not return a bow.
When a Great Officer is seen by the ruler of a state,
the ruler bows for the condescension of his visit.
When an Officer is seen by a Great Officer,
the Great Officer bows for the condescension of his visit.
When two people of the same state meet for the first time,
the host bows for the condescension of the visit.
A ruler toward an Officer
does not return the bow;
but if the Officer is not his subject,
he does return the bow.
A Great Officer toward his own subjects,
though they be lowly,
must return their bow.
Men and women return bows to each other.
2.9 The ruler of a state, in his spring hunting, does not surround the marsh;
a Great Officer does not take a whole herd;
an Officer does not take fawns or eggs.
2.10 In a bad year
when the grain does not ripen,
the ruler, in his meals, does not offer the sacrificial lungs;
his horses are not fed with grain;
the royal roads are not kept clear;
and at sacrificial ceremonies, the musical instruments are not suspended.
A Great Officer does not eat fine millet;
an Officer, when drinking wine, does not have music.
Unless there is a reason,
the ruler does not remove his jade ornaments from his person;
unless there is a reason, a Great Officer
does not remove his suspended instruments;
unless there is a reason, an Officer does not remove his *qín* or *sè*.
When an Officer has made a presentation to the ruler of a state,
on another day,
if the ruler asks him,
"Where did you get that?"
he bows twice, touches his head to the ground, and then answers.
When a Great Officer goes abroad on private business,
he must request permission.
Upon his return,
he must have something to present.
When a Shì travels privately beyond the borders,
he must request permission.
Upon returning,
he must report back.
If the ruler commends his toil,
he bows;
if the ruler asks about his journey,
he bows and then responds.
2.11 When the ruler of a state leaves his state,
those who stop him say:
"How can you abandon the Shèjì!"
For a Dàfū,
they say:
"How can you abandon the Zōngmiào!"
For a Shì,
they say:
"How can you abandon the Fénmù!"
The ruler of a state dies for the Shèjì,
a Dàfū dies for his charges,
and a Shì dies for his duties.
2.12 The one who rules over all under heaven
is called the Tiānzǐ.
When receiving the Zhūhóu in audience,
distributing offices, delegating administration, and assigning tasks based on merit,
he calls himself "Yǔ yīrén".
When ascending the steps to the throne or presiding over sacrifices:
for internal rites he is called "the Filial King So-and-so",
and for external rites he is called "the Succeeding King So-and-so".
When presiding over the Zhūhóu
and communicating with the spirits and deities,
he is called "The Tiānwáng So-and-so Fǔ".
When he passes away,
it is said, "The Tiānwáng has collapsed".
In the rite of recalling the soul, they say,
"Tiānzǐ, return!"
When announcing the mourning,
it is said, "The Tiānwáng has ascended to the heights".
When his tablet is placed in the temple
and his ancestral tablet is established,
he is called Dì.
Before the Tiānzǐ has concluded the mourning period,
he calls himself "Yǔ xiǎozǐ".
He is named during his life,
and he is also named after his death.
2.13 The Tiānzǐ has a Hòu,
Fūrén,
Shìfù,
Pín,
Qī,
and Qiè.
The Tiānzǐ establishes the heavenly offices,
starting with the Six Dà:
called the Dàzǎi,
Dàzōng,
Dàshǐ,
Dàzhù,
Dàshì,
and Dàbǔ,
who preside over the Six Statutes.
The Tiānzǐ's Five Guān:
called the Sītú,
Sīmǎ,
Sīkōng,
Sīshì,
and Sīkòu,
who preside over the Five Groups.
The Tiānzǐ's Six Fǔ:
called the Sītǔ,
Sīmù,
Sīshuǐ,
Sīcǎo,
Sīqì,
and Sīhuò,
who preside over the Six Duties.
The Tiānzǐ's Six Gōng:
called the earth workers,
metal workers,
stone workers,
wood workers,
animal workers,
and grass workers,
who preside over the fashioning of the six materials.
When the Five Guān present their tribute,
it is called Xiǎng.
2.14 The head of the Five Guān
is called Bó;
he manages the regions.
When he is introduced to the Tiānzǐ,
he is called "Official of the Tiānzǐ".
If he is of the same surname as the Tiānzǐ,
he is called "Bófù";
if of a different surname, he is called "Bójiù".
When addressing the Zhūhóu,
he calls himself "Elder of the Tiānzǐ";
abroad he is called Gōng;
in his own state he is called Jūn.
The head of a province,
when entering the Tiānzǐ's state, is called Mù.
If he is of the same surname as the Tiānzǐ,
he is called "Shūfù";
if of a different surname, he is called "Shūjiù";
abroad he is called Hóu;
in his own state he is called
"Jūn".
Among the Dōngyí, Běidí, Xīróng, and Nánmán,
though their rulers be great, they are called Zǐ.
Internally they call themselves "Bùgǔ",
and externally they call themselves "Wáng lǎo".
Minor Hóu of various regions,
when entering the Tiānzǐ's state, are called "So-and-so";
abroad they are called Zǐ;
they call themselves
"Gū".
The Tiānzǐ stands before the screen.
When the Zhūhóu face north to see the Tiānzǐ,
it is called Jìn.
When the Tiānzǐ stands in the space between the gate and the screen,
with the Gōng facing east
and the Zhūhóu facing west,
it is called Cháo.
2.15 When Zhūhóu meet before the appointed time, it is called Yù;
meeting at a border place is called Huì.
When a Zhūhóu sends a Dàfū to inquire after another Zhūhóu, it is called Pìn;
making an agreement of faith is called Shì;
presiding over a sacrificial animal is called Méng.
2.16 When a Zhūhóu meets the Tiānzǐ, he says, "Your servant, Hóu So-and-so of Such-and-such place";
when speaking to the people,
he calls himself
"Guǎrén".
When in mourning clothes,
he is called "the Heir, the Gū".
When attending sacrifices:
for internal rites he is "the Filial Son, Hóu So-and-so of Such-and-such place",
and for external rites he is "the Great-grandson, Hóu So-and-so of Such-and-such place".
His death is called Hōng;
in the recall rite they say, "So-and-so Fǔ, return!"
After the burial,
when the successor meets the Tiānzǐ, it is called Lèijiàn.
Pronouncing the posthumous name is called Lèi.
When a Zhūhóu sends someone as an envoy to another Zhūhóu,
the envoy calls himself
"the Elder of my Guǎjūn".
The Tiānzǐ is reverently grand;
the Zhūhóu are brilliant and majestic;
the Dàfū are numerous and dignified;
the Shì move with measured steps;
the commoners are attentive and alert.
The Tiānzǐ's consort is called Hòu;
a Zhūhóu's is called Fūrén;
a Dàfū's is called Rúrén;
a Shì's is called Fùrén;
a commoner's is called Qī.
Gōng and Hóu have Fūrén,
Shìfù,
Qī,
and Qiè.
A Fūrén refers to herself before the Tiānzǐ
as
"Lǎofù";
before other Zhūhóu
as
"Guǎ xiǎojūn";
before her own ruler
as
"Xiǎotóng".
From the Shìfù downwards,
they call themselves "Bìzǐ".
Children use their own names before their parents.
A Dàfū of the various states,
when entering the Tiānzǐ's state,
is called "Shì So-and-so";
he calls himself "the Accompanying Minister So-and-so".
Abroad he is called Zǐ;
in his own state he is called "the Elder of my Guǎjūn".
As an envoy he calls himself
"So-and-so".
2.17 One does not say the Tiānzǐ has "gone out";
the personal name of a Zhūhóu is not used during his life.
A Jūnzǐ does not personally handle offensive matters;
when a Zhūhóu loses his territory,
his name is used;
when he extinguishes a state of the same surname,
his name is used.
In the rites of a minister:
he does not remonstrate openly.
If he remonstrates three times and is not heard,
he leaves.
In a son's service to his parents:
if he remonstrates three times and is not heard,
he follows them with wailing and tears.
2.18 When the ruler is ill
and takes medicine,
the minister tastes it first.
When a parent is ill
and takes medicine,
the son tastes it first.
If a physician's family has not practiced for three generations,
one does not take his medicine.
Comparisons of people must be made within their own class.
2.19 When asking about the age of the Tiānzǐ,
the reply is:
"I have heard
that he has begun to wear robes of such-and-such many chǐ."
When asking about the age of a Guójūn:
if he is an adult, it is said: "He is able to attend to the affairs of the Zōngmiào and Shèjì";
if he is young,
it is said:
"He is not yet able to attend to the affairs of the Zōngmiào and Shèjì."
When asking about the son of a Dàfū:
if he is an adult, it is said:
"He is able to drive a chariot";
if he is young, it is said:
"He is not yet able to drive a chariot."
When asking about the son of a Shì:
if he is an adult, it is said:
"He is able to manage the reception of guests";
if he is young, it is said:
"He is not yet able to manage the reception of guests."
When asking about the son of a Shùrén:
if he is an adult, it is said:
"He is able to carry firewood";
if he is young, it is said:
"He is not yet able to carry firewood."
2.20 When asking about the wealth of a Guójūn,
the reply mentions the extent of his lands
and the products of his mountains and marshes.
When asking about the wealth of a Dàfū,
it is said: "He has a Zǎi to manage his laborers,
and his sacrificial vessels and robes are not borrowed."
When asking about the wealth of a Shì,
the reply is given in the number of his chariots.
When asking about the wealth of a Shùrén,
the reply is given in the number of his livestock.
2.21 The Tiānzǐ sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
sacrifices to the four directions,
sacrifices to the mountains and rivers,
sacrifices to the Wǔsì,
all completed within the year.
The Zhūhóu sacrifice to their respective directions.
They sacrifice to the mountains and rivers,
sacrifice to the Wǔsì,
all completed within the year.
A Dàfū sacrifices to the Wǔsì,
all completed within the year.
A Shì sacrifices to his ancestors.
2.22 In all sacrifices,
if there has been a tradition of discontinuance, no one dares to revive it;
if there has been a tradition of performance, no one dares to discontinue it.
Sacrificing to that which one should not sacrifice to
is called Yínsì.
Yínsì brings no blessing.
2.23 The Tiānzǐ uses a Xīniú,
the Zhūhóu use a Féiniú,
the Dàfū use a Suǒniú,
the Shì use a sheep and a pig.
A younger son does not perform the sacrifice;
if he sacrifices, he must inform the Zōngzǐ.
2.24 In the rites for sacrificing in the Zōngmiào:
an ox is called Yīyuán Dàwǔ,
a pig is called Gāngliè,
a piglet is called Túféi,
a sheep is called Róumáo,
a cock is called Hànyīn,
a dog is called Gēngxiàn,
a pheasant is called Shūzhǐ,
a rabbit is called Míngshì,
dried meat is called Yǐnjì,
dried fish is called Shāngjì,
fresh fish is called Tǐngjì,
water is called Qīngdí,
wine is called Qīngzhuó,
glutinous millet is called Xiānghé,
foxtail millet is called Xiāngqí,
panicled millet is called Míngzī,
rice is called Jiāshū,
leeks are called Fēngběn,
salt is called Xiáncuó,
jade is called Jiāyù,
silk offerings are called Liàngbì.
2.25 The death of a Tiānzǐ is called
"Bēng",
that of a Zhūhóu is called
"Hōng",
that of a Dàfū is called
"Zú",
that of a Shì is called
"Bùlù",
and that of a Shùrén is called
"Sǐ".
When on the bed, the body is called Shī,
when in the coffin, it is called Jiù.
The death of winged birds is called Jiàng,
that of four-legged beasts is called Zì.
Dying by the hand of the enemy is called Bīng.
Sacrificing to a grandfather, he is called "Huáng Zǔkǎo",
a grandmother, "Huáng Zǔbǐ".
A father is called "Huáng Kǎo",
a mother, "Huáng Bǐ".
A husband is called "Huáng Pì".
When alive, they are called Fù, Mǔ, and Qī;
when deceased, they are called Kǎo, Bǐ, and Pín.
If one dies at a great age, it is called Zú;
if one dies young, it is called Bùlù.
2.26 In looking at the Tiānzǐ,
the gaze does not go above his collar,
nor below his belt;
for a Guójūn,
the gaze is level with his harness strap;
for a Dàfū,
the gaze is level;
for a Shì,
one looks five paces ahead.
In all looking:
looking above the face indicates arrogance,
looking below the belt indicates sorrow,
looking sideways indicates craftiness.
2.27 At the Ruler's command,
the Dàfū and Shì practice their duties.
In the bureau, one speaks of bureau business;
in the treasury, one speaks of treasury business;
in the armory, one speaks of armory business;
at court, one speaks of court business.
At court, one does not speak of dogs or horses.
To stop court business and look around,
if there is no unusual matter,
there must be unusual thoughts.
Therefore, to stop court business and look around,
the Jūnzǐ calls it rusticity.
At court, one speaks of ritual,
asks about ritual,
and replies according to ritual.
At the great banquet, one does not ask about divination,
nor does one boast of wealth.
2.28 In all introductory gifts:
the Tiānzǐ uses Chàng;
the Zhūhóu use a Guī;
a Qīng uses a lamb;
a Dàfū uses a wild goose;
a Shì uses a pheasant;
a Shùrén's gift is a bolt of cloth;
a boy lays down his gift and withdraws.
In the wild or in the army, there are no formal gifts;
using a chin-strap,
an arm-guard,
or an arrow,
is acceptable.
The introductory gifts for women are
oriental raisin tree fruits, hazelnuts,
dried meat, spiced meat,
jujubes, and chestnuts.
2.29 When presenting a woman to the Tiānzǐ,
it is said: "To complete the Bǎixìng";
to a Guójūn,
it is said: "To prepare the wine and drink";
to a Dàfū,
it is said:
"To prepare the sweeping and sprinkling."
3.1 During the mourning for Gōngyí Zhòngzǐ,
Tángōng wore the mourning head-cloth.
Zhòngzǐ passed over his grandson and established his son as heir;
Tángōng said:
"How can this be?
I have not heard of this before."
He hurried to see Zǐfú Bózǐ at the right of the gate,
and said:
"Zhòngzǐ passed over his grandson and established his son as heir;
why is this?"
Bózǐ said:
"Zhòngzǐ is also following the ancient way.
In the past, Wén Wáng passed over Bóyìkǎo and established Wǔ Wáng;
Wēizǐ passed over his grandson Tú and established Yǎn;
Zhòngzǐ is also following the ancient way."
Zǐyóu asked Kǒngzǐ about it,
Kǒngzǐ said:
"No!
Establish the grandson."
3.2 In serving one's parents, one may conceal their faults but not confront them;
when attending to them on either side, there is no fixed method for their nourishment;
one serves them diligently until their death,
and observes mourning for three years.
In serving one's ruler, one may confront him but not conceal his faults;
when attending to him on either side, there is a fixed method for his nourishment;
one serves him diligently until his death,
and observes mourning for three years.
In serving one's teacher, one neither confronts him nor conceals his faults;
when attending to him on either side, there is no fixed method for his nourishment;
one serves him diligently until his death,
and observes mourning in the heart for three years.
3.3 Jì Wǔzǐ finished his bed-chamber;
the burial place of the Dù clan was under the western steps.
He requested that they be buried together there,
and it was granted.
Upon entering the palace, one did not dare to wail.
Wǔ Zǐ said:
"Joint burial was not an ancient practice;
since the time of Zhōu Gōng,
there has been no change to this.
I agree with the major principles but not the minor details;
why is that?"
He then ordered the mourning wail.
3.4 When the mother of Zǐ Shàng died, he did not observe mourning for her.
The disciples asked Zǐ Sī, saying:
"In the past, did your late father
observe mourning for a divorced mother?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"Then why do you not make Bái observe mourning for her?
What is the reason?"
Zǐ Sī said:
"In the past, my late father never deviated from the Way;
when the Way was exalted, he followed it in its exaltation;
when the Way was diminished, he followed it in its diminution.
How could I, Jí, match that?
She who was Jí's wife
was Bái's mother;
she who is no longer Jí's wife
is no longer Bái's mother."
Thus, the Kǒng family's practice of not mourning a divorced mother
began with Zǐ Sī.
3.5 Kǒng Zǐ said:
"To bow and then touch the forehead to the ground
is a gentle expression of compliance;
to touch the forehead to the ground and then bow
is a solemn expression of the utmost sincerity.
In the three-year mourning,
I follow the practice of the utmost sincerity."
3.6 When Kǒng Zǐ had succeeded in performing the joint burial at Fáng,
he said:
"I have heard that
in ancient times there were graves but no mounds;
but I, Qiū,
am a man of the east, west, south, and north,
and I cannot leave the spot unmarked."
Thereupon he raised a mound over it,
four feet high.
Kǒng Zǐ returned first,
while his disciples followed later.
It rained heavily,
and when they arrived,
Kǒng Zǐ questioned them,
saying:
"Why have you come so late?"
They replied:
"The grave at Fáng collapsed."
Kǒng Zǐ did not respond.
They repeated it three times.
Kǒng Zǐ shed tears and said:
"I have heard that
in ancient times they did not repair graves."
3.7 Kǒng Zǐ wailed for Zǐ Lù in the central courtyard.
When someone came to offer condolences,
the Master bowed to him.
After he finished wailing,
he brought in the messenger and asked about the circumstances.
The messenger said:
"He was pickled."
Thereupon he ordered that the pickled meat be covered.
3.8 Zēng Zǐ said:
"At the grave of a friend,
when the grass has grown for a year, one no longer wails."
3.9 Zǐ Sī said:
"In mourning, the encoffining takes place after three days;
for everything attached to the body,
there must be sincerity and good faith,
so that there is no cause for regret.
The burial takes place after three months;
for all that is attached to the coffin,
there must be sincerity and good faith,
so that there is no cause for regret.
Three years is the ultimate limit for mourning;
even when it is over, the deceased is not forgotten.
Therefore, a gentleman has a lifelong sorrow,
but not a single morning's anxiety.
Thus, on the anniversary of a death, he does not enjoy music."
3.10 Kǒng Zǐ was orphaned while young
and did not know where his father's grave was.
He performed the encoffining at the Crossroads of Wǔ Fù.
Those who saw it
all thought it was a burial.
In its meticulousness,
it was indeed an encoffining.
He inquired of the mother of Màn Fù of Zōu,
and only then was he able to perform the joint burial at Fáng.
3.11 When there is mourning in the neighborhood,
one does not sing while pounding grain;
when there is an encoffining in the village,
one does not sing in the lanes.
The mourning cap has no tassels.
3.12 The lineage of Yǒu Yú used earthenware coffins;
the lineage of Xià Hòu used a brick enclosure;
the people of Yīn used inner and outer coffins;
the people of Zhōu used wall-screens and funeral fans.
The people of Zhōu used the inner and outer coffins of the Yīn
for the burial of those who died in the oldest stage of premature death;
they used the brick enclosure of the Xià Hòu for the burial
of those in the middle and youngest stages of premature death;
and they used the earthenware coffin of the Yǒu Yú
for the burial of infants for whom no mourning was worn.
3.13 The lineage of Xià Hòu favored black;
for the great matter of encoffining, they used the dusk;
in military affairs, they rode black horses;
for sacrifices, they used dark-colored victims.
The people of Yīn favored white;
for the great matter of encoffining, they used midday;
in military affairs, they rode white horses;
for sacrifices, they used white victims.
The people of Zhōu favored red;
for the great matter of encoffining, they used the sunrise;
in military affairs, they rode red horses with white bellies.
For sacrifices, they used red victims.
3.14 When the mother of Mù Gōng died,
he sent a messenger to ask Zēng Zǐ:
"What should be done?"
He replied:
"I, Shēn, heard from my father:
The sorrow of weeping and wailing,
the feelings of trimmed and untrimmed mourning,
and the diet of congee and gruel,
extend from the Son of Heaven down to all.
The linen screen
belongs to Wèi;
the silk screen
belongs to Lǔ."
3.15 Jìn Xiàn Gōng was about to kill his Shì Zǐ, Shēn Shēng;
Prince Chóng Ěr said to him:
"Why do you not speak of your intent to the Duke?"
The Shì Zǐ said:
"I cannot.
The Ruler finds peace in Lí Jī;
if I did so, I would wound the Duke's heart."
[Chóng Ěr] said:
"Then why not flee?"
The Shì Zǐ said:
"I cannot.
The Ruler says I wish to murder my ruler;
is there any state in the world without a father?
Where could I go with such a charge?"
He sent a messenger to take leave of Hú Tū, saying:
"I, Shēn Shēng, have committed an offense
in not heeding your words, elder;
thus I have come to my death.
I do not dare to begrudge my death.
Nevertheless,
my ruler is old,
his son is young,
and the state is in much distress.
If you, elder, do not come forth to plan for my ruler, [the state will suffer].
If you indeed come forth to plan for my ruler,
I shall die having received your favor."
He bowed twice, touching his head to the ground,
and then died.
Thus he was known as Gōng Shì Zǐ.
There was a man of Lǔ who performed the auspicious sacrifice in the morning and sang in the evening;
Zǐ Lù laughed at him.
The Master said:
"Yóu,
will your reproaching of others
never cease?
The three-year mourning period
is indeed a long time."
When Zǐ Lù went out,
the Master said:
"Is it really too much?
To sing once the month has passed is acceptable."
3.17 Lǔ Zhuāng Gōng fought with the people of Sòng at Chéng Qiū.
Xiàn Bēn Fù was the charioteer,
and Bǔ Guó was the spearman on the right.
The horses were startled,
the army was defeated,
and the Duke fell from the chariot.
A reserve chariot offered him the mounting strap.
The Duke said:
"The one chosen by divination failed to perform."
Xiàn Bēn Fù said:
"On other days we were not defeated,
but today we were;
this shows a lack of courage."
He then died for the cause.
While the stable-boy was washing the horses,
he found a stray arrow in the fleshy part of a horse's haunch.
The Duke said:
"It was not his fault."
He then composed a eulogy for him.
The practice of having eulogies for Shì
began with this.
3.18 Zēng Zǐ was lying ill,
very weak.
Yuè Zhèng Zǐ Chūn sat at the side of the bed,
Zēng Yuán and Zēng Shēn sat at his feet,
and a young servant sat in the corner holding a torch.
The servant said:
"How grand and beautiful!
Is that not the mat of a Dà Fū?"
Zǐchūn said:
"Stop!"
Zéngzǐ heard this,
was startled
and said,
"Ah!"
(The boy) said:
"It is flowery and lustrous;
is it not a Great Officer's mat?"
Zéngzǐ said:
"Yes,
this was a gift from Jìsūn.
I have not been able to change it.
Yuán,
get up and change the mat."
Zéng Yuán said:
"Your illness is grave,
and you cannot be moved.
Hopefully we can wait until morning
to respectfully change it."
Zéngzǐ said:
"Your love for me is not like his;
a gentleman loves others according to virtue,
while a petty person loves others with indulgence.
What do I seek?
That I may die in the right way is enough for me."
They lifted and supported him to change it.
Before he was settled back on the mat, he passed away.
3.19 When death first occurs,
the grief is intense as if there is no end;
after the encoffining,
one looks around anxiously as if seeking something and not finding it;
after the burial,
one looks uneasy as if waiting for someone who does not arrive.
At the Liàn sacrifice, one is full of sighs;
at the Xiáng sacrifice, one feels a sense of resignation.
3.20 In Zhūlóu, they performed the recall of the soul with arrows;
this probably began from the battle at Shēngxíng.
The practice of Lǔ women wearing the zhuā headdress when offering condolences
began from the defeat at Táitái.
3.21 During the mourning for the mother-in-law of Nángōng Tāo's wife,
the Master instructed them on the zhuā, saying:
"Do not make it too prominent;
do not make it too broad.
Use hazel wood for the hairpin,
one foot long,
and the hair-band should be eight inches."
3.22 When Mèng Xiànzǐ performed the Shàn sacrifice,
he hung up the musical instruments but did not play music;
he approached his concubines but did not enter the inner chamber.
The Master said:
"Xiànzǐ is one degree above other men!"
3.23 After Kǒngzǐ performed the Xiáng sacrifice,
for five days he played the qín but it did not produce a melody;
after ten days, he performed songs to the shéng.
3.24 Yǒuzǐ, probably after the Xiáng sacrifice,
wore silk shoes
and a woven hat-string.
3.25 There are three cases where death does not receive condolences:
those killed through cowardice, those crushed by falling objects,
and those who drowned.
Zǐlù was in mourning for his sister;
he could have ended the mourning,
but he did not.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Why do you not end it?"
Zǐlù said:
"I have few siblings and I cannot bear to."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The former kings established the rites,
so that even the common people on the road
would all find it unbearable."
Zǐlù heard this
and then ended the mourning.
3.26 Tàigōng was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū,
but for five generations,
they were all brought back to be buried in Zhōu.
A gentleman said:
"Music delights in its origin,
and ritual does not forget its root.
The ancients had a saying:
'When a fox dies, its head points toward its home hill';
this is benevolence."
3.27 When Bóyú's mother died,
he was still wailing after a year.
The Master heard it and said:
"Who is wailing?"
The disciples said:
"It is Lǐ."
The Master said:
"Ah!
That is too much."
Bóyú heard this
and then ended his wailing.
3.28 Shùn was buried in the wilds of Cāngwú;
his three wives probably did not follow him there.
Jì Wǔzǐ said:
"Zhōugōng probably practiced joint burial."
At the funeral of Zéngzǐ,
he was bathed in the kitchen.
3.29 During the dàgōng mourning, one abandons their regular studies.
Some say:
"During dàgōng mourning,
chanting is permissible."
3.30 When Zǐzhāng was ill,
he called Shēn Xiáng and told him:
"A gentleman's death is called 'the end,'
while a petty person's is called 'death.'
Today, am I not close to the former?"
3.31 Zéngzǐ said:
"The offering at the beginning of death,
is it not like leftovers on the shelf?"
Zéngzǐ said:
"The practice of not setting a designated place for wailing during xiǎogōng mourning
is the custom of common alleys.
When Zǐsī wailed for his sister-in-law, he set a designated place,
and the women led the leaping;
when Shēn Xiáng wailed for Yán Sī, it was the same."
3.32 In ancient times,
the seams of the cap were vertical;
nowadays
they are horizontal;
thus the mourning cap's reversing of the auspicious style
is not according to antiquity.
Zéngzǐ said to Zǐsī:
"Jí,
when I was in mourning for my parent,
no water or congee entered my mouth for seven days."
Zǐsī said:
"When the former kings established the rites,
those who would exceed them were to bend down to reach them,
and those who could not reach them
were to stand on tiptoe to attain them.
Therefore, when a gentleman is in mourning for his parent,
no water or congee enters his mouth for three days,
so that he must use a staff before he can rise."
3.33 Zéngzǐ said:
"If the xiǎogōng mourning is not extended for late notification,
then distant brothers will end up having no mourning dress;
how can this be right?"
3.34 At the funeral of Bógāo,
before the messenger from the Kǒng family had arrived,
Rǎnzǐ took bundles of silk
and a team of horses
and presented them.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"How strange!
This only makes me appear insincere in the rites for Bógāo."
Bógāo died in Wèi,
and notice was sent to Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Where shall I wail for him?
For a brother,
I wail in the ancestral temple;
for a friend of my father,
I wail outside the gate of the ancestral temple;
for a teacher,
I wail in the inner chamber;
for a friend,
I wail outside the door of the inner chamber;
for an acquaintance,
I wail in the open field.
To do it in the field
would be too distant;
to do it in the inner chamber
would be too solemn.
Since he was introduced to me by Cì,
I will wail for him at the residence of the Cì family."
He then ordered Zǐgòng to act as host,
saying:
"For those who come to wail because of you,
bow to them;
for those who come because they knew Bógāo,
do not bow to them."
3.35 Zéngzǐ said:
"If one is ill during mourning
and must eat meat or drink wine,
there must be the flavor of plants and trees added to it.
This refers to things like ginger and cinnamon."
3.36 Zǐxià lost his son and then lost his sight.
Zéngzǐ went to offer condolences and said:
"I have heard that
when a friend loses his sight, one should wail for him."
Zéngzǐ wailed,
and Zǐxià also wailed,
saying:
"O Heaven!
I am without guilt."
Zéngzǐ said angrily:
"Shāng,
how can you be without guilt?
You and I served the Master between the Zhū and Sì rivers,
but you retired to grow old by the Xīhé river,
and caused the people of Xīhé
to mistake you for the Master;
this is your first guilt.
and you caused the people to hear nothing of your grief;
that is your second fault.
You lost your son,
and you lost your sight;
that is your third fault.
And yet you say, "What fault have I?"
Zǐxià threw down his staff, bowed, and said:
"I have been wrong!
I have been wrong!
I have lived apart from the group in solitude
for too long indeed."
3.37 When a person stays inside during the day,
it is appropriate to inquire about their illness;
when they stay outside at night,
it is appropriate to offer condolences.
Therefore, unless there is a great reason, a Jūnzǐ
does not sleep outside;
unless he is performing a fast,
or is ill,
he does not stay inside day and night.
3.38 When Gāo Zǐgāo was in mourning for his parents,
he wept tears of blood for three years
and never showed his teeth in a smile;
the Jūnzǐ considered this a difficult achievement.
3.39 Regarding the mourning garments,
rather than have them be inappropriate for the occasion,
it is better to have no mourning garments at all.
Those in *zīcuī* mourning
do not sit at the edge of the mat;
those in *dàgōng* mourning do not perform arduous labor in their mourning clothes.
3.40 When Kǒngzǐ went to Wèi,
he encountered the funeral of an old host.
He went in and wailed for him with great sorrow.
Upon coming out,
he told Zǐgòng to unhitch the outside horse from the carriage and present it as a funeral gift.
Zǐgòng said:
"At the funerals of your disciples,
you have never unhitched an outside horse;
to unhitch an outside horse for an old host,
is this not perhaps too much?"
The Master said:
"Just now when I went in and wailed for him,
I encountered a surge of grief and shed tears.
I detest the idea of my tears having nothing to follow them.
Little one, go and do it."
3.41 When Kǒngzǐ was in Wèi,
there was someone conducting a funeral,
and the Master observed it,
saying:
"How well he conducts the mourning!
It is sufficient to serve as a model.
Little ones, take note of it."
Zǐgòng said:
"What did the Master find so good about it?"
He replied:
"When going to the grave, he seemed full of yearning;
when returning, he seemed lost in doubt."
Zǐgòng said:
"Is that not better than returning quickly to perform the *yú* sacrifice?"
The Master said:
"Little ones, take note of it;
I have not yet been able to achieve this."
3.42 At the mourning for Yán Yuān,
meat from the *xiáng* sacrifice was presented.
Kǒngzǐ went out to receive it;
he went back inside,
played the *qín*, and then ate it.
3.43 Kǒngzǐ was standing with his disciples;
he folded his hands with the right hand uppermost,
and the various disciples all did the same.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"You disciples are indeed eager to learn!
As for me, I do so because of the mourning for my elder sister."
Then the various disciples all put the left hand uppermost.
3.44 Kǒngzǐ rose early,
and with his hands behind his back, trailing his staff,
he wandered by the door,
singing:
"The Tài Shān is crumbling!
The roof-beam is breaking!
The wise man is withering!"
After singing, he went in
and sat facing the door.
Zǐgòng heard it and said:
"If the Tài Shān crumbles,
where then shall I look up?
If the roof-beam breaks
and the wise man withers,
then on whom shall I rely?
The Master is likely to be ill."
He then hurried inside.
The Master said:
"Cì!
Why have you come so late?
The Xià Hòu clan encoffined the dead at the top of the eastern steps,
as if he were still the host;
the Yīn people encoffined between the two pillars,
where the host and guest stand on either side;
the Zhōu people encoffined at the top of the western steps,
as if he were a guest.
Now, I, Qiū, am a man of Yīn.
Last night,
I dreamt that I was sitting between the two pillars with offerings before me.
No enlightened king has arisen,
and who in the world can honor me as their master?
I am likely to die."
He took to his bed and died seven days later.
At the mourning for Kǒngzǐ,
the disciples were in doubt as to what mourning dress they should wear.
Zǐgòng said:
"In the past, when the Master mourned for Yán Yuān
it was like mourning for a son
but without the mourning dress;
and the same when he mourned for Zǐlù.
Let us mourn for the Master
as for a father but without the mourning dress."
3.45 At the mourning for Kǒngzǐ,
Gōngxī Chì was the master of ceremonies:
the decoration of the coffin,
the wall-curtains, the fans, and the ropes
were after the fashion of Zhōu;
the high ornaments
were after the fashion of Yīn;
the silk streamers on the banners
were after the fashion of Xià.
3.46 At the mourning for Zǐzhāng,
Gōngmíng Yí was the master of ceremonies.
The pall was of red silk,
with white borders at the four corners,
as was the practice for an officer of Yīn.
3.47 Zǐxià asked Kǒngzǐ:
"How should one live when there is a blood feud for one's parents?"
The Master said:
"He should sleep on straw with a shield for his pillow, hold no office,
and not live under the same sky with the enemy;
if he meets him in the marketplace or at court,
he should not turn back for a weapon but fight him immediately."
Zǐxià said:
"May I ask how one should live when there is a blood feud for one's brother?"
The Master said:
"He may hold office, but not in the same state;
if he is on a mission with the ruler's command,
even if he meets him, he should not fight."
Zǐxià said:
"May I ask how one should live when there is a blood feud for a paternal uncle
or a cousin?"
The Master said:
"He should not be the leader in seeking revenge;
if the principal party is capable of it,
then he should hold his weapon and follow behind them."
3.48 At the mourning for Kǒngzǐ,
the disciples all went out wearing their mourning headbands.
When they were living together they wore the headbands,
but when they went out they did not.
3.49 Keeping the grave clear
was not the practice of antiquity.
3.50 Zǐlù said:
"I have heard from the Master:
'In the rites of mourning,
rather than have the sorrow be insufficient while the ritual is in excess,
it is better that the ritual be insufficient while the sorrow is in excess.
In the rites of sacrifice,
rather than have the reverence be insufficient while the ritual is in excess,
it is better that the ritual be insufficient while the reverence is in excess.'"
3.51 Zéngzǐ went to offer condolences in Fùxià;
the host had already performed the *zǔ* sacrifice,
filled the wheel ruts,
but then pushed the coffin back to its place;
he made the women descend and then performed the rites.
A follower asked:
"Is this according to the rites?"
Zéngzǐ said:
"The *zǔ* sacrifice means the beginning of departure;
since it is just the beginning,
why should it be impossible to return and stay?"
The follower then asked Zǐyóu:
"Is this according to the rites?"
Zǐyóu said:
"The putting of rice into the mouth is done under the window,
the smaller dressing of the corpse is done inside the door,
the larger dressing of the corpse is done at the eastern steps,
the encoffining is done in the guest's place,
the *zǔ* sacrifice is done in the courtyard,
and the interment is done at the grave;
all these are to move the deceased further and further away.
Therefore, in mourning affairs there is progress but no retreat."
Zéngzǐ heard of this and said:
"How much superior he is
in his understanding of the *zǔ* sacrifice!"
3.52 Zéngzǐ went to offer condolences wearing a fur robe with the outer garment over it;
Zǐyóu went to offer condolences with his fur robe showing.
Zéngzǐ pointed to Zǐyóu and said to others:
"That man
is said to be well-versed in the rites,
yet how is it that he shows his fur robe when offering condolences?"
When the host had completed the minor dressing of the corpse,
he bared his shoulder and bound up his hair;
Zǐyóu hurried out,
put on his fur robe, belt, and headband, and entered again.
Zēngzǐ said:
"I was wrong,
I was wrong;
that man is correct."
3.53 When Zǐxià, after ending his mourning period, came to see the Master,
he was given a qín;
he tried to tune it but it would not be in harmony,
and he played it but it did not produce a complete melody.
He stood up and said:
"My grief is not yet forgotten.
The former kings established the rites,
and I do not dare to exceed them."
When Zǐzhāng, after ending his mourning period, came to see the Master,
he was given a qín;
he tuned it and it was in harmony,
and he played it and it produced a complete melody.
He stood up and said:
"The former kings established the rites,
and I do not dare not to reach the required standard."
3.54 At the mourning for Sīkòu Huìzǐ,
Zǐyóu wore the hemp mourning robe and the headband of male hemp.
Wénzǐ declined this, saying:
"You honored Mímóu's younger brother by being his friend,
and now you honor him by wearing this mourning dress;
I venture to decline it."
Zǐyóu said:
"It is according to the rites."
Wénzǐ withdrew and returned to wailing.
Zǐyóu hurried and took his place among the officers.
Wénzǐ again declined, saying:
"You honored Mímóu's younger brother by being his friend,
and now you honor him by wearing this mourning dress,
and you further honor him by attending his funeral;
I venture to decline."
Zǐyóu said:
"I firmly request to do so."
Wénzǐ withdrew,
supported the rightful heir to stand facing south, and said:
"You honored Mímóu's younger brother by being his friend,
and now you honor him by wearing this mourning dress,
and you further honor him by attending his funeral;
how could I, Hǔ, dare not return to my proper place?"
Zǐyóu then hurried and took his place as a guest.
3.55 At the mourning for Jiāngjūn Wénzǐ,
after the mourning period was over,
a man from Yuè came to offer condolences.
The host wore the shēnyī robe
and the cooked silk cap,
waiting for him in the ancestral temple,
with tears and snot running down.
Zǐyóu watched this and said:
"The son of the Jiāngjūn of the Wén family is almost there!
This is the ritual of those who have lost the rites;
his actions are appropriate."
3.56 In childhood, one is named;
at the capping ceremony, one receives a style name;
at fifty, one is addressed by seniority;
after death, one receives a posthumous title;
this is the way of Zhōu.
The headband represents reality.
Digging a hole in the center of the room to bathe the body,
breaking the stove to support the feet,
and when the burial takes place,
breaking through the ancestral temple wall and crossing through the courtyard
to exit from the main gate;
this is the way of Yīn.
Scholars follow this.
3.57 When Zǐliǔ's mother died,
Zǐshuò asked to prepare the funeral requirements.
Zǐliǔ said:
"How will you do it?"
Zǐshuò said:
"I request to sell the mother of our concubine-born younger brother."
Zǐliǔ said:
"How could one sell another's mother to bury his own mother?
This cannot be done."
After the burial,
Zǐshuò wanted to use the remainder of the condolence money to prepare sacrificial vessels.
Zǐliǔ said:
"This cannot be done.
I have heard that
