a superior man does not profit his house from a funeral;
let it be distributed among our poor brothers."
3.58 The superior man says:
"If one plans for someone's army,
if it is defeated, he dies for it;
if one plans for someone's state or city,
if it is in danger, he shares in its ruin."
3.59 Gōngshū Wénzǐ climbed the hill of Xiáqiū,
and Qú Bóyù followed him.
Wénzǐ said:
"How pleasant is this hill!
When I die, I want to be buried here."
Qú Bóyù said:
"Since you, Sir, find it pleasant,
then I, Yuàn, request to be buried before you."
3.60 There was a man of Biàn whose mother died,
and he wept like a child.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"His grief is indeed grief,
but it is difficult to maintain.
As for the rites,
they are made to be transmissible,
and they are made to be continuous.
Therefore, wailing and leaping have their proper measures."
3.61 When Shúsūn Wǔshū's mother died,
after the minor dressing,
the bearers went out the door;
once out the door, he bared his shoulder
and threw away his cap, binding his hair.
Zǐyóu said:
"He knows the rites."
3.62 When supporting the ruler,
the Master of Diviners supports on the right,
and the Master of Archers supports on the left;
when the ruler dies, they lift him in this way.
3.63 For the husband of a maternal aunt,
the wife of a maternal uncle,
and the mutual mourning between these two husbands,
the superior man has not spoken of it.
Some say: if living at the same hearth, they wear the three-month mourning.
3.64 In matters of mourning,
one should appear hurried;
in auspicious matters,
one should appear calm and composed.
Therefore, though mourning is urgent,
one does not skip the proper steps;
though auspicious matters are deliberate,
one is not idle.
Being too agitated is coarse;
being too negligent is like a common person.
The superior man is composed and dignified.
3.65 Concerning funeral equipment,
the superior man is ashamed to have it all prepared;
things that can be done in one or two days,
the superior man does not do beforehand.
3.66 Regarding mourning dress:
a brother's son is like one's own son,
as he is drawn close and brought forward;
the lack of mourning for a sister-in-law or brother-in-law
is because they are pushed away and kept distant;
the light mourning for aunts and sisters
is because there are others who have received them and will treat them with more weight.
3.67 When eating beside someone in mourning,
one never eats to satiety.
3.68 Zēngzǐ was standing by the side of the gate with a guest,
when one of his disciples hurried out.
Zēngzǐ said:
"Where are you going?"
The disciple replied:
"My father has died,
and I am going out to wail in the lane."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Return,
and wail in your own quarters."
Zēngzǐ then faced north and offered his condolences.
3.69 Kǒngzǐ said:
"To treat the dead as if they were completely dead
is inhuman and should not be done;
to treat the dead as if they were still alive
is unwise and should not be done.
For this reason,
the bamboo vessels are not fit for use,
the earthenware is not fit for washing,
the wood is not finely carved,
the qín and sè are strung but not tuned,
the yú and shēng are complete but not in harmony,
and there are bells and chimes but no stands to hang them on.
They are called 'spirit articles,'
to treat them as belonging to the spirits."
3.70 Yǒuzǐ asked Zēngzǐ, saying:
"Did you ask the Master about mourning?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"I heard him say:
'In mourning, one should desire to quickly become poor,
and after death, one should desire to quickly decay.'"
Yǒuzǐ said:
"Those are not the words of a superior man."
Zēngzǐ said:
"I, Shēn, heard them from the Master."
Yǒuzǐ again said:
"Those are not the words of a superior man."
Zēngzǐ said:
"I, Shēn, along with Zǐyóu, heard them."
Yǒuzǐ said:
"Indeed,
then the Master must have said them for a specific reason."
Zēngzǐ told these words to Zǐyóu.
Zǐyóu said:
"How remarkable!
The words of Yǒuzǐ resemble those of the Master.
Formerly, when the Master was staying in Sòng,
he saw the Sīmǎ of Huán building a stone outer coffin for himself,
which was not finished in three years.
The Master said:
"If it is as extravagant as this,
it is better to rot quickly after death."
This desire for the body to rot quickly after death
was said on account of Huán Sīmǎ.
When Nángōng Jìngshū returned,
he was sure to carry treasures when attending court.
The Master said:
"If it is as much about wealth as this,
it is better for the mourning period to bring poverty quickly."
This desire for the mourning period to bring poverty quickly
was said on account of Jìngshū."
Zēngzǐ told the words of Zǐyóu to Yǒuzǐ,
and Yǒuzǐ said:
"Indeed,
I previously said
that these were not the words of the Master."
Zēngzǐ said:
"How do you know this?"
Yǒuzǐ said:
"When the Master was in office at Zhōngdū,
he prescribed an inner coffin of four inches
and an outer coffin of five inches.
By this, I know he did not wish for quick rotting.
In the past, when the Master lost the position of Sīkòu in Lǔ
and was about to go to Jīng,
he first sent Zǐxià,
and then followed up by sending Rǎn Yǒu.
By this, I know he did not wish for quick poverty."
3.71 When Chén Zhuāngzǐ died,
the announcement was made to Lǔ.
The people of Lǔ wished not to wail for him,
so Duke Miù summoned Xiànzǐ and questioned him.
Xiànzǐ said:
"The Great Officers of antiquity
did not let even a greeting accompanied by dried meat go beyond their borders;
though one might wish to wail for them,
how could they do so?
Today's Great Officers
share in the administration of the central states;
though one might wish not to wail,
how could they not wail?
Furthermore, I have heard
that wailing follows two paths:
there is wailing out of love,
and there is wailing out of fear."
The Duke said:
"True.
If so, then what should be done?"
Xiànzǐ said:
"I request that he be wailed for in the temple of a different surname."
Thereupon, they joined in wailing for him at the Xiàn family temple.
3.72 Zhòng Xiàn said to Zēngzǐ:
"The Xiàhòushì used spirit vessels,
to show the people that the dead have no consciousness;
the Yīn people used sacrificial vessels,
to show the people that the dead have consciousness;
the Zhōu people used both,
to show the people their doubt."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Is it not so?
Is it not so?
For spirit vessels
are vessels for the ghosts;
sacrificial vessels
are vessels for the living.
As for the people of antiquity,
why would they treat their parents as dead?"
3.73 Gōngshū Mù had a brother by the same mother but a different father who died,
and he asked Zǐyóu about it.
Zǐyóu said:
"Should it be the Dàgōng mourning?"
Dí Yí had a brother by the same mother but a different father who died,
and he asked Zǐxià about it.
Zǐxià said:
"I have not heard of this before;
however, the people of Lǔ wear the Qícuī mourning for it."
Dí Yí performed the Qícuī mourning.
Today's practice of Qícuī mourning for such brothers
began with the question of Dí Yí.
3.74 The mother of Zǐsī died in Wèi.
Liǔ Ruò said to Zǐsī:
"You
are the descendant of a Sage.
People from all directions look to you to observe the rites;
you should be careful about this."
Zǐsī said:
"Why should I be careful?
I have heard:
When there is the rite
but not the wealth,
the gentleman does not perform it.
When there is the rite
and the wealth
but not the proper time,
the gentleman does not perform it.
Why should I be careful?"
3.75 Xiànzǐ Suǒ said:
"I have heard:
In antiquity, there was no reduction of mourning;
those above and below each observed mourning based on their kinship.
Téng Bówén wore Qícuī mourning for Mèng Hǔ,
who was his uncle;
he wore Qícuī mourning for Mèng Pí,
who was also his uncle."
3.76 Hòumù said:
"Regarding mourning,
I heard Xiànzǐ say:
'In mourning,
one cannot but think deeply and long about it.
When buying a coffin, I see that the exterior and interior are smooth;
when I die, it should be the same.'"
3.77 Zēngzǐ said:
"Before the corpse has been decorated,
the hall is curtained off.
After the minor dressing, the curtain is removed."
Zhòngliángzǐ said:
"Because the husbands and wives are in a state of disorder from grief,
the hall is curtained off.
After the minor dressing, the curtain is removed."
3.78 Regarding the offerings at the minor dressing,
Zǐyóu said:
"They should be in the east."
Zēngzǐ said:
"They should be in the west,
for where the dressing is done, there is the mat."
That the offerings at the minor dressing are in the west
is a later error in the rites of Lǔ.
3.79 Xiànzǐ said:
"The sackcloth robe and the fine linen skirt
are not from antiquity."
3.80 Zǐpú died.
The wailers called out his name, Miè.
Zǐgāo
said:
"How rustic this is!"
The wailers then changed their way.
3.81 At the mourning for the mother of Dù Qiáo,
there were no ritual assistants in the house,
as it was considered neglectful.
3.82 The Master said:
"When death has just occurred,
those wearing lambskin robes and black caps
should simply change them."
Lambskin robes and black caps—
the Master did not wear them when offering condolences.
3.83 Zǐyóu asked about the implements for mourning.
The Master said:
"They should be in proportion to whether the family has wealth or not."
Zǐyóu said:
"How is the wealth or lack thereof to be measured?"
The Master said:
"If there is wealth,
do not exceed the rites;
if there is a lack thereof,
as long as the head, feet, and body are covered during the dressing,
and the burial is completed,
with the coffin lowered and the grave sealed,
who could possibly find fault with that?"
3.84 Sīshì Bēn said to Zǐyóu:
"I request that the dressing of the corpse be done on the bed."
Zǐyóu said:
"Yes."
Xiànzǐ heard of this
and said:
"How arrogant is Shūshì,
to take it upon himself to grant people the rites!"
3.85 Duke Xiāng of Sòng buried his wife
with a hundred jars of pickled meat.
Zēngzǐ said:
"Having already called them spirit vessels,
he then went and filled them."
3.86 At the mourning for Mèng Xiànzǐ,
the Sītú's subordinates returned the contributions of money.
The Master said:
"This is acceptable."
3.87 Regarding the reading of the list of funeral gifts,
Zēngzǐ said:
"This is not from antiquity;
this is making the announcement twice."
3.88 Chéng Zǐgāo was lying ill.
Qìng Yí entered,
and requested, saying:
"Your illness is critical.
If it should lead to the great illness,
then what should be done?"
Zǐgāo said:
"I have heard this:
In life, one should be of benefit to others;
in death, one should not be a harm to others.
Even if in life I have not been of benefit to others,
should I then harm others in death?
When I die,
then choose a piece of land that is not fit for cultivation to bury me."
3.89 Zǐxià asked Fūzǐ, saying:
"In the mourning for a ruler's mother or wife."
"In residence, speech, food, and drink, one should be easy and composed."
3.90 When guests arrive,
and there is no place to lodge them.
Fūzǐ said:
"When they are alive, they shall lodge with me;
when they are dead, I shall provide for their encoffining."
3.91 Guó Zǐgāo said:
"Burial
is concealment;
concealment
is because of the desire that people should not see the body.
Therefore,
the clothing is sufficient to adorn the body,
the coffin fits around the clothing,
the outer coffin (guǒ) fits around the coffin,
and the earth fits around the outer coffin.
Why then return to turn the soil and plant trees upon it?"
3.92 At the mourning for Kǒngzǐ,
some came from Yān to observe,
and they stayed with the Zǐxià clan.
Zǐxià said:
"Is it the Sage's burial of others
or others' burial of the Sage?
What is there for you to observe?
Formerly, Fūzǐ spoke of it, saying:
'I have seen mounds shaped like halls,
seen them like embankments,
seen them like covered large houses,
and seen them like axe-heads.
I follow the axe-head shape.'
This refers to the 'horse-mane' (mǎliè) mound.
Now, in one day, the pounding boards were moved three times
to finish the mound;
is this still following Fūzǐ's intent?"
3.93 Women do not use kudzu (gé) belts.
3.94 When offering fresh seasonal produce,
it is like the offerings at the new moon.
3.95 After the burial,
everyone removes their mourning garments according to their degree.
3.96 The chí ornaments should resemble the eaves (zhòngliù).
3.97 When a ruler (jūn) ascends the throne, he has his inner coffin (bēi) made;
it is lacquered once a year,
and stored away.
3.98 Recalling the soul (fù),
wedging the teeth,
binding the feet,
the mouth-offering (fàn),
setting out the decorations,
and screening the hall are all done together.
The father and brothers order the messengers to announce the death.
3.99 When a ruler's soul is recalled (jūnfù),
it is done at the Small Chamber, the Great Chamber,
the Small Ancestral Temple, the Great Ancestral Temple,
the Gate of the Armory (Kùmén), and the four outskirts.
3.100 During mourning, the body is not stripped—
is it because of the offerings?
Or because of the sacrificial meat?
Once encoffined,
after ten days, the materials for the grave and the spirit articles (míngqì) are displayed.
The morning offering is at sunrise;
the evening offering is while the sun is still out.
In the mourning for parents,
wailing has no set time,
but if sent on a mission, one must ensure he returns for the offerings.
3.101 At the first anniversary (liàn) sacrifice,
the liàn robe has a yellow lining
and quàn borders;
a kudzu (gé) waist-band;
hemp shoes without toe-caps;
ear-plugs of horn;
a deerskin robe with wide sleeves;
it is permissible to wear the inner garment over it.
3.102 While there is a coffin in the house,
if news of the death of a distant brother arrives,
even if it is for the sī degree, one must go;
if it is not a brother,
even if it is a neighbor, one does not go.
For acquaintances,
those whose brothers do not live with them are all condoled.
3.103 The Tiānzǐ has four layers of coffins;
a hide coffin of water buffalo and rhinoceros skin covers them,
its thickness is three inches;
one coffin of lǐ wood,
and two coffins of zǐ wood;
all four layers fit closely.
The coffin bands are two longitudinal and three transverse,
with one wedge for each band.
The cypress outer coffin (guǒ) is made of pieces six feet long.
3.104 When the Tiānzǐ wails for a Zhūhóu,
he wears the juébiàn cap, the headband, and the chún robe;
or it is said:
he orders an official to wail for him,
and he does not have music at his meals for the sake of the deceased.
3.105 For the encoffining of the Tiānzǐ,
the space is filled with wood and plastered, using the dragon-hearse (lóngchún) as the outer coffin,
with axe-patterns (fǔ) placed on top of the outer coffin,
and the plastering of the structure completed;
this is the ritual of the Tiānzǐ.
3.106 Only for the mourning of the Tiānzǐ
are there separate groups by surname to wail.
3.107 Lǔ Āi Gōng delivered the eulogy (lěi) for Kǒng Qiū, saying:
"Heaven has not left the venerable elder,
and no one is left to assist me in my position;
alas, how sorrowful!
Nífù!"
3.108 When the state loses a large district or city,
the Gōng, Qīng, Dàfū, and Shì all wear the yàn cap
and wail in the Grand Temple (Dàmiào)
for three days;
the ruler (jūn) does not have full meals.
Some say:
the ruler has full meals and wails to the Spirit of the Land (Hòutǔ).
3.109 Kǒngzǐ disliked those who wailed in the open fields.
3.110 One who has not yet held office
does not dare to present a mourning gift (shuì) to others on his own;
if he presents a gift,
it must be by the order of his father or elder brother.
3.111 Only after all the Shì have entered do the morning and evening leapings occur.
3.112 At the xiáng sacrifice, white silk (gǎo) is worn;
in that same month, the dàn sacrifice is performed;
in the following month, music is resumed.
3.113 For a Shì, the ruler bestows a funeral canopy (yì).
4.1 For the death of a ruler's eldest son in the oldest stage of premature death (zhàngshāng),
three chariots are provided;
for a duke's son by a concubine in the oldest stage of premature death,
one chariot;
for a Dàfū's eldest son in the oldest stage of premature death,
one chariot.
4.2 At the mourning of a Gōng,
the heads of the various high offices
carry staffs.
4.3 For a Dàfū, the ruler,
when the burial is about to take place,
offers condolences at the house;
when the coffin is taken out,
he orders the pulling of the hearse;
after three steps it stops;
this is done three times,
and then the ruler retires;
the same is done at the ancestral temple,
and the same at the place of sorrowful parting (āicì).
4.4 At fifty, one who has no chariot
does not cross the border to offer condolences to others.
4.5 When Jì Wǔzǐ was ill in bed,
Jiǎo Gù entered to see him without removing his qíshuāi garment,
and said:
"This Way
is about to perish;
a Shì should only remove the qíshuāi at the gate of the ruler's palace."
Wǔzǐ said:
"Is it not good?
A gentleman (jūnzǐ) makes small things manifest."
When it came to his mourning,
Zēng Diǎn leaned against his gate and sang.
4.6 When a Dàfū offers condolences:
"If he arrives while the rites are in progress,
it is declined.
When offering condolences to someone,
one does not have music on that day.
A woman does not cross the border to offer condolences to others.
On the day of offering condolences,
one does not drink wine or eat meat.
To offer condolences at a burial, one must hold the ropes for pulling the hearse;
if following the hearse to the grave-site,
one must hold the ropes (fú)."
4.7 During mourning,
if a Gōng offers condolences,
there must be someone to return the bow;
even a friend, a neighbor, or a house-guest will do.
The condolence says:
"Our lonely ruler has sent me to assist."
The host says:
"[He] condescends to visit."
If the ruler meets the coffin on the road,
he must send someone to offer condolences.
At the mourning of a Dàfū,
a son by a concubine (shùzǐ) does not receive condolences.
4.8 If the brother of one's wife dies, having succeeded his father,
one wails for him in the principal chamber;
the son acts as the host,
baring the shoulder, wearing the mourning turban (miǎn), wailing, and leaping;
the husband enters and stands to the right of the gate;
he has a man stand outside the gate to inform those who come;
those who were intimate with the deceased enter and wail;
if the father is still alive,
the wailing is done in the wife's chamber;
if it is not the successor to the father,
the wailing is done in a different chamber.
4.9 While there is a coffin in the house,
on hearing of the death of a distant brother,
one wails in a side chamber;
if there is no side chamber,
one wails to the right inside the gate;
if it is in the same state,
one goes to wail for him.
4.10 Zǐzhāng died.
Zēngzǐ was in mourning for his mother;
he went to wail for him wearing the *zīcuī* mourning dress.
Someone said:
"The *zīcuī* is not used for paying a visit of condolence."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Was mine a visit of condolence?"
4.11 At the mourning for Yǒu Ruò,
Duke Dào paid a visit of condolence.
Zǐyóu acted as the usher,
and stood on the left.
4.12 At the mourning for Wáng Jī of Gǔ in Qí,
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ wore the *dàgōng* mourning dress for her.
Someone said:
"Since she was married from Lǔ,
he therefore wore the mourning dress of a sister for her."
Someone else said:
"She was his maternal grandmother,
and therefore he wore mourning for her."
4.13 At the mourning for Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
Duke Mù of Qín sent a messenger to offer condolences to Prince Chóng'ěr,
and furthermore said:
"I have heard
that losing a state usually happens at such a time,
and gaining a state also usually happens at such a time.
Although you, my son, are solemnly in the midst of your mourning dress,
mourning cannot be prolonged,
and the opportunity must not be lost.
May you, young man, consider this."
Chóng'ěr told this to Jiù Fàn.
Jiù Fàn said:
"May you, young man, decline it.
A person in mourning has no treasure;
benevolence and love for kin are his treasures.
What does the death of a father mean?
If one uses it to seek profit,
who in the world could speak well of it?
May you, young man, decline it."
Prince Chóng'ěr said to the guest:
"The ruler has kindly condoled with the exiled servant Chóng'ěr.
Having lost my person and my father having died,
I was unable to join in the wailing and weeping of grief,
and thus caused the ruler concern.
What does the death of a father mean?
How could I dare have other ambitions,
and thereby disgrace the ruler's righteousness?"
He kowtowed but did not bow in return;
he wailed and then rose;
and having risen, he did not speak privately.
Zǐxiǎn reported the mission to Duke Mù.
Duke Mù said:
"How benevolent is Prince Chóng'ěr!
By kowtowing without bowing,
he showed he did not yet consider himself the successor;
hence he did not complete the bow.
By wailing and rising,
he showed love for his father.
By rising and not speaking privately,
he kept himself far from profit."
4.14 Placing a curtain around the coffin
was not an ancient practice;
it began with Jìng Jiāng wailing for Mù Bó.
4.15 The rites of mourning
are the height of sorrow and grief.
To regulate grief
is to follow the changes;
the gentleman remembers those who gave him his beginning.
The *fù* (calling back the soul)
is the way of exhausted love,
and contains the heart of prayer;
it is looking for the return from the darkness
and is the way of seeking from ghosts and spirits.
Facing the north
is the meaning of seeking in the darkness.
Bowing and kowtowing
is the deepest concealment of sorrow and grief;
kowtowing
is the extreme of such concealment.
For the feeding, rice and cowries are used,
because one cannot bear the mouth to be empty;
it is not for the purpose of nourishment,
but simply using what is fine.
The *míng*
is the banner of clarity.
Because the dead can no longer be distinguished,
a flag is used to mark them.
Out of love for them,
they are recorded;
out of respect for them,
the way is fully followed.
The *zhòng*
is the way of the master;
the Yīn people attached the *zhòng* to the tablet;
the Zhōu people separated the *zhòng* from the tablet.
The offerings are made with plain vessels
because the living have hearts of plain grief;
only in the rites of sacrifice
does the master exhaust his own efforts;
how can he know what the spirits enjoy?
It is simply that the master has a heart of purification and respect.
Leaping and wailing
are the height of grief.
There is a set number for them,
which serves as a regulated refinement.
Baring the shoulder and binding the hair
are changes;
being distressed
is the change of grief.
Removing ornaments
is removing beauty;
baring the shoulder and binding the hair
is the extreme of removing ornaments.
When to bare the shoulder and when to cover it
are the regulations of grief.
Wearing the *biàn* cap and kudzu mourning bands for burial
is the way of communion with the spirits;
it contains a heart of respect.
The Zhōu people used the *biàn* cap for burial;
the Yīn people used the *xǔ* cap for burial.
Giving gruel to the host, the hostess, and the household manager
is because of their exhaustion;
the ruler commands them to eat it.
Returning to wail and ascending the hall
is returning to where the deceased used to act;
the hostess entering the chamber
is returning to where she used to provide care.
Condolences offered when returning from the burial to wail
are the height of grief;
one returns and the deceased is gone;
they are lost;
at this time, the feeling is most extreme.
The Yīn offered condolences after the mound was raised;
the Zhōu offered condolences after returning to wail.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The Yīn were already sincere,
but I follow the Zhōu."
Burying in the north, with the head to the north,
was the universal rite of the Three Dynasties;
it was because they go to the darkness.
When the mound is raised,
the master offers gifts,
and the invoker invites the corpse of the *yú* sacrifice to stay for the night.
After returning to wail,
the master and the officials inspect the victim for the *yú* sacrifice.
The officials set out the mat and offerings to the left of the tomb;
then they return,
and perform the *yú* sacrifice at midday.
The *yú* sacrifice is performed on the day of burial
because one cannot bear to be separated for a single day.
In that month,
the *yú* sacrifice replaces the daily offerings.
When the wailing until exhaustion is over, it is called "completion of the matter";
on that day,
the auspicious sacrifice replaces the mourning sacrifice.
The next day,
the deceased is enshrined with the grandfather.
The transition to the auspicious sacrifice
leading up to the enshrinement
must happen on this day
to maintain connection, for one cannot bear that for a single day there should be no place for the spirit to rest.
The Yīn performed the enshrinement after the *liàn* sacrifice;
the Zhōu performed the enshrinement after the wailing until exhaustion.
Kǒngzǐ considered the Yīn practice good.
4.16 When a ruler attends the mourning of a subject,
he is preceded by a sorcerer and an invoker with peach branches and reed brooms, and men holding spears—
this is because of his dislike for death;
it is how he is distinguished from the living.
4.17 In mourning, there is the way of death.
This is why the former kings found it difficult to speak of.
4.18 The morning visit to the temple during mourning
follows the filial heart of the deceased;
because of the grief of leaving their home,
they therefore go to the temples of the grandfather and father before departing.
The Yīn performed the morning visit and then enshrined the body in the ancestral temple;
the Zhōu performed the morning visit and then proceeded to burial.
4.19 Kǒngzǐ said:
"He who made the spirit articles
understood the way of mourning;
they are complete as objects but cannot be used."
How sad!
If the dead were to use the vessels of the living,
would it not lead to the use of human sacrifices?
They are called spirit articles
because they are for the spirits.
Clay carriages and straw figures
have existed since ancient times;
they follow the way of spirit articles.
Kǒngzǐ thought that he who made the straw figures was good,
but he who made the tomb figurines was not benevolent—
did it not lead to the use of human beings?
4.20 Duke Mù asked Zǐsī:
"Is wearing mourning for a former ruler
an ancient practice?"
Zǐsī said:
"The gentlemen of old
advanced people with ritual
and dismissed people with ritual;
therefore, there was the rite of wearing mourning for a former ruler."
The gentlemen of today,
when they promote a person, it is as if they would place them on their knees;
when they dismiss a person, it is as if they would cast them into an abyss.
If they do not become the leaders of conflict,
is that not good enough!
Why should there be any return to the mourning dress?"
4.21 During the mourning for Dào Gōng,
Jì Zhāo Zǐ asked Mèng Jìng Zǐ, saying:
"What should we eat for the ruler?"
Jìng Zǐ said:
"Eating congee
is the universal rite of the world.
That we three ministers cannot dwell in the ducal house
is known by everyone everywhere.
If I force myself to become emaciated, I could do so,
but would it not make people suspect that I am not truly emaciated out of genuine emotion?
I, therefore, will eat regular food."
4.22 When Sītú Jìng Zǐ of Wèi died,
Zǐ Xià went to condole.
The host had not yet performed the minor dressing,
but Zǐ Xià wore the mourning headband when he went.
Zǐ Yóu went to condole,
after the host had already performed the minor dressing.
Zǐ Yóu took out the headband and wailed.
Zǐ Xià asked:
"Did you hear this somewhere?"
He replied:
"I heard it from the Master:
'If the host has not yet changed his garments, one does not wear the headband.'"
4.23 Zēng Zǐ said:
"Yàn Zǐ can be said to
have understood ritual;
he possessed reverence and respect."
Yǒu Ruò said:
"Yàn Zǐ wore a single fox-fur robe for thirty years.
There was only one offering carriage at his funeral,
which returned after reaching the grave.
For the ruler of a state, there are seven bundles of offerings
and seven offering carriages;
for a Great Officer, five bundles
and five offering carriages.
How could Yàn Zǐ have understood ritual?"
Zēng Zǐ replied:
"When a state lacks the Way,
a gentleman is ashamed to perform rituals to the full.
When a state is extravagant,
he shows them frugality;
when a state is frugal,
he shows them the proper ritual."
4.24 When the mother of Guó Zhāo Zǐ died,
he asked Zǐ Zhāng:
"At the burial at the grave,
where should the men and women be positioned?"
Zǐ Zhāng said:
"At the funeral of Sītú Jìng Zǐ,
the Master assisted, and
the men faced west,
while the women faced east."
Guó Zhāo Zǐ said:
"Ah!
No."
He continued:
"In my funeral, it shall be this way:
you take charge of it;
let guests be guests
and hosts be hosts—
the women shall follow the men and all face west."
4.25 At the mourning for Mù Bó,
Jìng Jiāng wailed during the day;
at the mourning for Wén Bó,
she wailed day and night.
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"She knows ritual."
At the mourning for Wén Bó,
Jìng Jiāng leaned against his bed and did not wail,
saying:
"In the past, when I had this son,
I thought he would become a worthy man,
but I never saw him frequenting the ducal house;
now that he has died,
none of his friends or fellow officials have shed a tear,
yet the women of the inner chambers all wail and lose their voices.
This son
must have been very neglectful of ritual!"
4.26 When the mother of Jì Kāng Zǐ died,
her undergarments were displayed.
Jìng Jiāng said:
"A woman, if not adorned,
does not dare to see her parents-in-law.
Now guests are coming from all directions;
why are undergarments displayed here?"
She ordered them to be removed.
4.27 Yǒu Zǐ and Zǐ Yóu were standing together,
and saw a child yearning for his parents.
Yǒu Zǐ said to Zǐ Yóu:
"I have never understood the jumping in mourning;
I have long wished to abolish it.
If genuine emotion lies in this child's behavior,
could that be the real thing?"
Zǐ Yóu said:
"In ritual:
there are those who minimize emotion;
there are those who create objects for a reason;
and there are those who simply act directly on their raw feelings,
which is the way of the Róng and Dí barbarians.
The way of ritual is not like that.
When people are joyful, they are elated;
when elated, they sing;
when singing, they sway;
when swaying, they dance;
when dancing, they may become indignant;
when indignant, they become sorrowful;
when sorrowful, they sigh;
when sighing, they beat their breasts;
and when beating their breasts, they jump.
To regulate and temper these emotions—
this is what is called ritual.
When a person dies,
others would naturally find him repulsive;
when he can no longer do anything,
they would naturally turn their backs on him.
Therefore,
the shrouds and coverlets are prepared,
and the coffin ornaments and fan-screens are set up,
so that people will not find the deceased repulsive.
Upon the initial death,
offerings of dried meat and sauce are made;
when the body is about to be moved,
a farewell offering is made;
after the burial, offerings of food are made,
though no one has ever seen the deceased enjoy them.
Since ancient times,
these practices have never been abandoned,
so that people will not turn their backs on the deceased.
Therefore, what you criticize in the ritual
is not actually a defect of the ritual."
4.28 Wú invaded Chén,
cutting off the sacrifices and killing the pestilence-stricken.
As the army was returning and leaving the border,
the Grand Minister Pǐ of Chén was sent as an envoy to the army.
Fū Chāi said to the Usher Yí:
"This man is very talkative;
why not ask him:
'An army must have a reputation;
what will people call this army?'"
what will they call it?"
Grand Minister Pǐ replied:
"The invaders of old
did not cut off sacrifices,
did not kill the pestilence-stricken,
and did not capture those with grey hair.
Now this army
has killed the pestilence-stricken;
will it not be called an army that kills the pestilence-stricken?"
Fū Chāi asked:
"If I return your land
and send back your sons,
then what will it be called?"
He replied:
"If the King punishes the crimes of our humble city
and then compassionately pardons us,
how could the army
then lack a good name?"
4.29 Yán Dīng was good at observing mourning.
When death first occurred,
he looked flustered as if seeking something but failing to find it.
At the encoffining,
he looked longing as if following someone but failing to catch up.
After the burial,
he looked desolate, as if he could not wait for the deceased's return before resting.
4.30 Zǐ Zhāng asked:
"The Shū says:
'Gāo Zōng did not speak for three years,
and when he did speak, everyone was delighted.'
Was this really so?"
Zhòng Ní said:
"Why should it not be so?
In ancient times, when a Son of Heaven died,
the royal heir left the government to the Prime Minister for three years."
4.31 Zhī Dào Zǐ died,
and before he was buried,
Lord Píng was drinking wine.
Shī Kuàng and
Lǐ Diào were in attendance,
and the bells were being struck.
Dù Kuì came from outside,
heard the sound of the bells,
and asked:
"Where is he?"
Someone said:
"In the inner chambers."
Dù Kuì entered the chambers,
ascended the steps one by one,
poured some wine,
and said:
"Kuàng, drink this."
He poured another cup
and said:
"Diào, drink this."
He poured another cup,
sat facing north in the hall, and drank it.
He descended
and hurried out.
Píng Gōng called him back and had him enter,
saying:
"Guì,
earlier I thought your heart might have something to tell me,
which is why I did not speak to you;
why did you make Kuàng drink?"
He replied:
"The days of Zǐ and Mǎo are not for music;
since Zhì Dào Zǐ is in the hall,
this is a great Zǐ and Mǎo day indeed.
Kuàng is the Grand Master of Music,
yet he did not advise you,
which is why I made him drink."
"Why did you make Tiáo drink?"
He replied:
"Tiáo is your favorite servant,
yet for the sake of one drink or one meal,
he forgot his ruler's grief;
that is why I made him drink."
"Why did you drink?"
He replied:
"Guì is the Cook;
not only should I provide knives and spoons,
but I also dared to concern myself with preventing errors;
that is why I drank."
Píng Gōng said:
"I, too, have faults;
pour a cup and make me drink."
Dù Guì washed the cup and raised it.
The Duke said to his attendants:
"When I die,
you must not abolish this cup."
Until today,
when the offerings are finished,
they raise the cup
and call it the Dù jǔ.
4.32 Gōngshū Wénzǐ died,
and his son Shù requested a posthumous title from the ruler,
saying:
"The days and months move on
and the burial is approaching.
I request a name to replace his own."
The ruler said:
"In the past, when the state of Wèi suffered from famine,
the Master made porridge for the hungry of the state;
is this not benevolence (Huì)?
In the past, when the state of Wèi was in trouble,
the Master used his life to protect me;
is this not constancy (Zhēn)?
The Master managed the government of Wèi,
refined its ranks and systems,
and interacted with the four neighbors;
the altars of Wèi were not disgraced;
is this not refinement (Wén)?
Therefore, let the Master be called Zhēn Huì Wénzǐ."
4.33 Shí Dài Zhòng died,
leaving no legitimate heir
but six sons by concubines.
They divined to determine who should be the successor.
They were told:
"He who bathes and wears jade ornaments will receive the omen."
Five of them all bathed and wore jade ornaments;
Shí Qí Zǐ said:
"Who, while observing the mourning of a parent,
would bathe and wear jade ornaments?"
He did not bathe or wear jade ornaments.
Shí Qí Zǐ received the omen.
The people of Wèi believed the tortoise had knowledge.
4.34 Chén Zǐchē died in Wèi;
his wife and his family steward plotted to bury someone alive with him.
The decision was settled,
and then Chén Zǐkàng arrived.
They informed him, saying:
"The Master was ill
and has no one to care for him in the underworld;
we request to bury someone with him."
Zǐkàng said:
"Burying someone with the dead
is contrary to ritual;
nevertheless,
for one who is ill and needs care,
who would be better than his wife and steward?
If it can be stopped,
then I wish to stop it;
if it cannot be stopped,
then I wish for you two to be the ones used."
Thus, it was not carried out.
4.35 Zǐlù said:
"How tragic is poverty!
In life, one has no means to provide nourishment;
in death, one has no means to observe ritual."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Eating beans and drinking water while exhausting one's joy—
that is called filial piety.
Folding the hands and feet,
and being buried without an outer coffin,
in accordance with one's wealth—
that is called ritual."
4.36 Wèi Xiàn Gōng fled into exile;
when he returned to Wèi
and reached the outskirts,
he was about to distribute cities to his followers before entering.
Liǔ Zhuāng said:
"If everyone had stayed to guard the state,
then who would have held the reins and followed you?
If everyone had followed you,
then who would have guarded the state?
For the ruler to return to his state and show favoritism,
would that not be impermissible?"
The distribution was not carried out.
4.37 In Wèi, there was a Grand Historian named Liǔ Zhuāng,
who was bedridden with illness.
The Duke said:
"If his illness becomes critical,
even if I am at a sacrifice, you must inform me."
The Duke bowed twice with his head to the ground and requested of the personator, saying:
"I have a minister named Liǔ Zhuāng;
he is not merely my minister,
but a minister of the state.
Hearing that he is dying,
I request to go to him."
He went without removing his sacrificial robes
and subsequently used them as a shroud for him.
He gave him the town of Qiúshì and the district of Pānshì,
wrote the deed and placed it in the coffin,
saying:
"For generations to come, for ten thousand descendants,
let this never be changed."
4.38 Chén Qiánxī was bedridden with illness;
he gathered his brothers
and commanded his son Zūnyǐ, saying:
"When I die,
you must make a large coffin for me
and have my two maidservants flanking me."
When Chén Qiánxī died,
his son said:
"Burying people with the dead
is contrary to ritual;
how much more so in the same coffin?"
Thus, they were not killed.
4.39 Zhòng Suì died at Chuí;
on the Rénwǔ day, the Yì sacrifice was still held;
the Wàn dancers entered, but the flutes (Yuè) were removed.
Zhòngní said:
"This is contrary to ritual;
when a high minister dies, the Yì sacrifice is not held."
4.40 The mother of Jì Kāngzǐ died.
Gōngshū Ruò was then young.
At the encoffinment,
Bān requested to use a mechanical device for the interment.
They were about to follow his suggestion
when Gōngjiān Jiǎ said:
"This cannot be!
Lǔ has its traditions:
the ducal house uses the large pillars,
and the three families use the Huán pillars.
Bān,
if you use someone's mother to test your ingenuity,
how could you not be allowed to do so?
But should you not refrain from using her to test your ingenuity?
Is it not distressing?
Alas!"
They did not follow his suggestion.
4.41 There was a battle at Láng.
Gōngshū Yúrén encountered those carrying staves entering the stronghold to rest,
and said:
"The service required of them is indeed distressing,
and the burden placed on them is indeed heavy.
If the gentlemen cannot plan for them,
and the officers cannot die for them,
this is unacceptable!
I have already spoken my mind."
Together with his young neighbor Wāng Qǐ, he went forth,
and they both died there.
The people of Lǔ wished not to perform the mourning rite for a minor (Shàng) for Wāng Qǐ,
and they asked Zhòngní about it.
Zhòngní said:
"He was able to take up the shield and spear to defend the state;
even if you wish not to treat him as a minor,
is that not also permissible?"
4.42 Zǐlù was leaving Lǔ
and said to Yán Yuān:
"What will you give me as a parting gift?"
He replied:
"I have heard this:
when leaving one's state,
one weeps at the graves and then departs;
when returning to one's state,
one does not weep
but visits the graves and then enters."
He asked Zǐlù:
"What will you advise me?"
Zǐlù said:
"I have heard this:
when passing a grave, one bows from the carriage;
when passing a shrine, one dismounts."
4.43 Gōngyǐn Shāngyáng and Chén Qìjí pursued the Wú army,
and caught up with them.
Chén Qìjí said to Gōngyǐn Shāngyáng:
"It is the King's business;
it is proper for you to take your bow in hand."
He took the bow in hand.
"Shoot them."
He shot at them,
killed one man,
and put his bow back in its case.
Again they caught up,
and Chén spoke to him again;
he killed two more men.
Each time he killed a man,
he covered his eyes.
He stopped his driver and said:
"In the court, I do not sit among the high officials;
at feasts, I do not participate;
having killed three men,
it is enough to return and report the mission accomplished."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the midst of killing,
there was still ritual propriety."
4.44 The feudal lords attacked Qín.
Cáo Huán Gōng died during the meeting.
The lords requested to place jade in the mouth of the deceased,
and they allowed the dressing of the corpse.
4.45 Xiāng Gōng went to court in Jīng;
Kāng Wáng died.
The people of Jīng said:
"You must request to dress the corpse."
The people of Lǔ said:
"This is not according to ritual."
The people of Jīng forced him.
A shaman first brushed the coffin.
The people of Jīng regretted it.
4.46 At the funeral of Téng Chéng Gōng,
Lǔ sent Zǐshū Jìngshū to offer condolences
and present the message;
Zǐfú Huìbó served as the assistant.
When they reached the suburbs,
because it was the anniversary of the death of Yìbó,
Jìngshū would not enter.
Huìbó said:
"This is state business;
one cannot, for the private matter of an uncle,
fail to carry out public affairs."
They then entered.
4.47 Āi Gōng sent someone to offer condolences to Kuì Shàng,
meeting him on the road.
Kuì Shàng stepped aside from the road,
drew the outline of a house on the ground, and received the condolences there.
Zéngzǐ said:
"Kuì Shàng did not understand ritual as well as the wife of Qǐ Liáng.
Zhuāng Gōng of Qí made a surprise attack on Jǔ at Duó,
and Qǐ Liáng died there.
His wife met his coffin on the road and wailed for him piteously.
Zhuāng Gōng sent someone to offer her condolences.
She replied:
'If my lord's servant was not free from guilt,
then his body should be exposed in the marketplace or court,
and his wife and concubines should be taken as prisoners;
if my lord's servant was free from guilt,
then there is the dilapidated hut of his ancestors.
My lord should not demean his command by offering condolences on the road.'"
4.48 At the funeral of the young son Niè,
Āi Gōng wanted to use the lowering-ropes.
He asked Yǒu Ruò.
Yǒu Ruò said:
"It may be done;
your three ministers still use them."
Yán Liǔ said:
"For the Son of Heaven, there is the dragon hearse and the outer coffin cover;
for the feudal lords, there is the hearse and the coffin cover;
—because of the elm-juice lubricant, the ropes were provided.
Those three ministers have discarded the hearse but still use the ropes,
which is a misappropriation of ritual that misses the mark.
Why should my lord imitate them?"
4.49 When the mother of Dào Gōng died,
Āi Gōng wore the zīcuī mourning dress for her.
Yǒu Ruò said:
"To wear zīcuī for a concubine,
is that ritual?"
The Duke said:
"Could I help it?
The people of Lǔ regard her as my wife."
4.50 Jì Zǐgāo was burying his wife;
they trampled on someone's grain.
Shēn Xiáng reported this to him,
saying:
"Please compensate them for it."
Zǐgāo said:
"The Mèng clan did not punish me for this,
and my friends did not abandon me for this.
Because I am the head of the town here,
if I were to buy a path for a burial,
it would be difficult for my successors to continue the practice."
4.51 For one who serves in office but does not yet have a salary,
if the ruler sends a gift, it is called a 'contribution';
when sent on a mission, he refers to his ruler as 'my little ruler';
if he has left office and the ruler dies,
he does not wear mourning for him.
4.52 At the sacrifice of repose, the personator is established,
and there are a small table and a mat.
When the final wailing is finished, the taboo on the name begins;
the service to the living is finished, and the service to the spirit has begun.
After the final wailing,
the steward takes a wooden-clapper bell to proclaim in the palace, saying:
"Discard the old taboo and observe the new one."
This is done from the door of the bedchamber to the Kù gate.
4.53 With a name of two characters, one does not avoid both at once.
The mother of the Master was named Zhēngzài.
When he said 'zài', he did not use 'zhēng';
when he said 'zhēng', he did not use 'zài'.
4.54 When there is a cause for sorrow in the army,
they wear plain white clothes and wail outside the Kù gate.
The messenger chariot does not carry bow-cases or quiver-covers.
4.55 If someone's ancestral house is burned,
there is wailing for three days.
Therefore it is said:
"When the new temple caught fire,
there was also wailing for three days."
4.56 Kǒngzǐ was passing by the side of Mount Tài.
There was a woman wailing at a grave most sorrowfully.
The Master leaned forward on the crossbar of his carriage and listened.
He sent Zǐgòng to ask her, saying:
"Your wailing
sounds as if you have suffered repeated sorrows."
She said:
"Indeed.
Formerly, my father-in-law was killed by a tiger;
my husband also died by one;
and now my son has also died by one."
The Master said:
"Why do you not leave this place?"
She said:
"There is no oppressive government here."
The Master said:
"Disciples, remember this:
oppressive government is more fierce than a tiger
indeed."
4.57 Among the people of Lǔ, there was one named Zhōu Fēng.
Āi Gōng held a ritual gift and requested to see him,
but he said "It is not possible."
The Duke said:
"Shall I then give it up?"
He sent someone to ask him,
saying:
"The Yǒuyú clan did not display trust to the people, yet the people trusted them;
the Xiàhòu clan did not display reverence to the people, yet the people revered them.
What was done to obtain this from the people?"
He replied:
"Among the ruins and graves,
one does not display sorrow to the people, yet the people are sorrowful.
Within the altars of land and grain and the ancestral temples,
one does not display reverence to the people, yet the people are reverent.
The people of Yīn made oaths, and the people began to rebel.
The people of Zhōu made covenants, and the people began to doubt.
If there are no ritual principles,
loyalty, trust, or sincerity of heart with which to preside over them,
even if you bind them firmly,
will the people not disperse?"
4.58 During mourning, one does not think about one's dwelling;
in one's grief, one does not endanger one's person.
Not thinking about the dwelling
is because there is no temple;
not endangering the person
is because one must not be without descendants.
4.59 Yánlíng Jìzǐ went to Qí.
On his return,
his eldest son died,
and was buried between Yíng and Bó.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yánlíng Jìzǐ
is one in Wú who is well-versed in ritual."
He went to observe the burial.
The pit was not so deep as to reach the groundwater.
The dressing was with the clothes of the season.
After the burial, the mound was raised;
its length and width covered the pit,
and its height was such that one could lean on it.
Once the mound was raised,
he bared his left shoulder,
and circled the mound to the right three times while wailing,
saying:
"That the bones and flesh return to the earth
is fate.
As for the soul and spirit, they can go anywhere;
they can go anywhere."
Then he proceeded on his way.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"As for Yánlíng Jìzǐ's practice of ritual,
is it not indeed in accordance with it!"
4.60 During the mourning for Zhūloú Kǎo Gōng,
the Ruler of Xú sent Róng Jū to offer condolences and present mouth-gems,
saying:
"My humble ruler has sent Róng Jū to sit and perform the mouth-gem rite (hán), presenting the jade of a marquis;
he has commissioned Róng Jū to use it for the hán."
The officer of ceremonies said:
"Among the feudal lords who have graced our humble state with their presence,
those who follow the simple rites follow the simple,
and those who follow the elaborate rites follow the elaborate;
a mixture of the simple and elaborate has never occurred."
Róng Jū replied:
"Róng Jū has heard:
in serving one's ruler, one dares not forget his ruler,
nor does one dare to neglect his ancestors.
Formerly, our late ruler Jū Wáng, when campaigning in the west, crossed the Hé River;
in all things he used these words.
Róng Jū
is a man of Lǔ
and dares not forget his ancestors."
When Zǐsī’s mother died in Wèi,
the news was sent to Zǐsī,
and Zǐsī wailed in the ancestral temple.
His disciples arrived and said:
"A mother of the Shù clan has died;
why do you wail in the temple of the Kǒng clan?"
Zǐsī said:
"I am in error,
I am in error."
He then went to wail in another room.
4.61 When the Son of Heaven dies,
after three days the Invoker (Zhù) first puts on mourning dress;
after five days the heads of departments put on mourning dress;
after seven days the men and women within the capital put on mourning dress;
after three months the whole world puts on mourning dress.
The foresters provide the wood for the hundred sacrifices;
those trees fit for the inner and outer coffins are cut down.
For those who do not arrive,
their sacrifices are abolished
and the person is executed.
4.62 There was a great famine in Qí.
Qián Áo prepared food by the roadside
to wait for those who were starving and feed them.
A starving man, covering his face with his sleeve and dragging his shoes,
came stumbling along.
Qián Áo, holding food in his left hand
and a drink in his right,
said:
"Hey! Come and eat."
The starving man raised his eyes and looked at him,
saying:
"It is precisely because I would not eat 'Hey, come' food
that I have come to this state."
Qián Áo followed him and apologized;
but in the end, he would not eat and died.
Zéngzǐ heard of this
and said:
"Was it not unnecessary?
At the 'Hey,' he might have left,
but at the apology, he might have eaten."
4.63 In the time of Zhūloú Dìng Gōng,
there was someone who murdered his father.
The officers reported it.
The Duke, startled and losing his seat, said:
"This is my fault."
He said:
"I once learned how to judge such a case:
if a minister murders his ruler,
all who hold office should kill him without pardon;
if a son murders his father,
all who are in the palace should kill him without pardon.
Kill the man,
destroy his house,
flood the palace site and turn it into a pond.
The ruler should wait more than a month before raising his cup again."
4.64 When Zhào Wénzǐ of Jìn completed his house,
the Great Officers of Jìn held a celebration.
Zhāng Lǎo said:
"How beautiful and high!
How beautiful and bright!
Here you will sing;
here you will wail;
here you will gather the clans of the state."
Wénzǐ said:
"If I, Wǔ, am able to sing here,
to wail here,
and to gather the clans of the state here,
it will be to preserve my head and neck to follow my late predecessors to Jiǔjīng."
He faced north, bowed twice, and touched his head to the ground.
The superior man called this a good song of praise and a good prayer.
4.65 Zhòngní’s pet dog died.
He sent Zǐgòng to bury it,
saying:
"I have heard
that a worn-out curtain is not thrown away,
as it is used to bury a horse;
a worn-out canopy is not thrown away,
as it is used to bury a dog.
I, Qiū, am poor
and have no canopy;
when you cover it with earth,
also give it a mat
so its head does not sink into the dirt."
When a carriage horse died,
it was buried with a curtain.
4.66 When the mother of Jìsūn died,
Āi Gōng offered condolences.
Zéngzǐ and Zǐgòng also went to offer condolences.
The gatekeeper, because the ruler was there,
would not let them in.
Zéngzǐ and Zǐgòng entered the stable and adjusted their appearance.
Zǐgòng entered first;
the gatekeeper said:
"I have already announced you earlier."
Zéngzǐ entered later,
and the gatekeeper made way for him.
When they crossed the inner eaves,
the ministers and Great Officers all vacated their seats,
and the Duke descended one step and bowed to them.
A superior man commented:
"If the way of perfect decorum is followed,
its influence travels far."
4.67 When an armored soldier of the Yáng Gate died,
Zǐhǎn, the Minister of Works, entered and wailed for him with great sorrow.
A spy from Jìn in Sòng
returned and reported to the Lord of Jìn:
"An armored soldier of the Yáng Gate died,
and Zǐhǎn wailed for him with great sorrow,
and the people were pleased;
perhaps they cannot be attacked."
Kǒngzǐ heard this and said:
"How well they spy on a state!
The Shī says:
'Whenever people have a funeral,
crawl on hands and knees to help them.'
Even if it were not just Jìn,
who in the world could withstand them?"
4.68 During the mourning for Lǔ Zhuāng Gōng,
after the burial,
the mourning headband was not worn when entering the Treasury Gate.
After the officers and Great Officers finished the wailing of the final sacrifice,
hemp was no longer worn when entering.
4.69 There was an old friend of Kǒngzǐ named Yuán Ràng.
When his mother died,
the Master helped him polish the outer coffin.
Yuán Ràng climbed onto the wood and said:
"It has been a long time since I expressed myself in music."
He sang:
"Striped like the head of a leopard,
soft as the hand of a girl."
The Master passed by as if he had not heard him.
His followers said:
"Should you not break off with him?"
The Master said:
"I, Qiū, have heard
that those close should not lose their bond of kinship,
and old friends should not lose their bond of friendship."
4.70 Zhào Wénzǐ and Shūyù were looking over the Jiǔyuán.
Wénzǐ said:
"If the dead could rise again,
with whom should I go?"
Shūyù said:
"Would it be Yáng Chǔfù?"
Wénzǐ said:
"His conduct was upright in the state of Jìn,
but he could not preserve his own life;
his wisdom is not worthy of praise."
"Would it be Jiù Fàn?"
Wénzǐ said:
"He saw profit and did not consider his ruler;
his benevolence is not worthy of praise.
I would go with Suí Wǔzǐ;
he profited his ruler without forgetting himself,
and planned for himself without neglecting his friends."
The people of Jìn said Wénzǐ was a judge of character.
Wénzǐ's inward character was so retiring as if his clothes were too heavy for him,
and his speech was so hesitant as if the words could not come out of his mouth.
Of the scholars he recommended to the state of Jìn for the management of granaries and treasuries,
there were more than seventy families;
during his life, he did not share in their profits,
and at his death, he did not entrust his son to them.
4.71 Shūzhòng Pí taught Zǐliǔ.
When Shūzhòng Pí died,
his wife, a woman of Lǔ,
wore the frayed mourning dress (cuī) and the knotted headband (miùzhì).
Shūzhòng Yǎn reported this,
requesting the fine hemp mourning dress (suìcuī) and the round headband (huánzhì),
saying:
"Formerly, when I mourned for my aunts and sisters, I also did this,
and no one forbade me."
He retired
and made his wife wear the fine hemp mourning dress and the round headband.
4.72 There was a man of Chéng whose elder brother died, but he did not wear the mourning dress for him.
Hearing that Zǐgāo was going to be the Governor of Chéng,
he then wore the mourning dress.
The people of Chéng said:
"The silkworm produces silk, but the crab has its shell;
the bee has its cap, but the cicada has its tassels;
the brother died, but it was for Zǐgāo that he wore the mourning dress."
4.73 When the mother of Lèzhèng Zǐchūn died,
he did not eat for five days.
He said:
"I regret this.
If for my own mother I cannot express my true feelings,
where else should I apply my true feelings?"
4.74 In a year of drought,
Mù Gōng summoned Xiànzǐ and questioned him about it,
saying:
"Heaven has not rained for a long time.
I wish to expose a cripple to the sun; how would that be?"
Xiànzǐ said:
"Heaven has not rained for a long time,
yet to expose a person's infirmity to the sun
is cruel.
Would that not be unacceptable?"
"In that case, I wish to expose a shamaness to the sun; how would that be?"
Xiànzǐ said:
"If Heaven does not rain,
yet you expect it from a foolish woman
and seek it through her,
is that not quite far-fetched?"
"What if I move the market?"
Xiànzǐ said:
"When the Son of Heaven dies,
the market is held in the lanes for seven days.
When a feudal lord dies,
the market is held in the lanes for three days.
To move the market for this cause
would surely be acceptable."
4.75 Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the joint burials of the people of Wèi,
they keep the coffins apart;
in the joint burials of the people of Lǔ,
they join them together.
How excellent that is!"
5.1 The system of ranks and emoluments established by the kings:
Gōng, Hóu, Bó, Zǐ, and Nán
—five grades in all.
Among the feudal lords: Shàng Dàfū Qīng,
Xià Dàfū,
Shàng Shì, Zhōng Shì, and Xià Shì
—five grades in all.
The territory of the Son of Heaven is one thousand lǐ square.
A Gōng or Hóu's territory is one hundred lǐ square;
a Bó's territory is seventy lǐ square;
a Zǐ or Nán's territory is fifty lǐ square.
Those whose territory cannot reach fifty lǐ
do not have direct access to the Son of Heaven;
they are attached to the feudal lords
and are called Fùyōng.
The lands of the Sāngōng of the Son of Heaven are equivalent to those of a Gōng or Hóu.
The Qīng of the Son of Heaven are equivalent to a Bó.
The Dàfū of the Son of Heaven are equivalent to a Zǐ or Nán.
The Yuánshì of the Son of Heaven are equivalent to a Fùyōng.
5.2 The regulation:
A farm consists of one hundred mǔ.
Regarding the division of the hundred mǔ:
A top-grade farmer supports nine people;
the next supports eight;
the next supports seven;
the next supports six;
and a low-grade farmer supports five.
For commoners in government service,
their emoluments are graded according to this scale.
A Xià Shì of a feudal lord is equivalent to a top-grade farmer.
His salary is sufficient to replace his labor in plowing.
A Zhōng Shì receives twice the salary of a Xià Shì.
A Shàng Shì receives twice the salary of a Zhōng Shì.
A Xià Dàfū receives twice the salary of a Shàng Shì.
A Qīng
receives the salary of four Dàfū.
A Ruler
receives the salary of ten Qīng.
In a secondary state, a Qīng
receives the salary of three Dàfū.
A Ruler
receives the salary of ten Qīng.
In a small state, a Qīng
receives twice the salary of a Dàfū.
A Ruler receives the salary of ten Qīng.
5.3 A Shàng Qīng of a secondary state
holds a rank equivalent to the Zhōng Qīng of a great state.
A Zhōng Qīng is equivalent to its Xià Qīng.
A Xià Qīng is equivalent to its Shàng Dàfū.
A Shàng Qīng of a small state
holds a rank equivalent to the Xià Qīng of a great state.
A Zhōng Qīng is equivalent to its Shàng Dàfū.
A Xià Qīng is equivalent to its Xià Dàfū.
For those states that have Zhōng Shì and Xià Shì,
their numbers each constitute one-third of the grade above them.
5.4 Within the Four Seas, there are nine provinces (Jiǔ Zhōu).
Each province is one thousand lǐ square.
In each province,
thirty states of one hundred lǐ are established,
sixty states of seventy lǐ,
and one hundred and twenty states of fifty lǐ,
totaling two hundred and ten states.
Famous mountains and great marshes are not granted as fiefs;
the remainder are used for Fùyōng and intervening lands.
For the eight provinces,
each province has two hundred and ten states.
5.5 Within the capital district (Xiànnèi) of the Son of Heaven,
there are nine states of one hundred lǐ,
twenty-one states of seventy lǐ,
sixty-three states of fifty lǐ,
totaling ninety-three states.
Famous mountains and great marshes are not distributed;
the remainder are used to provide emoluments for the Shì
and as intervening lands.
5.6 In all the nine provinces,
there are one thousand seven hundred and seventy-three states.
The Yuánshì of the Son of Heaven
and the Fùyōng of the feudal lords are not included in this number.
5.7 The area within one hundred lǐ of the Son of Heaven is for the support of officials.
The area within one thousand lǐ is for his use.
5.8 Beyond the one thousand lǐ,
Regional Chiefs (Fāngbó) are established.
Five states constitute a group (Shǔ),
and a group has a head (Zhǎng).
Ten states constitute a union (Lián),
and a union has a leader (Shuài).
Thirty states constitute a division (Zú),
and a division has a director (Zhèng).
Two hundred and ten states constitute a province (Zhōu),
and a province has a Chief (Bó).
For the eight provinces, there are eight Bó,
fifty-six Zhèng,
one hundred and sixty-eight Shuài,
and three hundred and thirty-six Zhǎng.
The eight Bó each lead their subordinates
to be under the two Elder Statesmen (Lǎo) of the Son of Heaven.
They divide the world into left and right,
and are called the Two Chiefs (Èr Bó).
5.9 The area within one thousand lǐ is called the Diàn district.
Beyond the one thousand lǐ,
it is called Cǎi,
and then Liú.
5.10 The Son of Heaven has:
three Gōng,
nine Qīng,
twenty-seven Dàfū,
and eighty-one Yuánshì.
5.11 A great state has:
three Qīng;
all are appointed by the Son of Heaven;
five Xià Dàfū,
and twenty-seven Shàng Shì.
5.12 A secondary state has:
three Qīng;
two Qīng are appointed by the Son of Heaven,
and one Qīng is appointed by its own ruler;
five Xià Dàfū,
and twenty-seven Shàng Shì.
5.13 A small state has:
two Qīng;
both are appointed by its own ruler;
five Xià Dàfū,
and twenty-seven Shàng Shì.
5.14 The Son of Heaven sends his Dàfū to serve as the Three Inspectors (Sānjiàn),
to oversee the states of the Regional Chiefs,
with three persons for each state.
The feudal lords within the capital district (Xiànnèi) of the Son of Heaven
receive salaries;
5.15 the external feudal lords
inherit their positions.
5.16 The regulation:
the Sāngōng
are of the first degree of rank with robes of embroidered patterns;
if there is an addition,
it is a special grant.
It does not exceed nine degrees of rank.
The ruler of a secondary state
does not exceed seven degrees;
the ruler of a small state
does not exceed five degrees.
A Qīng of a great state
does not exceed three degrees;
a lower Qīng has two degrees;
a Qīng of a small state
and a Xià Dàfū have one degree.
5.18 In all cases of employing the people's talents,
they must first be evaluated.
After evaluation and differentiation, they are employed;
after they undertake duties, they are given ranks;
after their positions are fixed, they are given salaries.
When conferring rank upon someone in court,
it is done together with the Shì.
When punishing someone in the market,
it is done together with the masses to reject him.
Therefore, the house of a Gōng does not keep a punished man,
a Dàfū does not maintain one,
and if a Shì encounters one on the road, he does not speak with him.
They are banished to the four quarters,
to go wherever they please.
They are not reached by the administration,
and there is no desire for them to live.
5.20 In the relations of the *Zhūhóu* to the *Tiānzǐ*,
every year there is a small mission,
every three years a large mission,
and every five years an audience.
5.21 The *Tiānzǐ* makes a tour of inspection once every five years.
5.22 In the second month of the year,
he goes on an eastern tour of inspection, reaching *Dàizōng*,
where he performs the *chái* sacrifice and gazes from afar to sacrifice to the mountains and rivers;
he gives audience to the *Zhūhóu*;
he inquires after those a hundred years old and visits them in person.
He commands the *Dàshī* to present the poems
to observe the customs of the people;
he commands the market officials to submit prices
to observe what the people like and dislike,
and whether their intentions are excessive or their preferences perverse.
He commands the *Diǎnlǐ* to examine the seasons and months,
to fix the days,
and to standardize the pitch-pipes;
the systems of ritual and music and the forms of clothing are rectified.
For the spirits of mountains and rivers,
if any sacrifice is not performed,
it is considered irreverence;
for those who are irreverent,
the ruler reduces their territory.
Regarding ancestral temples,
if any are not in order,
it is considered a lack of filial piety;
for those who are unfilial,
the ruler demotes their rank.
Those who change the rituals and alter the music
are considered disobedient;
for those who are disobedient,
the ruler banishes them.
Those who change the systems and clothing
are considered rebels;
those who rebel are punished by the ruler.
Those who have merit and virtue towards the people
have their land increased and their honors advanced.
In the fifth month,
he goes on a southern tour of inspection, reaching *Nányuè*,
following the ritual of the eastern inspection.
In the eighth month,
he goes on a western tour of inspection, reaching *Xīyuè*,
following the ritual of the southern inspection.
In the eleventh month,
he goes on a northern tour of inspection, reaching *Běiyuè*,
following the ritual of the western inspection.
Upon returning,
he reports at the temples of his ancestors and father, *Nǐ*,
using a single victim.
5.23 When the *Tiānzǐ* is about to set out,
he performs the *lèi* sacrifice to *Shàngdì*,
the *yí* sacrifice to the *Shè*,
and visits the temple of his father, *Nǐ*;
when the *Zhūhóu* are about to set out,
they perform the *yí* sacrifice to the *Shè*
and visit the temple of their fathers, *Nǐ*.
5.24 When the *Tiānzǐ* meets with the *Zhūhóu* without a specific matter, it is called a *cháo* audience;
they examine rituals, rectify punishments, and unify virtues
to honor the *Tiānzǐ*.
When the *Tiānzǐ* bestows music upon the *Zhūhóu*,
he uses the *zhù* to present it;
when bestowing music upon the *Bó*, *Zǐ*, and *Nán*,
he uses the *táo* to present it.
5.25 As for the *Zhūhóu*,
only after being granted bows and arrows
may they go on military expeditions;
only after being granted axes and battle-axes
may they carry out executions;
only after being granted the *guī* ladle
may they brew sacrificial *chàng* wine.
If they have not been granted the *guī* ladle,
they obtain the *chàng* wine from the *Tiānzǐ*.
5.26 Only after the *Tiānzǐ* issues the command for instruction
are schools established.
The *Xiǎoxué* is located to the left of the south of the ruler’s palace;
the *Dàxué* is in the suburbs.
For the *Tiānzǐ* it is called *Bìyōng*;
for the *Zhūhóu* it is called *Pàngōng*.
5.27 When the *Tiānzǐ* is about to set out on a military expedition,
he performs the *lèi* sacrifice to *Shàngdì*,
the *yí* sacrifice to the *Shè*,
and visits the temple of his father, *Nǐ*;
he performs the *mà* sacrifice at the place to be attacked.
He receives his mandate at the ancestral temple
and receives the strategy at the academy.
He sets out on the expedition,
captures the guilty,
and upon his return,
offers the *shìdiàn* sacrifice at the academy,
reporting with the interrogation of prisoners and the left ears of the slain.
5.28 When the *Tiānzǐ* and the *Zhūhóu*
have no specific business,
they hold three hunts a year.
The first is for dried meat offerings,
the second is for guests,
and the third is to fill the ruler’s kitchen.
To have no business and not hunt
is called irreverence;
to hunt without following rituals
is called wasting Heaven’s resources.
The *Tiānzǐ* does not surround the prey completely;
the *Zhūhóu* do not wipe out an entire herd.
When the *Tiānzǐ* kills a beast, the *dàsuí* banner is lowered;
when a *Zhūhóu* kills one, the *xiǎosuí* banner is lowered;
when a *Dàfū* kills one, the *zuǒchē* assistant carriage is stopped.
Once the *zuǒchē* stops,
then the common people may hunt.
When the otters offer up fish,
then the foresters enter the marshes and weirs.
When the wolves offer up beasts,
then the hunting begins.
When the pigeons are transformed into hawks,
then the nets and snares are set.
When the grass and trees wither and fall,
then people enter the mountain forests.
Before insects have gone into hibernation,
fire is not used for hunting.
They do not take fawns,
they do not take eggs,
they do not kill the pregnant,
they do not kill immature things,
and they do not overturn nests.
5.29 The *Zhǒngzǎi* regulates the national expenditure;
it must be at the end of the year,
after the five grains have all been gathered,
that the national expenditure is regulated.
The use of land, whether large or small,
depends on the abundance or scarcity of the harvest.
Using an average of thirty years to regulate the national expenditure,
he measures income to determine expenses,
with one-tenth used for sacrifices.
During mourning,
there are no sacrifices for three years,
except for the sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, and the *Shè* and *Jì*,
for which they step over the coffin ropes to perform the rituals.
For mourning, one-tenth of three years' income is used.
For mourning and sacrifices,
if resources are insufficient, it is called distress;
if there is a surplus, it is called waste.
In sacrifices,
in a bountiful year they are not extravagant,
and in a bad year they are not stingy.
A state without nine years of stored reserves
is called insufficient;
without six years of reserves
is called an emergency;
without three years of reserves,
it is said that the state is no longer a state.
From three years of farming,
there must be one year’s worth of food;
from nine years of farming,
there must be three years’ worth of food.
Taking an average of thirty years,
though there be droughts or floods,
the people will not have the color of hunger,
and only then may the *Tiānzǐ* eat his meals
with daily musical accompaniment.
For the *Tiānzǐ*, the enshrinement takes seven days
and the burial takes seven months.
For the *Zhūhóu*, the enshrinement takes five days
and the burial takes five months.
For *Dàfū*,
*shì*,
and commoners,
the enshrinement takes three days
and the burial takes three months.
The three-year mourning period
applies from the *Tiānzǐ* down;
the commoners use the *xuànfēng* method for burial.
A burial is not stopped for rain;
there is no mound raised and no trees planted;
in mourning, one does not attend to other matters;
this applies from the *Tiānzǐ* down to the commoners.
Mourning follows the rank of the deceased,
while sacrifices follow the rank of the living.
Younger sons do not perform the primary sacrifices.
5.30 The *Tiānzǐ* has seven ancestral temples:
three for the *zhāo* ancestors and three for the *mù* ancestors,
which with the temple of the *Dàzǔ* make seven.
The *Zhūhóu* have five temples:
two for the *zhāo* ancestors and two for the *mù* ancestors,
which with the temple of the *Dàzǔ* make five.
The *Dàfū* have three temples:
one for the *zhāo* ancestor and one for the *mù* ancestor,
which with the temple of the *Dàzǔ* make three.
A *shì* has one temple;
commoners sacrifice in their inner chambers.
5.31 The ancestral temple sacrifices of the *Tiānzǐ* and the *Zhūhóu* are:
the spring sacrifice called *Yuè*,
the summer sacrifice called *Dì*,
the autumn sacrifice called *Cháng*,
and the winter sacrifice called *Zhēng*.
The Tiānzǐ sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
the Zhūhóu sacrifice to the Shèjì,
and the Dàfū sacrifice to the Wǔsì.
The Tiānzǐ sacrifices to the famous mountains and great rivers of the world:
the Wǔyuè are ranked with the Sāngōng,
and the Sìdú are ranked with the Zhūhóu.
The Zhūhóu sacrifice to those famous mountains and great rivers that are within their own territories.
5.32 The Tiānzǐ and Zhūhóu sacrifice to those spirits within their lands whose states have perished and who have no successors.
5.33 For the Tiānzǐ, the Yuè sacrifice is performed separately;
the Dì,
the Cháng,
and the Zhēng sacrifices are performed collectively.
For the Zhūhóu, if they perform the Yuè, they do not perform the Dì;
if they perform the Dì, they do not perform the Cháng;
if they perform the Cháng, they do not perform the Zhēng;
if they perform the Zhēng, they do not perform the Yuè.
For the Zhūhóu, the Yuè
is performed separately;
for the Dì,
some are performed separately and some collectively;
for the Cháng,
it is collective;
for the Zhēng,
it is collective.
5.34 For the Tiānzǐ, the sacrifices to the Shèjì both use the Dàláo;
for the Zhūhóu, the sacrifices to the Shèjì both use the Shǎoláo.
For the ancestral temple sacrifices of the Dàfū and Shì:
if they have land, they perform the sacrifice;
if they have no land, they only make seasonal offerings.
The Shùrén in spring offer chives,
in summer offer wheat,
in autumn offer millet,
and in winter offer rice.
The chives are accompanied by eggs,
the wheat by fish,
the millet by a sucking pig,
and the rice by a wild goose.
The ox used for the sacrifice to Heaven and Earth
has horns like silkworm cocoons or chestnuts;
the ox for the ancestral temple
has horns that can be grasped by the hand;
the ox for guests
has horns a foot long.
A Zhūhóu does not kill an ox without cause,
a Dàfū does not kill a sheep without cause,
a Shì does not kill a dog or a pig without cause,
and a Shùrén does not eat delicacies without cause.
5.35 Ordinary side dishes do not exceed the grade of the sacrificial animal;
everyday robes do not exceed the grade of sacrificial robes;
living quarters do not exceed the grade of the ancestral temple.
5.36 In ancient times:
for public fields,
labor was contributed but no tax was levied.
In markets,
ground-rent was charged for stalls but no tax was levied on goods.
At customs barriers,
there was inspection but no taxation.
Forests, foothills, rivers, and marshes
were entered at proper times and were not prohibited.
For the guī fields, there was no taxation.
5.37 When employing the labor of the people,
it did not exceed three days in a year.
5.38 Fields and residential lands were not sold,
and burial grounds were not requested for other use.
5.39 The Sīkōng holds the measures
to measure the land,
to settle the people among mountains, rivers, marshes, and wetlands,
according to the four seasons.
He estimates the distance of the land
and undertakes works according to the people's strength.
In all cases of employing the people:
he assigns the tasks of the elderly to the old
and provides them with the food of the robust.
5.40 In all matters of settling the people and utilizing materials,
it must be based on Heaven and Earth,
and the cold, heat, dryness, and moisture;
wide valleys and great rivers require different systems.
The people living among them have different customs:
their temperaments, whether hard or soft, heavy or light, slow or fast, have different balances,
their blending of the five flavors differs,
their tools and implements have different designs,
and their clothing has different suitabilities.
Cultivate their teachings
without changing their customs;
standardize their governance
without changing what is suitable for them.
The Zhōngguó, Róng, and Yí—
the peoples of the five regions—
all have their own natures,
which cannot be shifted.
In the East they are called Yí;
they wear their hair loose and tattoo their bodies,
and some do not eat cooked food.
In the South they are called Mán;
they tattoo their foreheads and cross their feet,
and some do not eat cooked food.
In the West they are called Róng;
they wear their hair loose and dress in skins,
and some do not eat grain.
In the North they are called Dí;
they wear feathers and fur and live in caves,
and some do not eat grain.
The Zhōngguó,
Yí, Mán, Róng, and Dí
all have their comfortable dwellings,
harmonious flavors,
suitable clothing,
convenient implements,
and prepared tools.
The peoples of the five regions
have mutually unintelligible languages
and different desires.
To convey their intentions
and communicate their desires:
in the East the interpreters are called Jì,
in the South they are called Xiàng,
in the West they are called Dídī,
and in the North they are called Yì.
5.41 In all cases of settling the people,
measure the land to establish settlements,
and determine the area to settle the people.
The land, the settlement, and the people's dwellings
must be in proportion with one another.
There should be no uncultivated land
and no idle people.
Use food with economy and perform labor in proper season;
the people will then all feel secure in their dwellings,
enjoy their work and encourage achievement,
and honor the ruler and be affectionate toward their superiors;
only then are schools established.
5.42 The Sītú cultivates the Liùlǐ to regulate the nature of the people,
clarifies the Qījiào to stimulate the virtue of the people,
standardizes the Bāzhèng to prevent excess,
unifies morality to harmonize customs,
nourishes the aged to promote filial piety,
cares for the orphaned and solitary to reach those in need,
promotes the worthy to honor virtue,
and dismisses the unworthy to diminish evil.
He orders the Xiāng
to select those who do not follow the teachings and report them.
The elders all assemble at the Xiáng;
on the first day,
they practice archery and prize achievement,
and they practice the district rites and prize seniority.
The Dà Sītú leads the eminent scholars of the state
to participate in the service there.
If they do not change,
he orders the Right Xiāng of the capital
to select those who do not follow the teachings and move them to the Left;
he orders the Left Xiāng of the capital
to select those who do not follow the teachings and move them to the Right,
following the same procedure as the first rite.
If they do not change,
they are moved to the outskirts,
following the same procedure as the first rite.
If they do not change,
they are moved to the distant countryside,
following the same procedure as the first rite.
If they do not change,
they are banished to remote regions
and for the rest of their lives are not ranked among the people.
He orders the Xiāng
to evaluate the Xiùshì
and promote them to the Sītú;
they are called Xuǎnshì.
The Sītú evaluates the most refined of the Xuǎnshì and promotes them to the Great School;
they are called Jùnshì.
Those promoted to the Sītú
are not subject to service in their districts;
those promoted to the Great School
are not subject to service under the Sītú;
they are called Zàoshì.
The Yuèzhèng honors the four arts
and establishes the four teachings,
following the Shī, Shū, Lǐ, and Yuè of the former kings to form Zàoshì.
In spring and autumn, they are taught the Lǐ and Yuè;
in winter and summer, they are taught the Shī and Shū.
The Wángdàzǐ, the other princes,
the eldest sons of the various feudal lords,
the legitimate sons of the Gōngqīng, Dàfū, and Yuánshì,
and the eminent ones selected from the state
all gather there.
In all cases, entry into the school is based on seniority.
When they are about to graduate,
the Xiǎoxū, Dàxū,
and Xiǎo Yuèzhèng
select those who do not follow the teachings
to report them to the Dà Yuèzhèng.
The Dà Yuèzhèng reports them to the King.
The King orders the Sāngōng,
the Nine Ministers, Dàfū, and Yuánshì to all enter the school.
If they do not change,
the King personally inspects the school.
If they still do not change,
the King for three days does not have meat served
and banishes them to remote regions.
In the West, the place is called Jí;
in the East, it is called Jì;
and for the rest of their lives, they are not ranked among the people.
The Dà Yuè Zhèng evaluated the most outstanding among the selected students
to report them to the Wáng,
and promoted them to the Sīmǎ,
calling them Jìnshì.
The Sīmǎ distinguished and evaluated their talents for office;
he evaluated the worthiest among the Jìnshì
to report them to the Wáng
and determine their assessment.
Only after the assessment was fixed were they given office;
only after they were appointed to office were they given rank;
only after their position was fixed were they given a salary.
If a Dàfū neglected his duties,
he would never hold office for the rest of his life,
and upon death, he was buried with the rites of a Shì.
If there was a mobilization,
then the Dà Sītú was commanded to instruct the Shì in the use of chariots and armor.
In all cases of practicing skills and evaluating strength,
they went to the four quarters,
baring their arms and legs,
and competing in archery and charioteering.
All those who serve superiors through their skills are:
Zhù, Shǐ, archers, charioteers, physicians, diviners, and the various craftsmen.
All those who serve superiors through their skills
do not undertake a second task,
do not change their office,
