and when leaving their home districts, they do not rank alongside the Shì.
Those who serve in a private household,
when leaving their home districts, do not rank alongside the Shì.
5.43 The Sīkòu rectified the punishments
and clarified the laws to hear litigations and lawsuits.
He must conduct the "three inquiries."
If there was an intent but no written evidence, the case was not heard.
When applying a punishment, follow the lighter option;
when granting a pardon, follow the heavier option.
5.44 In all cases of establishing the five punishments,
they must conform to the principles of Heaven;
the severity of the penalty must correspond to the offense.
In all cases of hearing lawsuits involving the five punishments,
one must trace the intimacy between father and son
and establish the righteousness between ruler and minister to weigh the matter.
One must carefully consider the order of severity
and cautiously measure the degree of gravity to distinguish them.
One must apply all of one’s intelligence
and exert one’s loyalty and compassion to exhaustively examine it.
For doubtful cases,
they were shared broadly with the people;
if the people also doubted,
the person was pardoned.
One must examine comparisons of small and great cases to finalize the matter.
Once the verdict was finalized,
the Shǐ reported the completion of the case to the Zhèng,
and the Zhèng heard it.
The Zhèng reported the completion of the case to the Dà Sīkòu,
and the Dà Sīkòu heard it beneath the jujube trees.
The Dà Sīkòu reported the completion of the case to the Wáng,
and the Wáng commanded the Sāngōng to participate in hearing it.
The Sāngōng reported the completion of the case to the Wáng,
and the Wáng thrice sought grounds for mercy,
before finally determining the punishment.
In all cases of applying punishments and penalties,
even the light ones are not pardoned.
Punishment (Xíng) means form (Xíng);
form means completion;
once completed, it cannot be changed;
therefore, the Jūnzǐ devotes his full mind to it.
Those who split words to break the laws,
who confuse names to change systems,
and who follow heterodox ways to throw the government into disorder,
shall be put to death.
Those who create licentious music, strange clothing, extraordinary skills,
and extraordinary implements to cast doubt among the people,
shall be put to death.
Those whose conduct is false yet persistent,
whose speech is false yet eloquent,
whose learning is erroneous yet extensive,
and who follow what is wrong yet make it appear glossy to cast doubt among the people,
shall be put to death.
Those who make false claims about ghosts and spirits,
auspicious days, and divination to cast doubt among the people,
shall be put to death.
Regarding these four types of execution,
no hearings are allowed.
In all cases of maintaining prohibitions to unify the people,
errors are not pardoned.
Ceremonial jade tablets and gold-ornamented libation cups
are not to be sold in the market.
Official robes and official carriages
are not to be sold in the market.
Vessels of the ancestral temple
are not to be sold in the market.
Sacrificial animals are not to be sold in the market.
Weapons of war are not to be sold in the market.
Utensils that do not meet the standard measurements
are not to be sold in the market.
War chariots that do not meet the standard measurements
are not to be sold in the market.
Cloth and silk whose fineness or coarseness does not match the standard count,
and whose width and length do not match the standard measurements,
are not to be sold in the market.
Improper colors that confuse the proper colors
are not to be sold in the market.
Elaborate embroideries, pearls, and jade ornaments
are not to be sold in the market.
Ceremonial clothing and prepared food
are not to be sold in the market.
Five grains out of season
and fruits that are not yet ripe
are not to be sold in the market.
Timber not yet ready for felling
is not to be sold in the market;
birds, beasts, fish, and turtles not yet ready for being killed
are not to be sold in the market.
At the barrier gates, prohibitions are maintained for inspection;
strange clothing is prohibited,
and strange speech is noted.
5.45 The Dàshǐ is in charge of the rites;
he holds the bamboo records
and observes the posthumous names and prohibitions.
5.46 The Tiānzǐ fasts and purifies himself to receive admonitions.
When the Sīhuì brings the year-end reports
to verify them with the Tiānzǐ,
the Zhǒngzǎi fasts and purifies himself to receive the verification.
The Dà Yuè Zhèng,
the Dà Sīkòu,
and the Overseers of the Market,
these three officials, with their year-end reports,
follow in the verification with the Tiānzǐ.
The Dà Sītú,
the Dà Sīmǎ,
and the Dà Sīkōng fast and purify themselves to receive the verifications,
while the various officials each take their year-end reports
to be verified by these three high officials.
The Dà Sītú,
the Dà Sīmǎ,
and the Dà Sīkōng take the year-end reports of the various officials
to be verified with the Tiānzǐ,
and the various officials fast and purify themselves to receive the verification.
Afterwards,
they give rest to the aged and encourage the farmers,
completing the year's affairs
and determining the state expenditures.
5.47 In all cases of nourishing the aged:
the Yǒuyú family used the Rite of Banqueting;
the Xiàhòu family used the Rite of Entertainment;
the Yīn people used the Rite of Feeding;
and the Zhōu people refined and used all of them together.
Those of fifty were nourished in their townships;
those of sixty were nourished in the capital;
those of seventy were nourished in the college;
this extended to the Zhūhóu.
5.48 At eighty, they bowed to the ruler's command
by sitting and bowing their heads to the ground twice;
the Gǔ also did the same.
At ninety, they sent someone else to receive the command.
At fifty, they were given different grains;
at sixty, they had meat daily;
at seventy, they had two additional savory dishes;
at eighty, they were constantly provided with delicacies;
at ninety,
their food and drink did not leave their chambers,
and their meals and drinks could follow them wherever they wandered.
At sixty, their funeral requirements were prepared annually;
at seventy, they were prepared seasonally;
at eighty, they were prepared monthly;
at ninety, they were attended to daily;
only the inner and outer shrouds, the coverlet, and the head-covering
were prepared after death.
At fifty, decline begins;
at sixty, without meat they are not full;
at seventy, without silk they are not warm;
at eighty, without another person they are not warm;
at ninety,
they are not warm even with another person.
At fifty, they used a staff at home;
at sixty, they used a staff in their township;
at seventy, they used a staff in the capital;
at eighty, they used a staff in the court;
for those of ninety,
if the Tiānzǐ wished to ask them anything,
he would go to their chambers
and bring delicacies with him.
At seventy, they did not have to wait for the end of the court audience;
at eighty, there was a monthly inquiry after their welfare;
at ninety, there were daily rations provided.
At fifty, they were not subject to labor service;
at sixty, they did not serve in military duties;
at seventy, they did not participate in the business of receiving guests;
at eighty, they were exempt from the duties of fasting and mourning.
At fifty, one received rank;
at sixty, one no longer attended the college in person;
at seventy, one retired from government service.
For mourning, they only wore the Cuī má garments.
5.49 The Yǒuyú-shì nourished the national elders at the Shàngxiáng,
and nourished the common elders at the Xiàxiáng.
The Xiàhòu-shì nourished the national elders at the Dōngxù,
and nourished the common elders at the Xīxù.
The Yīn people nourished the national elders at the Yòuxué,
and nourished the common elders at the Zuǒxué.
The Zhōu people nourished the national elders at the Dōngjiāo,
and nourished the common elders at the Yúxiáng:
The Yúxiáng was located in the western suburbs of the capital.
The Yǒuyú-shì wore the Huáng cap when sacrificing,
and the Shēnyī robe when nourishing the aged.
The Xiàhòu-shì wore the Shōu cap when sacrificing,
and the Yànyī robe when nourishing the aged.
The Yīn people wore the Xǔ cap when sacrificing,
and the Gǎoyī robe when nourishing the aged.
The Zhōu people wore the Miǎn cap when sacrificing,
and the Xuányī robe when nourishing the aged.
For all Three Kings, the nourishing of the aged always involved a verification of their years.
For those of eighty years, one son was exempt from government service;
for those of ninety years, the entire household was exempt from government service.
For those with chronic disabilities who could not be cared for without another person,
one person was exempt from government service.
During mourning for parents,
one was exempt from government service for three years.
During mourning of Qīcuī or Dàgōng,
one was exempt from government service for three months.
When about to move to the territory of another feudal lord,
one was exempt from government service for three months.
When moving one's household from the territory of another feudal lord,
one was exempt from government service for a full year.
5.50 One who is young and fatherless is called Gū.
One who is old and childless is called Dú.
An old man without a wife is called Jīn.
An old woman without a husband is called Guǎ.
These four
are the destitute people of Heaven who have no one to whom they can tell their grievances;
all receive regular rations of food.
5.51 The mute, the deaf, the lame,
those with contracted limbs, those with missing limbs, dwarfs, and the various artisans,
were each fed according to their service.
5.52 On the roads:
men keep to the right,
women keep to the left,
and carriages follow the center.
When walking with someone of one's father's age, one follows behind;
with someone of one's elder brother's age, one walks slightly behind in a wing formation;
friends do not get ahead of each other.
Light burdens are carried by both together;
heavy burdens are divided;
those with graying hair are not to carry things in their hands or on their heads.
An elderly Jūnzǐ does not travel on foot;
an elderly commoner does not eat without meat.
5.53 A Dàfū does not borrow sacrificial vessels.
If sacrificial vessels are not yet completed,
he does not manufacture vessels for casual banquets.
5.54 A square lǐ comprises nine hundred mǔ of fields.
An area ten lǐ square
comprises one hundred units of one square lǐ,
making ninety thousand mǔ of fields.
An area one hundred lǐ square
comprises one hundred units of ten lǐ square,
making nine billion mǔ of fields.
An area one thousand lǐ square
comprises one hundred units of one hundred lǐ square,
making nine trillion mǔ of fields.
5.55 From Héngshān to the Nánhé,
it is nearly a thousand lǐ.
From the Nánhé to the Jiāng,
it is nearly a thousand lǐ.
From the Jiāng to Héngshān,
it is over a thousand lǐ.
From the Dōnghé to the Eastern Sea,
it is over a thousand lǐ.
From the Dōnghé to the Xīhé,
it is nearly a thousand lǐ.
From the Xīhé to the Liúshā,
it is over a thousand lǐ.
To the west, it does not exhaust the Liúshā;
to the south, it does not exhaust Héngshān;
to the east, it does not reach the Eastern Sea;
to the north, it does not exhaust Héngshān.
In all within the Four Seas,
cutting off the long to supplement the short,
the area is three thousand lǐ square,
making eighty-one trillion mǔ of fields.
An area one hundred lǐ square
makes nine billion mǔ of fields:
mountains, hills, forests, foothills,
rivers, marshes, ditches, canals,
city walls, suburbs, palaces, houses, roads, and alleys—
removing one-third for these,
the remainder is six billion mǔ.
5.56 In ancient times, eight chǐ of the Zhōu scale made a bù;
now, six chǐ and four cù of the Zhōu scale make a bù.
An ancient hundred mǔ
is equivalent to today's one hundred forty-six mǔ and thirty bù.
An ancient hundred lǐ
is equivalent to today's one hundred twenty-one lǐ, sixty bù, four chǐ, two cù, and two fēn.
5.57 An area one thousand lǐ square
comprises one hundred units of one hundred lǐ square.
If thirty states of one hundred lǐ square are enfeoffed,
the remainder is seventy units of one hundred lǐ square.
If sixty more states of seventy lǐ square are enfeoffed,
— which amounts to twenty-nine units of one hundred lǐ square
and forty units of ten lǐ square.
The remainder is forty units of one hundred lǐ square
and sixty units of ten lǐ square.
If one hundred twenty more states of fifty lǐ square are enfeoffed,
— which amounts to thirty units of one hundred lǐ square.
— The remainder
is ten units of one hundred lǐ square
and sixty units of ten lǐ square.
Famous mountains and large marshes are not granted as fiefs;
the remainder is treated as attached territories or fallow fields.
Feudal lords who have merit
take from the fallow fields for their emoluments;
those whose land is reduced
return it to the fallow fields.
Within the Tiānzǐ's metropolitan domain:
An area one thousand lǐ square comprises one hundred units of one hundred lǐ square.
If nine units of one hundred lǐ square are enfeoffed,
the remainder is ninety-one units of one hundred lǐ square.
If twenty-one more states of seventy lǐ square are enfeoffed,
— which amounts to ten units of one hundred lǐ square
and twenty-nine units of ten lǐ square.
— The remainder
is eighty units of one hundred lǐ square
and seventy-one units of ten lǐ square.
If sixty-three more states of fifty lǐ square are enfeoffed,
— which amounts to fifteen units of one hundred lǐ square
and seventy-five units of ten lǐ square.
— The remainder
is sixty-four units of one hundred lǐ square
and ninety-six units of ten lǐ square.
5.58 A Xiàshì of a feudal lord receives an emolument sufficient to feed nine people,
a Zhōngshì feeds eighteen people,
and a Shàngshì feeds thirty-six people.
A lower Dàfū feeds seventy-two people,
and a Qīng feeds two hundred eighty-eight people.
A ruler feeds two thousand eight hundred eighty people.
A Qīng of a second-rank state feeds two hundred sixteen people,
and the ruler feeds two thousand one hundred sixty people.
A Qīng of a small state feeds one hundred forty-four people,
and the ruler feeds one thousand four hundred forty people.
As for the Qīng of a second-rank state
who are appointed by their own ruler,
they are treated like the Qīng of a small state.
The Dàfū of the Tiānzǐ serve as the Sānjiàn;
those who inspect the states of the feudal lords
have an emolument equal to a Qīng of a feudal lord,
and a rank equal to the ruler of a second-rank state;
their emolument is taken from the lands of the Fāngbó.
When the Fāngbó come to court the Tiānzǐ,
each has a city for bathing and grooming within the Tiānzǐ's domain,
ranked equal to a Yuánshì.
The heirs of feudal lords inherit the state,
but Dàfū do not inherit their rank.
Employment is based on virtue;
rank is based on merit.
Before rank is bestowed,
they are treated as the Tiānzǐ's Yuánshì
in order to rule their states.
The Dàfū of feudal lords
do not inherit rank or emolument.
5.59 The six rites:
capping, marriage, mourning, sacrifice, local feasting, and meetings.
The seven teachings:
father and son, brothers,
husband and wife, ruler and minister,
seniors and juniors, friends, and guests.
The eight government functions:
food and drink, clothing,
works and services, distinctions and ranks,
linear measures, capacity measures, numerical calculations, and regulations.
6.1 In the first month of spring,
the sun is in Yíngshì,
the Shēn constellation is central at dusk,
and the Wěi constellation is central at dawn.
Its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ.
Its divine ruler is Tàihào,
and its protective spirit is Gùmáng.
Its creatures are the scaly ones.
Its musical note is Jué.
Its pitch-pipe corresponds to Dàcù.
Its number is eight.
Its taste is sour,
and its smell is rank.
Its sacrifice is to the Door,
and the spleen is the first part offered.
6.2 The east wind thaws the ice,
the hibernating insects begin to stir,
fish rise to the ice,
otters sacrifice fish,
and the wild geese arrive.
6.3 The Son of Heaven resides in the Left Wing of the Green Brightness Hall (Qīng Yáng Zuǒ Gè).
He rides in the phoenix-bell carriage (Luán Lù),
yokes the azure dragons (Cāng Lóng),
carries the green banner (Qīng Qí),
wears green robes (Qīng Yī),
and wears azure jade (Cāng Yù) ornaments.
He eats wheat and mutton,
and his vessels are coarse and perforated.
6.4 In this month,
the Beginning of Spring (Lì Chūn) occurs.
Three days before the Beginning of Spring,
the Grand Historian (Dà Shǐ) reports to the Son of Heaven, saying:
"On such-and-such a day is the Beginning of Spring;
the flourishing virtue resides in Wood."
The Son of Heaven then fasts.
On the day of the Beginning of Spring,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Three Ducal Ministers (Sān Gōng), the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng), the Feudal Lords (Zhū Hóu), and the Grand Masters (Dà Fū)
to welcome the spring in the eastern suburb (Dōng Jiāo).
Upon returning,
he rewards the Ducal Ministers, Feudal Lords, and Grand Masters in the court.
6.5 He commands the Chancellor (Xiàng) to spread virtue and harmonize orders,
to carry out celebrations and bestow favors,
reaching down to the millions of people.
Rewards and gifts are then distributed,
ensuring none are inappropriate.
6.6 He then commands the Grand Historian (Dà Shǐ) to guard the records and uphold the laws,
to observe the movements of the sun, moon, stars, and constellations in the heavens,
so that their regular paths do not err
and the celestial order is not lost,
using the beginnings as the standard.
6.7 In this month,
the Son of Heaven uses a chosen day (Yuán Rì) to pray for grain to the Highest Emperor (Shàng Dì).
Having chosen an auspicious day (Yuán Chén),
the Son of Heaven personally carries the plow (Lěi Sì),
placing it between the armored attendant (Bǎo Jiè) and the driver,
and leads the Three Ducal Ministers (Sān Gōng), the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng), the Feudal Lords (Zhū Hóu), and the Grand Masters (Dà Fū)
to personally plow the Sacred Field (Dì Jí).
The Son of Heaven pushes the plow three times,
the Ducal Ministers five times,
and the Ministers and Feudal Lords nine times.
Upon returning,
he holds a goblet in the Great Hall (Dà Qǐn),
where the Three Ducal Ministers, Nine Ministers, Feudal Lords, and Grand Masters all attend,
and it is called the "Wine of Labor" (Láo Jiǔ).
6.8 In this month,
the Qi of Heaven descends,
and the Qi of Earth ascends;
Heaven and Earth harmonize,
and plants and trees begin to sprout.
The King orders the commencement of agricultural affairs,
commanding the officials to dwell in the eastern suburb (Dōng Jiāo).
All repair the boundaries and borders,
and carefully examine the paths and trails.
They skillfully evaluate the hills and mounds,
slopes and heights, plains and marshes,
determining what is suitable for the soil
and what the five grains require for growth,
so as to teach and guide the people;
they must do this personally.
Once the field work is organized,
and the standards of alignment are first established,
the farmers will not be confused.
6.9 In this month,
he commands the Director of Music (Yuè Zhèng) to enter the school and practice dancing.
He also repairs the sacrificial canons.
He commands sacrifices to mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
but for the victims, females must not be used.
6.10 The felling of trees is prohibited.
Do not overturn nests,
do not kill young insects,
those yet in the womb, the newly born, or fledglings.
Do not take fawns or eggs.
Do not gather large crowds,
and do not build inner or outer city walls (Chéng Guō).
Cover exposed bones and bury remains.
6.11 In this month,
one must not raise an army;
to raise an army will surely bring heavenly calamity.
Do not let military actions arise;
they must not start from us.
Do not change the Way of Heaven,
do not sever the Principles of Earth,
and do not disrupt the Order of Man.
6.12 If in the first month of spring (Mèng Chūn) the ordinances of summer are carried out,
then wind and rain will be untimely,
plants and trees will shed their leaves early,
and the state will frequent terrors.
If the ordinances of autumn are carried out, the people will suffer great pestilence,
whirlwinds and torrential rains will arrive together,
and weeds like goosefoot, darnel, fleabane, and mugwort will spring up at once.
If the ordinances of winter are carried out, then floods will cause ruin,
frost and snow will be severe,
and the first seeds will not sprout.
6.13 In the second month of spring (Zhòng Chūn),
the sun is in Kuí.
At dusk, Hú is at the meridian;
at dawn, Jiàn Xīng is at the meridian.
Its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ.
Its sovereign is Dà Hào,
and its spirit is Gù Máng.
Its creatures are the scaly ones.
Its musical note is Jiǎo,
and its pitch-pipe corresponds to Jiá Zhōng.
Its number is eight.
Its flavor is sour,
and its smell is rank.
Its sacrifice is at the door (Hù),
and the spleen is the first part offered.
6.14 The rain waters begin;
the peach trees begin to blossom;
the orioles (Cāng Gēng) sing;
hawks transform into doves.
6.15 The Son of Heaven resides in the Great Temple of the Green Brightness Hall (Qīng Yáng Dà Miào).
He rides in the phoenix-bell carriage (Luán Lù),
yokes the azure dragons (Cāng Lóng),
carries the green banner (Qīng Qí),
wears green robes (Qīng Yī),
and wears azure jade (Cāng Yù) ornaments.
He eats wheat and mutton.
His vessels are coarse and perforated.
In this month,
he ensures the safety of budding sprouts,
nurtures the young and small,
and cares for orphans.
Choosing an auspicious day (Yuán Rì),
he commands the sacrifice to the people’s Altar of the Soil (Shè).
He commands the officials to inspect the prisons,
remove fetters and handcuffs,
stop floggings and torture,
and cease all litigations and trials.
6.16 In this month,
the dark birds (Xuán Niǎo) arrive.
On the day they arrive,
the Great Sacrifice (Dà Láo) is offered to the High Progenitor (Gāo Méi).
The Son of Heaven personally attends,
and the Queen leads the Nine Concubines (Jiǔ Pín) to assist.
He then honors those with whom he has consorted,
presenting them with bow cases,
and granting them bows and arrows
before the High Progenitor.
6.17 In this month,
day and night are of equal length (Rì Yè Fēn).
Thunder begins to sound,
and lightning starts.
Hibernating insects all stir,
opening their burrows and beginning to emerge.
Three days before the thunder sounds,
a bell with a wooden clapper (Duó) is shaken to command the millions of people, saying:
"The thunder is about to sound.
If any fail to be cautious in their conduct and movements,
the children they bear will be incomplete,
and there will surely be ominous calamities."
At the equinox,
they standardize measures of length and capacity,
balance weights and stones (Shí),
check the peck (Dǒu) and bushel (Yǒng) measures,
and rectify weights and leveling beams.
6.18 In this month,
the plowmen take a brief rest.
They repair the gates and doors;
the side-rooms and temples are all put in order.
No great works should be undertaken
that would interfere with agricultural affairs.
In this month,
do not exhaust the rivers and marshes,
do not drain the ponds and embankments,
and do not burn the mountain forests.
6.19 The Son of Heaven then offers a fresh lamb when opening the ice-houses,
first presenting it in the ancestral temples.
6.20 On the first Dīng day,
he commands the Director of Music (Yuè Zhèng) to practice dancing
and perform the vegetable offering (Shì Cài).
The Son of Heaven then leads the Three Ducal Ministers (Sān Gōng), the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng), the Feudal Lords (Zhū Hóu), and the Grand Masters (Dà Fū) to personally go and observe it.
On the middle Dīng day,
he again commands the Director of Music to enter the school and practice music.
6.21 In this month,
sacrifices do not use animal victims,
but use jade tablets (Guī Bì)
and offer skins and silks (Pí Bì) instead.
6.22 If in the second month of spring (Zhòng Chūn) the ordinances of autumn are carried out,
then the state will suffer great floods,
cold air will arrive in force,
and invaders and soldiers will come to attack.
If the ordinances of winter are carried out,
the Yang Qi will not prevail,
the wheat will not ripen,
and the people will frequently rob one each other.
If the ordinances of summer are carried out,
the state will suffer a great drought,
warm air will arrive too early,
and insect pests (Míng) will cause damage.
6.23 In the last month of spring,
the sun is in Wèi.
At dusk, the Qī Xīng constellation is at the center;
at dawn, the Qiān Niú constellation is at the center.
Its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ.
Its sovereign is Dà hào,
and its spirit is Gōu máng.
Its creatures are the scaly ones.
Its musical note is Jué,
and its pitch-pipe corresponds to Gū xiǎn.
Its number is eight.
Its flavor is sour,
its smell is rank,
its sacrifice is to the door,
and of the internal organs, the spleen is offered first.
6.24 The tóng tree begins to bloom;
field mice are transformed into quails;
rainbows begin to appear;
and duckweed begins to grow.
6.25 The Tiān zǐ dwells in the Right Side-room of the Qīng yáng Palace.
He rides in the luan-chariot,
driven by azure dragon-horses,
carrying the azure banner.
He wears azure robes
and azure jade ornaments.
He eats wheat and mutton.
His vessels are coarse and open to allow passage.
6.26 In this month,
the Tiān zǐ presents the yellow robes to the former sovereigns.
He orders the Zhōu mù to inspect the boats,
turning them over and back five times.
When it is reported to the Tiān zǐ that "the boats are fully prepared,"
the Tiān zǐ begins to travel by boat.
He presents sturgeon in the ancestral temple
and prays for the fulfillment of the wheat crop.
6.27 In this month,
the vital energy is in full vigor,
and the yáng energy is released and spread.
Things that curl out and
things that bud forth all emerge.
One should not remain indoors.
The Tiān zǐ spreads virtue and practices kindness.
He orders the Yǒu sī to open the granaries,
give to the poor and needy,
and relieve the destitute.
He opens the treasuries,
distributes silks and coins,
and bestows them throughout the world.
He encourages the Zhū hóu,
invites famous scholars,
and honors the worthy.
6.28 In this month,
he orders the Sī kōng, saying:
"The seasonal rains are about to fall,
and the waters below will rise.
Inspect the states and cities;
survey the plains and wilds.
Repair the dikes and embankments,
clear the channels and ditches,
and open up the roads
so there are no obstructions.
As for hunting, the various nets (jū fú and luó wǎng),
the bird-screens, and the poisoned bait for beasts
must not be taken out through the nine gates."
6.29 In this month,
he orders the Yě yú not to cut down mulberry or wild mulberry trees.
The cooing doves flutter their wings,
and the hoopoes alight on the mulberry trees.
Prepare the frames, stands, mats, and baskets.
The Hòu fēi fast and purify themselves;
they personally go to the eastern fields to pick mulberry leaves.
They forbid women from merely spectating
and reduce their other duties to encourage the silk-work.
When the silk-work is completed,
the cocoons are divided and the silk is weighed to show the merit
in providing for the sacrificial robes of the suburban and ancestral temples,
so that none dare be idle.
In this month,
he orders the Gōng shī to command the various artisans to inspect the materials in the five storehouses:
metals and iron,
hides, leather, and sinews,
horns and ivory,
feathers and arrow-shafts,
grease, glue, cinnabar, and lacquer,
ensuring none are of poor quality.
6.30 The various artisans all perform their duties.
The inspectors make daily proclamations:
"Do not act contrary to the season,
nor create extravagant or cunning things to unsettle the mind of the superior."
6.31 At the end of this month,
an auspicious day is chosen
for a grand musical performance.
The Tiān zǐ then leads the Sān gōng, Jiǔ qīng, Zhū hóu, and Dà fū to personally witness it.
6.32 In this month,
the bulls and stallions are brought together
to roam with the females in the pastures.
The sacrificial animals,
colts, and calves
are brought forth,
and their numbers are recorded.
6.33 He orders the state exorcism,
and at the nine gates, the ritual of dismembering and warding off is performed
to conclude the spring energy.
6.34 If in the last month of spring the ordinances of winter are followed,
then cold energy will break out at times;
plants and trees will wither;
and the state will experience great fear.
If the ordinances of summer are followed,
then the people will suffer many diseases and epidemics;
seasonal rains will not fall;
and the mountain forests will yield no harvest.
If the ordinances of autumn are followed,
then the sky will often be gloomy and overcast;
excessive rains will fall early;
and military conflicts will arise.
6.35 In the first month of summer,
the sun is in Bì.
At dusk, the Yì constellation is at the center;
at dawn, the Wù nǚ constellation is at the center.
Its days are Bǐng and Dīng.
Its sovereign is Yán dì;
its spirit is Zhù róng.
Its creatures are the feathered ones.
Its musical note is Zhǐ,
and its pitch-pipe corresponds to Zhòng lǚ.
Its number is seven.
Its flavor is bitter,
and its smell is scorched.
Its sacrifice is to the hearth;
of the internal organs, the lungs are offered first.
The mole-crickets chirp;
earthworms emerge;
the king-melons grow;
and the bitter herbs go to seed.
6.36 The Tiān zǐ dwells in the Left Side-room of the Míng táng.
He rides in the vermilion chariot,
driven by red horses with black manes,
carrying the red banner.
He wears vermilion robes
and red jade ornaments.
He eats beans and chicken.
His vessels are tall and coarse.
6.37 In this month,
the Beginning of Summer occurs.
Three days before the Beginning of Summer,
the Tà shǐ reports to the Tiān zǐ, saying:
"On such-and-such a day is the Beginning of Summer;
the flourishing virtue is in fire."
The Tiān zǐ then fasts.
On the day of the Beginning of Summer,
the Tiān zǐ personally leads the Sān gōng, Jiǔ qīng, and Dà fū
to welcome the summer in the southern suburbs.
Upon their return,
he bestows rewards
and enfeoffs the Zhū hóu.
Proclamations of favor and gifts are carried out,
and there is no one who is not pleased and joyful.
6.38 He then orders the Yuè shī
to practice the combination of rites and music.
He orders the Tài wèi
to recommend the outstanding and talented,
to promote the worthy and good,
and to elevate those of great character.
He bestows ranks and grants stipends,
ensuring they correspond to the positions.
In this month,
nurture what is growing and increase what is rising;
let nothing be destroyed or brought down.
Do not start earthworks,
do not mobilize large crowds,
and do not cut down large trees.
In this month,
the Tiān zǐ begins to wear thin linen.
He orders the Yě yú to travel to the fields and plains
to encourage the farmers and comfort the people on behalf of the Tiān zǐ,
so that no time is lost.
6.39 He orders the Sī tú to inspect the districts and borders;
he orders the farmers to work diligently
and not rest in the capital.
In this month,
drive away beasts so they do not harm the five grains;
do not conduct large hunts.
The farmers then harvest the wheat;
the Tiān zǐ tastes the wheat with pork,
first presenting it in the ancestral temple.
In this month,
gather and store various medicinal herbs.
The delicate grasses die;
the harvest time of wheat arrives.
Settle light penalties,
decide minor offenses,
and release those in light confinement.
When the sericulture is completed,
the Queen and consorts present the cocoons.
Then the cocoon tax is collected,
distributed according to the number of mulberry trees,
with high and low, old and young treated as one,
to provide for the sacrificial robes of the suburban and ancestral temples.
6.40 In this month,
the Son of Heaven drinks *zhòu* wine,
and employs ritual and music.
6.41 If in Mèng Xià the ordinances of Autumn are followed,
then bitter rains will frequently come,
the five grains will not flourish,
and the people of the four borders will enter the fortified places.
If the ordinances of Winter are followed,
then the grass and trees will wither early,
followed by great floods
that destroy the city walls and moats.
If the ordinances of Spring are followed,
then locusts will become a disaster,
violent winds will arrive,
and the flowering grasses will not produce fruit.
6.42 In the month of Zhòng Xià,
the sun is in Dōng Jǐng,
at dusk Kàng is at the meridian,
and at dawn Wēi is at the meridian.
Its days are Bǐng and Dīng.
Its sovereign is Yán Dì,
its spirit is Zhù Róng.
Its creatures are the feathered,
its musical note is Zhǐ,
and its pitch pipe corresponds to Ruí Bīn.
Its number is seven.
Its taste is bitter,
its smell is scorched.
Its sacrifice is that of the stove,
and the lungs are offered first.
6.43 When Minor Heat arrives,
the praying mantis is born.
The shrike begins to cry,
and the mockingbird ceases its song.
6.44 The Son of Heaven dwells in the Great Temple of the Míng Táng;
he rides in the vermilion carriage,
driven by red horses with black manes,
carrying the red banner.
He wears vermilion robes
and red jade ornaments.
He eats beans and chicken.
His vessels are tall and coarse.
He nurtures the strong and handsome.
6.45 In this month,
the music masters are commanded to repair the small drums, large drums, and hand drums;
to tune the *qín* zithers, *sè* zithers, pipes, and flutes;
to handle the shields, axes, halberds, and feathers;
to harmonize the *yú* organs, *shēng* organs, *chí* flutes, and reeds;
and to put in order the bells, chimes, *zhù* starters, and *yǔ* stoppers.
6.46 The officials are commanded to pray and sacrifice for the people to the mountains, rivers, and the hundred sources;
the Great Yù sacrifice to the Sovereign is performed,
using the full set of music.
Then the hundred districts are commanded
to perform the Yù sacrifice to the hundred lords, ministers, and officials who have benefited the people,
to pray for the ripening of the grain.
6.47 The farmers then present the broomcorn millet.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven then tastes the millet with a chick,
accompanied by cherries,
and first presents them in the ancestral temple.
6.48 The people are ordered not to cut indigo for dyeing,
not to burn wood for ash,
and not to bleach cloth in the sun.
The gates and gates of the villages are not to be closed,
and at the passes and markets there should be no searches.
For those in heavy imprisonment, their cases are reviewed,
and their food is increased.
6.49 Mares are separated from the herd,
and the leaping stallions are tethered;
the regulations for horses are distributed.
6.50 In this month,
the day is at its longest.
Yīn and Yáng struggle,
and life and death are partitioned.
The superior man fasts and practices abstinence;
in his dwelling, he must remain secluded,
and not be restless.
He halts music and sensual pleasures,
and none should be brought forward.
He minimizes flavors
and does not seek rich blends.
He moderates his desires,
steadies his heart and spirit,
and the various officials keep their affairs quiet and do not impose punishments,
to stabilize that which is accomplished by the serene Yīn.
6.51 The deer shed their antlers,
and the cicadas begin to sing.
The *bànxià* plant grows,
and the hibiscus blooms.
6.52 In this month,
one should not use fire in the southern quarter.
One may dwell in high and bright places,
one may look out over great distances,
one may ascend mountains and hills,
and one may stay in towers and pavilions.
6.53 If in Zhòng Xià the ordinances of Winter are followed,
then hail and frost will damage the grain,
the roads will be impassable,
and sudden troops will arrive.
If the ordinances of Spring are followed,
then the five grains will ripen late,
the hundred pests will arise at their time,
and the state will suffer famine.
If the ordinances of Autumn are followed,
then grass and trees will shed their leaves,
fruits will ripen early,
and the people will suffer from epidemics.
6.54 In the month of Jì Xià,
the sun is in Liǔ,
at dusk Huǒ is at the meridian,
and at dawn Kuí is at the meridian.
Its days are Bǐng and Dīng.
Its sovereign is Yán Dì,
its spirit is Zhù Róng.
Its creatures are the feathered.
Its musical note is Zhǐ,
and its pitch pipe corresponds to Lín Zhōng.
Its number is seven.
Its taste is bitter,
its smell is scorched.
Its sacrifice is that of the stove,
and the lungs are offered first.
The warm winds begin to arrive,
the crickets dwell in the walls,
the hawks then learn to hunt,
and rotting grass becomes fireflies.
6.55 The Son of Heaven dwells in the right side-chamber of the Míng Táng;
he rides in the vermilion carriage,
driven by red horses with black manes,
carrying the red banner.
He wears vermilion robes
and red jade ornaments.
He eats beans and chicken,
and his vessels are tall and coarse.
6.56 The masters of the fisheries are ordered to strike the scaly dragons and take the alligators,
and to present the large turtles and take the soft-shelled turtles.
The men of the marshes are ordered to bring in materials and reeds.
6.57 In this month,
the four supervisors are ordered to collect the required fodder from the hundred districts,
to nourish the sacrificial animals.
The people are ordered to all put forth their strength
to serve August Heaven, the High Deity, and the spirits of the famous mountains, great rivers, and the four directions,
to sacrifice to the spirits of the ancestral temple and the altars of land and grain,
so as to pray for blessings for the people.
6.58 In this month,
the female officials are ordered to dye colors,
and the embroidered patterns
must follow the ancient laws,
without any error or deviation.
Black, yellow, blue-green, and red,
all must be of good quality,
and none dare be deceitful or false,
to provide for the sacrificial robes of the suburban and ancestral temples,
to make banners and emblems,
and to distinguish the degrees of noble and common, high and low.
6.59 In this month,
the trees and plants are at their height;
the foresters are ordered to enter the mountains and inspect the timber,
but there must be no felling.
One may not begin earthworks,
one may not convene the feudal lords,
one may not raise troops or move the masses,
and no great affairs should be undertaken,
so as not to disturb the nurturing energy.
Do not issue orders and wait for fulfillment,
lest it hinder the work of Shén Nóng.
The floods are at their peak,
and Shén Nóng is about to finish his work;
if great affairs are undertaken, there will be heavenly disaster.
6.60 In this month,
the earth is moist and the heat is humid;
great rains frequently fall.
Burning and clearing weeds and letting water run
is beneficial for killing the grass,
as if using hot soup.
This can fertilize the fields
and improve the strength of the soil.
6.61 If in Jì Xià the ordinances of Spring are followed,
then the grains and fruits will fall prematurely,
the state will have many cases of wind-coughing,
and the people will migrate.
If the ordinances of Autumn are followed,
then the hills and marshes will have floods,
the crops will not ripen,
and there will be many disasters among women.
If the ordinances of Winter are followed,
then cold winds will arrive out of season,
hawks and falcons will strike early,
and the people of the four borders will enter the fortified places.
6.62 The Center is Earth.
Its days are Wù and Jǐ.
Its sovereign is Huáng Dì,
its spirit is Hòu Tǔ.
Its creatures are the naked ones.
Its musical note is Gōng.
Its pitch pipe corresponds to the Gōng of Huángzhōng.
Its number is five.
Its flavor is sweet.
Its smell is fragrant.
Its sacrifice is to the Zhōngliù.
In the sacrifice, the heart is offered first.
The Son of Heaven dwells in the grand chamber of the Grand Temple.
He rides in the Grand Carriage,
drawn by yellow horses with black manes,
carrying the yellow banner,
wearing yellow robes,
and wearing yellow jade.
He eats millet and beef.
His vessels are round and wide.
6.63 In the first month of autumn,
the sun is in Yì.
At dusk, Jiànxīng is on the meridian;
at dawn, Bì is on the meridian.
Its days are Gēng and Xīn.
Its deity is Shǎohào,
and its spirit is Rùshōu.
Its creatures are the hairy ones.
Its musical note is Shāng,
and its pitch pipe corresponds to Yízé.
Its number is nine.
Its flavor is acrid,
and its smell is rank.
Its sacrifice is to the gate;
in the sacrifice, the liver is offered first.
6.64 Cool winds arrive,
white dew falls,
and the cold cicada chirps.
Hawks sacrifice birds,
and executions begin to be carried out.
6.65 The Son of Heaven dwells in the Left Wing of the Zǒngzhāng.
He rides in the war chariot,
drawn by white horses with black manes,
carrying the white banner,
wearing white robes,
and wearing white jade.
He eats hemp seed and dog meat.
His vessels are angular and deep.
6.66 In this month,
the Lì Qiū occurs.
Three days before the Lì Qiū,
the Grand Scribe informs the Son of Heaven, saying:
"On such-and-such a day is the Lì Qiū;
the fullness of virtue is in Metal."
The Son of Heaven then fasts and purifies himself.
On the day of the Lì Qiū,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Sāngōng, the Jiǔqīng, the Feudal Lords, and the Grand Masters
to welcome the autumn in the western suburbs.
Upon returning,
he rewards military commanders and warriors at court.
The Son of Heaven then orders the generals and commanders
to select soldiers and sharpen weapons,
to choose and train the brave and outstanding,
to give sole responsibility to those with merit,
in order to campaign against the unrighteous.
He investigates and punishes the tyrannical and negligent,
in order to clarify likes and dislikes,
and bring harmony to those in distant lands.
In this month,
the officials are ordered to revise legal regulations,
repair the prisons,
prepare the shackles and fetters,
prohibit wickedness,
be cautious in punishing the depraved,
and strive to capture and seize them.
The judges are ordered to examine injuries,
inspect wounds,
look at fractures,
and scrutinize the verdicts.
In deciding lawsuits,
they must be upright and impartial.
Execute the guilty
and strictly carry out punishments.
Heaven and Earth begin to be austere;
it is not permitted to show indulgence.
In this month,
the farmers present the grain.
The Son of Heaven tastes the new crop,
first offering it in the ancestral shrine.
The hundred officials are ordered
to begin gathering the harvest,
repair the dikes and embankments,
carefully inspect the dams,
in order to prepare for floods.
They repair houses and chambers,
plaster walls and enclosures,
and mend the inner and outer city walls.
In this month,
do not enfeoff feudal lords
or establish high officials.
Do not cede territory,
send out great envoys,
or send out great gifts of silk.
6.67 If in the first month of autumn the ordinances of winter are followed,
then the Yin Qi will greatly prevail,
shelled insects will ruin the grain,
and enemy troops will arrive.
If the ordinances of spring are followed,
then the state will suffer drought,
the Yang Qi will return,
and the five grains will not bear fruit.
If the ordinances of summer are followed,
then the state will have many fire disasters,
cold and heat will be unseasonable,
and the people will suffer many malarial fevers.
6.68 In the mid-month of autumn,
the sun is in Jiǎo.
At dusk, Qiānniú is on the meridian;
at dawn, Zīxī is on the meridian.
Its days are Gēng and Xīn.
Its deity is Shǎohào,
and its spirit is Rùshōu.
Its creatures are the hairy ones.
Its musical note is Shāng,
and its pitch pipe corresponds to Nánlǚ.
Its number is nine.
Its flavor is acrid,
and its smell is rank.
Its sacrifice is to the gate;
in the sacrifice, the liver is offered first.
6.69 The swirling winds arrive,
the wild geese arrive,
and the swallows return.
The flocks of birds store up food.
6.70 The Son of Heaven dwells in the Grand Temple of Zǒngzhāng.
He rides in the war chariot,
drawn by white horses with black manes,
carrying the white banner,
wearing white robes,
and wearing white jade.
He eats hemp seed and dog meat.
His vessels are angular and deep.
6.71 In this month,
nourish the elderly and frail,
bestow stools and canes,
and provide them with congee and food.
6.72 The Superintendent of Robes is ordered
to prepare and refurbish the robes and garments.
The embroidery must follow the regular patterns,
the sizes have small and large,
and the lengths have short and long.
Garments have their proper measures;
one must follow the ancient precedents.
The caps and belts have their regular rules.
6.73 The officials are ordered
to re-emphasize the strictness of the hundred punishments.
Executions and killings must be appropriate;
let there be no perversion or distortion.
If there is perversion or inappropriateness,
one will in turn suffer calamity.
6.74 In this month,
the Zǎi and Zhù are ordered
to inspect the sacrificial animals.
Check if they are complete and without blemish,
examine the fodder and grain they eat,
look at their fatness or leanness,
and inspect their color.
They must be matched by category,
their size measured,
and their length observed;
everything must be within the proper measure.
When these five requirements are fully met,
Shàngdì will then accept the offering.
6.75 The Son of Heaven then performs the Nuó exorcism
in order to release the Autumn Qi.
6.76 With dog meat he tastes the hemp seed,
first offering it in the ancestral shrine.
6.77 In this month,
it is permissible to build inner and outer city walls,
establish capitals and towns,
dig storage pits and cellars,
and repair round and square granaries.
6.78 The officials are ordered
to urge the people to harvest.
They make an effort to store vegetables
and accumulate a great deal.
They then encourage the planting of wheat;
let no one miss the season.
If anyone misses the season,
they will be punished without doubt.
6.79 In this month,
day and night are divided equally.
Thunder begins to cease its sound.
Hibernating insects seal their holes.
The Qi of killing gradually increases,
the Yang Qi daily declines,
and the waters begin to dry up.
6.80 When day and night are divided equally,
then standardize measures of length and capacity,
balance weights and scales,
rectify the Jūn and Shí weights,
and harmonize the Dǒu and Yǒng measures.
In this month,
regulations for the passes and markets are eased,
to attract traveling merchants,
and goods and commodities are brought in
to facilitate the affairs of the people.
People gather from all four directions,
and those from distant regions all arrive,
so that wealth is not lacking,
the ruler has no shortage of supplies,
and the hundred affairs are thus accomplished.
6.81 In all great undertakings,
do not go against the celestial numbers;
one must follow the timing
and carefully accord with their categories.
6.82 If in the second month of autumn the ordinances of spring are carried out,
then the autumn rains will not fall,
plants and trees will blossom and flourish,
and the state will be filled with fear.
If the ordinances of summer are carried out,
then the state will suffer a drought,
hibernating insects will not hide,
and the five grains will sprout again.
If the ordinances of winter are carried out,
then wind disasters will frequently arise,
retreating thunder will sound early,
and plants and trees will die prematurely.
6.83 In the last month of autumn,
the sun is in *Fáng*,
at dusk *Xū* is at the center,
at dawn *Liǔ* is at the center.
Its days are *gēng* and *xīn*.
Its sovereign is *Shǎo Hào*,
its deity is *Rù Shōu*.
Its creatures are the hairy ones.
Its musical note is *shāng*,
the pitch-pipe is *Wú Yì*.
Its number is nine.
Its flavor is acrid,
its smell is rank.
Its sacrifice is at the door,
the liver is the first part offered.
6.84 Wild geese arrive as guests.
Sparrows enter the great water to become clams.
Chrysanthemums have yellow flowers.
Dholes sacrifice beasts and slaughter birds.
6.85 The *Tiān Zǐ* resides in the Right Wing of the *Zǒng Zhāng*,
rides in a war chariot,
yokes white horses with black manes,
displays white banners,
wears white robes,
and wears white jade.
He eats hemp and dog meat;
his vessels are angular and deep.
6.86 In this month,
commands and orders are strictly reiterated.
The hundred officials, high and low, are ordered to focus on gathering inward,
to harmonize with the storage of heaven and earth,
and nothing should be allowed to leak out.
6.87 Then the *Zhǒng Zǎi* is ordered
that agricultural activities be fully concluded;
the totals of the five grains are tallied,
and the harvest from the Emperor’s ritual field is stored in the Sacred Granary,
being careful to show reverence and diligence.
6.88 In this month,
frost begins to fall,
then the hundred artisans take a rest.
6.88 Then the officials are ordered, saying:
“The cold air has arrived in full force;
the strength of the people cannot bear it,
let them all move indoors.”
6.89 On the first *dīng* day,
the *Yuè Zhèng* is ordered to enter the academy to practice wind instruments.
6.90 In this month,
the great feast for the Sovereigns and the *cháng* sacrifice are held,
and the victims are announced as ready to the *Tiān Zǐ*.
6.91 He assembles the *Zhū Hóu*,
regulates the hundred districts,
receives the new moon days for the coming year,
along with the laws for the light or heavy taxes the *Zhū Hóu* levy on the people,
the amounts of tribute and service,
using the distance and the suitability of the land as the measure,
to provide for the affairs of the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples,
without any private gain.
6.92 In this month,
the *Tiān Zǐ* instructs in hunting,
to practice the five arts of war,
and he distributes the regulations for horses.
The charioteers and the seven grooms are ordered to yoke the teams,
displaying flags and banners.
Chariots are assigned according to rank
and arranged outside the gate-screen.
The *Sī Tú* tucks the whip in his belt
and faces north to swear them in.
The *Tiān Zǐ* puts on martial attire,
holding his bow and arrows to hunt,
and orders the Master of Sacrifice to offer the captured game to the four directions.
6.93 In this month,
plants and trees turn yellow and shed their leaves,
then wood is cut to make charcoal.
6.94 Hibernating insects all huddle in their burrows,
and all plaster their entrances shut.
Judicial punishments are expedited,
so as not to detain the guilty.
Those with undeserved salaries or ranks
and those receiving inappropriate support are reduced.
6.95 In this month,
the *Tiān Zǐ* tastes the rice with dog meat,
first offering it in the ancestral temples.
6.96 If in the last month of autumn the ordinances of summer are carried out,
then the state will suffer great floods,
winter stores will rot and fail,
and the people will suffer many colds and sneezes.
If the ordinances of winter are carried out,
then the state will have many thieves and rebels,
the borders will not be at peace,
and the land will be divided.
6.97 If the ordinances of spring are carried out,
then warm winds will arrive,
the people’s spirit will become lax and lazy,
and armies will be raised but not settled.
6.97 In the first month of winter,
the sun is in *Wěi*,
at dusk *Wēi* is at the center,
at dawn the *Qī Xīng* are at the center.
Its days are *rén* and *guǐ*.
Its sovereign is *Zhuān Xū*,
its deity is *Xuán Míng*.
Its creatures are the shelled ones.
Its musical note is *yǔ*,
the pitch-pipe is *Yìng Zhōng*.
Its number is six.
Its flavor is salty,
its smell is rotten.
Its sacrifice is at the road,
the kidneys are the first part offered.
6.98 Water begins to freeze,
the earth begins to harden.
Pheasants enter the great water to become large clams.
Rainbows hide and are not seen.
6.99 The *Tiān Zǐ* resides in the Left Wing of the *Xuán Táng*,
rides in a black chariot,
yokes black horses,
displays black banners,
wears black robes,
and wears black jade.
He eats broomcorn millet and pork;
his vessels are wide and enclosed.
6.100 In this month,
the Start of Winter occurs.
Three days before the Start of Winter,
the *Tài Shǐ* reports to the *Tiān Zǐ*, saying:
“On such-and-such a day is the Start of Winter;
the full power of virtue resides in Water.”
The *Tiān Zǐ* then fasts.
On the day of the Start of Winter,
the *Tiān Zǐ* personally leads the *Sān Gōng*, the *Jiǔ Qīng*, and the *Dà Fū*
to welcome the winter in the northern suburbs.
Upon returning,
he rewards those who died in service,
and shows compassion to orphans and widows.
6.101 In this month,
the *Tài Shǐ* is ordered to smear the tortoise shells and stalks with blood,
to interpret the cracks and examine the hexagrams for good and bad fortune.
Through this, partiality and factionalism are investigated,
so that no crimes remain hidden.
6.102 In this month,
the *Tiān Zǐ* begins to wear furs.
6.103 The officials are ordered, saying:
“The qi of heaven rises upward,
the qi of earth descends,
heaven and earth do not commune,
all is closed up and blocked, thus forming winter.”
The hundred officials are ordered to carefully cover and store things.
The *Sī Tú* is ordered to inspect stores and accumulations,
ensuring that nothing remains uncollected.
Repairs are made to city walls,
gates and hamlets are guarded,
bolts and locks are repaired,
keys and latches are checked carefully,
seals are secured,
the borders are prepared,
fortresses are made sound,
passes and bridges are scrutinized,
and narrow paths are blocked.
6.104 Regulations for mourning are prepared,
the distinctions of robes and garments are clarified,
the thickness of inner and outer coffins is examined,
the size and height of grave plots and burial mounds,
and the degrees of depth and thickness
according to the ranks of high and low.
6.105 In this month,
the *Gōng Shī* is ordered to evaluate achievements,
to display the ritual vessels,
and to inspect measures and standards.
Let none create excessive or artful novelties to unsettle the ruler’s mind.
Excellence in workmanship must be the primary goal.
Artisans engrave their names on objects,
to examine their sincerity.
If the workmanship is improper,
their crime must be punished,
so as to exhaust the truth of the circumstances.
6.106 In this month,
the great *Zhēng* sacrifice and drinking are held.
6.107 The Son of Heaven then prays for the coming year to the *Tiānzōng*,
and performs the great animal sacrifices at the *Gōngshè* and the neighborhood gates.
He performs the *Là* sacrifice to the ancestors and the *Wǔsì*,
and rewards the farmers to let them rest.
6.108 The Son of Heaven then orders the generals and commanders to lecture on martial arts,
and practice archery, charioteering, and wrestling.
6.109 In this month,
he orders the *Shuǐyú* and the *Yúshī*
to collect taxes from the waters, springs, ponds, and marshes.
None shall dare to encroach upon or exploit the common people,
so as to cause the Son of Heaven to incur resentment from those below.
If there are any such cases,
they shall be punished without pardon.
6.110 If the ordinances of spring are followed in *Mèngdōng*,
then the freezing and closing will not be tight,
the breath of the earth will leak upward,
and many people will become refugees.
If the ordinances of summer are followed,
the state will have many violent winds,
it will not be cold during winter,
and hibernating insects will reappear.
If the ordinances of autumn are followed,
snow and frost will be untimely,
small military skirmishes will frequently arise,
and the land will be encroached upon.
6.111 In the month of *Zhòngdōng*,
the sun is in *Dǒu*,
at dusk *Dōngbì* is centered,
and at dawn *Zhěn* is centered.
Its days are *Rén* and *Guǐ*.
Its emperor is *Zhuānxū*,
and its spirit is *Xuánmíng*.
Its creatures are the shelled ones.
Its musical note is *Yǔ*,
and its pitch-pipe corresponds to *Huángzhōng*.
Its number is six.
Its taste is salty,
and its smell is rotten.
Its sacrifice is that of the Path,
and the kidneys are offered first.
6.112 The ice becomes even stronger,
and the earth begins to crack.
The *hédàn* bird no longer sings,
and tigers begin to mate.
6.113 The Son of Heaven resides in the *Xuántáng* of the *Dàmiào*.
He rides in the dark carriage,
drawn by iron-black horses,
carries the dark banner,
wears black robes,
and wears dark jade.
He eats millet and pork,
and his vessels are wide and deep.
6.114 He organizes the affairs for those who died in service.
He orders the officials, saying:
"No earthworks shall be undertaken.
Be careful not to uncover what is covered,
do not uncover houses
or mobilize large crowds,
so as to keep things solid and closed.
If the breath of the earth leaks,
it is called 'opening the chambers of Heaven and Earth.'
All hibernating insects will then die,
the people will surely suffer epidemics,
followed by deaths.
This month is called *Chàngyuè*."
6.115 In this month,
the *Yǎnyǐn* is ordered
to reiterate the palace commands,
inspect the gates,
and be careful with the chambers;
they must be doubly closed.
Reduce the work of the women and do not allow licentiousness;
even if there are noble relatives or close favorites,
none shall be exempt from the prohibition.
6.116 Then the *Dàqiú* is ordered:
the glutinous rice and paddy must be complete,
the yeast and malt must be timely,
the soaking and steaming must be clean,
the water and springs must be fragrant,
the pottery must be of good quality,
and the temperature of the fire must be correct.
These six things must be used together.
The *Dàqiú* supervises this,
and there should be no error.
6.117 The Son of Heaven orders the officials
to pray and sacrifice to the Four Seas, Great Rivers, Famous Sources, Deep Marshes, Wells, and Springs.
6.118 In this month,
if there are farmers who have not stored their harvests,
or horses, cattle, and livestock that are straying,
they may be taken without questioning.
In the mountains, forests, marshes, and wetlands,
if there are those who can gather wild vegetables
or hunt birds and beasts,
the *Yějǔ* shall guide them.
If there are those who encroach or rob from each other,
they shall be punished without pardon.
In this month
the winter solstice occurs.
Yin and Yang struggle,
and all living things are stirred.
The *Jūnzǐ* fasts and practices abstinence,
and must stay in seclusion.
He wishes his body to be at peace,
removes music and beautiful sights,
and forbids desires.
He quiets his form and nature;
affairs should be still,
so as to await the settling of Yin and Yang.
6.119 Rue begins to grow,
the iris comes out,
earthworms knot,
elks' antlers shed,
and the water in the springs moves.
6.120 At the winter solstice,
trees are felled,
and bamboo is taken for arrows.
In this month,
one may dismiss officials who have no duties
and discard equipment that is of no use.
6.121 Plaster the palace courts and the neighborhood gates,
and build prisons;
this is how one assists the closing and storing of Heaven and Earth.
6.122 If the ordinances of summer are followed in *Zhòngdōng*,
then the state will suffer drought,
gloomy mists will prevail,
and thunder will sound.
If the ordinances of autumn are followed,
then the sky will rain liquid,
melons and gourds will not form,
and the state will have great wars.
If the ordinances of spring are followed,
then locusts will cause destruction,
the springs will all dry up,
and the people will suffer from many skin diseases.
6.123 In the month of *Jìdōng*,
the sun is in *Wùnǚ*,
at dusk *Lóu* is centered,
and at dawn *Dǐ* is centered.
Its days are *Rén* and *Guǐ*.
Its emperor is *Zhuānxū*,
and its spirit is *Xuánmíng*.
Its creatures are the shelled ones.
Its musical note is *Yǔ*,
and its pitch-pipe corresponds to *Dàlǚ*.
Its number is six.
Its taste is salty,
and its smell is rotten.
Its sacrifice is that of the Path,
and the kidneys are offered first.
6.124 Wild geese fly north,
and magpies begin to nest.
6.125 Pheasants crow,
and hens hatch.
6.126 The Son of Heaven resides in the right side-hall of the *Xuántáng*.
He rides in the dark carriage,
drawn by iron-black horses,
carries the dark banner,
wears black robes,
and wears dark jade,
eats millet and pork,
and his vessels are wide and deep.
6.126 He orders the officials to perform the Great *Nàn* exorcism,
to dismember victims at the sides,
and to bring out the earthen ox,
so as to send away the cold qi.
6.127 Birds of prey strike swiftly and fiercely.
Then the sacrifices to the mountains and rivers are completed,
along with those to the great ministers of the emperors
and the spirits of heaven and earth.
6.128 In this month,
the *Yúshī* is ordered to begin fishing.
The Son of Heaven goes in person
and tastes the fish,
first offering them in the ancestral temple.
6.129 The ice is then at its height,
and the waters and marshes are solid to their core.
He orders the collection of ice,
and the ice is brought in.
He orders that the people be told
to bring out the five kinds of seeds.
He orders the farmers to plan for the collective plowing,
repair the plows and shares,
and prepare the field tools.
6.130 He orders the *Yuèshī* to hold a grand ensemble of wind instruments and then conclude.
6.131 Then he orders the *Sìjiān* to collect the ranked firewood and brushwood,
to provide for the burnt offerings at the suburban altars, the ancestral temple, and the hundred sacrifices.
In this month,
the sun reaches the end of its course in its mansions,
the moon reaches the end of its course in its cycles,
and the stars return to their places in the sky.
The number of days is nearly completed,
and the year is about to start anew.
Devote the farmers exclusively to their work,
and let them not be employed for any other tasks.
6.132 The Tiānzǐ then, together with the Gōng, Qīng, and Dàfū,
regulates the national laws
and discusses the seasonal ordinances
to prepare for the suitability of the coming year.
6.133 He then orders the Dàshǐ to arrange the rank of the Zhūhóu,
to levy sacrificial victims from them
to provide for the offerings to Huángtiān, Shàngdì, and the Shèjì.
He then orders the states of the same surname
to provide the fodder and grain for the Qǐnmiào.
He orders the Zǎi to record the amount of land held by the Qīng and Dàfū down to the Shùmín,
and to levy sacrificial victims
to provide for the sacrifices to the mountains, forests, and famous rivers.
All the people within the Jiǔzhōu of the world
without exception offer their labor
to provide for the sacrifices to Huángtiān, Shàngdì, the Shèjì, the Qǐnmiào, the mountains, forests, and famous rivers.
6.134 If in the last month of winter the ordinances of autumn are carried out,
then white dew will descend early,
shelled insects will become a plague,
and those on the four borders will enter the fortifications for protection.
If the ordinances of spring are carried out,
then many fetuses and young will be harmed,
the state will suffer from many chronic diseases,
and this is called disobedience.
If the ordinances of summer are carried out,
then floods will ruin the state,
seasonal snow will not fall,
and ice and frost will dissolve.
7.1 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the ruler dies and a Shìzǐ is born,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The Qīng, Dàfū, and Shì follow the Shèzhǔ,
facing north
at the south of the western steps.
The Dàzhù wears the Bìmiǎn,
holds a bundle of silk,
ascends from the western steps to the top of the stairs,
but does not enter the hall,
and orders that there be no wailing.
The Zhù cries out three times
and announces, saying:
'The son of so-and-so is born,
and I venture to announce it.'
He then ascends,
places the silk on the table to the east of the coffin,
wails,
and descends.
All the Zhǔrén, Qīng, Dàfū, and Shì,
and those in the Fángzhōng,
all wail but do not leap.
After completing one outburst of grief,
they return to their positions.
Then the morning offering is made.
The Xiǎozǎi ascends and takes away the silk.
After three days,
all the Zhǔrén, Qīng, Dàfū, and Shì
take their original positions
facing north.
The Dàzǎi, Dàzōng, and Dàzhù all wear the Bìmiǎn.
The Shǎoshī carries the child in mourning clothes;
the Zhù goes first,
the child follows,
and the Zǎi and Zōngrén follow him.
Upon entering the gate,
those wailing stop,
and the child ascends from the western steps.
He faces north before the coffin.
The Zhù stands at the southeast corner of the coffin.
The Zhù cries out three times
and says:
'So-and-so, the son of so-and-so,
following the officials,
ventures to appear.'
The child bows, touches his forehead to the ground,
and wails.
The Zhù, Zǎi, Zōngrén, all the Zhǔrén,
Qīng, Dàfū, and Shì
wail and leap three times three times,
then descend
and return to their positions in the east,
where all bare their shoulders.
The child leaps,
and those in the Fángzhōng also leap
three times three times.
They put on the mourning clothes again,
take up their staffs,
and then go out.
The Dàzǎi orders the Zhù and Shǐ
to announce the name everywhere to the Wǔsì and the mountains and rivers."
7.2 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the burial has already taken place and then the Shìzǐ is born,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The Dàzǎi and Dàzōng follow the Dàzhù and announce it at the Nì.
After three months,
the name is given at the Nì,
and the name is announced everywhere, reaching the Shèjì, Zōngmiào, and the mountains and rivers."
7.3 Kǒngzǐ said:
"When a Zhūhóu goes to the Tiānzǐ,
he must announce it to the Zǔ
and make an offering at the Nì.
He wears the Miǎn and goes out to hold court,
and orders the Zhù and Shǐ to announce it to the Zōngmiào and the mountains and rivers.
Then he gives orders to the Wǔguān of the state and then departs,
making the road sacrifice as he goes out.
The announcements
are completed in five days;
to exceed this
is not in accordance with the rites.
All announcements
use sacrificial victims and silk.
Upon returning,
it is also done like this.
When Zhūhóu meet each other,
they must announce it to the Nì,
and wear court dress to go out and hold court.
He orders the Zhù and Shǐ to announce it to the Wǔmiào
and the mountains and rivers he will pass.
He also gives orders to the Wǔguān of the state
and makes the road sacrifice as he goes out.
Upon returning,
he must personally announce it to the Zǔ and Nì.
Then he orders the Zhù and Shǐ to announce it to all those who were previously announced,
and after that he hears court affairs and enters."
7.4 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If there are two simultaneous funerals,
what should be done?
Which should come first and which last?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In burial,
first the light and then the heavy;
as for the offerings,
first the heavy and then the light; this is the rite.
From the opening of the coffin until the burial,
no offerings are made.
In conducting the burial, one does not wail in the mourning shed;
after returning from the burial, offerings are made,
and then one takes leave at the coffin,
and then completes the burial matters.
For the Yú sacrifice,
first the heavy and then the light,
which is the rite."
7.5 Kǒngzǐ said:
"Even if a Zōngzǐ is seventy,
he should not be without a chief wife;
if one is not a Zōngzǐ,
it is acceptable to be without a chief wife."
7.6 Zēngzǐ asked:
"When about to perform the capping ceremony for a son,
and the guest for the capping arrives,
they bow and yield to each other and enter,
but if they hear of a mourning for which Zīcuī or Dàgōng is worn,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If it is a mourning within the family, the ceremony is canceled;
if it is an external mourning, the capping is performed but without the toast of sweet wine,
the prepared food is removed and the floor is swept,
and they take their positions and wail.
If the guest for the capping has not yet arrived,
then the ceremony is canceled.
If one is about to cap a son and the appointed day has not yet come,
but there is mourning of Zīcuī, Dàgōng, or Xiǎogōng,
then the capping is performed while wearing the mourning clothes."
"When the mourning is over, is the cap not changed?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When the Tiānzǐ bestows the Miǎn and Biàn robes upon a Zhūhóu or Dàfū in the Tàimiào,
they return and set out an offering,
wear the bestowed robes,
and on such an occasion there is the capping with a toast of wine,
but no capping with a toast of sweet wine.
If the father is deceased and the capping is performed,
then after being capped,
one sweeps the ground
and sacrifices at the Nì;
after the sacrifice,
one sees the paternal uncles,
and then feasts the guest of the capping."
7.7 Zēngzǐ asked:
"In what kind of sacrifice
is the practice of the general toast not performed?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I have heard that
for the Xiǎoxiáng,
the Zhǔrén performs the Liàn sacrifice but does not perform the general toast;
a toast is offered to the guests,
but the guests do not raise the cup;
this is the rite."
In the past,
Lǔ Zhāogōng performed the *liàn* sacrifice and then offered the toast to the guests and travelers;
this was contrary to ritual.
When Xiàogōng performed the *dàxiáng* sacrifice,
he did not perform the libation toast;
this was also contrary to ritual."
7.8 Zēngzǐ asked,
"During a mourning period of *dàgōng*,
can one participate in the matters of food offerings and libations?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Is it only for *dàgōng*?
From *zhǎncuī* on down, all may participate;
this is the ritual."
Zēngzǐ said,
"Should one not refrain from using light mourning clothes
to assist in more solemn duties?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"That is not what I mean.
In the mourning for a *tiānzǐ* or *zhūhóu*,
those wearing *zhǎncuī* perform the libations;
for a *dàfū*,
those wearing *zīcuī* perform them;
for a *shì*,
then friends perform them.
If there are not enough,
then they are taken from those in *dàgōng* and below;
if there are still not enough,
then they revert to those in heavier mourning."
Zēngzǐ asked,
"Can those in *xiǎogōng* participate in sacrifices?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Why only *xiǎogōng*?
From *zhǎncuī* on down, they may participate in sacrifices;
this is the ritual."
Zēngzǐ said,
"Should one not refrain from using light mourning for solemn sacrifices?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"In the funeral sacrifices of a *tiānzǐ* or *zhūhóu*,
those not wearing *zhǎncuī* do not participate;
for a *dàfū*,
those wearing *zīcuī* participate;
for a *shì*,
if those for the sacrifice are not enough,
then they are taken from brothers and those in *dàgōng* and below."
7.9 Zēngzǐ asked,
"If one is an acquaintance
and wears mourning dress, can he participate in the sacrifice?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"One in *sī* mourning does not perform their own sacrifices,
how then could he assist others?"
7.10 Zēngzǐ asked,
"If one has taken off the mourning clothes,
can one participate in the matters of food offerings and libations?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"To remove the mourning garments and perform libations
is contrary to ritual;
but to act as an assistant or usher is permissible."
7.11 Zēngzǐ asked,
"In the marriage ritual, if the silk offerings have been presented
and an auspicious day has been chosen,
but then the girl's father or mother dies,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The groom sends someone to offer condolences.
If the groom's father or mother dies,
then the girl's family also sends someone to offer condolences.
In mourning for a father, the father is named;
in mourning for a mother, the mother is named.
If the parents are deceased,
then the paternal uncle or his wife are named.
As for the groom,
after the burial,
his paternal uncle delivers a message to the girl's family, saying,
'The son of So-and-so is in mourning for his parent,
and cannot at this time become your relative through marriage;
he has sent me to deliver this message.'
The girl's family gives their assent,
but does not dare to marry her off to another;
this is the ritual.
When the groom
has ended the mourning,
the girl's parents send someone to request the marriage;
if the groom does not take her,
only then may she be married to another;
this is the ritual.
If the girl's father or mother dies,
the groom also follows this procedure."
7.12 Zēngzǐ asked,
"During the personal fetching of the bride,
if the girl is on the road
and the groom's father or mother dies,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The girl changes her clothes, putting on a plain linen *shēnyī*,
with a white silk head-tie, and hastens to the mourning.
If the girl is on the road
and her own father or mother dies,
then the girl returns."
"If the groom goes to fetch the bride personally,
and the girl has not yet arrived,
but there is a death requiring *zīcuī*
or *dàgōng* mourning,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The man does not enter,
but changes into mourning clothes in an outer apartment;
the girl enters,
and changes into mourning clothes in an inner apartment;
thereafter they take their positions and wail."
Zēngzǐ asked,
"When mourning is over, do they not resume the marriage ritual?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"As for a sacrifice,
if the time has passed, it is not performed;
this is the ritual.
Why then should one go back to the beginning?"
7.13 Kǒngzǐ said,
"In the family that marries off a daughter,
for three nights they do not extinguish the candles,
thinking of the separation.
In the family that takes a wife,
for three days they do not play music,
thinking of her succeeding the deceased parents.
After three months, she is presented in the ancestral temple,
and is called the 'arrived wife.'
A day is chosen to sacrifice to the deceased father,
completing the status of a wife."
7.14 Zēngzǐ asked,
"If a girl dies before being presented in the ancestral temple,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"She is not moved to the ancestral altar,
she is not associated with the late mother-in-law,
the husband does not carry a staff, wear straw sandals, or stay in a mourning shed;
she is returned for burial to her own family,
showing that she had not yet completed her status as a wife."
7.15 Zēngzǐ asked,
"In taking a wife,
if an auspicious day has been set and the girl dies,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The groom wears *zīcuī* and goes to offer condolences,
and after the burial, he removes
it.
If the husband dies, the girl also does the same."
Zēngzǐ asked,
"Can a mourning have two chief mourners
and an ancestral temple have two tablets;
is this ritual?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"In heaven there are not two suns,
on earth there are not two kings;
in the *cháng*, *dì*, *jiāo*, and *shè* sacrifices,
there are no two supreme beings.
I have not known this to be the ritual.
In the past, Qí Huángōng frequently raised troops
and made a false tablet to take with him.
Upon his return,
he stored it in the ancestral temple.
That an ancestral temple should have two tablets
began with Huángōng.
As for having two chief mourners at a funeral,
in the past, Wèi Línggōng went to Lǔ
and happened upon the funeral of Jì Huánzǐ.
The Ruler of Wèi requested to offer condolences,
and Āigōng declined;
but being unable to refuse the request,
the Duke acted as the host,
and the guest entered to offer condolences.
Kāngzǐ stood at the right of the gate,
facing north;
the Duke bowed and yielded, ascending by the eastern steps
and facing west;
the guest ascended by the western steps to offer condolences.
The Duke bowed,
rose,
and wailed;
Kāngzǐ bowed with his head to the ground at his position,
and the officers did not correct it.
The practice today of having two chief mourners
stems from the error of Jì Kāngzǐ."
7.16 Zēngzǐ asked,
"In ancient times, when an army marched,
did they necessarily take the tablets of the shrines already removed with them?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"When the *tiānzǐ* made a tour of inspection,
he took the tablets of the removed shrines with him,
carrying them in the purification carriage;
this meant he necessarily had those he honored with him.
Now,
to take the tablets of all seven shrines with him,
that is an error.
Among the seven shrines or five shrines, there should be no empty places for tablets;
the only times there are empty places for tablets
is when the *tiānzǐ* passes away,
or a *zhūhóu* passes away, or leaves his state,
or when the collective *xiá* sacrifice is performed for the ancestors;
only then are they without tablets."
I heard from Lǎo Dān:
"When the Tiānzǐ passes away,
or a ruler of a state dies,
the Zhù takes the spirit tablets of the various temples and stores them in the Grand Ancestral Temple;
this is the ritual.
After the completion of the wailing at the conclusion of the mourning rites and the finalizing of the sacrificial business,
each tablet returns to its own temple.
When a ruler leaves his state,
the Dàzǎi takes the spirit tablets of the various temples to follow him;
this is the ritual.
In the Xiá sacrifice at the ancestral temple,
the Zhù welcomes the tablets of the four temples.
When the tablets
leave or enter a temple, the way must be cleared."
So said Lǎo Dān.
7.17 Zēng Zǐ asked:
"In ancient times, when an army marched
without moving the spirit tablets,
what tablet was used?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The Tablet of the Command."
Zēng Zǐ asked:
"What does that mean?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When the Tiānzǐ or the Zhūhóu are about to set out,
they must announce it to the ancestors and the immediate deceased father with offerings of coins, silk, skins, and jade tablets.
They then carry them forth
and place them in the Carriage of Purification for the journey.
At every place they lodge,
they set out offerings before entering the lodging.
Upon returning, they must announce it,
set out offerings, and when finished,
collect the coins and jade,
store them between the two staircases,
and only then do they go out.
This is to honor the command."
7.18 Zǐyóu asked:
"To mourn a foster mother as one would a mother,
is that according to the ritual?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It is not according to the ritual.
In ancient times,
a male child had a tutor outside
and a foster mother inside;
they were commissioned by the ruler's command to teach the son.
What mourning garment should there be?
In the past,
Lǔ Zhāogōng lost his mother when young.
He had a good foster mother,
and when she died,
the Duke could not bear it
and wished to mourn for her.
The officials heard of it
and said:
'According to ancient ritual,
there is no mourning garment for a foster mother.
Now if the ruler wears mourning for her,
it would go against ancient ritual and disrupt the laws of the state.
If you insist on doing it,
the officials will record it to leave for future generations.
Would that not be unacceptable?'
The Duke said:
'In ancient times, the Tiānzǐ wore the Liàn crown when living in leisure.'
The Duke could not bear it,
so he wore the Liàn crown to mourn his foster mother.
Mourning for a foster mother
began with Lǔ Zhāogōng."
7.19 Zēng Zǐ asked:
"When the Zhūhóu meet the Tiānzǐ in a group,
and after entering the gate
they cannot complete the ritual,
how many causes are there for abandonment?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Four."
He asked to hear them.
He said:
"A fire in the Grand Temple,
a solar eclipse,
the death of the Hòu,
or rain soaking the robes and causing loss of composure,
then it is abandoned.
If the Zhūhóu are all present and there is a solar eclipse,
they follow the Tiānzǐ to save the sun,
each with the color of his direction and his weapons.
If there is a fire in the Grand Temple,
they follow the Tiānzǐ to save it from the fire,
but without using directional colors or weapons."
7.20 Zēng Zǐ asked:
"When Zhūhóu meet each other,
and after bowing and yielding they enter the gate,
but cannot complete the ritual,
how many causes are there for abandonment?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Six."
He asked to hear them.
He said:
"The passing of the Tiānzǐ,
a fire in the Grand Temple,
a solar eclipse,
the death of the Hòu or the Fūrén,
or rain soaking the robes and causing loss of composure,
then it is abandoned."
7.21 Zēng Zǐ asked:
"Regarding the Tiānzǐ's sacrifices of Cháng, Dì, Jiāo, Shè, and the Wǔsì,
when the Fǔ and Guǐ vessels are already set out,
and the Tiānzǐ passes away
or the Hòu dies,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It is abandoned."
7.22 Zēng Zǐ asked:
"If during a sacrifice a solar eclipse occurs,
or a fire breaks out in the Grand Temple,
