what should be done about the sacrifice?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Proceed quickly with the sacrifice and that is all.
If the sacrificial animals have arrived
but have not yet been slaughtered,
then it is abandoned."
7.23 When the Tiānzǐ passes away
and has not yet been placed in the coffin,
the Wǔsì sacrifices are not performed.
After being placed in the coffin, the sacrifices are performed;
during those sacrifices,
the personator enters,
eats three mouthfuls of rice, there is no encouragement to eat,
and after the rinsing of the mouth there is no returning of the toast, and that is all.
From the opening of the coffin until the return from wailing,
the Wǔsì sacrifices are not performed.
After the burial, the sacrifices are performed,
and the Zhù completes the offerings, and that is all.
7.24 Zēng Zǐ asked:
"When the Zhūhóu sacrifice to the Shèjì,
and the Zǔ and Dòu vessels are already set out,
and they hear of the Tiānzǐ's passing
or the Hòu's death,
or if their own ruler dies
or his Fūrén dies,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It is abandoned.
From the death until the encoffinment,
and from the opening of the coffin until the return from wailing,
they follow the pattern of the Tiānzǐ."
7.25 Zēng Zǐ asked:
"In the sacrifice of a Dàfū,
when the Dǐng and Zǔ vessels are already set out,
and the Biān and Dòu vessels are already arranged,
and the ritual cannot be completed,
how many causes are there for abandonment?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Nine."
He asked to hear them.
He said:
"The passing of the Tiānzǐ,
the death of the Hòu,
the death of the Ruler,
the death of the Fūrén,
a fire in the Ruler's Grand Temple,
a solar eclipse,
mourning of three years,
the Zīcuī mourning,
or the Dàgōng mourning;
in all these cases, it is abandoned.
External mourning
from Zīcuī downwards
may proceed.
In the sacrifice during Zīcuī mourning,
the personator enters,
eats three mouthfuls, there is no encouragement,
and after the rinsing of the mouth there is no returning toast, and that is all.
During Dàgōng mourning, there is a returning toast, and that is all.
During Xiǎogōng or Sī mourning,
it is just the business within the room and that is all.
The reason why the Shì are different
is that during Sī mourning they do not sacrifice;
as for what they do sacrifice to, if they have no mourning obligation toward the deceased, then they sacrifice."
Zēng Zǐ asked:
"During the three years of mourning,
does one go to offer condolences?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"During the three years of mourning,
after the Liàn sacrifice, one does not stand in groups
and does not travel in a line.
The gentleman uses ritual to adorn his emotions.
To offer condolences and wail while in the three years of mourning—
is that not being insincere?"
Zēng Zǐ asked:
"If a Dàfū or Shì has a private mourning,
and it is time to remove it,
but he is also wearing mourning for his ruler,
how should he remove the private mourning?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"While the mourning for the ruler is on his person,
he does not dare to wear private mourning clothes;
so what is there to remove?
In such a case, the time passes and he does not perform the removal ceremony.
After the mourning for the ruler
is removed, he then performs the Yīnjì sacrifice.
This is the ritual."
7.26 Zēngzǐ asked:
"In the mourning for parents,
is it permissible not to remove the mourning garments?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The former kings established the rites;
not to perform a ceremony after the proper time has passed
is the rite.
It is not that one cannot refrain from removing them,
but one fears exceeding the regulations.
Therefore, the superior man does not offer sacrifices after the proper time has passed;
this is the rite."
7.27 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If a ruler dies
and has already been encoffined,
and then a minister has the mourning for his own parents,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He should return to live at home.
When there are major services at the ruler's court,
he goes to the ruler's place,
but for the morning and evening wailing, he does not."
Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the ruler's coffin has already been moved for burial,
and the minister has the mourning for his parents,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He returns home to wail and then returns to follow the ruler's funeral procession."
Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the ruler has not yet been encoffined,
and the minister has the mourning for his parents,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He returns home for the encoffining,
then returns to the ruler's place.
If there are major services at home, he returns there;
for the morning and evening wailing at the ruler's, he does not attend.
For a Dàfū,
the Shìlǎo manages the family affairs;
for an Officer (Shì),
then the sons and grandsons manage the affairs.
If the wife (Nèizǐ) of a Dàfū
has major services,
she also goes to the ruler's place,
but for the morning and evening wailing, she does not."
7.28 For those of lower rank not to deliver a eulogy for those of higher rank,
and for the young not to deliver a eulogy for the old,
is the rite.
Only the Tiānzǐ
invokes Heaven to eulogize a person.
For feudal lords (Zhūhóu) to eulogize one another
is contrary to the rites.
7.29 Zēngzǐ asked:
"When a ruler goes beyond the borders of his state
with the preparations for the three-year mourning period,
taking an inner coffin (Bēi) with him,
if the ruler dies,
how should his return be handled?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If they have prepared the burial clothes and encoffining,
then the son wears hemp,
the Biànzhì headgear,
the Shūcuī mourning garment,
hemp sandals (Fēi),
and carries a staff.
They enter through the gate of the watchtower (Quē)
and ascend by the western steps.
If it is like the minor dressing (Xiǎoliàn),
then the son wears the Miǎn and follows the coffin,
entering through the main gate
and ascending by the eastern steps (Zuòjiē).
The ruler, the Dàfū, and the Shì follow the same rule."
Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the funeral procession of a ruler has already started
and one hears of the mourning for one's parents,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Complete the service.
After the burial is finished, then return home,
not waiting for the successor's orders."
Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the funeral procession for one's parents has already started
and reached the road,
and one hears of the death of the ruler,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Complete the service.
After the burial is finished,
change the mourning clothes and go to the ruler's."
7.30 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the Zōngzǐ is a Shì
and a cadet son (Shùzǐ) is a Dàfū,
how should the sacrifice be performed?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Sacrifice with the higher-grade victim at the house of the Zōngzǐ.
The invoker (Zhù) shall say:
'The filial son So-and-so for the assistant son (Jièzǐ) So-and-so presents his regular service.'
If the Zōngzǐ has committed an offense
and is living in another state,
and the cadet son is a Dàfū,
when he performs the sacrifice,
the invoker shall say:
'The filial son So-and-so makes the assistant son So-and-so conduct his regular service.'
The acting head (Shèzhǔ) does not perform the Yàn sacrifice,
does not perform the Lǚ toast,
does not request blessings (Jiǎ),
does not perform the Suí sacrifice,
and does not offer associate sacrifices (Pèi).
He sets out the offerings for the guests,
the guests set them down but do not lift them to drink,
and the sacrificial meat is not distributed.
His words to the guests shall be:
'My elder lineage brother, younger lineage brother, or the Zōngzǐ is in another state,
and has sent me to deliver these words.'"
7.31 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the Zōngzǐ has left and is in another state,
and a cadet son who holds no rank is living at home,
may he perform the sacrifice?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He may sacrifice!"
Zēngzǐ asked:
"How should the sacrifice be performed?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He should look towards the grave and build an altar,
and sacrifice there at the proper seasons.
If the Zōngzǐ has died, he reports it at the grave and then sacrifices at home.
After the Zōngzǐ has died, the cadet son states his own name but does not use the word 'filial' (Xiào),
and this continues until his own death.
Among the followers of Zǐyóu,
there were cadet sons who performed sacrifices in this way,
following this principle.
Those who sacrifice today
do not prioritize its underlying meaning,
and thus they are in error regarding the sacrifice."
7.32 Zēngzǐ asked:
"Must there be a personator (Shī) at the sacrifice?
Is it permissible if there is only the Yàn offering?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In sacrificing to one who has completed the full term of life, there must be a personator;
the personator must be a grandson.
If the grandson is young,
then someone is made to carry him.
If there is no grandson,
then someone of the same surname may be chosen.
In sacrificing to a minor (Shāng), there must only be the Yàn offering,
for they did not complete the full term.
To sacrifice to one who completed the full term without a personator
is to treat them as a minor."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"There is the Yin Yàn
and the Yang Yàn."
Zēngzǐ asked:
"Minors are not given the accessory sacrifice (Fù).
What is meant by Yin Yàn and Yang Yàn?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If a Zōngzǐ dies as a minor,
a cadet son does not become his successor.
At his auspicious sacrifice,
a single victim (Tèshēng) is used.
In the sacrifice for a minor, they do not lift
the lungs,
there is no Qízuǒ tray,
no dark liquor (Xuánjiǔ),
and no announcement that the service is successfully completed;
this is called the Yin Yàn.
For all minors
and those who died without heirs,
the sacrifice is held at the house of the Zōngzǐ,
at the bright spot of the room,
with the wine jars in the eastern chamber;
this is called the Yang Yàn."
7.33 Zēngzǐ asked:
"If the funeral procession has already started and reached the main road (Gèng),
and an eclipse of the sun occurs,
should there be any change in the procedure,
or not?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Formerly,
I followed Lǎo Dān in assisting at a burial in Xiàngdǎng.
When we reached the main road,
an eclipse of the sun occurred.
Lǎo Dān said:
'Qiū!
Stop the hearse,
move to the right side of the road,
and cease the wailing to await the passing of the celestial change.'
Once it became bright, we returned to the road and proceeded.
He said:
'This is the rite.'
After returning from the burial,
I, Qiū, asked him, saying:
'A hearse is something that should not be turned back;
when an eclipse of the sun occurs,
one does not know how long it will last;
would it not be better to continue the journey?'"
Lǎo Dān said:
"When the feudal lords pay court to the Tiānzǐ,
they set out when they see the sun
and they rest when the sun sets,
making an offering;
when a Dàfū is sent on a mission,
he sets out when he sees the sun
and he rests when the sun sets.
A coffin should not be brought out early
nor stay out late at night.
Those who travel while seeing the stars—
are they not only criminals and those rushing to the funeral of their parents?
If there is a solar eclipse,
how could one not see the stars?
Moreover, when a Jūnzǐ performs the rites,
he does not use the illness of a relative to cause distress."
I heard this from Lǎo Dān.
7.34 Zēngzǐ asked,
"When one on a mission for the ruler dies in a lodging,
the rites say:
'At a public lodging, the soul is summoned;
at a private lodging, the soul is not summoned.'
In any state to which one is sent,
if the lodging is assigned by an official,
then it is a public lodging;
what then is meant by a private lodging where the soul is not summoned?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"What a fine question!
Houses belonging to the families of Qīng, Dàfū, or Shì
are called private lodgings;
public hostels and places built by the Duke
are called public lodgings.
'Summoning the soul in a public lodging' refers to this."
7.35 Zēngzǐ asked,
"For a child who dies in the lowest stage of premature death:
if they are buried in a brick-lined grave in the garden,
and then carried on a frame to the site,
it is because the distance is short.
Now, if the tomb is far,
how should the burial be conducted?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I heard from Lǎo Dān:
'In the past, Shǐ Yì had a son who died
in the lowest stage of premature death.
Because the tomb was far,'
Shào Gōng said to him:
'Why not place him in a coffin and shroud him within the palace?'
Shǐ Yì said:
'How would I dare to do so?'
Shào Gōng spoke of it to Zhōu Gōng,
and Zhōu Gōng said:
'Why should it not be permitted?'
Shǐ Yì then did so.
Using a coffin and shrouding the coffin for the lowest stage of premature death
began with Shǐ Yì."
7.36 Zēngzǐ asked,
"If a Qīng or Dàfū is about to act as a personator for the Duke,
has already received the invitation for the vigil,
and then has a death in his own family requiring the Zīcuī mourning,
what should be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He goes out
and stays in a public lodging to await the event;
this is the ritual."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When a personator goes out wearing the cap and robes,
the Qīng, Dàfū, and Shì must all dismount for him.
The personator must salute by leaning on the crossbar,
and he must have outriders in front."
7.37 Zǐxià asked,
"When the wailing for the three-year mourning has ended,
and one does not avoid military matters—
is this the ritual
or was it started by the officials?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the Xià Hòu clan, for the three-year mourning,
they returned to their duties after the coffin was placed in the hall.
The people of Yīn returned to their duties after the burial.
The Record says:
'A Jūnzǐ does not take a person away from his kin,
nor can he be taken away from his kin.'
Does it not refer to this?"
Zǐxià said:
"Is it then wrong that
military matters are not avoided?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I heard from Lǎo Dān:
'In the past, Bó Qín, Duke of Lǔ, did this for a specific reason.
Today, as for those who use the three-year mourning period
to follow their own advantage,
I do not know about them!'"
8.1 When Wén Wáng was the heir apparent,
he paid court to Wáng Jì
three times a day.
At the first crow of the cock, he dressed,
went outside the door of the bedchamber,
and asked the attendant of the inner eunuchs:
"Is the King well today?"
The inner eunuch said:
"He is well."
Wén Wáng was then happy.
When it reached midday,
he went again
and did the same.
When it reached evening,
he went again
and did the same.
If there was any disharmony in the King's health,
the inner eunuch would inform Wén Wáng,
and Wén Wáng's face would show worry,
and he could not walk with a steady step.
When Wáng Jì's appetite returned,
then Wén Wáng also returned to his normal state.
When the meal was served,
he would certainly be present
to see if it was at the correct temperature.
When the meal was removed,
he asked what had been eaten.
He commanded the master of the kitchen:
"Do not serve anything that has been warmed over!"
The master replied:
"Yes,"
and then he withdrew.
Wǔ Wáng followed this practice
and did not dare to add anything to it.
When Wén Wáng was ill,
Wǔ Wáng did not remove his cap or belt while nursing him.
If Wén Wáng ate one bowl of food,
he also ate one bowl;
if Wén Wáng ate a second bowl,
he also ate a second bowl.
After twelve days, there was a recovery.
Wén Wáng said to Wǔ Wáng:
"What did you dream?"
Wǔ Wáng replied:
"I dreamt that the Dì gave me nine years."
Wén Wáng said:
"What do you think it meant?"
Wǔ Wáng said:
"There are nine states in the west;
will the King eventually bring peace to them?"
Wén Wáng said:
"No.
In antiquity, age was called niánlíng;
teeth are also called líng.
I am one hundred, and you are ninety;
I give three of my years to you."
Wén Wáng was ninety-seven when he died,
and Wǔ Wáng was ninety-three when he died.
When Chéng Wáng was young
and could not preside over the throne,
Zhōu Gōng acted as regent,
ascending the throne to govern.
He applied the Laws for the Heir Apparent to Bó Qín,
wanting to make Chéng Wáng understand the Way of father and son, ruler and minister, and elder and younger;
if Chéng Wáng made an error,
then he would beat Bó Qín
so as to show Chéng Wáng the Way of an heir apparent.
This was from when Wén Wáng was the heir apparent.
8.2 In the education of the heir apparent and the Shì,
it must be according to the season.
In spring and summer, they learn the shield and spear;
in autumn and winter, they learn the feathers and flute;
all in the Dōng Xù.
The Junior Music Master teaches the shield,
and the Dàxū assists him.
The Flute Master teaches the spear,
and the Assistant Flute Master assists him.
The Xū beat the drums to the Nán music.
In spring they recite and in summer they play the strings,
and the Grand Music Master instructs them.
At the Gǔzōng, in autumn they learn the Rites,
and those who hold the Rites instruct them;
in winter they read the Documents,
and those in charge of the Documents instruct them.
The Rites are in the Gǔzōng,
and the Documents are in the Shàng Xiáng.
8.3 In all sacrifices and the nourishing of the elderly,
the rites of requesting words
and gathering for discourse
are all instructed by the Junior Music Master in the Dōng Xù.
The Grand Music Master teaches the dance with shield and battle-axe,
and the explanations of the discourses.
As for the command to request words,
the Grand Music Master provides the numbers,
and the Dà Sī Chéng discusses and explains them in the Dōng Xù.
8.4 For all who sit in attendance with the Dà Sī Chéng,
those far and near are separated by three mats
so they may ask questions.
When finished, they lean against the wall.
If the list of matters is not yet completed,
they do not ask questions.
8.5 In all learning,
the *Chūnguān* performs the *Shìdiàn* sacrifice to the former teachers in the spring;
it is the same in autumn and winter.
Whenever a school is first established,
a *Shìdiàn* must be performed to the former sages
and former teachers;
when performing these rites,
silk fabrics must be used.
In all *Shìdiàn* ceremonies,
there must be a general assembly;
if there is a national misfortune, this is not the case.
8.6 Whenever there is a Great Harmonious Music performance,
it must be followed by the ritual of nourishing the elderly.
Whenever a discourse is held in the *Jiāo*,
virtuous and talented men must be selected from there.
Some are advanced because of their virtue;
some are promoted because of their achievements;
some are praised because of their words.
Those with minor skills are all cautioned
to await further discourse.
If they appear three times and excel in one of these areas,
then their rank is advanced
according to their order,
and they are called *Jiāorén*.
They are sent afar to the *Chéngjūn*,
and eventually take the cup from the superior vessel.
8.7 When first establishing a school,
after the ritual vessels have been prepared and the silk used,
the *Shìcài* is then performed.
There is no dancing and no handing over of ritual implements,
and then they withdraw.
They host the guest in the *Dōngxù*;
there is a single offering of wine;
it is acceptable to have no assistant and to hold a discourse.
Teaching the *Shìzǐ*.
8.8 In all cases, the Three Kings taught the *Shìzǐ* using *Lǐ* and *Yuè*.
*Yuè*
is for cultivating the internal;
*Lǐ*
is for cultivating the external.
When *Lǐ* and *Yuè* are intertwined within
and manifest in form without,
then their completion results in joy,
respectfulness, and gentle refinement.
A *Dàfù* and a *Shǎofù* are appointed to nurture him,
desiring him to know the Way of father and son, and ruler and minister.
The *Dàfù* examines the Way of father and son, and ruler and minister to demonstrate it to him;
the *Shǎofù* assists the *Shìzǐ*
so that he may observe the *Dàfù*’s virtuous conduct and carefully explain it to him.
The *Dàfù* is in front,
the *Shǎofù* is behind;
inside, there is the *Bǎo*,
and outside, there is the *Shī*.
Thus, through teaching and explanation, virtue is perfected.
As for the *Shī*,
they teach him through various matters and explain virtue to him;
as for the *Bǎo*,
they are cautious regarding his person to support him and guide him back to the Way.
The *Jì* says:
“In *Yú*, *Xià*, *Shāng*, and *Zhōu*,
there were the *Shī* and *Bǎo*,
and there were the *Yí* and *Chéng*;
they established the four *Fǔ* and the three *Gōng*.
It was not necessary to fill every post;
they only sought the right person.”
This means employing the capable.
The *Jūnzǐ* says: “When virtue is perfected,
teaching is respected;
when teaching is respected, offices are upright;
when offices are upright, the state is well-governed.”
This refers to the ruler.
*Zhòngní* said:
“In the past, *Zhōugōng* acted as regent,
ascending the throne to govern.
He applied the *Shìzǐ Fǎ* to *Bóqín*
in order to perfect *Chéngwáng*.
I have heard it said:
‘For one who is a minister,
if sacrificing his life benefits the ruler, he does it.’
How much more so should he use his person to benefit his ruler?
*Zhōugōng* was more than capable of doing this!”
For this reason, one must know how to be a son
before one can be a father;
one must know how to be a minister
before one can be a ruler;
one must know how to serve others
before one can command others.
*Chéngwáng* was young
and could not ascend the throne;
as he was the *Shìzǐ*,
there was nothing for him to do.
Therefore, the *Shìzǐ Fǎ* was applied to *Bóqín*,
causing him to live with *Chéngwáng*,
desiring to make *Chéngwáng* know
the righteousness of father and son, ruler and minister, and senior and junior.
The ruler in relation to the *Shìzǐ*:
by kinship, he is the father;
by status, he is the ruler.
Having the affection of a father
and the dignity of a ruler,
he can then encompass and possess the world.
For this reason,
one cannot but be cautious in nurturing the *Shìzǐ*.
To perform one action and obtain three benefits
is only possible through the *Shìzǐ*.
This refers to his ranking by age in the school.
Therefore, when the *Shìzǐ* is ranked by age in the school,
the people of the state observe it and say:
“He who will be my ruler
yields to me based on age; why is this?”
The answer is:
“Since his father is alive, *Lǐ* dictates it so.”
Thus, the masses understand the Way of father and son.
Secondly, they say:
“He who will be my ruler yields to me based on age;
why is this?”
The answer is:
“Since the ruler is alive, *Lǐ* dictates it so.”
Thus, the masses understand the righteousness of ruler and minister.
Thirdly, they say:
“He who will be my ruler yields to me based on age;
why is this?”
The answer is:
“He treats the elderly as elderly.”
Thus, the masses understand the protocols of senior and junior.
Therefore, while the father is alive, he acts as a son;
while the ruler is alive, he is called a minister.
Occupying the protocols of a son and a minister
is how he honors the ruler and loves his kin.
Thus, he learns to be a father and son,
he learns to be a ruler and minister,
and he learns to be a senior and junior.
When the ways of father and son,
ruler and minister,
and senior and junior are attained,
then the state is well-governed.
A saying goes:
“When the *Yuèzhèng* oversees the studies
and the *Fùshī* oversee the completion,
once there is one great and good person,
the myriad states will be upright.”
This refers to the *Shìzǐ*.
*Zhōugōng* ascended the throne.
The *Shùzǐ* who regulates the members of the ducal clan
taught them filial piety, brotherly respect, harmony, friendship, and fatherly love,
clarifying the righteousness of father and son
and the order of senior and junior.
When they attended court before the Duke:
in the Inner Court,
they faced east with the north as the place of honor;
if there were noble ministers,
they were arranged by age.
In the Outer Court,
they were arranged by office;
the *Sīshì* managed this.
In the Ancestral Temple,
they were in the same positions as in the Outer Court.
The *Zōngrén* assigned duties
according to rank and office.
When ascending to partake of the leftovers, making offerings, or receiving the cup,
it was done according to the primary heirs.
The *Shùzǐ* managed them;
even if someone had the three appointments of rank,
they did not overstep their father or elder brother.
During the Duke's great affairs,
they were ordered by the fineness or coarseness of their mourning garments.
Even in the mourning of the ducal clan, it was the same,
following the chief mourner in order.
If the Duke held a feast with the clan,
then those of different surnames were guests,
the *Shànzǎi* was the host,
and the Duke was ranked by age with his paternal uncles and brothers.
In clan meals, the rank decreased by one level with each generation.
8.9 In the army,
they guarded the *Gōngní*.
If the Duke had affairs beyond the borders,
the *Shùzǐ* would lead those of the ducal clan who had no duties to guard the Duke's palace;
the *Zhèngshì* guarded the *Tàimiào*,
the paternal uncles guarded the noble palaces and noble rooms,
and the sons and grandsons guarded the lower palaces and lower rooms.
8.10 As for the grandsons of the *Wǔmiào*,
as long as the ancestral temple has not been destroyed,
even if they are commoners,
when they have their capping ceremony
or take a wife,
they must inform the clan head;
when they die,
a funeral notice must be sent;
at the *liàn* and *xiáng* sacrifices, they inform him.
Regarding the mutual relations of the clan members:
if one should condole but does not,
or should wear the mourning headband but does not,
the officials shall punish them.
As for the gifts of horses and carriages,
funeral money, assistance,
and the burial jade,
there are specific regulations for all.
If a member of the *Gōngzú* commits a capital offense,
he is strangled by the *Diànrén*.
For crimes involving corporal punishment,
he is subjected to light or heavy beating,
which is also reported to the *Diànrén*.
Members of the *Gōngzú* are not subjected to castration.
When the case is concluded,
the officials report the verdict to the *Gōng*.
For a capital offense,
they say: "The crime of so-and-so falls under the *dàpì*";
for a corporal punishment offense,
they say: "The crime of so-and-so falls under the *xiǎopì*."
The *Gōng* says:
"Pardon him."
The officials say again:
"It is according to the law."
The *Gōng* says again:
"Pardon him."
The officials say again:
"It is according to the law."
After the third pardon,
if there is no response,
the official exits
and delivers the punishment to the *Diànrén*.
The *Gōng* then sends someone to pursue him, saying:
"Even so,
you must pardon him."
The official responds:
"It is too late!"
He reports back to the *Gōng*,
who then wears plain white clothes and abstains from full meals,
changing his routine for the deceased,
as if for a relative of that rank.
Although he does not wear formal mourning attire,
he personally wails for him.
8.11 Members of the *Gōngzú* attend court at the Inner Court,
to show intimacy within the clan.
Even if some are noble, they are ranked by age,
to clarify the relationship between fathers and sons.
At the Outer Court, they are ranked by office,
to treat those of different surnames appropriately.
Within the ancestral temple,
positions are based on rank,
to honor virtue.
The *Zōngrén* assigns tasks based on office,
to respect the worthy.
Ascending to eat the leftovers and receiving the cup are done by the eldest heir,
which is the way to honor the ancestors.
Mourning rites are ordered by the weight of the garments,
so as not to infringe upon personal kinship.
When the *Gōng* feasts with his clan, it is done by age,
and thus the way of filial piety and fraternal duty is achieved.
In their communal meals, the ranking decreases by one degree with each generation,
reflecting the diminishing degrees of kinship.
In battle, they guard the *Gōngmǐ*,
showing the depth of filial love.
The principal sons guard the *Dàmiào*,
to honor the ancestral line,
and thus the way of ruler and subject is manifested.
Uncles and elder brothers guard the noble chambers,
while younger sons and brothers guard the lower chambers,
and thus the way of yielding is achieved.
8.12 Descendants within five generations,
as long as the ancestral temple has not been dismantled,
even if they have become commoners, when they are capped
or take a wife, they must report it,
and their deaths must be announced,
so as not to forget their kinship.
Though the kinship is not severed, being ranked among commoners
is due to a lack of ability.
Respectfully offering condolences, visiting the bereaved, and giving funeral gifts
is the way of harmony and friendship.
In ancient times,
when the office of the *Shùzǐ* was well-managed,
the state had proper order.
When the state has order,
the people in the various regions follow the correct direction.
Regarding the crimes of the *Gōngzú*,
though they are kin, they are not allowed to violate the authority of the officials;
this is the correct method,
and it is the way to show consideration for the common people.
Punishing them in private
is so as not to cause the people of the state to witness the punishment of brothers.
The ruler does not offer condolences,
does not wear mourning clothes,
and wails in the temple of a different surname,
because the offender has disgraced the ancestors and must be distanced.
Wearing plain clothes and living outside,
and not listening to music,
is mourning him privately,
showing that the bond of flesh and blood is never severed.
The *Gōngzú* are not subjected to castration,
so as not to cut off their lineage.
8.13 When the *Tiānzǐ* inspects the school,
the drums are beaten at dawn to summon everyone,
which is how the multitude is alerted.
Once the multitude has arrived,
only then does the *Tiānzǐ* arrive.
He then orders the officials to perform their duties.
They establish the ranks and regulations
and offer sacrifices to the former teachers
and former sages.
When the officials finish their tasks,
they report back.
At the start of the nourishment ceremony:
he goes to the *Dōngxù*,
performs the *shìdiàn* sacrifice to the former elders,
and then sets out the seats for the *Sānlǎo*,
the *Wǔgēng*,
and the other elders.
He goes to inspect the food and examine the sweet wine,
and the delicacies for nourishing the elderly
are all prepared;
then songs are chanted,
and they retire to cultivate the practice of filial nourishment.
Returning,
they ascend to sing the *Qīng Miào*,
and after singing, there is discourse,
to complete the rite.
They speak of the way of father and son,
ruler and subject,
and elder and youth;
harmonizing with the ultimate reach of virtuous sounds,
this is the greatest of rites.
Below, the flutes play the *Xiàng*,
and they dance the *Dà Wǔ*.
The great assembly is gathered for these matters
to connect with the spirits
and to promote those of virtue.
Correcting the positions of ruler and subject
and the grades of noble and humble,
the righteousness of superior and inferior is carried out.
The officials report that the music has ended,
and the *Wáng* then orders the *Gōng*,
*Hóu*, *Bó*,
*Zǐ*, *Nán*, and the various officials, saying:
"Return
and nourish the old and the young at the *Dōngxù*."
Ending it with benevolence.
8.14 Therefore,
when the sages record these matters,
they consider them with greatness,
love with respect,
act according to ritual,
cultivate with filial nourishment,
order them with righteousness,
and end them with benevolence.
8.15 Therefore, whenever the people of old undertook a matter,
everyone knew the completeness of their virtue.
The *jūnzǐ* of old,
when undertaking great matters,
were always careful about the beginning and the end;
how could the people then not understand?
The *Yuè Mìng* says:
"In thinking of the beginning and the end, let your standard be in learning."
The *Shìzǐ zhī Jì* says:
Morning and evening, he went to the outside of the door of the *Dàqǐn*,
and asked the *nèishù*:
"How is the health today?"
The *nèishù* said:
"Today it is peaceful."
The *Shìzǐ* then showed a joyful expression.
If there was any lack of comfort,
the *nèishù* would tell the *Shìzǐ*,
and the *Shìzǐ*'s expression would be filled with worry.
When the *nèishù* said "He has returned to his original state,"
only then would he also return to his original state.
When the morning and evening meals were served,
the *Shìzǐ* would certainly be present
to check the temperature.
When the food was cleared away,
he asked what had been eaten.
He made sure to know what was served,
gave instructions to the *shànzǎi*,
and then retired.
If the *nèishù* said "He is ill,"
the *Shìzǐ* would personally purify himself and wear dark garments to care for him.
He would respectfully inspect
the dishes prepared by the *shànzǎi*.
He would personally taste
the medicine for the illness.
If the tasting showed the food was good,
the *Shìzǐ* could also eat;
if the ruler ate little,
the *Shìzǐ* would also not eat to satisfaction;
this continued until the ruler returned to health,
and only then would he also return to his normal state.
9.1 Formerly, when *Zhòngní* was present as a guest at the *Zhà* sacrifice,
after the ceremony was finished,
he went out and walked above the gatehouse towers,
where he sighed deeply.
The sigh of *Zhòngní*
was likely a sigh for the state of *Lǔ*.
Yán Yǎn was by his side and asked:
"Master, why do you sigh?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When the Great Way was practiced,
and during the eras of the heroes of the Three Dynasties (Sāndài),
I, Qiū, was not able to reach those times,
but I have a record of them.
When the Great Way was practiced,
the world was shared by all.
The virtuous and capable were chosen,
sincerity was emphasized and harmony cultivated.
Thus, people did not treat only their own parents as parents,
nor only their own children as children.
The aged were provided for until their end,
the able-bodied had employment,
the young were provided with growth,
and the widowers, widows, orphans, the childless, and the disabled
were all supported.
Men had their roles,
and women had their homes.
Wealth was disliked if it was wasted on the ground,
but it did not have to be hidden for one's own use;
physical labor was disliked if it did not come from oneself,
but it was not necessarily performed for oneself.
For this reason,
intrigues were shut down and did not arise,
and robberies, thefts, and rebellious outrages did not occur,
so that outer doors did not need to be closed.
This was called the Great Unity (Dàtóng).
Now the Great Way has become obscure,
and the world is shared only within families.
Everyone treats only their own parents as parents,
and only their own children as children.
Wealth and labor are for oneself.
The great men establish hereditary succession as the ritual.
City walls, moats, and ditches are made for security.
Ritual and righteousness are the guiding principles:
to regulate ruler and subject,
to deepen the bond between father and son,
to harmonize brothers,
to bring concord to husband and wife,
to establish institutions,
to arrange fields and hamlets,
to honor the brave and wise,
and to claim merit for oneself.
Therefore, intrigues arise from this,
and warfare starts because of it.
Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, Chéng Wáng, and Zhōu Gōng
were the chosen ones of this period.
These six gentlemen
were never anything but careful regarding ritual.
They used it to manifest righteousness,
to verify sincerity,
to expose errors,
to model benevolence and emphasize yielding,
and to show the people the constant norms.
If anyone did not follow this,
those in power were removed,
and the masses regarded them as a calamity.
This was called the Lesser Prosperity (Xiǎokāng)."
9.2 Yán Yǎn asked again:
"Is ritual truly so urgent?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Indeed, ritual
is what the ancient kings used to receive the Way of Heaven
and to govern human emotions.
Therefore, those who lose it die,
and those who attain it live.
The Shī states:
'Look at that rat, it has a body;
a man who has no ritual—
a man who has no ritual,
why does he not die quickly!'
For this reason, ritual
must be rooted in Heaven,
patterned after Earth,
arrayed among the ghosts and spirits,
and extended to funerals, sacrifices,
archery, charioteering, capping, marriage,
audiences, and diplomatic visits.
Thus the sages used ritual to show these things,
so the world, the states, and the families could be set right."
9.3 Yán Yǎn asked again:
"The Master's exhaustive discourse on ritual—
may I hear more of it?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I wished to observe the way of Xià,
so I went to Qǐ,
but there was insufficient evidence;
however, I obtained the Xiàshí.
I wished to observe the way of Yīn,
so I went to Sòng,
but there was insufficient evidence;
however, I obtained the Kūnqián.
The meaning of Kūnqián
and the order of the Xiàshí—
I used these to observe it.
9.4 "The origin of ritual
began with food and drink.
They roasted millet and split open piglets;
they dug hollows in the ground for jars and drank with their hands;
they used straw drumsticks and clay drums;
yet they were still able to convey their respect to the ghosts and spirits.
When someone died,
they would climb onto the roof and shout,
announcing:
'Gāo!
Come back, so-and-so!'
After that, they fed the deceased raw grain and offered cooked meat in straw.
Thus they looked to heaven and buried in the earth;
the body and animal soul descend,
while the conscious spirit is above.
Therefore, the dead face north
and the living face south,
all following the original ways.
9.5 "In ancient times, the former kings
had no palaces or houses.
In winter they lived in caves,
and in summer in nests of branches.
They had no knowledge of fire for transformation,
so they ate the fruits of plants and trees
and the flesh of birds and beasts,
drinking their blood
and swallowing their fur and feathers.
They had no hemp or silk,
and wore feathers and skins.
9.6 "Later sages arose,
and then cultivated the benefits of fire,
casting metal and molding earth
to make terraces, towers, palaces, houses, windows, and doors.
They used fire to bake, roast,
boil, and broil.
They made sweet wine and vinegar.
They worked hemp and silk
to make cloth and fabric,
using them to nourish the living and bury the dead,
and to serve the ghosts, spirits, and the High Lord.
All followed the original beginnings.
9.7 "Therefore, the dark water is in the room,
the sweet wine and clear wine are by the door,
the millet wine is in the hall,
and the clarified wine is below.
They set out the sacrificial animals,
prepare the tripods and stands,
array the qín, sè, flutes, lithophones, bells, and drums,
and refine the prayers and blessings,
to bring down the spirits from above and their ancestors.
To regulate ruler and subject,
to deepen the bond between father and son,
to harmonize brothers,
to align superior and inferior;
husband and wife have their proper places.
This is called receiving the blessings of Heaven.
9.8 "They craft the invocations and titles,
offer dark water in sacrifice,
present the blood and fur,
place raw meat on the stands,
cook the sacrificial meats,
use mats of rushes,
cover with coarse cloth,
wear washed silk,
offer sweet wine and clear wine,
and present roasted and broiled meats.
The ruler and his wife exchange offerings,
to gratify the spirits and souls.
This is called the Union of the Invisible.
9.9 "Afterward they withdraw and join in boiling the meats,
dismembering the dogs, pigs, oxen, and sheep,
and filling the fǔ, guǐ, biān, and dòu vessels and the soup cauldrons.
The invoker reports with filial piety,
and the blessing is reported with kindness.
This is called the Great Auspiciousness.
This is the great completion of ritual.
9.10 Kǒngzǐ said:
"Alas, how sad!
I observe the way of Zhōu,
and Kings Yōu and Lì damaged it.
If I leave Lǔ, where should I go?
The Border (Jiāo) and Great Ancestral (Dì) sacrifices of Lǔ
are contrary to ritual;
the legacy of Zhōu Gōng has surely declined!
The Jiāo sacrifice of Qǐ is to Yǔ;
the Jiāo sacrifice of Sòng is to Xiè.
These are the duties maintained by the Son of Heaven.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
while the feudal lords sacrifice to the spirits of the land and grain.
9.11 "The prayers and blessings dare not change their ancient constants.
This is called the Great Magnitude (Dàjiǎ).
9.12 "If the words of prayers and blessings
are hidden away by the lineage officials, invokers, shamans, and scribes,
it is contrary to ritual;
this is called a darkened state (Yōuguó).
If the clear wine and the jiǎ-cups reach the personators and the ruler out of order,
it is contrary to ritual;
this is called an usurping ruler."
9.13 "For the *Miǎn*, *Biàn*, weapons, and armor to be stored in private households,
is contrary to the *Lǐ*,
and this is called intimidating the ruler.
9.14 "For a *Dàfū* to have a full complement of officials,
for sacrificial vessels not to be borrowed,
and for musical instruments to be fully provided,
is contrary to the *Lǐ*,
and this is called disordering the state.
9.15 "Therefore, one who serves in the public sphere is called a *Chén*,
while one who serves in a household is called a *Pú*.
During the three-year mourning period,
or for one who has newly married,
for one year no duties are assigned.
To enter the court in mourning garments,
or to live mixed and on equal footing with household *Pú*,
is contrary to the *Lǐ*,
and this is called the ruler and the *Chén* sharing the state.
Therefore, the *Tiānzǐ* has fields to settle his descendants,
the *Zhūhóu* have states to settle their descendants,
and the *Dàfū* have *Cǎi* to settle their descendants;
this is called the system of regulations.
Thus, when the *Tiānzǐ* visits the *Zhūhóu*,
he must reside in their ancestral temple,
and if he does not enter with the ritual records,
this is called the *Tiānzǐ* destroying the laws and disordering the discipline.
For the *Zhūhóu*, except for inquiring after illness or condoling a death,
to enter the house of a *Chén*
is called the ruler and *Chén* engaging in levity.
9.16 "For this reason,
the *Lǐ* are the great handle of the ruler,
used to distinguish suspicions and clarify subtleties,
to host the ghosts and spirits,
to examine the system of regulations,
and to distinguish *Rén* and *Yì*;
they are the means to govern the administration and secure the ruler.
Therefore, if the administration is not correct,
then the ruler's position is endangered;
if the ruler's position is endangered,
then the high ministers will rebel,
and the lesser officials will steal.
If punishments are severe and customs are corrupt,
then the laws will lack constancy.
If laws lack constancy,
then the *Lǐ* will lack rank.
If the *Lǐ* lack rank,
then the *Shì* will not serve.
If punishments are severe and customs are corrupt,
then the people will not return their allegiance;
this is called a diseased state.
9.17 "Therefore, the administration
is that by which the ruler preserves himself.
For this reason, the administration
must be rooted in *Tiān*,
and through blending descend as mandates.
When the mandate descends to the *Shè*, it is called blending with the Earth;
when it descends to the ancestral temple, it is called *Rén* and *Yì*;
when it descends to the mountains and rivers, it is called undertaking tasks;
when it descends to the *Wǔsì*, it is called the system of regulations.
This is the means by which the *Shèngrén* secures his person.
9.18 "Therefore, the *Shèngrén* forms a triad with Heaven and Earth,
and stands alongside the ghosts and spirits
to govern the administration.
He abides in what they preserve,
which is the order of the *Lǐ*;
he enjoys what they delight in,
which is the governance of the people.
Thus, Heaven produces the seasons and Earth produces wealth;
man—his father gives him life and his teacher instructs him.
These four,
the ruler uses correctly,
so the ruler stands in a position free from error.
9.19 "Therefore, the ruler is one who is enlightened by others,
not one who enlightens others.
The ruler is one who is nourished by others,
not one who nourishes others.
The ruler is one who is served by others,
not one who serves others.
Thus, if the ruler enlightens others, he will make errors;
if he nourishes others, he will be insufficient;
if he serves others, he will lose his position.
Therefore, the common people take the ruler as their pattern to govern themselves,
nourish the ruler to secure themselves,
and serve the ruler to make themselves manifest.
Thus, when the *Lǐ* are realized and roles are fixed,
people will all cherish their deaths and worry about their lives.
9.20 "Therefore, use men's wisdom but remove their craftiness;
use men's courage but remove their anger;
use men's *Rén* but remove their greed.
9.21 "Therefore, when the state faces calamity,
a ruler dying for the *Shèjì* is called *Yì*,
while a *Dàfū* dying for the ancestral temple is called an extraordinary event.
9.22 "Therefore, the *Shèngrén* is able to treat the world as one family
and the *Zhōngguó* as one person,
not because of a mere thought,
but because he must know their feelings,
be open to their *Yì*,
be clear about their benefits,
and understand their calamities;
only then can he accomplish this.
9.23 "What are human feelings?
Joy, anger, grief, fear, love, hate, and desire;
these seven
are things men can do without learning.
What is human *Yì*?
Kindness in the father,
filial piety in the son,
goodness in the elder brother,
fraternal respect in the younger brother,
*Yì* in the husband,
obedience in the wife,
benevolence in the elders,
compliance in the youth,
*Rén* in the ruler,
and loyalty in the *Chén*;
these ten
are what are called human *Yì*.
Cultivating trust and promoting harmony
are called human benefits.
Strife, plunder, and mutual killing
are called human calamities.
Therefore, as for the means by which the *Shèngrén* governs the seven human feelings,
cultivates the ten *Yì*,
promotes trust and harmony,
prizes courtesy and yielding,
and removes strife and plunder,
if he sets aside the *Lǐ*, by what else could he govern them?
Drinking, eating, and the relation between male and female—
man's greatest desires reside therein.
Death, poverty, and suffering—
man's greatest dislikes reside therein.
Thus, desires and dislikes
are the great starting points of the heart.
Men hide their hearts,
and they cannot be measured or fathomed;
beauty and ugliness are both in their hearts, but not visible in their expressions.
If one wishes to unify them and examine them to the end,
if he sets aside the *Lǐ*, what else is there?
9.24 "Therefore, man
is the virtue of Heaven and Earth,
the intersection of *Yīn* and *Yáng*,
the meeting of ghosts and spirits,
and the refined energy of the *Wǔxíng*.
9.25 "Therefore, Heaven holds the *Yáng*
and hangs out the sun and stars;
Earth holds the *Yīn*
and opens up through the mountains and rivers.
Distributing the *Wǔxíng* throughout the four seasons,
after they are in harmony, the moon is born.
Thus, in three periods of five days it is full,
and in three periods of five days it is waning.
The movements of the *Wǔxíng*
successively exhaust one another.
The *Wǔxíng*, the four seasons, and the twelve months
revert to being each other's root.
The five tones, the *Liùlǜ*, and the twelve tubes
revert to being each other's *Gōng*.
The five flavors, the six harmonies, and the twelve meals
revert to being each other's substance.
The five colors, the six patterns, and the twelve garments
revert to being each other's substance.
9.26 "Therefore, man
is the heart of Heaven and Earth,
the tip of the *Wǔxíng*,
one who is born eating flavors, distinguishing sounds, and wearing colors.
Therefore, when the *Shèngrén* acts,
he must take Heaven and Earth as the root,
*Yīn* and *Yáng* as the starting point,
the four seasons as the handle,
the sun and stars as the record,
the moon as the measure,
the ghosts and spirits as the companions,
the *Wǔxíng* as the substance,
the *Lǐ* and *Yì* as the tools,
human feelings as the field,
and the *Sìlíng* as the livestock.
By taking Heaven and Earth as the root,
things can be raised.
By taking *Yīn* and *Yáng* as the starting point,
feelings can be seen.
By taking the four seasons as the handle,
tasks can be encouraged.
By taking the sun and stars as the record,
tasks can be arranged.
By taking the moon as the measure,
achievements can be regulated.
By taking the ghosts and spirits as companions,
tasks can be guarded.
By taking the *Wǔxíng* as the substance,
tasks can be repeated.
By taking the *Lǐ* and *Yì* as the tools,
the practice of tasks can be examined.
By taking human feelings as the field,
people are made the profound interior.
By taking the *Sìlíng* as the livestock,
drinking and eating have their source.
What are the *Sìlíng*?
The *Lín*, the *Fèng*, the *Guī*, and the *Lóng*;
these are called the *Sìlíng*.
Therefore, when the *Lóng* is kept as livestock,
the fish and sturgeon do not scatter in alarm.
When the Fèng is treated as a domestic animal,
the birds are not startled.
When the Lín is treated as a domestic animal,
the beasts do not flee in terror.
When the Guī is treated as a domestic animal,
human feelings are not lost.
9.27 "Therefore the former kings grasped the milfoil and the Guī,
arranged the sacrifices,
buried the silks,
proclaimed the words of prayer and blessing,
and established systems and regulations.
Thus the state had Lǐ,
the officials had governance,
affairs had specific duties,
and Lǐ had order.
9.28 "Therefore the former kings were concerned that Lǐ might not reach those below.
9.29 "Therefore they sacrificed to the Dì at the suburb,
so as to determine the position of Heaven;
they sacrificed to the Shè in the state,
so as to arrange the benefits of the Earth;
they sacrificed at the ancestral temple, so as to root themselves in Rén;
they sacrificed to mountains and rivers, so as to host the ghosts and spirits;
and they performed the five sacrifices, so as to root themselves in human affairs.
Thus the master of ceremonies and the invoker were in the temple,
the Sāngōng were in the court,
and the Sānlǎo were in the school.
Before the King
was the Wū and behind him was the Shǐ;
diviners, musicians, and attendants were all on his left and right.
The King was in the
center with a mind of Wúwéi,
so as to maintain ultimate uprightness.
9.30 "Therefore, when Lǐ is performed at the suburb,
the hundred spirits receive their duties there;
when Lǐ is performed at the Shè,
all products can be fully realized;
when Lǐ is performed at the ancestral temple,
filial piety and parental kindness are practiced there;
when Lǐ is performed for the five sacrifices,
correct laws are exemplified there.
Therefore, from the suburb, Shè, ancestral temple, mountains and rivers, to the five sacrifices,
these are the cultivation of Yì and the repository of Lǐ.
9.31 "For this reason, Lǐ
must be rooted in the Dàyī,
which divided to become Heaven and Earth,
revolved to become Yīn and Yáng,
transformed to become the four seasons,
and arranged to become ghosts and spirits.
Its descent is called mandate,
and its office is in Heaven.
9.32 "Lǐ must be rooted in Heaven,
move upon the Earth,
be arranged in affairs,
and change according to the seasons,
harmonizing with the divisions of skills.
Its residence in humans is called nourishment;
it is practiced through goods, labor,
and yielding:
in drinking, eating,
capping, marriage,
mourning, sacrifice,
archery, charioteering,
court audiences, and diplomatic visits.
9.33 "Therefore Lǐ and Yì
are the great principles of humanity,
used to promote sincerity and cultivate harmony,
and to strengthen the joints of human flesh
and the binding of sinews and bones.
They are the great principles for nourishing the living, seeing off the dead, and serving the ghosts and spirits.
They are the great channel for reaching the Tiāndào and following human feelings.
9.34 "Therefore, only the sage knows that Lǐ cannot be abandoned.
Thus, to ruin a state, destroy a family, or perish a person,
one must first discard their Lǐ.
Therefore, Lǐ is to humans
what yeast is to wine;
the Jūnzǐ uses it to become substantial,
while the Xiǎorén uses it to become superficial.
9.35 "Therefore the sage-kings cultivated the handle of Yì
and the order of Lǐ
to govern human feelings.
Thus human feelings
are the field of the sage-king.
He cultivates Lǐ to plow it,
displays Yì to plant it,
explains learning to weed it,
roots in Rén to gather it,
and spreads music to bring peace to it.
Therefore Lǐ
is the substance of Yì.
If it harmonizes with Yì,
then even if a Lǐ was not something the former kings had,
it can be initiated based on Yì.
Yì is the division of skills
and the measure of Rén.
Those who harmonize with skills
and explain Rén
will become strong if they attain it.
Rén
is the root of Yì
and the substance of compliance;
those who attain it will be honored.
Therefore, governing a state without Lǐ
is like plowing without a plowshare.
Performing Lǐ without rooting it in Yì
is like plowing without planting.
Pursuing Yì without explaining it through learning
is like planting without weeding.
Explaining through learning
without uniting it with Rén
is like weeding without harvesting.
Uniting with Rén
without bringing peace through music
is like harvesting without eating.
Bringing peace through music
without reaching compliance
is like eating without getting fat.
When the four limbs are correct,
and the skin is full and firm,
that is the prosperity of a person.
When father and son are devoted,
brothers are harmonious,
and husband and wife are in concord,
that is the prosperity of the family.
When great ministers follow the law,
minor officials are incorruptible,
offices are ordered,
and ruler and subject correct each other,
that is the prosperity of the state.
The Tiānzǐ uses virtue as his carriage
and music as his driver.
The Zhūhóu associate through Lǐ,
the Dàfū are ordered by law,
the Shì examine each other through sincerity,
and the Bǎixìng maintain each other through harmony;
this is the prosperity of the world.
This is called Dàshùn.
Dàshùn
is the constant way to nourish the living, see off the dead, and serve the ghosts and spirits.
Thus, great affairs accumulate without becoming stagnant,
move together without confusion,
and small actions are performed without error.
It is deep yet penetrating,
flourishing yet ordered.
They are connected yet do not overlap,
and move without harming each other;
this is the height of compliance.
Therefore, by being clear about compliance,
one can then maintain safety in times of danger.
9.36 "Therefore, differences in Lǐ,
whether abundant
or reduced,
are used to sustain feelings and harmonize in danger.
Thus, how the sage-kings practiced compliance:
they did not let those on mountains live by rivers,
nor those on islands live on the plains,
and they did not let things fall into ruin.
They used water, fire, metal, and wood,
and ate and drank according to the seasons.
They matched men and women
and distributed ranks and positions
according to age and virtue.
They employed the people according to compliance.
Thus, there were no disasters of floods, droughts, or insects,
and the people had no calamities of famine or ominous diseases.
Thus, Heaven did not withhold its Way,
Earth did not withhold its treasures,
and humans did not withhold their feelings.
Thus, Heaven sent down sweet dew,
Earth brought forth sweet springs,
the mountains yielded vessels and chariots,
and the Hé brought forth the Hétú.
The Fènghuáng and Qílín were all in the suburbs,
and the Guī and Lóng were in the palace ponds;
as for the eggs and embryos of the other birds and beasts,
they could all be looked down upon and observed.
This was for no other reason than that
the former kings were able to cultivate Lǐ to reach Yì
and embody sincerity to reach compliance;
this is the reality of compliance."
10.1 Lǐqì (The Ritual Vessels),
are therefore the Great Preparation.
The Great Preparation is abundant virtue.
Lǐ removes crookedness
and increases beautiful qualities.
When established, they are correct;
when applied, they are effective.
In a person,
it is like the outer skin of bamboo;
or like the heart of pine and cypress.
These two are the great principles of the world.
Thus, they pass through the four seasons without changing their branches or leaves.
Therefore, when a Jūnzǐ has Lǐ,
he is harmonious externally and has no resentment internally.
Thus, all things cherish Rén,
and the ghosts and spirits enjoy his virtue.
10.2 When the former kings established the rites,
they had a basis and they had ornamentation.
Loyalty and good faith
are the basis of rites;
righteousness and principles
are the ornamentation of rites.
Without the basis, they cannot be established;
without the ornamentation, they cannot be practiced.
10.3 Rites
harmonize with the seasons of Heaven,
utilize the resources of Earth,
are in accord with the ghosts and spirits,
harmonize with the hearts of men,
and are that which orders the myriad things.
Therefore, the seasons of Heaven have their productions;
the geography of Earth has its suitabilities;
the offices of men have their abilities;
and the various properties of things have their benefits.
Therefore, if Heaven does not produce it
and Earth does not nourish it,
the *Jūnzǐ* does not use it for rites,
and the ghosts and spirits will not accept it as an offering.
To live in the mountains and use fish and turtles for rites,
or to live in the marshes and use deer and pigs for rites,
the *Jūnzǐ* calls this "not knowing the rites."
Therefore, one must take the fixed resources of the state
to establish the great constants of rites
and the great order of rites,
based on the breadth or narrowness of the land,
the simplicity or abundance of the rites,
and the quality of the harvest.
Therefore, even though the harvest is greatly reduced,
the masses are not fearful or anxious.
Thus, the ruler's regulation of rites is moderate.
10.4 In rites,
timeliness is the most important,
accordance is next,
the substance is next,
suitability is next,
and proportion is next.
*Yáo* handed the throne to *Shùn*,
*Shùn* handed the throne to *Yǔ*.
*Tāng* exiled *Jié*,
*Wǔ Wáng* attacked *Zhòu*.
These were matters of timeliness.
The *Shī* says:
"It was not that he changed his plans,
but that he followed his ancestral filial piety."
10.5 The sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
the affairs of the ancestral temple,
the way of father and son,
and the righteousness of ruler and minister,
are the order.
10.6 The affairs of the *Shè* and *Jì*, the mountains and rivers,
and the sacrifices to ghosts and spirits,
are the substance.
10.7 The items used in mourning and sacrifice,
and the interaction with guests,
are the righteousness.
10.8 To sacrifice with a lamb
or a piglet,
such that all the hundred officers are satisfied;
to sacrifice with a *Dàláo*,
such that there is not necessarily a surplus;
this is what is called proportion.
The *Zhūhóu* take the tortoise as a treasure
and the *guī* jade as a symbol of authority.
Families do not treasure tortoises,
do not store *guī*,
and do not have gate-towers,
meaning there is a sense of proportion.
10.9 In rites,
there are instances where abundance is valued:
the *Tiānzǐ* has seven temples,
the *Zhūhóu* five,
the *Dàfū* three,
and the *Shì* one.
The *Tiānzǐ* has twenty-six *dòu* vessels,
the *Zhūgōng* sixteen,
the *Zhūhóu* twelve,
the upper *Dàfū* eight,
and the lower *Dàfū* six.
A *Zhūhóu* has seven attendants and seven *láo* sacrifices,
a *Dàfū* has five attendants and five *láo* sacrifices.
The *Tiānzǐ* has five layers of mats,
the *Zhūhóu* three layers,
and the *Dàfū* two layers.
When the *Tiānzǐ* dies, he is buried after seven months,
with five layers of coffin-cloths and eight *shà* ornaments;
the *Zhūhóu* are buried after five months,
with three layers and six *shà*;
the *Dàfū* are buried after three months,
with two layers and four *shà*.
These are cases where abundance is valued.
10.10 There are instances where simplicity is valued:
the *Tiānzǐ* has no attendants.
In sacrificing to Heaven, a single victim is used.
When the *Tiānzǐ* visits a *Zhūhóu*,
the *Zhūhóu* serves a calf for his meal.
When *Zhūhóu* visit each other,
the libation uses *yùchàng* wine,
but there are no offerings in *biān* and *dòu* vessels.
The *Dàfū*'s diplomatic gifts consist of dried and pickled meat.
The *Tiānzǐ* eats once,
the *Zhūhóu* twice,
the *Dàfū* and *Shì* three times;
those who eat for labor have no fixed number.
The *Dàlù* carriage has one set of tassels,
while the secondary carriage has seven sets.
*Guī* and *zhāng* jades are used singly,
while *hǔ* and *huáng* are used in pairs.
For the sacrifice to ghosts and spirits, a single mat is used.
When the *Zhūhóu* hold court,
a *Dàfū* reports individually,
while *Shì* report in groups.
These are cases where simplicity is valued.
10.11 There are instances where large size is valued:
the capacity of palaces,
the measurements of vessels,
the thickness of inner and outer coffins,
and the size of burial mounds.
These are cases where large size is valued.
10.12 There are instances where small size is valued:
in the ancestral temple sacrifice,
the noble offer with a *jué*,
the humble offer with a *sàn*;
the superior lift the *zhì*,
the inferior lift the *jiǎo*.
The vessels for the five offerings:
outside the gate is the *fǒu*,
inside the gate is the *hú*,
and the ruler's vessel is the earthenware *wǔ*.
These are cases where small size is valued.
10.13 There are instances where height is valued:
the hall of the *Tiānzǐ* is nine feet high,
the *Zhūhóu*'s seven feet,
the *Dàfū*'s five feet,
and the *Shì*'s three feet.
The *Tiānzǐ* and *Zhūhóu* have gate-towers.
These are cases where height is valued.
10.14 There are instances where low position is valued:
the highest respect uses no altar,
but sacrifices on the swept ground.
The stands for the *Tiānzǐ* and *Zhūhóu* omit the *jìn* stand,
while the *Dàfū* and *Shì* use the *yì*
and *jìn* stands.
These are cases where low position is valued.
10.15 There are instances where ornamentation is valued:
the *Tiānzǐ* wears the dragon robe,
the *Zhūhóu* the *fǔ* pattern,
the *Dàfū* the *fú* pattern,
and the *Shì* a black robe and madder-red skirt.
For the crown of the *Tiānzǐ*,
there are red and green strings with twelve tassels,
the *Zhūhóu* nine,
the upper *Dàfū* seven,
the lower *Dàfū* five,
and the *Shì* three.
These are cases where ornamentation is valued.
10.16 There are instances where plainness is valued:
the highest respect has no ornamentation;
in the company of one's father's kin, there is no formal posturing;
the *Dàguī* is not carved;
the *Dàgēng* is not seasoned;
the *Dàlù* carriage is plain and has a grass mat;
the sacrificial wine vessel is covered with coarse cloth
and has a wooden ladle.
These are cases where plainness is valued.
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"Rites
must be examined!
When rites are different,
they are not excessive
and not deficient."
This is what is meant.
It refers to proportion.
10.17 Where rites value abundance,
it is because they express the outward mind;
virtue is manifested and spread,
extending to all things,
with great principles and abundant objects.
In such cases,
how could they not value abundance?
Therefore, the *Jūnzǐ* takes pleasure in this manifestation.
Where rites value simplicity,
it is because they express the inward mind.
The attainment of virtue's production is subtle and refined;
looking at the things of the world, none are worthy to match its virtue.
In such cases,
how could they not value simplicity?
Therefore, the *Jūnzǐ* is cautious when alone.
10.18 The sages of old
regarded the inward as honorable
and the outward as joyful,
simplicity as noble,
and abundance as beautiful.
Therefore, when the former kings established the rites,
they could not be too many,
nor could they be too few;
they had only to be in proportion.
10.19 Therefore,
when a *Jūnzǐ* sacrifices with the *Dàláo*,
it is called *Lǐ*;
when a *Pǐshì* sacrifices with the *Dàláo*,
it is called *Rǎng*.
*Guǎn Zhòng* had engraved *Guǐ* and red *Hóng*,
*Shānjié* and *Zǎozhuì*,
which the *Jūnzǐ* considered excessive.
*Yàn Píngzhòng* sacrificed to his ancestors,
but a pig's shoulder did not even cover the *Dòu*.
He wore washed clothes and a laundered cap to court;
the *Jūnzǐ* considered this parsimonious.
10.20 Therefore,
when a *Jūnzǐ* performs *Lǐ*,
he must not be incautious;
it is the discipline of the masses;
if the discipline is scattered, the masses will be in disorder.
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"When I fight, I conquer;
when I sacrifice, I receive blessings;
this is because I have surely obtained the *Dào*."
The *Jūnzǐ* says:
"In sacrifices, one does not pray for favors,
does not signal too early,
does not delight in mere size,
does not consider only auspicious events as good,
the sacrificial animals need not be overly fat or large,
and the offerings need not be of many varieties."
10.21 *Kǒngzǐ* said:
"How could *Zāng Wènzhòng* know *Lǐ*!
*Xiàfù Fúqí* reversed the order of sacrifice
and he did not stop him.
He burned firewood at the *Ào*;
as for the *Ào*,
it is the sacrifice of the old woman,
with food served in a basin
and drink in a jar."
is like the body.
If the body is incomplete,
the *Jūnzǐ* calls it an incomplete person.
If it is arranged inappropriately,
it is also like being incomplete.
*Lǐ* has great aspects and small aspects,
conspicuous aspects and subtle aspects.
The great must not be diminished,
the small must not be increased,
the conspicuous must not be hidden,
and the subtle must not be enlarged.
Therefore, there are three hundred major rituals
and three thousand minor rituals,
but their ultimate purpose is one.
No one enters a room except through the door.
Regarding *Lǐ*, the *Jūnzǐ*
exhausts his emotions and fulfills his caution,
attaining respect and sincerity,
attaining beauty, elegance, and sincerity.
Regarding *Lǐ*, the *Jūnzǐ*
acts directly in some cases,
acts circuitously and diminishes in others,
follows the constant and grades them,
follows the natural order and criticizes,
makes cuts and spreads them out,
pushes forward and advances,
lets go and adds refinement,
lets go and does not reach the limit,
and follows the order and gathers.
The rituals of the *Sāndài* were one;
the people followed them together.
Some used white and some used blue-green;
the *Xià* created them and the *Yīn* followed them.
10.23 In *Zhōu*, the *Shǐ* sat,
and was instructed and encouraged by *Wǔfāng*;
their ritual was like this,
and their *Dào* was one.
In *Xià*, the *Shǐ* stood until the sacrifice ended;
in *Yīn*, the *Shǐ* sat.
In *Zhōu*, the travel-toast was offered to six *Shǐ*;
*Zéngzǐ* said:
"The *Zhōu* ritual is like a *Jiù*!"
10.24 The *Jūnzǐ* says:
"Rituals that are close to human emotions
are not the most perfect.
In the *Jiāo*, blood is used;
in the Great Banquet, raw meat is used;
in the triple offering, barely seared meat is used;
in the single offering, cooked meat is used."
Therefore,
the *Jūnzǐ*’s approach to *Lǐ*
is not to act out his emotions arbitrarily;
this has an origin.
Therefore, seven *Jiè* are used to meet each other;
otherwise, it would be too blunt.
One arrives after three declinations and three yieldings;
otherwise, it would be too abrupt.
Thus, when the people of *Lǔ* are to perform a service for *Shàngdì*,
they must first perform a service at the *Pàngōng*.
When the people of *Jìn* are to perform a service for the *Hé*,
they must first perform a service at the *Èchí*.
When the people of *Qí* are to perform a service for *Tàishān*,
they must first perform a service at the *Pèilín*.
Being tied for three months,
keeping watch for seven days,
and fasting for three days—
this is the height of caution.
10.25 Therefore, rituals have ushers and heralds,
and music has assistants to guide the steps;
this is the height of gentleness.
*Lǐ*
returns to the root and follows the ancient way,
not forgetting its beginning.
Therefore, in funerary matters, there is no herald;
in court matters, music is used.
For the use of *Lǐjiǔ*,
*Xuánjiǔ* is honored.
For the use of the carving knife,
the *Luán* knife is valued.
For the comfort of fine mats,
coarse straw mats are also provided.
Therefore,
when the former kings established *Lǐ*,
there must be a primary principle;
thus they can be recounted and studied extensively.
10.26 The *Jūnzǐ* says:
"One who has no regulation within
cannot examine things with discernment.
If one wishes to examine things without following *Lǐ*,
one will not succeed.
Therefore, doing things without *Lǐ*
will not lead to respect.
Speaking without *Lǐ*
will not lead to being believed.
Thus it is said:
*Lǐ*
is the perfection of things."
10.27 Therefore,
when the former kings of old established *Lǐ*,
they followed the nature of materials to express their principles.
Thus, when performing great matters,
they must follow the seasons of Heaven;
when performing morning and evening rites, they must follow the sun and moon;
for high places, they must use hills;
for low places, they must use rivers and marshes.
Therefore, when the seasons of Heaven bring rain and moisture,
the *Jūnzǐ* exerts himself with unremitting effort.
10.28 Therefore,
the former kings of old
valued virtue,
honored the *Dào*, and employed the capable.
They raised the worthy and placed them in office;
they gathered the masses and took oaths with them.
Therefore, they served Heaven based on Heaven's patterns,
they served Earth based on Earth's patterns,
they ascended famous mountains to report to Heaven,
and used auspicious land to sacrifice to the Emperor in the *Jiāo*.
When they reported to Heaven,
the *Fènghuáng* descended,
and the turtles and dragons appeared.
When they sacrificed to the Emperor in the *Jiāo*,
the wind and rain were moderate,
and the cold and heat arrived in their proper times.
Therefore, when the Sage stood facing south,
the world was greatly governed.
10.29 The *Tiāndào* is the ultimate teaching;
the Sage possesses the ultimate virtue.
Upon the ancestral hall,
the *Léi* vessel is on the *Zuò*,
and the *Xī* vessel is on the west.
Below the ancestral hall,
the suspended drum is on the west,
and the *Yìng* drum is on the east.
The Lord is on the *Zuò*,
and the Lady is in her room.
The sun rises in the east,
and the moon rises in the west;
this is the division of *Yīn* and *Yáng*
and the positions of husband and wife.
10.30 The Lord pours from the *Xī* and *Xiàng* in the west,
and the Lady pours from the *Léi* vessel in the east.
Rituals interact above,
and music responds below;
this is the height of harmony.
is to return to what it arose from;
music
is to rejoice in what it has accomplished.
Therefore, the former kings established *Lǐ* to regulate affairs,
and cultivated music to guide the will.
Thus, by observing their *Lǐ* and music,
whether there is order or chaos can be known.
*Qú Bóyù* said:
"The *Jūnzǐ* is one who reaches the essence."
Thus, by observing a vessel,
one knows the skill of the craftsman;
by observing what is emitted,
one knows the wisdom of the person.
Thus it is said:
The *Jūnzǐ* is cautious about that which he gives to others.
10.32 Within the Dà Miào, how reverent it is!
The Jūn personally leads the sacrificial victim,
and the Dàfū assist with the silks and follow.
The Jūn personally prepares the sacrifice,
and the Fūrén presents the unfermented wine.
The Jūn personally carves the victim,
and the Fūrén presents the wine.
The Qīng and Dàfū follow the Jūn,
and the Mìngfù follow the Fūrén.
How profound and deep is their reverence!
How sincere and constant is their loyalty!
How earnest is their desire that the spirits enjoy the offering!
When the victim is led in, an announcement is made in the courtyard;
when the blood and hair are presented, an announcement is made in the inner chamber;
when the soup is set, an announcement is made in the hall.
These three announcements are made in different positions,
for it is the way of seeking the spirit without yet having found it.
The sacrifice is set in the hall,
and the Bàng sacrifice is performed outside.
Therefore it is said:
"Is he there?
Is he here?"
10.33 The ritual of a single libation represents simplicity;
three libations represent ornamentation;
five libations represent detailed observation;
seven libations represent spiritual power.
10.34 The Dà Xiǎng banquet—is it not an affair of the Wáng?
The three sacrificial victims, the fish, and the dried meat
are the delicacies of the Sì Hǎi and the Jiǔ Zhōu.
The offerings of the Biān and Dòu vessels
are the harmonious essences of the four seasons.
The presentation of metal
signifies harmony.
Bundles of silk with a jade bì disk on top
honor virtue.
The tortoise shell is placed in the front row
for its foreknowledge.
Metal follows it
to show sincerity.
Cinnabar, lacquer, silk, floss, bamboo, and arrows
are resources shared with the people.
As for the rest, there are no fixed goods;
each brings what their state possesses,
and thus distant things are presented.
When the guests depart,
the Sì Xià music is played to see them off;
this shows the gravity of ritual.
10.35 Sacrificing to Dì at the Jiāo altar
is the height of reverence.
The sacrifice at the Zōngmiào
is the height of benevolence.
The Sànglǐ
is the height of loyalty.
Preparing the sacrificial garments and vessels
is the height of benevolence.
The use of silks for bīnkè
is the height of righteousness.
Therefore, if a jūnzǐ wishes to observe the Way of rén and yì,
ritual is its foundation.
The jūnzǐ says:
"Sweetness can receive harmony;
whiteness can receive colors.
A person of loyalty and trustworthiness
can learn ritual.
If there is no person of loyalty and trustworthiness,
then ritual cannot function in a vacuum.
Thus, finding the right person is what is valued."
10.36 Kǒngzǐ said:
"Reciting the three hundred poems of the Shī
is not equal to a single libation.
The ritual of a single libation
is not equal to the Dà Xiǎng banquet.
The ritual of the Dà Xiǎng
is not equal to the Dà Lǚ sacrifice.
When the Dà Lǚ is complete,
it is still not equal to the sacrifice to Dì.
Do not lightly discuss ritual!"
10.37 Zǐlù served as the steward for the Jì family.
When the Jì family performed sacrifices,
they waited until it was dark to begin;
when the day was not long enough,
they continued by candlelight.
Although they had appearances of great effort
and hearts of solemn reverence,
everyone was exhausted and weary.
The yǒusī leaned against things while attending the sacrifice;
this was a great lack of reverence.
On another day of sacrifice
where Zǐlù assisted,
the affairs of the inner chamber met at the threshold,
the affairs of the hall met at the steps.
They began the rites at first light
and retired by late morning.
Kǒngzǐ heard of this and said:
"Who says that Yóu does not know ritual?"
11.1 For the Jiāo sacrifice, a single victim is used,
but for the Shèjì, the Great Victim is used.
When the Tiānzǐ visits the zhūhóu,
the lords use a calf for his meal;
when the zhūhóu visit the Tiānzǐ,
the Tiānzǐ bestows on them the ritual of the Great Victim;
this is the principle of valuing sincerity.
Therefore, the Tiānzǐ does not eat a pregnant animal,
nor is such used in sacrificing to Dì.
The Dàlù chariot has one set of tassels,
the Xiānlù has three sets,
and the Cìlù has five sets.
For the Jiāo sacrifice, blood is offered;
for the Dà Xiǎng, raw meat;
for the three libations, parboiled meat;
for the single libation, cooked meat.
Supreme reverence does not focus on the taste
but values the fragrance.
When the zhūhóu act as guests,
the libation uses fragrant yùchàng wine.
The libation is used for its scent.
In the Dà Xiǎng banquet,
they merely value dried and spiced meat.
11.2 In the Dà Xiǎng banquet,
the Jūn sits on three layers of mats to return the toast.
For the assistant of the three libations,
the Jūn sits on a single mat to return the toast.
This is the superior descending to meet the inferior.
In the Dà Xiǎng and the spring Dì sacrifice there is music,
but in the simple meal and the autumn Cháng sacrifice there is no music;
this follows the principle of Yīn and Yáng.
All drinking
nourishes the Yáng energy;
all eating
nourishes the Yīn energy.
Therefore, there are the spring Dì and the autumn Cháng sacrifices.
In spring, the orphans are feasted,
and in autumn, the elderly are fed;
the principle is the same.
Yet for the simple meal and the autumn Cháng sacrifice, there is no music.
Drinking
nourishes the Yáng energy,
therefore there is music;
eating
nourishes the Yīn energy,
therefore there is no sound.
All sound
belongs to Yáng.
11.4 The Dǐng and Zǔ are odd in number while the Biān and Dòu are even;
this is the principle of Yīn and Yáng.
The contents of the Biān and Dòu
are products of water and land.
They do not dare use common tastes but value variety;
this is the principle of communicating with the divine spirits.
11.5 When the guest enters the great gate, the Sì Xià music is played
to show ease combined with reverence.
When the cup is finished, the music ends;
Kǒngzǐ repeatedly sighed in admiration of this.
When the pledge-cup is set down, the musicians go up to sing
to express virtue.
The singers are above
and the gourds and bamboos are below;
this values the human voice.
Music arises from the Yáng,
and ritual is created from the Yīn;
when Yīn and Yáng are in harmony, all things thrive.
11.6 The presentation of silks has no fixed direction;
this is to distinguish the suitability of different lands
and to regulate the intervals for those far and near.
The tortoise shell is in the front row
for foreknowledge;
the bells follow it,
and harmony is placed among them.
Skins of tigers and leopards
show the subduing of the fierce.
Bundles of silk with a jade bì disk on top
are for outgoing virtue.
11.7 Having a hundred courtyard torches
began with Qí Huán Gōng.
Dàfū playing the Sì Xià music
began with Zhào Wén Zǐ.
11.8 Audiences at court.
Private meetings by Dàfū
are contrary to ritual.
A Dàfū carries a jade guī scepter when sent on a mission
to extend trust;
they do not dare have private meetings
to show ultimate reverence.
Why then should private gifts and private meetings
occur in the courts of the zhūhóu?
One who is a minister
has no private foreign relations;
they do not dare have a double heart toward their Jūn.
11.9 A Dàfū feasting his Jūn
is contrary to ritual.
If a Dàfū is overbearing and the Jūn kills him,
it is righteous;
this practice began with the Sān Huán.
For the Tiānzǐ, there is no ritual for a guest;
no one dares act as a host to him.
When the Jūn goes to his minister's house,
he ascends by the Zuòjiē;
the minister does not dare to claim the house as his own.
In the audience ritual,
the Son of Heaven does not descend from the hall to see the feudal lords.
Descending from the hall to see the feudal lords
is a lapse in ritual by the Son of Heaven,
which began from Yí Wáng onwards.
11.10 For feudal lords to have instruments suspended on all four sides,
to sacrifice with a white bull,
to strike jade chimes,
to use red shields and set up metal bells,
to wear ceremonial caps and perform the Dà Wǔ dance,
and to ride in the Dà Lù carriage
are ritual usurpations by the feudal lords.
Building towers over gates and setting up screen walls in the path,
having reverse stands for cups,
wearing embroidered axe-patterns
and cinnabar-red inner garments
are ritual usurpations by the Dà fū.
Therefore, when the Son of Heaven is weak,
the feudal lords usurp power.
When the Dà fū are strong,
the feudal lords are coerced.
In such a state, they value each other according to rank,
see each other for goods,
and bribe each other for profit,
and the rituals of the world fall into chaos.
Feudal lords do not dare to treat the Son of Heaven as their ancestor,
and Dà fū do not dare to treat the feudal lords as their ancestor.
For a public temple to be established in a private household
is contrary to ritual;
this began with the Sān Huán.
11.11 The Son of Heaven preserves the descendants of the two preceding dynasties,
which is out of respect for the worthy.
Respecting the worthy does not extend beyond two dynasties.
A feudal lord does not treat a refugee lord as a subject.
Therefore, in antiquity, the position of a refugee lord was not hereditary.
11.12 When the ruler faces south,
it is in response to the principle of Yáng.
When the subject faces north,
it is in response to the ruler.
