11.13 The retainers of a Dà fū do not perform the jǐ shǒu kowtow,
not to honor the household retainer,
but to avoid the ritual due to the ruler.
When a Dà fū makes an offering, the ruler does not personally receive it;
when the ruler gives a gift, the recipient does not bow in person,
lest the ruler respond with a bow to him.
11.14 When the villagers performed the exorcism ritual,
Kǒngzǐ stood on the eastern steps in court robes
to reassure the household spirits.
11.15 Kǒngzǐ said,
"If one shoots according to the music,
how can one listen?
How can one shoot?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"If a scholar
is asked to shoot
and is unable,
he declines on account of illness.
This is the significance of the suspended bow."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Fasting for three days
and using it for one,
one still fears being irreverent;
if drums are beaten for two days,
how can this be?"
11.16 Kǒngzǐ said,
"To perform the Yì sacrifice inside the Kù Mén,
the Bèng sacrifice in the east,
and the morning market in the west,
is to lose the proper way."
11.17 The Shè sacrifice is to the earth and focuses on the Yīn energy.
The ruler faces south below the northern wall,
responding to the principle of Yīn.
The day used is the Jiǎ day,
as it is the beginning of the days.
The Dà Shè of the Son of Heaven must receive frost, dew, wind, and rain to communicate with the Qi of Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, the altar of a lost state is covered with a roof,
so it does not receive the Yáng of Heaven.
The Bó Shè has a window in the north,
to let the Yīn be illuminated.
The Shè is the means to divinize the Way of the Earth.
The Earth carries the myriad things;
Heaven hangs down its signs.
We take resources from the Earth
and take laws from Heaven;
therefore, we honor Heaven and feel close to the Earth.
Thus, the people are taught to give beautiful repayment.
The household centers on the Zhōng Liù and the state centers on the Shè,
to show the foundation.
Only for the Shè ritual
do the people all leave their neighborhoods.
Only for the Shè hunt
do the people of the state all set out.
Only for the Shè,
do the administrative districts provide the sacrificial grain,
as a way to repay the foundation and return to the beginning.
11.18 In the last month of spring, the fire is brought out
for the purpose of burning.
Then they review the chariots and taxes
and inspect the ranks of soldiers,
and the ruler personally makes an oath at the Shè altar
to practice military maneuvers.
Moving them to the left and to the right,
making them sit and rise,
to observe their familiarity with changes;
they release animals for them
and entice them with gains
to see that they do not violate orders.
The goal is to make their wills submissive
and not greedy for gain;
therefore, in battle they are victorious,
and in sacrifice they receive blessings.
11.19 When the Son of Heaven visits the four quarters,
he first performs the Chái sacrifice.
11.20 The Jiāo sacrifice
welcomes the arrival of the longest day,
a great repayment to Heaven that centers on the Sun.
The altar is built in the southern suburb,
to approach the position of Yáng.
They sweep the ground and sacrifice,
focusing on simplicity.
The vessels are made of pottery and gourds
to symbolize the nature of Heaven and Earth.
It is held in the suburb,
so it is called the Jiāo.
The victim is a red bull,
as red is esteemed.
A calf is used
to value sincerity.
Regarding the use of the Xīn day for the Jiāo:
when the Zhōu first performed the Jiāo, the day was the solstice.
Divining for the Jiāo:
the order is received in the ancestral temple,
and the tortoise shell is prepared in the temple of the late father,
which is the principle of honoring ancestors and feeling close to one's father.
On the day of divination,
the King stands at the marsh,
personally listening to the proclamations,
which is the principle of receiving instruction and admonition.
The orders are presented within the Kù Mén
to warn the hundred officials.
The orders from the Dà Miào
are to warn the common people.
On the day of the sacrifice,
the King wears the leather cap to hear the sacrificial reports,
showing the people reverence for the superior.
Those in mourning do not wail,
they do not dare wear mourning clothes,
they sprinkle and sweep the roads,
and the villages light field-torches.
Without orders, the people obey the superior.
On the day of the sacrifice,
the King wears the ceremonial robe to symbolize Heaven,
wearing the ceremonial cap
with twelve jade strings on the pendants,
which follows the number of Heaven.
He rides in a plain chariot,
valuing its simplicity.
The banner has twelve streamers,
decorated with dragons and the sun and moon
to symbolize Heaven.
Heaven hangs down its signs,
and the sages take them as a model.
The Jiāo is how the Way of Heaven is made clear.
If the bull for the Lord is not auspicious,
it is used as the bull for Jì.
The bull for the Lord must be in the stall for three months,
while the bull for Jì only needs to be prepared.
This is to distinguish between serving the celestial gods and the human spirits.
The myriad things have their root in Heaven,
and man has his root in his ancestors;
this is why they are paired with Shàngdì.
The Jiāo sacrifice
is a great repayment to the root and a return to the beginning.
11.21 The Son of Heaven performs the Great Là sacrifice to the eight spirits.
The Yīqí clan began the Là sacrifice.
As for Là,
it means to search.
In the twelfth month of the year,
the myriad things are gathered together to be searched for and offered a feast.
In the Là sacrifice:
the primary focus is the Xiān Sè
and sacrifice is made to the Sī Sè.
Sacrifice is made to the hundred kinds of seeds
to repay the harvest.
A feast is offered to the husbandmen, the watchmen of the fields, the huts and field-path markers,
and the birds and beasts;
it is the height of benevolence
and the perfection of righteousness.
The gentlemen of old,
whoever they employed, they surely repaid them.
They welcome the cats
because they eat field mice;
they welcome the tigers
because they eat field boars;
they welcome and sacrifice to them.
Sacrificing to the dikes and the ditches
is a matter of duty.
It says:
“Earth, return to your dwelling;
water, return to your chasms;
insects, do not arise;
grasses and trees, return to your marshes.”
Wearing the *Píbìan* and *Sùfú*, they sacrifice.
The *Sùfú*
is used for sending off the deceased.
Belts of kudzu and staves of hazel wood
represent the reductions of mourning.
The *Là* sacrifice
is the height of benevolence
and the perfection of righteousness.
To sacrifice wearing yellow robes and a yellow cap
is to give rest to the farmers.
The country folk wear the yellow cap;
the yellow cap
is the dress of the fields.
11.22 The *Dàluóshì*
is the official of the Son of Heaven who manages birds and beasts,
and the feudal lords pay tribute through him.
Arriving in a straw hat
is to honor the dress of the fields.
The *Luóshì* presents deer and women
and instructs the guests to announce it.
This is to warn the feudal lords, saying:
“Those who love hunting
and love women will lose their states.”
The Son of Heaven plants melons and flowering plants,
kinds that are not harvested for storage.
The Eight *Là* are used to record the four directions.
If the harvest is not successful in the four directions,
the Eight *Là* is not performed there,
in order to be cautious with the people's resources.
In directions where the harvest is successful,
the *Là* is then performed,
to move the people to joy.
Once the *Là* is finished and the harvest collected,
the people’s rest is complete.
Therefore, after the *Là* is over,
a gentleman does not initiate new labor.
11.23 The pickled vegetables in the regular *Dòu* vessels
are the harmonious essence of aquatic plants;
the meat pastes
are products of the land.
In the additional *Dòu* vessels, the pickles
are products of the land;
the meat pastes
are products of the water.
The offerings in the *Bīan* and *Dòu* vessels
are varieties from the water and the earth;
one does not dare use common, everyday flavors
but values a wide variety of items;
this is the meaning of communicating with the spiritual beings,
not the way of eating for flavor.
The offerings of the former kings
could be eaten
but were not to be craved.
The ceremonial robes and the Great Carriage
could be displayed
but were not to be objects of desire.
The *Wǔ* dance is vigorous
but not to be enjoyed for pleasure.
The majesty of the ancestral temple
is not for one's comfort.
The vessels of the ancestral temple
may be used
but not for personal convenience or benefit;
that which is used to communicate with the spiritual beings
cannot be the same as that used for comfort and pleasure.
Despite the excellence of wines and sweet spirits,
dark liquor and clear water are prioritized,
valuing the origin of the five flavors.
Despite the beauty of patterned and embroidered robes,
coarse cloth is prioritized,
returning to the beginning of women’s work.
Despite the comfort of mats made of reeds and bamboo,
those of rushes and straw are prioritized,
to make the meaning clear.
The great broth is not seasoned,
valuing its simple nature.
The great jade tablet is not carved,
beautifying its simple nature.
Despite the beauty of red lacquer and carved stands,
a plain carriage is used,
honoring its simplicity
and valuing its substance alone.
That which is used to communicate with spiritual beings
cannot be the same as that which is for extreme comfort and familiarity.
Only after this is it appropriate.
The *Dǐng* and *Zǔ* vessels are in odd numbers, while the *Bīan* and *Dòu* are in even numbers,
following the meaning of *Yīn* and *Yáng*.
The *Huángmù*
is the superior vessel for fragrant vapors.
“Yellow” (*Huáng*) signifies the center;
“Eyes” (*Mù*) are the clear and bright parts of the spirit.
This signifies pouring from the center and being clear and bright on the outside.
In sacrificing to Heaven,
they sweep the ground and sacrifice there,
relying on its simple substance.
Despite the excellence of vinegar and meat pastes,
boiled salt is prioritized,
valuing natural products.
Despite the utility of cutting knives,
the *Luándāo* is valued,
valuing its significance.
The sound is made harmonious, and then the cutting is done.
11.24 The Meaning of Capping:
When first capping a youth,
the black cloth cap is used.
In high antiquity, the cap was of plain cloth;
for purification, it was dyed black.
Regarding its tassels,
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
“I have not heard of them.
Once capped, the cap may be worn until it is worn out.”
The eldest son is capped at the eastern steps
to signify his succession.
The libation is performed at the guest’s position
to mark the completion of the ceremony.
The three additions of caps become increasingly noble
to illustrate his aspirations.
After capping him, a courtesy name is given
to show respect for his name.
The *Wěimào* cap
was the way of *Zhōu*.
The *Zhāngfǔ*
was the way of *Yīn*.
The *Wúzhuī*
was the way of the *Xiàhòu* clan.
The *Zhōu* used the *Bìan*,
the *Yīn* used the *Xǔ*,
and the *Xià* used the *Shōu*.
The three kings all used the *Píbìan* and the white pleated skirt.
There is no capping ceremony for a *Dàfū*,
but there is a marriage ceremony for him.
In ancient times,
one was fifty before receiving a noble rank;
how could there be a capping ceremony for a *Dàfū*?
That feudal lords have a capping ceremony
was an invention of the end of the *Xià*.
The eldest son of the Son of Heaven
is treated as a *Shì*.
In the world, no one is born noble.
Establishing feudal lords by hereditary succession
is to emulate the worthy.
Appointing people to office and rank
is done according to the levels of virtue.
Giving a posthumous title after death
is a modern practice;
in ancient times, there were no ranks in life
and no posthumous titles in death.
What the rites honor
is their underlying meaning.
If the meaning is lost
and only the numbers are displayed,
that is the work of the invokers and scribes.
Therefore, the numbers can be displayed,
but the meaning is difficult to know.
Knowing the meaning and reverently maintaining it
is how the Son of Heaven governs the world.
11.25 Only after Heaven and Earth unite do the myriad things flourish.
The marriage rite
is the beginning of ten thousand generations.
Taking a wife from a different surname
is a way to attach to the distant and emphasize the distinction.
The ritual silks must be sincere,
and the words must be humble.
Inform her with honesty and trust;
trust
is how one serves others;
trust
is the virtue of a wife.
Once united as equals,
she does not change throughout her life.
Therefore, if the husband dies, she does not remarry.
The man personally meets the bride,
the man preceding the woman;
this is the meaning of the hard and the soft.
Heaven precedes Earth,
and the ruler precedes the minister;
their meaning is the same.
Holding a ritual gift to meet one another
is to respectfully manifest the distinction.
When there is a distinction between men and women,
then father and son become close.
When father and son are close,
then righteousness arises.
When righteousness arises,
then the rites are created.
When the rites are created,
then the myriad things are at peace.
Without distinction and without righteousness,
it is the way of birds and beasts.
The groom personally drives the carriage and hands over the mounting cord,
to show his intimacy.
Why show intimacy?
It is to show affection.
Showing respect and affection
was how the former kings gained the world.
Going out through the great gate and leading the way,
the man leads the woman,
and the woman follows the man;
the duty of husband and wife begins from this.
A woman
is one who follows others.
In youth, she follows her father and elder brother;
when married, she follows her husband;
when her husband dies, she follows her son.
As for "husband" (fū),
he is a man of support;
as for "husband" (fū),
he is one who leads others with his wisdom.
Wearing the black cap and fasting
connects to the spirits and the Yīn and Yáng.
Since he is to be the master of the altars of land and grain
and the successor to his ancestors,
how can he not show the utmost respect?
Eating from the same sacrificial animal
signifies their shared status.
Therefore, a woman has no independent rank;
she follows the rank of her husband
and sits according to her husband's age.
The vessels used are made of pottery and gourds,
which shows respect for the ancient rites.
The three kings used pottery and gourds in the marriage feast.
The next morning,
the wife washes her hands and presents food;
after the father-in-law and mother-in-law have finished eating,
the wife eats the leftovers;
this is to show her secondary status.
The father-in-law and mother-in-law descend by the western steps,
while the wife descends by the eastern steps;
this signifies the handing over of the household to her.
In the marriage rite, music is not used;
this is the meaning of the dark Yīn.
Music
represents the Yáng energy.
In the marriage rite, congratulations are not offered;
it is simply the succession of generations.
11.26 In the sacrifices of the Yǒu Yú Shì,
they prioritized the use of vapor.
Sacrificing with blood, raw meat, and parboiled meat
was to use the vapor.
11.27 The Yīn people prioritized sound.
Before the fragrance was fully formed,
they purified the atmosphere with sound.
After three pieces of music were played,
only then did they go out to welcome the sacrificial animal.
The cries of the voices
were used to announce to the space between heaven and earth.
The Zhōu people prioritized scent.
For the libation, they used fragrant cháng-wine.
They mixed fragrant herbs with the cháng-wine.
The scent
reached down to the deep springs.
For the libation, they used the guī and zhāng jade vessels,
utilizing the essence of the jade.
After the libation,
they then welcomed the sacrificial animal,
to draw forth the Yīn energy.
Artemisia was mixed with millet and broomcorn;
the scent
reached the walls and roof of the house.
Therefore, after the offerings were set down,
they then burned the artemisia mixed with the animal fat.
In all sacrifices,
one must be careful in these matters.
The heavenly soul (hún-qì) returns to heaven,
while the earthly soul (xíng-pò) returns to the earth.
Therefore, in sacrifice,
one seeks for the meaning of the Yīn and Yáng.
The Yīn people first sought in the Yáng;
the Zhōu people first sought in the Yīn.
They gave instructions to the invoker in the inner room,
seated the personator in the hall,
used the sacrificial animal in the courtyard,
and presented the head in the inner room.
In the regular sacrifice,
the prayer was to the tablet;
in the searching sacrifice,
the prayer was at the bàng.
Not knowing where the spirit resides,
is it there? Is it here?
Or is it far away?
Sacrificing at the bàng
might be called seeking it at a distance.
The word bàng means "searching";
the word qí means "respect."
"Wealth" (fù) means "blessing."
"Head" (shǒu) means
"uprightness."
"Assistance" (xiāng)
means "to feast."
"Blessing" (gǔ)
means "longevity"
and "greatness."
"Personator" (shī)
means "to display."
The hair and blood
are to announce that the victim is a complete and unblemished creature.
To announce that the victim is complete
is the way to honor purity.
The blood sacrifice
is to present the full vigor.
Sacrificing the lungs, liver, and heart
honors the organs of breath.
Adding the lungs to the millet and broomcorn
and adding the clear water to the wines
is to repay the Yīn.
Taking the fat from the kidneys and burning it,
and presenting the head,
is to repay the Yáng.
Thinning the wine with clear water
honors what is new.
Whenever thinned,
it is to make it new.
It is called "bright water"
because the master of the sacrifice made this water clean.
The ruler bows twice and touches his head to the ground;
he bares his shoulder and personally cuts the meat,
which is the pinnacle of respect.
The pinnacle of respect
is submission.
Bowing
is submission;
touching the head to the ground
is extreme submission;
baring the shoulder
is the completion of submission.
In sacrifice, one is called "Filial Grandson" or "Filial Son,"
using titles according to their meaning;
calling oneself "Great-grandson So-and-so"
refers to the state and household.
In assisting at the sacrifice,
the host personally fulfills his respect
and carries out his excellence
without yielding to anyone.
In the sacrifices of raw, parboiled, and well-cooked meat,
how can we know that the spirit partakes of them?
The host simply fulfills his own respect.
Lifting the jiǎ and jué cups,
he signals the personator to be at ease.
In ancient times,
the personator stood when there was no business
and sat only after there was business.
The personator
is the image of the spirit.
The invoker
conveys the commands.
Straining the wine through couch grass
is to make the wine clear.
Thick wine was thinned with clear wine,
and the sacrificial gravy was thinned with thick wine;
this was like using clear water and clear wine to improve the old, seasoned wine.
In sacrifice, there are petitions,
there are thanksgivings,
and there are means to ward off evil.
The dark robes for fasting
are for the profound contemplation of the Yīn.
Therefore, a gentleman fasts for three days,
and he will surely see the one he is sacrificing to.
12.1 The sovereign king orders the Zhǒng Zǎi
to bestow virtue upon the masses of people.
12.2 When a son serves his parents:
at the first crowing of the cock,
they all wash their hands and rinse their mouths,
comb their hair, bind it with a headband, secure it with a hairpin, and tie the ends;
they brush their hair-piece, put on their cap, and fasten the chin-straps and tassels;
they put on the ceremonial robe, the knee-covers, and the large girdle,
and insert the tablet.
On the left and right they hang their accouterments:
on the left, the handkerchief, the knife, the whetstone, the small bodkin, and the metal fire-drill;
on the right, the thumb-ring, the arm-guard, the tube for pens, the perfume sachet, the large bodkin, and the wooden fire-drill;
they put on their leggings and fasten their shoe-strings.
12.3 When a wife serves her father-in-law and mother-in-law,
it is as she serves her own parents.
At the first crowing of the cock,
they all wash their hands and rinse their mouths,
comb their hair, bind it with a headband,
secure it with a hairpin, and tie the ends;
they put on their robes and girdles.
On the left they hang the handkerchief, the knife, the whetstone, the small bodkin, and the metal fire-drill;
on the right they hang the needle-case, the tube, the thread, and the silk floss;
they put on the sachet and the case, the large bodkin, and the wooden fire-drill;
they fasten their chin-straps
and tie their shoe-strings.
To go to the quarters of the *fùmǔ jiùgū*,
and upon arriving at the place,
lower the breath and soften the voice,
asking whether their clothes are too warm or too cold,
or if they have any illnesses, pains, or itches,
and respectfully rub or scratch them.
When going out or coming in,
sometimes preceding and sometimes following,
and respectfully supporting them.
When bringing water for washing,
the younger ones carry the basin,
the older ones carry the water,
requesting to pour the water for washing,
and when the washing is finished, they hand over the towel.
Asking what they desire and respectfully providing it,
with a gentle countenance to soothe them;
thick congee, thin congee, wine, sweet wine, vegetable soup, meat soup, beans, wheat, hemp seeds, rice, millet, fine millet, or glutinous millet—whatever they desire,
using dates, chestnuts, maltose, and honey to sweeten them,
using violets, marsh violets, elm seeds, elm bark, sowthistles, dried vegetables, rice water, and slippery mucilage to make them smooth,
and using fat or oil to enrich them,
the *fùmǔ jiùgū* must taste them before the children withdraw.
12.4 For sons and daughters who have not yet reached the age of *guān* or *jī*,
when the cock first crows,
they all wash their faces and rinse their mouths,
comb their hair and wrap it in a silk cloth,
brush the hair, tie it in *zǒngjiǎo*,
fasten their lapels and cap-strings,
and all wear *róngchòu*,
at dawn they pay their respects,
asking, "What have you eaten or drunk?"
If they have already eaten, they withdraw;
if they have not yet eaten,
they assist the elders in looking over the preparations.
12.5 For everyone inside and outside the household,
when the cock first crows,
all wash and rinse,
dress,
collect the pillows and mats,
sprinkle and sweep the rooms, halls, and courtyards,
spread the mats,
and each attends to their duties.
12.6 *Rùzǐ* sleep early and rise late,
according to their desire,
eating at no fixed time.
12.7 From the rank of *mìngshì* upwards,
fathers and sons live in different quarters.
At dawn they pay their respects,
presenting delicious and sweet foods with affection;
at sunrise they withdraw,
each attending to their duties;
at sunset they pay the evening respect,
presenting delicious and sweet foods with affection.
12.8 When *fùmǔ jiùgū* are about to sit,
they offer the mat and ask which direction they wish to face;
when they are about to lie down,
the elders offer the mat and ask where they wish to place their feet.
The younger ones hold the couch for them to sit on,
the attendants lift the small table,
they collect the mats and fine mats,
hang the quilts and store the pillows in cases,
roll up the mats and put them in covers.
12.9 The clothes of *fùmǔ jiùgū*,
quilts, fine mats, mats, pillows, and small tables are not to be transferred to others;
their staffs and sandals are to be treated with reverence,
and one does not dare to go near them.
As for the bowls and cups,
none dare use them unless for eating the leftovers;
and as for the regular food and drink,
unless it is leftovers,
none dare to eat or drink it.
12.10 While the parents are alive,
after the regular morning and evening meals,
the sons and wives assist in eating the leftovers;
after they have eaten, they consume the regular leftovers.
If the father is deceased and the mother is alive,
the *zhǒngzǐ* attends the meal,
and the other sons and wives assist in eating the leftovers as before;
the delicious, sweet, soft, and slippery foods are given to the *rùzǐ* as leftovers.
12.11 In the presence of *fùmǔ jiùgū*,
if they give an order,
one answers and responds respectfully.
Advancing, retreating, and turning around with caution and reverence,
ascending, descending, entering, exiting, and bowing with ease,
not daring to belch, sigh, sneeze, cough, yawn, stretch, stand on one leg, lean, or look sideways,
and not daring to spit or blow the nose;
if cold, not daring to put on more clothes;
if itching, not daring to scratch;
unless there is a respectful task,
not daring to bare the chest or shoulders;
not wading through water or tucking up the skirt;
the lining of undergarments and quilts should not be seen.
The saliva and nasal mucus of the parents should not be seen;
if the cap or sash is dirty,
one prepares ash-water to request washing them;
if the clothes are dirty,
one prepares ash-water to request laundering them;
if the clothes are torn or split,
one prepares needle and thread to request mending them.
Every five days,
heat water to request they bathe;
every three days prepare the hair-washing;
in between, if the face is dirty,
heat *pān* to request they wash the face;
if the feet are dirty,
heat water to request they wash the feet.
The younger serve the elder,
the low-ranking serve the high-ranking,
all following this pattern.
12.12 Men do not speak of inner affairs,
women do not speak of outer affairs.
Except for sacrifices or funerals,
they do not hand vessels to each other.
If they do hand something,
the woman receives it in a *fěi*;
if there is no *fěi*,
both sit down and place it on the ground before taking it.
Those inside and outside do not share a well,
do not share a bathhouse,
do not share sleeping mats,
do not share requests for borrowing items,
and men and women do not share clothes.
Inner words do not go out,
and outer words do not come in.
When a man enters the inner quarters,
he does not whistle or point;
when walking at night he uses a candle,
and if there is no candle, he stops.
When a woman goes out the door,
she must cover her face;
when walking at night she uses a candle,
and if there is no candle, she stops.
On the road,
men go by the right,
women go by the left.
Sons and wives who are filial and respectful,
regarding the orders of *fùmǔ jiùgū*,
do not resist or be lazy.
If they are given food or drink,
even if they do not like it,
they must taste it and wait;
if they are given clothes,
even if they do not want them,
they must wear them and wait;
if they are given a task
and someone else takes their place,
even if they do not want to give it up,
let the *gū* give it to them [the substitute],
and let the *gū* make them do it,
and then they return to it.
If the son's wife has a laborious task,
even if they love her dearly,
the *gū* lets her do it,
but rather allows her to rest frequently.
If a son's wife is not yet filial or respectful,
do not be resentful or angry,
but let the *gū* teach her;
if she cannot be taught,
only then be angry with her;
if she cannot be influenced by anger,
the son sends the wife away,
but does not announce the reason to the public.
If parents have faults,
lower the breath, use a pleasant countenance and a soft voice to admonish them;
if the admonition is not accepted,
increase in respect and filiality;
when they are pleased, admonish again;
if they are not pleased,
rather than let them get into trouble with the village or district,
it is better to admonish earnestly.
If the parents are angry and displeased
and beat the son until blood flows,
he does not dare to be resentful or angry,
but increases in respect and filiality.
If the parents have a maidservant's child or a child or grandchild by a concubine
and they love them dearly,
even after the parents have died,
one should respect them for a lifetime without fading.
If a son has two concubines,
and the parents love one of them,
while the son loves the other,
in regards to clothes and food,
or in the performance of duties,
he dares not prioritize his own preference over what the parents love,
and even after the parents have died, this should not fade.
If the son is very fond of his wife,
but the parents are not pleased,
he should send her away.
If the son is not fond of his wife,
but the parents say:
"She serves us well,"
the son should perform the rites of husband and wife towards her,
and for a lifetime this should not fade.
Though the parents have died,
when one is about to do something good,
thinking of bequeathing a good name to the parents,
one must carry it out.
When one is about to do something not good,
thinking of bequeathing shame and humiliation to the parents,
one must not carry it out.
12.13 When the *Jiù* has passed away, the *Gū* is elderly.
In the sacrifices
and for guests of the *Zhòngfù*,
she must request instructions from the *Gū* regarding every matter;
the *Jièfù* request instructions from the *Zhòngfù*.
If the *Jiù* or *Gū* employ the *Zhòngfù*,
she must not be idle, unfriendly, or disrespectful toward the *Jièfù*.
If the *Jiù* or *Gū* employ a *Jièfù*,
she does not dare to treat herself as an equal to the *Zhòngfù*;
she does not dare to walk side-by-side with her,
she does not dare to join in issuing orders,
and she does not dare to sit side-by-side with her.
For all daughters-in-law,
if not ordered to go to their private rooms,
they do not dare to withdraw.
When a daughter-in-law is about to perform any task,
whether great or small, she must request instructions from the *Jiù* and *Gū*.
Sons and their wives have no private goods,
no private livestock,
and no private vessels;
they do not dare to borrow items privately,
and they do not dare to give items privately.
If someone gives a daughter-in-law food, drink, clothes, fabric, sashes, handkerchiefs, fragrant roots, or orchids,
she receives them and offers them to the *Jiù* and *Gū*.
If the *Jiù* and *Gū* accept them, she is pleased,
as if she had just received a gift herself.
If they return the gift to her, she declines it;
if her declination is not accepted,
she receives it as if it were a new gift
and stores it to await a time of need.
If a daughter-in-law has private relatives or brothers and wishes to give something to them,
she must again request permission for that purpose,
and only after permission is granted does she give it to them.
12.14 The *Shìzǐ* and the *Shùzǐ*
reverently serve the *Zōngzǐ* and the *Zōngfù*.
12.15 Although they may be noble or wealthy,
they do not dare to enter the house of the *Zōngzǐ* with an air of nobility or wealth.
Even if they have many carriages and followers,
they leave them outside
and enter with a small and modest retinue.
If younger brothers or sons have tribute vessels, clothes, furs, quilts, carriages, or horses,
they must offer the best of them to the *Zōngzǐ*,
and only then dare to wear or use the next best.
If an item is not suitable to be offered,
they do not dare to enter the gate of the *Zōngzǐ* with it,
and they do not dare to impose their nobility or wealth upon their fathers, elder brothers, or the clan.
If they are wealthy,
they prepare two sacrificial animals,
offering the superior one to the *Zōngzǐ*.
The husband and wife both fast and show lineage respect there,
and only after the rites are finished do they dare to perform their private sacrifice.
12.16 Grains:
broomcorn millet, foxtail millet, rice, spiked millet,
white broomcorn millet, yellow spiked millet, ripened rice, and early-harvested rice.
Savory dishes:
beef soup with rice, mutton soup with rice, pork soup with rice, minced meat in brine, roasted beef.
Minced meat in brine and sliced beef; minced meat in brine and raw sliced beef.
Roasted mutton, sliced mutton, minced meat in brine, roasted pork.
Minced meat in brine, sliced pork, mustard sauce, raw sliced fish.
Pheasant, rabbit, quail, and partridge.
12.17 Drinks:
double-sweetened fermented liquor,
rice liquor (clear and with dregs),
broomcorn millet liquor (clear and with dregs),
spiked millet liquor (clear and with dregs).
Sometimes thin congee is used as sweet liquor:
broomcorn congee,
sour rice water, water, vinegar dregs, and thin rice water.
12.18 Wine: clear and white.
12.19 Delicacies:
parched grain, dumplings, powdered grain cakes, and congee.
12.20 Food pairings:
Snail sauce with Zizania rice,
pheasant soup;
wheat food,
dried meat soup,
chicken soup;
polished rice,
dog soup,
rabbit soup.
When mixing with grain, do not use smartweed.
For braised suckling pig,
wrap it in bitter herbs and stuff it with smartweed;
for braised chicken,
use brine sauce and stuff it with smartweed;
for braised fish,
use fish-egg sauce and stuff it with smartweed;
for braised turtle,
use brine sauce and stuff it with smartweed.
Dried meat,
ant egg sauce,
dried meat soup,
rabbit sauce,
elk skin,
fish sauce,
raw sliced fish,
mustard sauce,
raw elk meat,
minced meat in brine and sauce,
pickled peaches,
pickled plums,
and salt with eggs.
12.21 In all food, the consistency should correspond to spring;
for soups, the consistency should correspond to summer;
for sauces, the consistency should correspond to autumn;
for drinks, the consistency should correspond to winter.
12.22 In all seasoning,
in spring use more sour,
in summer more bitter,
in autumn more spicy,
in winter more salty;
harmonize them with smooth and sweet flavors.
12.23 Beef is suitable with rice,
mutton with broomcorn millet,
pork with foxtail millet,
dog meat with spiked millet,
wild goose with wheat,
fish with Zizania.
12.24 In spring, lamb and suckling pig are suitable, prepared with ox fat;
in summer, dried pheasant and dried fish, prepared with dog fat;
in autumn, calf and fawn, prepared with chicken fat;
in winter, fresh fish and wild goose, prepared with mutton fat.
12.25 Dried beef,
dried deer,
dried wild boar,
dried elk,
dried muntjac.
Elk, deer, wild boar, and muntjac
are all cut into large slices;
pheasant and rabbit are all served with vegetable garnish.
Small birds, partridge, cicadas, bees, wood-ear fungi,
water caltrops, Hovenia fruit, dates, chestnuts, hazelnuts,
persimmons, melons, peaches, plums, mume plums,
apricots, Chinese quinces, pears, ginger, and cinnamon.
12.26 For a *Dàfū*'s ordinary meal,
if there is raw sliced meat, there is no dried meat;
if there is dried meat, there is no raw sliced meat.
A *Shì* does not have two kinds of soup or sliced meat.
The elderly among the common people do not eat a meal without meat.
12.27 For raw sliced meat,
in spring use green onions,
in autumn use mustard.
For pork,
in spring use chives,
in autumn use smartweed.
Use green onions for solid fat,
scallions for liquid oil.
For the three sacrificial animals, use Evodia;
harmonize with vinegar;
for wild beasts, use plums.
Quail soup,
chicken soup,
partridge;
stuff them with smartweed.
Steamed bream and tench,
roasted squab,
pheasant;
these are fragrant and use no smartweed.
12.28 Do not eat young turtles.
For a wolf, remove the intestines;
for a dog, remove the kidneys;
for a wildcat, remove the spine;
for a rabbit, remove the rump;
for a fox, remove the head;
for a pig, remove the brain;
for a fish, remove the gall-bladder bone;
for a turtle, remove the rectal part.
For meat, it is called *tuō*;
for fish, it is called *zuò*;
for dates, it is called *xīn*;
for chestnuts, it is called *zhuàn*;
for peaches, it is called *dǎn*;
for quinces and pears, it is called *zuǎn*.
12.30 If an ox lows at night, the meat is rancid;
if a sheep has thin hair that is matted, the meat is rank;
if a dog has red thighs and is restless, the meat is foul-smelling;
if a bird has faded feathers and a raspy cry, the meat is fetid;
if a pig has a faraway look and overlapping eyelashes, the meat is fishy;
if a horse has a black spine and mottled forelegs, the meat is rank.
If a fledgling's tail is not a handful long,
do not eat it.
Also avoid the rump of a goose,
the fat of swans and owls,
the rump of a duck,
chicken liver,
goose kidneys,
the inner parts of a bustard,
and the stomach of a deer.
12.31 For raw meat, the finely sliced is called *kuài*,
the coarsely sliced is called *xuān*.
Some say: elk, deer, and fish are made into *zū*;
muntjac is made into *pìjī*;
wild boar is made into *xuān*;
rabbit is made into *wǎnpí*.
Slice green onions or scallions,
and place them in vinegar to soften the meat.
12.32 Regarding broth and food,
from the Zhūhóu down to the Shùrén, there is no difference in rank.
Dàfū do not have regular prescribed meals.
When a Dàfū is seventy, he has a cupboard.
The Tiānzǐ's cupboard
has five openings to the left
and five to the right.
Gōng, Hóu, and Bó have five in their inner chambers.
Dàfū have three in their cupboards.
Shì have one on their sideboards.
12.33 In all cases of nourishing the aged:
The Yǒu Yú clan used the Yàn ritual,
the Xià Hòu clan used the Xiǎng ritual,
the Yīn people used the Shí ritual,
and the Zhōu people cultivated and used them all together.
Generally, those of fifty are nourished in the township,
those of sixty are nourished in the capital city,
those of seventy are nourished in the school,
and this extends to the Zhūhóu.
For those of eighty,
when they receive a command from the ruler,
they bow once while sitting and then bow again with the head to the ground.
The blind do the same.
Those of ninety have someone else receive the command for them.
At fifty, they are provided with different grain.
At sixty, they have meat kept overnight.
At seventy, they are provided with two extra savory dishes.
At eighty, they have regular delicacies.
At ninety, their food and drink do not leave their bedchambers.
It is permissible for their delicacies and drinks to follow them wherever they wander.
At sixty, the funeral materials are prepared annually,
at seventy, seasonally,
at eighty, monthly,
and at ninety, they are maintained daily.
Only the jiǎo, jǐn, qīn, and mào
are made after death.
At fifty, the strength begins to decline.
At sixty, one is not full without meat.
At seventy, one is not warm without silk.
At eighty, one is not warm without another person.
At ninety, even with another person, one is not warm.
At fifty, one uses a staff in the house.
At sixty, one uses a staff in the township.
At seventy, one uses a staff in the capital city.
At eighty, one uses a staff at court.
For those of ninety,
if the Tiānzǐ wishes to ask them something,
he goes to their room and brings delicacies with him.
At seventy, one does not wait for the court to adjourn.
At eighty, the ruler sends monthly inquiries about their health.
At ninety, there is a daily allowance of food.
At fifty, one does not perform labor service.
At sixty, one does not participate in military service.
At seventy, one does not participate in the business of receiving guests.
At eighty, the duties of fasting and mourning do not apply to them.
At fifty, one receives a rank.
At sixty, one does not personally attend the school.
At seventy, one retires from office.
For all those from seventy and above,
only the shuāi and má garments are used for mourning.
Generally, the Sān Wáng, when nourishing the aged, would check the registers of age.
For those of eighty,
one son is exempt from public service.
For those of ninety,
the whole family is exempt from public service.
The blind are treated the same.
Whenever parents are alive,
the son, even if old himself, does not sit in the place of honor.
The Yǒu Yú clan nourished the elderly of the state in the Shàng Xiáng,
and the elderly of the commoners in the Xià Xiáng.
The Xià Hòu clan nourished the elderly of the state in the Dōng Xù,
and the elderly of the commoners in the Xī Xù.
The Yīn people nourished the elderly of the state in the Yòu Xué,
and the elderly of the commoners in the Zuǒ Xué.
The Zhōu people nourished the elderly of the state in the Dōng Jiǎo,
and the elderly of the commoners in the Yú Xiáng.
The Yú Xiáng was in the western suburbs of the capital city.
The Yǒu Yú clan wore the huáng cap when sacrificing
and the shēnyī when nourishing the aged.
The Xià Hòu clan wore the shōu cap when sacrificing
and the yànyī when nourishing the aged.
The Yīn people wore the xǔ cap when sacrificing
and the gǎoyī when nourishing the aged.
The Zhōu people wore the miǎn crown when sacrificing
and the xuányī when nourishing the aged.
12.34 Zéngzǐ said:
"When a filial son nourishes the aged,
he makes their hearts happy and does not go against their will.
He gladdens their ears and eyes and makes their sleeping quarters peaceful.
He serves them sincerely with food and drink.
The filial son's service lasts until the end of his life.
'Until the end of life' means
not just until the end of the parents' lives,
but until the end of his own life.
Therefore, what the parents love, he also loves.
Whom the parents respect, he also respects.
This extends even to their dogs and horses,
how much more so to people!"
Generally, in nourishing the aged,
the Wǔ Dì took them as models,
while the Sān Wáng begged them for words of advice.
The Wǔ Dì took them as models,
nourishing their physical bodies without begging for words.
If there were good deeds, they recorded them in the Dūnshǐ.
The Sān Wáng also took them as models,
but after nourishing the aged, they begged for words.
They also refined the etiquette.
Both had the Dūnshǐ.
12.35 For Chún'áo: fry fermented meat sauce,
place it on top of dry-land rice,
and pour fat over it.
This is called Chún'áo.
For Chúnmǔ: fry fermented meat sauce,
place it on top of broomcorn millet,
and pour fat over it.
This is called Chúnmǔ.
For the Páo:
Take a suckling pig or a young ram,
slaughter it and eviscerate it.
Fill its belly with dates.
Wrap it in reeds and straw.
Coat it with clay.
Roast it.
When the clay is dry,
break it off.
Wash the hands and rub the meat
to remove the thin membrane.
Make rice flour, wash and soak it to make a gruel,
then coat the pig with it and fry it in fat.
The fat must cover it.
Take a great cauldron of boiling water,
and in a small tripod, place fragrant dried meat inside.
Do not let the boiling water submerge the tripod.
Keep the fire going for three days and three nights without interruption.
Afterward, season it with vinegar and fermented meat sauce.
12.36 For Dǎozhēn:
Take the meat of beef, mutton, elk, deer, or muntjac, which must
be the tenderloin. For each kind, take the same amount as the beef. Pound it
on both sides.
Remove the nerves.
Cook it, take it out,
remove the membrane,
and soften the meat.
12.37 For Zì:
Take beef that must be freshly slaughtered.
Slice it thinly,
cutting across the grain.
Steep it in fine wine.
After one morning,
eat it with fermented meat sauce or vinegar and plum juice.
12.38 For Wèi'áo:
Pound the meat,
remove the membrane,
weave reeds,
and spread the beef upon them.
Sprinkle powdered cinnamon and ginger
over it and salt it.
Eat it when dry.
Mutton is prepared in the same way.
Elk, deer, and muntjac
are all prepared like beef and mutton.
If one desires moist meat,
soak it and fry it with fermented meat sauce.
If one desires dry meat,
pound it and eat it.
12.39 For Sǎn:
Take the meat of beef, mutton, and pork,
in equal parts, and mince them finely.
Mix with rice.
Use two parts rice to one part meat.
Form them into cakes and fry them.
12.40 For Gānláo:
Take one dog's liver,
wrap it
in its own caul fat and roast it until moist.
When the fat is scorched,
do not use smartweed.
Take rice, wash and soak it,
finely mince wolf's breast fat,
and mix it with the rice to make a gruel.
12.41 The Rites
begin with being careful about the distinction between husband and wife,
building houses and apartments,
and distinguishing between the exterior and interior.
Men reside in the exterior,
women reside in the interior.
The inner palace is deep and the gates are secured.
Gatekeepers and eunuchs guard them.
Men do not enter,
and women do not go out.
Men and women do not use the same clothes horse.
A wife does not dare to hang her clothes on her husband's rack,
nor does she dare to store them in her husband's boxes or baskets.
They do not dare to share the same bathhouse.
If the husband is not present,
she gathers his pillow, boxes, mats, and utensil covers and stores them away.
The young serving the old
and the lowly serving the noble
are all like this.
The ritual between husband and wife
continues until they reach seventy,
after which they share the same bed-chamber without separation.
Therefore, even though a concubine is old,
if she has not yet reached fifty,
she must be admitted to the husband's bed once every five days.
When one is about to be admitted,
she fasts and purifies herself,
rinses her mouth and washes,
is careful with her clothing,
combs her hair, uses a hairnet, pins her hair, and ties the ends,
uses a horn-comb to brush the hair over her forehead,
fastens her lapels and strings, and wears silk-stringed shoes.
Even for maid-servants and concubines,
their clothing and food
must come after those of their elders.
When the primary wife is not present,
a concubine being admitted dares not take the entire night for herself.
12.42 When the wife is about to give birth to a child,
and the month and time arrive,
she resides in a side chamber.
The husband sends someone twice a day to inquire about her,
and if she is in labor, he inquires in person.
The wife does not dare to see him,
but has the *mǔ* dress properly to respond.
Until the child is born,
the husband continues to send someone twice a day to inquire.
If the husband is fasting,
then he does not enter the gate of the side chamber.
When the child is born,
for a boy, a bow is hung on the left side of the gate;
for a girl, a sash is hung on the right side of the gate.
After three days,
they begin to carry the child;
the boy is taken for the archery ritual, but the girl is not.
12.43 When the *shìzǐ* of a state ruler is born,
it is reported to the ruler,
who then receives the child with the *dàláo*,
and the *zǎi* manages the preparations.
After three days,
an officer *shì* is chosen by divination to carry the child.
The one who receives an auspicious omen fasts for the night,
and in court robes, stands outside the chamber door.
He receives and carries the child.
The Master of Archery, with a bow of mulberry wood
and six arrows of wild-raspberry stalks,
shoots toward Heaven, Earth, and the four directions.
The *bǎo* receives the child and then carries him.
The *zǎi* offers ale to the one who carried the child
and rewards him with a bundle of silk.
The wife of an officer *shì*
or a concubine of a grandee *dàfū*
is appointed to suckle the child.
12.44 For all receptions of a child,
an auspicious day is chosen.
For the eldest son, the *dàláo* is used;
for commoners, a single piglet;
for an officer *shì*, a single pig;
for a grandee *dàfū*, the *shǎoláo*;
for the *shìzǐ* of a state ruler, the *dàláo*.
For those who are not the eldest son,
the ritual is reduced by one degree.
12.45 A separate room is made for the child within the palace.
From among the secondary wives and those who are suitable,
one is sought who is generous, kind,
mild, virtuous, respectful,
prudent, and of few words,
to serve as the *shī*;
the next serves as the *címǔ*,
and the next as the *bǎomǔ*.
They all reside in the child's room,
and no one else enters without business.
At the end of three months,
an auspicious day is chosen to trim the hair into tufts.
For a boy, these are "horns"; for a girl, they are a "bridle" style;
otherwise, the boy's is on the left and the girl's is on the right.
On this day,
the wife presents the child to the father.
People of high rank have new clothes made.
From the *mìngshì* downward,
all rinse their mouths and wash.
Both husband and wife rise early,
bathe and dress.
They prepare a meal as if for the first day of the month.
The husband enters the gate,
ascends by the eastern steps,
and stands facing west on the eastern platform.
The wife carries the child and comes out from the room,
standing by the lintel facing east.
The *mǔ* goes first
to assist, saying:
"The mother, [name], ventures on this day
to respectfully present the child."
The husband replies:
"With reverence, let him follow his models."
The father takes the child's right hand
and, smiling, gives him a name.
The wife replies:
"I will remember it for his fulfillment."
Then she turns to the left
and hands the child to the *shī*.
The *shī* then informs all the wives and secondary mothers of the name.
The wife then returns to her chamber.
The husband informs the *zǎi* of the name,
and the *zǎi* informs all the men of the name.
It is recorded:
"On such a year, month, and day, so-and-so was born,"
and it is stored away.
The *zǎi* informs the *lǘshǐ*,
who makes two copies:
one is stored in the Hamlet Office,
and the other is presented to the *zhōushǐ*.
The *zhōushǐ* presents it to the *zhōubó*,
who orders it to be stored in the District Office.
The husband enters to eat, according to the ritual of nourishment.
12.46 When the *shìzǐ* is born,
the ruler bathes and wears his court robes.
The wife does the same.
Both stand by the eastern steps facing west.
A *shìfù* carries the child and ascends by the western steps.
The ruler names him,
and then she descends.
The legitimate and concubine-born sons are presented in the outer chamber.
He strokes their heads and, smiling, names them.
The ritual follows the previous pattern,
but without formal speeches.
12.47 In all naming of children,
one does not use the day or month,
nor the name of a state,
nor the name of a hidden ailment.
The sons of a *dàfū* or a *shì*
do not dare to take the same name as the *shìzǐ*.
When a concubine is about to give birth,
and the month and time arrive,
the husband sends someone once a day to inquire.
At the end of the third month after the child is born,
she rinses, washes, and fasts early in the morning,
and is presented in the inner chamber.
She is received with rituals like those when she first entered the household.
After the ruler has eaten,
and the table is cleared,
he has her eat the leftovers alone,
and then she is admitted to his bed.
12.48 When a son by a concubine of a *gōng* is born,
he resides in the side chamber.
At the end of three months,
his mother bathes, wears her court robes, and is presented to the ruler.
An usher presents the child.
Whatever the ruler bestows, she accepts.
The ruler names him.
For the other sons,
he has an official name them.
12.49 For commoners who have no side chamber,
when the month and time arrive,
the husband leaves to stay in the public room.
His inquiries
and the ritual of the child seeing the father
do not differ from the above.
In all cases, if the father is alive,
and the grandson is presented to the grandfather,
the grandfather also names him.
The ritual is like that of a child seeing the father,
but without formal speeches.
12.50 Those who suckle the child
leave after three years.
If they are seen at the ruler's palace, they are treated with kindness.
The son of a *dàfū* has a *shímǔ*,
but the wife of a *shì* raises her child herself.
12.51 For the sons of *mìngshì* and above, and the sons of a *dàfū*,
they are presented after ten days.
When the eldest son is presented before he has eaten,
the father must take his right hand.
When other legitimate or concubine-born sons are presented after they have eaten,
the father must stroke their heads.
12.52 When the child is able to eat food,
he is taught to use his right hand.
When he is able to speak,
a boy responds with *wéi* and a girl with *yú*.
A boy wears a leather sash,
and a girl wears a silk sash.
At six years,
they are taught numbers and the names of the directions.
At seven years,
boys and girls do not share a mat
nor eat together.
At eight years,
in going out or coming in through gates or doors, and in taking their places for food and drink,
they must follow after their elders;
thus they are first taught yielding.
At nine years,
they are taught how to count the days.
At ten years,
they go out to follow an external teacher,
staying and sleeping away from home.
They learn writing and arithmetic.
Their clothing consists of robes and trousers not made of silk.
In their rituals, they follow the basic models.
Morning and evening, they learn the manners of youth,
and they request practice in being simple and sincere.
At thirteen years of age,
he learns music,
recites the *Shī*,
and performs the *Sháo* dance.
When he reaches full youth, he performs the *Xiàng* dance
and learns archery and charioteering.
At twenty, he undergoes the capping ceremony,
begins to learn the *Lǐ*,
is permitted to wear furs and silks,
and performs the *Dàxià* dance.
He practices filial piety and fraternal duty with sincerity,
and although he learns extensively, he does not yet teach others,
keeping his knowledge within and not yet entering public service.
At thirty, he takes a wife
and begins to manage the affairs of a man;
he learns extensively without a fixed limit
and follows his friends, observing their intentions.
At forty, he first enters government service;
according to the nature of things, he brings forth plans and deliberations.
If his principles harmonize with his superior, he follows and obeys;
if not, he leaves.
At fifty, he is appointed as a *Dàfū*
and takes charge of official administration.
At seventy, he retires from office.
12.53 Whenever a male bows,
he places his left hand on top.
12.54 A girl, at ten years of age, does not go out from the women's apartments.
Her *mǔ* teaches her to be pleasing in speech, docile in manner, and obedient.
She handles hemp and ramie,
manages silk and cocoons,
and weaves cloth, braids, and ribbons.
She learns women's tasks to provide clothing,
observes the sacrifices,
and prepares the wine and fluids, the *biān* and *dòu* vessels, and the pickled vegetables and meat sauces;
in the rites, she assists in setting out the offerings.
At fifteen, she undergoes the hair-pinning ceremony,
and at twenty, she is married.
If there is a special cause,
she is married at twenty-three.
If she is betrothed with full rites, she becomes a wife;
if she elopes, she becomes a concubine.
Whenever a female bows,
she places her right hand on top.
13.1 The *Tiānzǐ* wears a cap with jade bead-pendants,
with twelve strings of beads
hanging from the front and back of the rectangular board.
He wears the dragon-embroidered robe for sacrifices.
In the *xuánduān* robe, he greets the sun outside the Eastern Gate;
he listens to the announcement of the new moon outside the Southern Gate.
In an intercalary month,
the left leaf of the gate is closed
and he stands in the middle of it.
Wearing the *píbiàn* cap, he daily attends court
and thereupon eats.
At midday he eats the leftovers,
and music is played while he eats.
His daily meal is a *shǎoláo*;
on the first day of the month, it is a *dàláo*.
There are five drinks:
water, thin congee, wine, sweet spirits, and thick congee.
When he finishes eating,
he wears the *xuánduān* robe while at rest.
When he acts, the *Zuǒshǐ* records it;
when he speaks, the *Yòushǐ* records it.
The court musicians monitor the harmony of the sounds.
When the harvest is not successful,
the *Tiānzǐ* wears plain white clothes,
rides in a plain white chariot,
and eats without music.
13.2 The *Zhūhóu* wear the *xuánduān* robe for sacrifices,
the *bīmiǎn* robes for the morning court,
and the *píbiàn* cap to listen to the announcement of the new moon in the *Tàimiào*.
They wear court robes for the daily court in the inner court.
At court,
they enter as soon as the colors of dawn can be distinguished.
The ruler appears as the sun rises to see them,
then withdraws to the *Lùqǐn*
to attend to administration.
He sends someone to look after the *Dàfū*;
when the *Dàfū* have withdrawn,
he then goes to the *Xiǎoqǐn*
and removes his robes.
He also wears court robes to eat,
with a single victim, three *zǔ* stands, and the offering of the lungs.
In the evening, he wears the *shēnyī*
and offers the meat of the victim.
On the first day of the month, a *shǎoláo* is used,
with five *zǔ* stands and four *guǐ* vessels.
On *Zǐ* and *Mǎo* days, he eats millet and vegetable soup.
The *Fūrén* uses the same kitchen as the ruler.
The ruler does not kill an ox without a reason;
a *Dàfū* does not kill a sheep without a reason;
a *Shì* does not kill a dog or a pig without a reason.
The *Jūnzǐ* stays far away from the slaughterhouse and kitchen;
whatever has blood and breath,
he does not personally take its life.
If it does not rain by the eighth month,
the ruler does not have a full meal.
When the harvest is not successful,
the ruler wears hempen cloth and tucks his *hù* tablet into his sash by its base;
no tolls are collected at the passes and bridges;
forests and marshes are open and not taxed;
no earthwork projects are started;
and the *Dàfū* may not commission new chariots or horses.
13.3 The *Bǔrén* positions the tortoise shell;
the *Shǐ* marks the ink lines;
and the ruler determines the auspiciousness of the omens.
13.4 The ruler's chariot has a lambskin cover and a tiger-skin rug;
a *Dàfū*'s ceremonial chariot
has a deerskin cover and a leopard-skin rug,
as does his court chariot;
and an officer's ceremonial chariot
has a deerskin cover and a leopard-skin rug.
13.5 A *Jūnzǐ* in his dwelling always faces the door;
when sleeping, he always has his head to the east.
If there is a violent wind, sudden thunder, or heavy rain,
he must change his expression;
even at night, he must get up,
put on his robes and cap, and sit.
He washes his hands five times a day;
he washes his hair with millet water and his face with fine grain water.
For combing, he uses a comb of white-grained wood,
and when his hair is dry, an ivory comb.
When wine and appetizers are presented,
the musicians then ascend to sing.
For bathing, he uses two towels:
fine linen for the upper body and coarse linen for the lower body.
On leaving the tub, he steps onto a straw mat;
he repeatedly uses warm water
and then steps onto a rush mat.
He uses a cloth to dry his body,
puts on his shoes, and is offered a drink.
When he is about to go to the ruler's place,
he keeps a vigil and fasts overnight,
stays in the outer chamber,
and bathes.
The *Shǐ* presents the ivory *hù* tablet,
on which he writes his thoughts for his replies and his commissions.
After he has dressed,
he practices his movements and listens to the sound of his jade pendants,
and then goes out.
He bows at his private court;
he looks radiant;
and when he mounts his chariot, there is a brilliance about him.
The *Tiānzǐ* tucks the *tǐng* tablet into his sash,
representing the rectitude of the world.
The *Zhūhóu* use the *tú* tablet,
curved in front and straight behind,
representing their yielding to the *Tiānzǐ*.
The *Dàfū* use a tablet curved both in front and behind,
representing that there is nothing to which they do not yield.
13.6 When sitting in attendance,
one must move back on the mat;
if one does not move back,
then one must draw back and move away from the ruler's side.
One does not mount the mat from the front,
as that would be stepping over the mat.
When sitting, one leaves a foot of the mat empty in front.
When reading books
or eating,
one sits upright,
with the *dòu* vessels placed a foot away from the mat.
13.7 If the ruler grants food and treats him as a guest,
he orders him to make an offering,
and only then does he make it.
He first eats the rice and tastes all the delicacies,
then drinks and waits.
If there is a taster for the delicacies,
he waits for the ruler to eat
and then eats himself;
he eats the rice,
drinks, and waits.
When the ruler orders him to have some delicacies,
he takes those that are near;
if ordered to taste of various kinds,
he then may take whatever he wishes.
Whenever tasting a distant dish,
he must follow the sequence of the near dishes.
Before the ruler has covered his hand,
one does not dare to take the rice soaked in soup.
After the ruler has finished eating,
he then takes the rice soaked in soup;
when taking the rice soaked in soup,
it is done in three mouthfuls.
When the ruler's table has been removed,
he takes some of the rice and sauce,
goes out, and gives it to his attendants.
13.8 In all cases of assisting at a meal,
one does not eat to the full;
when eating at another's house, one does not sate himself.
Only water and thin congee are not used for offerings;
if one were to offer them,
it would be a sign of excessive self-abasement.
13.9 If the ruler grants him a cup of wine,
he leaves his mat, bows twice, touches his head to the ground, and receives it.
He returns to the mat and makes an offering,
drinks, and finishes the cup;
he then waits until the ruler has finished his cup,
and then hands back the empty cup.
When a Jūnzǐ drinks wine,
upon receiving one cup, his appearance is serious and respectful.
With the second cup, he is polite and articulate.
When the ritual is concluded
after the third cup,
he withdraws with a composed and easy manner.
Having withdrawn, he sits down to take his shoes;
he seeks a secluded spot and then puts them on.
Sitting on the left, he puts on the right shoe;
sitting on the right, he puts on the left shoe.
13.10 In all cases of wine vessels, the dark liquid must be placed in the superior position.
Only the Jūn faces the vessel directly.
Only when feasting country folk is all wine used.
A Dàfū places the vessel to the side and uses a Yù stand;
a Shì places the vessel to the side and uses a Jìn stand.
13.11 When first capped, one uses the black cloth cap.
This practice reaches down from the Zhūhóu.
After the capping ceremony, it may be discarded.
The dark cap with vermilion silk strings
is the cap of the Tiānzǐ.
The black cloth cap with embroidered tassels
is the cap of the Zhūhóu.
The dark cap with red silk strings
is the Zhūhóu’s cap for fasting.
The dark cap with grey-green silk strings
is the Shì’s cap for fasting.
The white silk cap with a dark band
is the cap for sons and grandsons.
The white silk cap with a plain white border
is the cap for the sacrifice after mourning.
Tassels hanging five inches
mark a scholar of idle leisure.
The dark cap with a white silk band
is the dress for those not yet ranked.
In the ordinary cap, the band is attached to the body;
this practice reaches down from the Tiānzǐ.
Only when there is business are the tassels attached.
At fifty, one does not go about with hair loose.
When parents have died, one does not wear the Máo hairstyle.
With the large silk cap, there are no tassels.
The dark cap with purple tassels
began with Lǔ Huán Gōng.
13.12 In the morning, one wears the black formal robe;
in the evening, the long robe.
The long robe has a cuff three times the width of the wrist.
The bottom seam is twice the width of the waist.
The lapel falls at the side.
The sleeve is long enough to allow the elbow to be drawn back.
The inner garment is long enough to overlap by a foot.
The collar is two inches wide.
The cuff is one foot two inches wide.
The border is one and a half inches wide.
Using silk to wrap cloth
is contrary to ritual.
A Shì does not wear woven patterns.
One who has no ruler does not wear two colors.
The upper garment is of a primary color;
the lower garment is of an intermediate color.
Unless in formal colors, one does not enter the gate of the palace.
In a single layer of fine or coarse linen, one does not enter the gate of the palace.
Wearing a fur robe with the fur outside, one does not enter the gate of the palace.
Wearing an uncovered fur robe, one does not enter the gate of the palace.
New silk floss makes the silk-lined robe;
old silk floss makes the wadded robe;
a single layer makes the unlined robe;
silk makes the lined garment.
13.13 Using white silk for the court dress
began with Jì Kāng Zǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Wearing the court dress to attend court,
one wears it after the first day of the month ceremony."
He also said:
"When the state does not follow the Way,
one does not wear the full dress of his rank."
Only the Jūn has the figured fur robe for inspections and oaths;
the "great fur robe" is not an ancient custom.
13.14 The Jūn wears a robe of white fox fur,
with an embroidered garment over it to show the fur.
The Jūn’s right attendant wears tiger fur;
the one on the left wears wolf fur.
A Shì does not wear white fox fur.
A Jūnzǐ wears a robe of grey fox fur with leopard-skin sleeves,
with a dark thin silk garment over it.
A fawn-skin robe with wild-dog sleeves
has a light green silk garment over it.
A lambskin robe with leopard-skin trim
has a black garment over it.
A fox-fur robe
has a yellow garment over it.
The embroidered garment over a fox-fur robe
is the dress of the Zhūhóu.
Robes of dog or sheep fur
do not have a show-garment,
as they are not for decoration;
one does not wear the show-garment.
The use of the show-garment with fur
is to display beauty.
At a funeral, one wears the robes closed,
not displaying all the decorations;
in the presence of the Jūn, one uses the show-garment,
displaying all the decorations.
Wearing the robe closed
is to contain the beauty;
therefore the Shī wears it closed,
and when holding the jade or tortoise-shell, it is worn closed;
when there is no ceremony, it is shown,
not daring to presume such fullness.
13.15 The tablet:
the Tiānzǐ uses precious jade;
the Zhūhóu use ivory;
a Dàfū uses bamboo decorated with fish-bones;
a Shì uses bamboo, and ivory at the base is permissible.
When seeing the Tiānzǐ or at archery,
one does not lay aside the tablet.
Laying aside the tablet when entering the Dàmiào
is not an ancient custom.
In the Xiǎogōng mourning, one does not lay aside the tablet;
but when performing duties and removing the mourning cap, one lays it aside.
After tucking it into the belt, one must wash his hands;
though one may hold things in court,
one does not always wash.
Whenever pointing or drawing in the presence of the Jūn,
one uses the tablet; when approaching to
receive a command from the Jūn,
one writes it on the tablet.
The tablet serves all such purposes;
hence it is decorated.
The tablet measures two feet and six inches;
its middle is three inches wide,
and its ends taper by one-sixth.
With a plain silk belt,
borders are all around.
A Dàfū has a plain silk belt,
with borders on the hanging ends.
A Shì has a belt of boiled silk,
with unhemmed edges and borders on the lower part.
A scholar at home wears a brocaded belt;
a disciple wears a plain white silk belt.
The loops and knots are made of silk cord.
The knee-cover: for the Jūn it is vermilion;
for a Dàfū it is plain white;
for a Shì it is of madder-dyed leather.
Rounded, tapered, or straight:
the Tiānzǐ’s is straight;
the Gōng and Hóu have the front and back square;
a Dàfū’s is square at the front
and has the corners cut off at the back;
for a Shì, front and back are regular.
The knee-cover is two feet wide at the bottom,
one foot wide at the top,
and three feet long.
Its neck is five inches;
at the shoulder, the leather belt
is two inches wide.
A Dàfū’s large belt is four inches wide.
For a mixed belt,
the Jūn’s is vermilion and green;
a Dàfū’s is dark with flowery patterns;
a Shì’s is black with a border
two inches wide,
wrapped twice to make four inches.
In all belts, there are unhemmed edges
without needlework.
Those of the first rank of commission have a red-yellow knee-cover and dark yoke-strap;
those of the second rank have a red knee-cover and dark yoke-strap;
those of the third rank have a red knee-cover and green yoke-strap.
The Tiānzǐ’s plain silk belt
is lined with vermilion
and has borders all around.
The Wánghòu wears the pheasant-embroidered robe;
the Fūrén wears the robe with embroidered pheasants;
these are three inches wide
and long enough to reach the belt.
The hanging ends of the girdle have a regulated length:
for a Shì, three feet;
for an official, two feet and five inches.
Zǐyóu said:
"Dividing the part below the belt into three,
the hanging ends occupy two parts."
The hanging ends, the knee-cover, and the knots all hang to the same level.
A Jūn’s lady of the first rank wears the robe with folded pheasant patterns.
Second rank wears the pheasant-embroidered robe;
first rank wears the plain white robe;
a Shì’s wife wears the black robe with a border.
Only the Shìfù are commissioned for the presentation of cocoons;
otherwise, women follow the rank of their husbands.
Whenever attending the Jūn,
the hanging ends of the girdle hang down,
the feet move as if gliding on a level surface,
the head is bowed like the eaves of a roof, the hands are clasped and hanging down,
the eyes look down while the ears listen to what is above.
One’s gaze is between the belt and the collar;
when listening, one inclines the left ear toward the speaker.
Whenever the Jūn summons
using three tallies:
with two tallies, one runs;
with one tally, one walks quickly.
At the office, one does not wait for his shoes;
when outside, one does not wait for his carriage.
13.16 For a *Shì* in relation to a *Dàfū*,
he does not dare to bow when greeting him, but bows when seeing him off.
For a *Shì* in relation to an honored person,
he bows first and then advances to face him;
if the honored person returns the bow, the *Shì* runs to avoid receiving it.
When a *Shì* speaks at the ruler's court,
if a *Dàfū* is deceased,
he refers to him by his posthumous name or courtesy name;
he refers to other *Shì* by their given names.
When speaking with a *Dàfū*,
he refers to *Shì* by their given names
and to *Dàfū* by their courtesy names.
At the residence of a *Dàfū*,
there are public taboos
but no private taboos.
In all sacrifices, there are no taboos;
in the ancestral temple, there are no taboos;
in teaching and when composing texts, there are no taboos.
13.17 The ancient *Jūnzǐ* necessarily wore jade pendants:
on the right, those sounding the notes *Zhǐ* and *Jué*;
on the left, those sounding *Gōng* and *Yǔ*.
When moving quickly, he kept time with the *Cǎi Qí*;
when walking, he kept time with the *Sì Xià*.
When turning around, his movements matched a circle;
when turning at an angle, his movements matched a square.
When advancing, he bowed;
when retreating, he raised his body;
only then would the jades chime together rhythmically.
Therefore, when the *Jūnzǐ* was in his carriage,
he heard the sounds of the *luán* and *hé* bells;
when walking, he heard the chiming of his jade pendants;
in this way, depraved and crooked thoughts
had no means to enter his heart.
13.18 When the ruler is present, he does not wear jade pendants visibly;
on the left, he ties the pendants;
on the right, he sets the pendants aside.
At home, he sets the pendants in place;
at court, he ties the pendants up.
During purification, he ties the pendants with a red string and wears a sparrow-colored knee-cover.
Every belt must have jade pendants,
except during mourning.
The jade pendants have an impact tooth.
For no reason does a *Jūnzǐ*
remove his jade from his person;
the *Jūnzǐ* compares his virtue to jade.
The *Tiānzǐ* wears white jade with dark silk cords;
the *Gōng* and *Hóu* wear *shānxuán* jade with vermilion cords;
the *Dàfū* wear *shuǐcāng* jade with pure-colored cords;
the *Shìzǐ* wears *yú* jade with dark green cords;
the *Shì* wear *ruǎn wén* jade with reddish-yellow cords;
*Kǒngzǐ* wore an ivory ring five inches in diameter
with dark green cords.
13.19 The regulations for a *Tóngzǐ*:
black cloth clothing with embroidered borders,
an embroidered sash,
tied together with cords; the embroidery
for binding the hair is all vermilion embroidery.
The hanging ends of the belt reach down—
if he is diligent in his duties, he gathers them up;
if he runs, he holds them in his arms.
A *Tóngzǐ* does not wear fur or silk,
does not wear shoes with toe-ornaments,
and does not wear the *sī* mourning garment.
When listening to instructions, he does not wear hemp.
When there is no business,
he stands to the north of the host, facing south.
When seeing a teacher,
he follows others in entering.
13.20 When attending a meal with a teacher, those of different ranks
perform the sacrifice last but begin eating first.
When a guest performs the sacrifice,
the host declines, saying:
“It is not worthy of being sacrificed.”
When the guest finishes the rice,
the host apologizes for the coarseness of the food.
If the host sets out his own sauce,
the guest clears it away himself.
Among those in one room,
if they are not guests,
one person clears the table.
Among those at a single meal,
one person clears the table.
At all banquet meals,
women do not clear the table.
13.21 When eating dates, peaches, or plums,
do not eat down to the pit.
For melons, sacrifice the top ring;
after eating the middle, discard the part that was held.
In eating fruit, follow the *Jūnzǐ*;
in eating cooked food, precede the *Jūnzǐ*.
When there is a celebratory occasion,
do not congratulate unless it is a gift from the ruler.
For one in mourning—
if he is diligent in his duties, he gathers his clothes;
if he runs, he holds them.
When *Kǒngzǐ* ate at the *Jì* clan’s residence,
he did not decline the sacrifice,
but ate the rice without eating the meat.
If the ruler bestows a carriage and horses,
he mounts them to bow in thanks;
if clothes,
he wears them to bow in thanks.
Until the ruler has given the command,
he does not dare to mount or wear them.
For a gift from the ruler,
he kowtows,
resting his palms on the ground.
For gifts of wine and meat,
he does not bow a second time.
For all gifts,
a *Jūnzǐ* and a *Xiǎorén* are not given on the same day.
13.22 When making an offering to the ruler,
a *Dàfū* sends a steward;
a *Shì* goes in person;
both bow twice and kowtow while sending it.
When presenting food to the ruler,
there are pungent herbs, peach branches, and reed brooms;
for a *Dàfū*, the broom is removed;
for a *Shì*, the pungent herbs are removed;
all are brought to the Master of the Kitchen.
A *Dàfū* does not bow in person,
to avoid the ruler returning the bow.
A *Dàfū* bows for the gift and withdraws;
a *Shì* waits for the assent and then withdraws,
bowing again,
though the ruler does not return the bow.
If a *Dàfū* personally gives a gift to a *Shì*,
the *Shì* bows to receive it,
and bows again at the *Dàfū*’s residence.
For clothes,
he does not wear them to bow.
If an equal is not home,
he bows at their house.
In making an offering to a superior,
one does not dare to let it be known directly.
A *Shì* does not offer congratulations to a *Dàfū*;
a lower *Dàfū* offers congratulations to an upper *Dàfū*.
While parents are alive,
in performing rites for others, he refers to himself through his father;
if someone gives him a gift,
he bows for it in his father’s name.
13.23 If the ritual is not grand,
the attire is not full.
Therefore, with the great fur robe, one does not expose the undergarment;
when riding in the state carriage, one does not bow to the crossbar.
13.24 When a father calls,
one answers with *wéi* and not *nuò*;
if one’s hand is holding a task, one drops it;
if food is in the mouth, one spits it out;
one runs without merely walking fast.
When parents are old,
one does not change his destination when going out
and does not exceed the time for return.
When a parent is ill, one’s expression and demeanor are not flourishing—
these are the minor details of a filial son.
After a father’s death, one cannot read his books,
for the moisture of his hands remains there;
after a mother’s death, one cannot drink from her cup,
for the moisture of her breath remains there.
13.25 When the ruler enters the gate,
the attendant brushes the central post;
the *Dàfū* stays between the doorpost and the central post;
the *Shì* attendant brushes the doorpost.
13.26 A guest does not enter through the center of the gate
and does not step on the threshold.
Public business is conducted from the west of the central post;
private business from the east of the central post.
13.27 The ruler and the personator of the dead walk with heels touching;
the *Dàfū* walks with feet following each other;
the *Shì* walks with half-steps.
When moving slowly, they all use these steps.
When moving quickly, they wish to lift the feet,
yet the hands and feet should not shift from their alignment.
Walking with a shuffling gait like a piglet, not lifting the feet,
gliding like a stream—
it is the same on the mat.
When walking upright,
the chin is level like an arrow.
When walking in a cap,
one moves with a light, lifting step.
When holding tortoise shell or jade,
one lifts the front of the foot and drags the heel,
with short, hurried steps.
13.28 In all walking, the demeanor should be easy and dignified.
13.29 In the ancestral temple, the demeanor is reverent;
at court, it is dignified and expansive.
13.30 The *Jūnzǐ*’s demeanor is relaxed and deliberate;
when seeing a superior, it is respectful and alert.
The appearance of the feet should be heavy;
the appearance of the hands should be respectful;
the appearance of the eyes should be steady;
the appearance of the mouth should be still;
the appearance of the voice should be quiet;
the appearance of the head should be upright;
the appearance of the breath should be solemn;
the appearance of standing should be virtuous;
the appearance of the countenance should be grave;
the appearance of sitting should be like a personator of the dead.
13.31 In private life, the demeanor is warm and gentle.
13.32 Whenever sacrificing,
one’s appearance and facial expression
should be as if one sees the person being sacrificed to.
13.33 The appearance of mourning is weary and haggard;
the facial expression is dejected;
the appearance of the gaze is apprehensive and searching;
the manner of speaking is hesitant and soft.
13.34 The military appearance is bold and vigorous;
the manner of speaking is stern and upright;
the facial expression is severe and solemn;
the appearance of the gaze is clear and bright.
The standing posture is distinct;
when in a lowly position, do not be sycophantic;
the head and neck must be centered;
stand firm like a mountain, and move with the proper time;
maintain an abundant spirit and a solid posture,
with a high-spirited and relaxed manner, and a countenance like jade.
13.35 Regarding self-appellations:
The Tiānzǐ says, “Yǔ Yī Rén.”
A Bó says, “The Tiānzǐ’s forceful servant.”
When the Zhūhóu address the Tiānzǐ,
they say, “Such-and-such land’s defensive servant, so-and-so”;
when in the border regions,
they say, “Such-and-such screen’s servant, so-and-so.”
To those of equal rank or below,
they say, “Guǎrén.”
The ruler of a small state says, “Gū”;
the usher also says, “Gū.”
A high Dàfū says, “Xiàchén”;
the usher says, “The Guǎjūn zhī Lǎo.”
A low Dàfū refers to himself by name;
the usher says, “Guǎ Dàfū.”
The Shìzǐ refers to himself by name;
the usher says, “The Guǎjūn zhī Shì.”
A Gōngzǐ says, “Chén Niè.”
A Shì says, “The servant of the courier service”;
to a Dàfū, he says, “Wài Sī.”
When a Dàfū sends a servant for private affairs,
if a personal servant ushers, he is called by name;
if a Gōngshì ushers, he says, “Guǎ Dàfū”
or “The Guǎjūn zhī Lǎo.”
When a Dàfū goes somewhere,
he must have a Gōngshì act as his guest.
14.1 In the past, Zhōugōng received the Zhūhóu in audience at their positions in the Míngtáng:
The Tiānzǐ stood facing south with his back to the axe-screen;
the Sāngōng
were before the central steps,
facing north, with the east being the place of honor.
The positions of the Zhūhóu
were to the east of the eastern steps,
facing west, with the north being the place of honor.
The states of the various Bó
were to the west of the western steps,
facing east, with the north being the place of honor.
The states of the various Zǐ
were at the east of the gate,
facing north, with the east being the place of honor.
The states of the various Nán
were at the west of the gate,
facing north, with the east being the place of honor.
The states of the Jiǔyí were outside the eastern gate,
