facing west, with the north being the place of honor.
The states of the Bāmán
were outside the southern gate,
facing north, with the east being the place of honor.
The states of the Liùróng
were outside the western gate,
facing east, with the south being the place of honor.
The states of the Wǔdí
were outside the northern gate,
facing south, with the east being the place of honor.
The states of the Jiǔcǎi
were outside the Yìngmén gate,
facing north, with the east being the place of honor.
Those from the four borders
reported their arrival generation after generation.
These were the positions in the Míngtáng of Zhōugōng.
The Míngtáng was that which
clarified the ranks of the Zhūhóu.
Formerly, when Yīn Zhòu threw the world into chaos,
he dried the flesh of Guǐhóu to feast the Zhūhóu.
Therefore, Zhōugōng assisted Wǔwáng in attacking Zhòu.
When Wǔwáng died,
Chéngwáng was young and weak.
Zhōugōng occupied the position of Tiānzǐ
to govern the world;
in the sixth year,
he received the Zhūhóu in audience at the Míngtáng,
established the rites and created the music,
and promulgated the weights and measures,
and the world was greatly submissive;
in the seventh year,
he returned the government to Chéngwáng.
Chéngwáng considered Zhōugōng to have performed meritorious service for the world;
therefore, he enfeoffed Zhōugōng in Qūfù,
with a territory of seven hundred lǐ
and a thousand leather-covered chariots,
and ordered the Lǔgōng to sacrifice to Zhōugōng generation after generation with the rites and music of the Tiānzǐ.
Therefore, the ruler of Lǔ,
in the first month of spring, rides in the dàlù chariot,
carrying the bow-case;
the banner has twelve streamers
with the emblems of the sun and moon;
he sacrifices to Shàngdì in the suburb,
pairing him with Hòujì.
These were the rites of the Tiānzǐ.
14.2 In the sixth month of midsummer,
the Dì sacrifice is used to sacrifice to Zhōugōng in the Dàmiào;
the victim used is a white bull;
the vessels used are the xī-zūn, xiàng-zūn,
and shānléi;
for the fragrant wine, the huángmù is used;
for the libation, the yùzàn ladle and
dàguī jade are used;
for the offerings, the yùdòu and
diāosuǎn are used;
for the cups, the yùzhǎn is used,
following the engraved style,
and added
are the bìsàn and the bìjiǎo;
for the meat-stands, the kuánjué are used.
In the upper hall, they sing the “Qīngmiào,”
and below, the flutes play the “Xiàng”;
with red shields and jade axes,
wearing ceremonial caps, they dance the “Dàwǔ”;
wearing the leather cap and plain silk skirt,
with the upper garment bared, they dance the “Dàxià.”
The “Mèi”
is the music of the Dōngyí;
the “Rèn”
is the music of the Nánmán.
Bringing the music of the Yí and Mán into the Dàmiào
signified the greatness of Lǔ in the world.
14.3 The ruler wears the rolled-dragon robe and crown, standing at the eastern steps;
his wife wears the fùhuī robe and stands in the inner chamber.
The ruler bares his shoulder to welcome the victim at the gate;
his wife presents the yùdòu and
biān vessels.
The Qīng and Dàfū assist the ruler;
the titled ladies assist his wife:
each carries out their duties.
If the officials neglect their duties, they are subject to severe punishment,
and the world was greatly submissive.
14.4 Therefore,
the summer Yuè, the autumn Cháng, and the winter Zhēng sacrifices,
the spring Shè and autumn Shěng,
followed by the great Là sacrifice,
are the sacrifices of the Tiānzǐ.
14.5 The Dàmiào
was the Tiānzǐ’s Míngtáng.
The Kùmén
was the Tiānzǐ’s Gāomén.
The Zhìmén
was the Tiānzǐ’s Yìngmén.
14.6 Sounding the wooden-clapper bell at court
is the administration of the Tiānzǐ.
14.7 Rafters carved with mountains and king-posts with duckweed,
the double-roofed temple with double eaves,
polished pillars and windows opening in all directions,
the counter-ledge for returning cups and the place for setting out the zūn,
the high ledge and the wide Kāngguī jade tablet,
and the carved screen;
these are the temple decorations of the Tiānzǐ.
14.8 The chariot with phoenix bells
was the carriage of the Yǒuyú Shì.
The hooked chariot
was the carriage of the Xiàhòu Shì.
The dàlù
was the carriage of the Yīn.
The chénglù
was the carriage of the Zhōu.
14.9 The banner of the Yǒuyú Shì,
the tassel-banner of the Xiàhòu Shì,
the great white banner of the Yīn,
and the great red banner of the Zhōu.
14.10 The Xiàhòu Shì used black horses
with black manes.
The Yīn people used white horses
with black heads.
The Zhōu people used yellow horses
with red manes.
14.11 The Xiàhòu Shì,
for sacrificial victims, preferred black;
the Yīn preferred white bulls;
the Zhōu preferred red bulls.
14.12 The tài-zūn
was the vessel of the Yǒuyú Shì.
The shānléi
was the vessel of the Xiàhòu Shì.
The zhù-zūn
was the vessel of the Yīn.
The xī-zūn and xiàng-zūn
were the vessels of the Zhōu.
14.13 For libation cups,
the Xiàhòu Shì used the zhǎn,
the Yīn used the jiǎ,
and the Zhōu used the jué.
14.14 Regarding the libation vessels,
the Xiàhòu Shì used the chicken-shaped tripod,
the Yīn used the jiǎ,
and the Zhōu used the yellow-eyed vessel.
14.15 Regarding their ladles,
the Xiàhòu Shì used the dragon ladle,
the Yīn used the carved ladle,
and the Zhōu used the cattail-patterned ladle.
14.16 Earth drums, straw mallets, and reed flutes
were the music of Yīqí Shì.
The clapping boards, jade chimes, and striking blocks,
the great qín, the great sè,
the medium qín, and the small sè,
are the musical instruments of the four dynasties.
14.17 The temple of Lǔ Gōng
is the Wén Shìshì.
The temple of Wǔ Gōng
is the Wǔ Shìshì.
14.18 The granary school
was the xiáng of the Yǒuyú Shì;
the xù
was the xù of the Xiàhòu Shì;
the Gǔzōng
was the school of the Yīn;
the Pàngōng
was the school of the Zhōu.
14.19 The Chóng tripod,
the Guàn tripod,
the great huáng jade,
and the Fēngfù tortoise shell
are the vessels of the Son of Heaven.
The Yuè halberd
and the great bow
are the military weapons of the Son of Heaven.
14.20 The Xiàhòu Shì used
footed drums.
The Yīn used
pillar drums;
the Zhōu used
hanging drums.
14.21 There was Chuí's Harmonious Bell,
Shū's Resonant Chime,
and Nǚwā's reed pipe.
14.22 The Xiàhòu Shì had dragon-shaped stands for bell-frames,
the Yīn had high teeth ornaments,
and the Zhōu had jade-adorned screens.
The Yǒuyú Shì used two dùn vessels,
the Xiàhòu Shì used four lián,
the Yīn used six hú,
and the Zhōu used eight guǐ.
14.23 Regarding meat stands,
the Yǒuyú Shì used the huán stand,
the Xiàhòu Shì used the jué stand,
the Yīn used the jǔ stand,
and the Zhōu used the fángzǔ stand.
14.24 The Xiàhòu Shì used the wooden jié dòu,
the Yīn used jade dòu,
and the Zhōu used ritual xiàn dòu.
14.25 The Yǒuyú Shì wore knee-covers,
the Xiàhòu Shì used the mountain design,
the Yīn used the fire design,
and the Zhōu used the dragon pattern.
14.26 The Yǒuyú Shì sacrificed the head,
the Xiàhòu Shì sacrificed the heart,
the Yīn sacrificed the liver,
the Zhōu sacrificed the lungs.
14.27 The Xiàhòu Shì valued clear water,
the Yīn valued sweet wine,
the Zhōu valued clarified wine.
14.28 The Yǒuyú Shì had fifty officials,
the Xiàhòu Shì had one hundred officials,
the Yīn had two hundred,
and the Zhōu had three hundred.
The streamers of the Yǒuyú Shì,
the silk-wrapped poles of the Xiàhòu Shì,
the high teeth ornaments of the Yīn,
and the jade-adorned screens of the Zhōu—
regarding all the clothing, vessels, and officials of the four dynasties,
Lǔ used them all.
For this reason,
Lǔ
followed the rituals of the King,
and the world has transmitted them for a long time.
Ruler and minister
have never assassinated each other;
rites and music, punishments and laws, administration and customs
have never been changed.
The world considers it a country that possesses the Way.
For this reason,
the world relies on it for rites and music.
15.1 In the untrimmed mourning dress,
the hair is bound with hemp;
for a mother,
the hair is bound with hemp,
and the mourning cap is made of cloth.
In the trimmed mourning dress,
unadorned hairpins are used until the end of mourning.
Men wear the cap and women wear hairpins;
men wear the mourning headband and women bind their hair.
The principle is:
for a man, there is the headband,
and for a woman, there is the binding of hair.
15.2 The rough staff
is made of bamboo;
the trimmed staff
is made of paulownia.
15.3 If the grandfather has died,
then one mourns for three years for a grandmother as the successor.
15.4 For parents
and the eldest son, one bows the head to the ground.
If a Dàfū offers condolences,
even if one is in the lightest mourning, one must bow the head to the ground.
A woman bows her head to the ground for her husband and her eldest son,
but for others she does not.
15.5 The male presiding mourner must be of the same surname,
and the female presiding mourner must be of a different surname.
15.6 One who acts as the successor to his father
wears no mourning for a divorced mother.
15.7 In treating relatives as relatives,
three generations expand to five,
and five expand to nine.
With reductions upward,
reductions downward,
and reductions sideways,
the degrees of kinship are concluded.
15.8 The King performs the dì sacrifice to the ancestor from whom his own ancestor sprang,
associating his ancestor with that one in the sacrifice,
and establishes four temples.
A son of a concubine who becomes a King
also does the same.
15.9 The founder of a secondary branch is the ancestor,
the one who succeeds him is the head of the Great Lineage,
and the one who succeeds a father is the head of a Small Lineage.
There is a lineage head whose position is shifted after five generations;
this is the one who succeeds the great-great-grandfather.
For this reason,
when the ancestor's tablet is shifted above,
the lineage headship changes below.
One honors the ancestor, and therefore respects the lineage head;
respecting the lineage head is the means by which one honors the ancestor and the father.
That a son of a concubine does not sacrifice to the ancestor
is to make clear who is the head of the lineage.
A son of a concubine does not wear the untrimmed mourning for his eldest son
because he does not succeed the ancestor or the father.
A son of a concubine does not sacrifice to those who died young or those without heirs;
those who died young or without heirs are associated with the ancestor's sacrifice to receive offerings.
15.10 That a son of a concubine does not sacrifice to his father
is to make clear who is the head of the lineage.
15.11 Treating relatives as relatives, honoring the honorable, and respecting the elders,
along with the distinction between men and women,
are the great principles of the human way.
15.12 Regarding those whose mourning follows another's,
if the person they follow dies,
then the mourning ceases.
Regarding those who follow by virtue of attachment,
even if the person they follow has died, they still wear mourning.
If a concubine leaves with her mistress,
then she does not wear mourning for her mistress's son.
15.13 According to the rites, unless one is a King, one does not perform the dì sacrifice.
15.14 A crown prince does not lower the mourning for his wife's parents;
his mourning for his wife
is the same as that of the legitimate son of a Dàfū.
15.15 If the father was an officer
and the son became the Son of Heaven or a feudal lord,
then the sacrifice is performed as the Son of Heaven or a feudal lord,
but the personator wears the robes of an officer.
If the father was the Son of Heaven or a feudal lord
and the son was an officer,
the sacrifice is performed as an officer,
and the personator wears the robes of an officer.
15.16 If a woman is divorced while in mourning,
she removes the mourning.
If she is in mourning for her parents
and is divorced before the liàn sacrifice,
she completes the three years of mourning.
If she is divorced after the liàn sacrifice,
she ceases the mourning.
If she returns before the liàn sacrifice,
she completes the one-year period;
if she returns after the liàn sacrifice,
she carries out the full mourning.
15.17 A mourning period of two full years
is the "three-year" mourning;
a mourning period of one full year
is the "two-year" mourning.
Mourning of nine months or seven months
lasts for three seasons;
mourning of five months
lasts for two seasons;
mourning of three months
lasts for one season.
Therefore, to sacrifice after one year
is the rite;
to remove mourning after one year
is the standard path.
The sacrifice is not performed for the sake of removing mourning.
If the burial takes place after three years, there must be two sacrifices.
The interval between these sacrifices is not the standard one, and then the mourning is ended.
In a household where the master’s mourning is of the *Dàgōng* degree,
if there is anyone for whom three years of mourning is required,
then these two sacrifices must be performed for them.
For friends,
there are only the *Yú* and *Fù* sacrifices.
If a *Shì*’s concubine has a son,
mourning of the *Sī* degree is worn for her;
if she has no son, it is not.
If one is born after the death of grandparents, paternal uncles, or elder brothers,
and the father wears retroactive mourning (*Shuì*) for them,
the son himself does not.
For the parents, wife, or eldest son of a ruler,
if the ruler has already ended his mourning before one hears of the death,
then retroactive mourning is not worn.
If the mourning was reduced to the *Sī* or *Xiǎogōng* degrees,
then it is worn retroactively.
For close ministers,
they wear whatever mourning the ruler wears.
For the rest,
they follow the ruler in wearing mourning,
but do not follow him in wearing retroactive mourning.
Even if the ruler has not yet heard of the death,
the ministers wear mourning for it.
15.18 At the *Yú* sacrifice,
the staff is not taken into the inner chamber;
at the *Fù* sacrifice,
the staff is not taken up into the hall.
15.19 For one who has been made the successor to the ruler’s mother,
when that mother dies,
he does not wear mourning for her relatives.
15.20 The mourning headband is reduced by one-fifth of its size;
the staff should be as thick as the headband.
15.21 A concubine mourning for the ruler’s eldest son
follows the same rules as the ruler’s wife.
When putting off mourning,
one begins with the heavier garments;
when changing mourning garments,
one begins with the lighter ones.
Unless there is business, the doors of the ancestral temple are not opened.
The wailing is always performed in the mourning shed (*Cì*).
15.22 Recalling the soul and writing the inscription
extend from the *Tiānzǐ* down to the *Shì*;
the wording is the same for all.
For a man, the personal name is used;
for a woman, the surname and seniority are written;
if the surname is unknown, the clan name is written.
15.23 The kudzu-cloth for *Zhǎncuī* is the same as the hemp for *Qīcuī*.
The kudzu-cloth for *Qīcuī* is the same as the hemp for *Dàgōng*;
when the hemp is the same,
they are worn together.
15.24 When the burial is hurried, the *Yú* sacrifice is hurried;
after three months, the wailing is ended.
15.25 If the mourning for both parents occurs at the same time,
the one buried first does not have the *Yú* or *Fù* sacrifices performed,
but waits for the later burial.
At that burial,
*Zhǎncuī* is worn.
15.26 A *Dàfū* reduces the mourning for his son by a concubine,
but that son’s son does not reduce it for his own father.
A *Dàfū* does not preside over the mourning of a *Shì*.
15.27 No mourning is worn for the parents of a foster mother (*Címǔ*).
15.28 When a man has been adopted as an heir by another,
his wife wears *Dàgōng* mourning for his adoptive parents.
15.29 When a *Shì* is associated in sacrifice with a *Dàfū*, the sacrificial victim is changed.
15.30 "Stepfather not living in the same house" refers to those who
must once have lived together.
Both have no heirs to succeed them.
Those who share property and sacrifice to their ancestors and fathers are considered to be living in the same house;
those who have heirs of their own are considered to be living in different houses.
15.31 One who wails for a friend
does so outside the door on the right, facing south.
15.32 When burying someone with another, the site is not determined by divination.
15.33 *Shì* and *Dàfū* may not be associated in sacrifice with *Zhūhóu*;
they are associated with grandfathers who were *Shì* or *Dàfū*.
Their wives are associated with the grandmothers.
A concubine is associated with the concubine-grandmother.
If there is no such person, they are associated with a relative of the same rank from a generation further back.
Association must follow the *Zhāomù* order.
*Zhūhóu* may not be associated with the *Tiānzǐ*;
but a *Tiānzǐ*, *Zhūhóu*, or *Dàfū* may be associated with a *Shì*.
15.34 For the legal mother of one's own mother,
if one's mother is dead, no mourning is worn.
15.35 For the head of a lineage (*Zōngzǐ*),
if his mother is alive, he performs the *Tàn* sacrifice for his wife.
15.36 One who is the heir to a foster mother
may wear mourning for a concubine-mother,
or for a concubine-grandmother.
15.37 The *Tàn* sacrifice is performed for parents, wife, and the eldest son.
15.38 Foster mothers and concubine-mothers
do not have sacrifices continued through successive generations.
15.39 A male who has been capped is not considered to have died prematurely (*Shāng*);
a female who has been pinned is not considered to have died prematurely.
15.40 One who is the heir to one who died prematurely
wears the mourning appropriate for him.
15.41 When a burial is long delayed,
only the chief mourner does not end the mourning;
the others, who wear hemp for the specified number of months,
end their mourning when that time has passed.
15.42 The bamboo hairpin is worn until the three years of mourning are completed.
Those in *Qīcuī* for three months and those in *Dàgōng* for the same period
wear straw sandals.
15.43 For the *Liàn* sacrifice,
when divining for the day and for the representative (*Shī*),
and inspecting the washing of the vessels,
one wears the mourning sash, the staff, and straw sandals.
When the officer announces that everything is prepared,
one then puts away the staff.
In divining for the day and for the *Shī*,
when the officer announces the completion of the business, one then takes up the staff
and bows as he sees the guests off.
At the *Dàxiáng* sacrifice,
one wears auspicious garments to divine for the *Shī*.
15.44 A son by a concubine living in his father's house
does not perform the *Tàn* sacrifice for his mother.
A son by a concubine does not take his place with a staff.
If the father does not preside over the mourning for a son by a concubine,
then that son's son may take his place with a staff.
While the father is alive,
if a son by a concubine mourns for his wife,
he may take his place with a staff.
15.45 When a *Zhūhóu* condoles with the minister of another state,
the ruler of that state acts as the host.
15.46 When a *Zhūhóu* condoles,
he must wear the skin cap and the *Xīcuī* garment.
Even if the person he is condoling for has already been buried,
the host must wear the *Miǎn*.
If the host has not yet put on mourning garments,
the ruler also does not wear the *Xīcuī*.
15.47 One nursing the sick does not wear mourning garments,
and then proceeds to preside over the mourning.
One who is not nursing, when entering a house of mourning,
does not change his own mourning garments.
One nursing a superior must change his garments;
one nursing an inferior does not.
15.48 If a concubine has no concubine-grandmother,
it is permissible to change the sacrificial victim and associate her with the legal wife.
15.49 For a wife's mourning, the *Yú* and the end of wailing (*Zùkū*)
are presided over by her husband or her son.
For the association sacrifice,
the father-in-law (*Jiù*) presides.
A *Shì* does not act in place of a *Dàfū*.
A *Shì* acting in place of a *Dàfū*
occurs only if he is the head of the lineage.
If the chief mourner has not yet ended his mourning,
and a brother arrives from another state,
the chief mourner does not wear the *Miǎn* to act as host for him.
The way of displaying the funeral vessels:
to display many but place only a few in the grave is permissible;
to display only a few but place them all in the grave is also permissible.
15.50 When hurrying to the mourning for a brother,
one goes first to the grave and then to the house,
taking his place and wailing.
For the mourning of an acquaintance,
one wails at the house and then goes to the grave.
15.51 A father does not dwell in the mourning shed (*Cì*) for any of his sons.
One who is a brother to a *Zhūhóu* wears *Zhǎncuī*.
For a death in the lowest degree of *Shāng*, *Xiǎogōng* is worn,
with the sash;
the washed hemp is not cut at the ends,
but is folded back and tied.
A wife is associated with her grandmother-in-law.
If there are three grandmothers-in-law,
she is associated with the one to whom she is most closely related.
15.52 If a wife died while her husband was a *Dàfū*,
and later the husband is no longer a *Dàfū*,
then when associating someone with her, the sacrificial victim is not changed.
If the wife died and later the husband becomes a *Dàfū*,
when associating someone with her,
the victim of a *Dàfū* is used.
15.53 One who is his father's heir
wears no mourning for a mother who has been divorced.
The reason for wearing no mourning
is that as the chief mourner, he cannot perform the sacrifices.
15.54 Cases where a woman carries a staff although she is not the chief mourner:
when her mother-in-law is alive, she carries a staff for her husband;
a mother carries a trimmed staff for her eldest son.
For a daughter still at home mourning for her parents,
if the chief mourner does not carry a staff,
then one of the children carries a staff.
15.55 For the *Sī* and *Xiǎogōng* degrees,
the *Miǎn* is worn at the *Yú* and the end of wailing.
If after the burial the *Yú* sacrifice is not hurried,
then even the chief mourner wears his cap;
when the time for the *Yú* arrives, they all wear the *Miǎn*.
For a brother,
when the mourning has already been ended;
when the time for his burial comes,
one puts on the mourning garments again.
At the hurried *Yú* and the end of wailing, the *Miǎn* is worn.
If the *Yú* sacrifice is not hurried, the mourning is ended.
Those who bury from afar, as well as those who return for the wailing, all wear their caps.
Upon reaching the suburbs, they then bare their heads (*Miǎn*), and then they return for the wailing.
When the Ruler (*Jūn*) comes to offer condolences,
even if it is not the proper time for baring the head,
the host must bare his head (*Miǎn*),
but he does not loosen his hempen bands.
Even if it is the Ruler of a different state,
he bares his head.
All close relatives bare their heads.
When ending the mourning for a child who died prematurely (*Shàng*),
the sacrifice must be performed in deep black (*Xuán*).
15.56 When ending the mourning for an adult (*Chéng sāng*),
the sacrifice
is performed in court robes and a white silk cap.
15.57 When hurrying to the mourning for a father,
one binds the hair (*Kuò fǎ*) in the hall,
bares the shoulder (*Tǎn*), descends the steps, and leaps (*Yǒng*).
One then puts on the mourning band (*Dié*) in the eastern part of the house.
When hurrying to the mourning for a mother,
one does not bind the hair,
but bares the shoulder in the hall,
descends the steps, and leaps.
One bares the head (*Miǎn*) in the eastern part of the house,
puts on the mourning band and takes one’s place, completes the leaping,
then goes out the door and ceases wailing.
Over three days, there are five wailings and three barings of the shoulder.
15.58 If a principal daughter-in-law (*Shì fù*) is not serving as the successor to her father-in-law (*Jiù*),
then her mother-in-law (*Gū*) observes the *Xiǎogōng* mourning for her.
16.1 According to the Rites (*Lǐ*):
None but a King (*Wáng*) performs the *Dì* sacrifice.
The King performs the *Dì* sacrifice to the ancestor from whom his line originated,
and associates his own first ancestor with him in the sacrifice.
The Feudal Lords (*Zhūhóu*) reach only to their Great Ancestor (*Dà Zǔ*).
When Great Officers (*Dàfū*) and Officers (*Shì*) have a great undertaking,
they report it to their Ruler,
and when joining the combined sacrifice (*Xiá*),
they reach back to their high-great-grandfather (*Gāozǔ*).
In the wilds of Mùyě,
was the great undertaking of Wǔ Wáng.
After the matter was finished and he withdrew,
he performed the *Chái* sacrifice to the Lord on High (*Shàngdì*),
prayed at the Altar of the Soil (*Shè*),
and established a sacrificial offering in the Mù chamber.
He then led the Feudal Lords of the world
in holding the *Dòu* and *Biān* vessels,
moving quickly and reverently.
He posthumously titled as Kings: Dà Wáng Dǎn Fù,
Wáng Jì Lì, and Wén Wáng Chāng;
so as not to approach the honorable with a humble status.
16.2 Above, one arranges the ancestors and the deceased father (*Nǐ*),
which is to honor the honorable;
below, one arranges the children and grandchildren,
which is to love one's kin;
laterally, one arranges the brothers,
gathering the clan together to eat,
ordering them according to the *Zhāomù* sequence,
and distinguishing them through ritual and righteousness.
By this, the Way of Humanity is exhausted.
When the Sage faces south to hear the affairs of the world,
there are five things he puts first,
and the common people are not among them.
The first is governing relatives;
the second is rewarding merit;
the third is promoting the worthy;
the fourth is employing the capable;
and the fifth is preserving affection.
If these five are achieved in the world,
the people will lack for nothing
and there will be none who are not provided for.
Among these five,
if even one thing is flawed,
the people will not find a natural death.
When the Sage faces south to govern the world,
he must begin from the Way of Humanity.
Establishing standards, degrees, and measures;
examining cultural regulations;
correcting the first day and the first month;
changing the colors of robes;
distinguishing emblems and titles;
varying tools and implements;
and differentiating clothes;
these are what can be changed along with the people.
But there are things that cannot be changed:
loving one's kin,
honoring the honorable,
respecting the elderly,
and the distinction between men and women;
these are what cannot be changed along with the people.
16.3 Those of the same surname follow the lineage head (*Zōng*),
joining the clan members together;
those of different surnames manage names,
governing the meetings between them.
When names are clear,
then the distinction between men and women is established.
If the husband
belongs to the rank of the fathers,
all the wives are in the rank of "mother."
If the husband
belongs to the rank of the sons,
all the wives are in the rank of "wife."
If one calls the wife of a younger brother "wife,"
could one then also call an elder brother's wife "mother"?
Names are the greatest part of human governance;
can one not be cautious?
16.4 At the fourth generation, one wears *Sī* (fine hemp),
which is the limit of mourning dress;
at the fifth generation, one bares the shoulder and head (*Tǎn Miǎn*),
which reduces the bond of the same surname.
At the sixth generation,
kinship bonds are exhausted.
If the collateral branches are distinguished above,
and the kinship ties are exhausted below,
can marriage then occur between them?
By binding them by the surname (*Xìng*) without distinction,
and connecting them through shared meals without separation,
even after a hundred generations, marriage is not permitted;
such was the Way of Zhōu.
16.5 There are six principles for mourning dress:
first, loving kin;
second, honoring the honorable;
third, names;
fourth, entering or leaving the lineage;
fifth, age;
and sixth, derivative mourning.
16.6 There are six types of derivative mourning:
mourning because of attachment,
mourning because of simple following,
mourning because of following one who has mourning dress but having none oneself,
mourning because of following one who has no mourning dress but having it oneself,
mourning that follows a heavy obligation but becomes light,
and mourning that follows a light obligation but becomes heavy.
16.7 Starting from benevolence (*Rén*) to lead one's kin,
ascending through the grades,
and reaching to the first ancestor,
this is called "lightening."
Starting from righteousness (*Yì*) to lead from the ancestor,
following down the sequence,
and reaching to the deceased father (*Nǐ*),
this is called "weighting."
One lightening and one weighting;
such is the nature of righteousness.
16.8 The Ruler has the way of gathering the clan,
but the clansmen must not use their kinship to treat the Ruler as a relative;
this is because of his position.
16.9 A son of a concubine (*Shù zǐ*) does not perform the sacrifices,
so as to make clear the position of the lineage head (*Zōng*).
A son of a concubine may not observe the three-year mourning for his eldest son,
because he does not succeed the ancestor.
A younger son who starts a new line is the founding ancestor (*Bié zǐ*),
and the one who succeeds that founder is the lineage head (*Zōng*).
One who succeeds a father is a Small Lineage head (*Xiǎo Zōng*).
There are lineages that do not change for a hundred generations,
and there are lineages that change after five generations.
The one that does not change for a hundred generations
is the line of the founding ancestor (*Bié zǐ*);
those who honor the successor of the founding ancestor from whom they originated
are the ones that do not change for a hundred generations.
Those who honor the successor of the high-great-grandfather (*Gāozǔ*)
are the ones that change after five generations.
Because one honors the ancestors, one respects the lineage head.
Respecting the lineage head
is the meaning of honoring the ancestors.
16.10 There are those who have a Small Lineage head but no Great Lineage head;
there are those who have a Great Lineage head but no Small Lineage head;
and there are those who have no lineage head and are not treated as lineage heads;
such are the sons of a Ruler (*Gōngzǐ*).
There is a way of lineage for the sons of a Ruler:
the sons of a Ruler's
concubine sons who are Officers (*Shì*) or Great Officers (*Dàfū*)
honor as lineage head the son of the legal wife who is an Officer or Great Officer;
this is the way of lineage for the sons of a Ruler.
16.11 For a severed branch of the clan, there is no transfer of mourning dress;
for those who are close are connected.
16.12 Starting from benevolence (*Rén*) to lead one's kin,
ascending through the grades,
and reaching to the ancestor;
starting from righteousness (*Yì*) to lead from the ancestor,
following down the sequence,
and reaching to the deceased father (*Nǐ*).
Therefore,
the Way of Humanity is to love one's kin.
Loving kin leads to honoring ancestors;
honoring ancestors leads to respecting the lineage head;
respecting the lineage head leads to gathering the clan;
gathering the clan leads to the ancestral temple being solemn;
the solemnity of the ancestral temple leads to the valuing of the Altars of Soil and Grain (*Shèjì*);
valuing the Altars of Soil and Grain leads to loving the hundred surnames;
loving the hundred surnames leads to punishments and penalties being hit upon the mark;
punishments hitting the mark leads to the common people being at peace;
the peace of the common people leads to sufficient wealth and utility;
sufficient wealth leads to the fulfillment of all aims;
the fulfillment of all aims leads to the forming of rituals and customs;
and once rituals and customs are formed, then there is joy.
The *Shī* says:
"Is it not brilliant? Is it not continuous?
May there be no weariness in the people."
This is what is meant.
17.1 It is heard that
one who sees a Jūnzǐ for the first time
should say:
“I have long desired to have my name heard by the Jiàngmìng.”
They should not go directly to the host.
If they are equals, they say:
“I have long desired to see you.”
If they rarely see each other, they say:
“I have heard your name.”
If they see each other frequently, they say:
“Morning and evening.”
A blind man says:
“I have heard your name.”
17.2 When visiting someone in mourning, one says:
“To be near.”
A youth says:
“To hear of the matters.”
When visiting for the mourning of a Gōng or Qīng,
then one says:
“To hear of the duties under the Sītú.”
17.3 If a Jūn is going elsewhere,
and a minister presents gold, jade, goods, or cowries to the Jūn,
then he says:
“I present horse provisions to the Yǒusī”;
equals say:
“A gift for your followers.”
17.4 When a minister presents Suì to the Jūn,
then he says:
“I present discarded clothes to the Gǔrén”;
equals say:
“Suì.”
For relatives and brothers, the term "discarded clothes" is not used;
they simply present them as Suì.
When a minister is in mourning for his Jūn
and offers goods or cowries to the Jūn,
then he says:
“I offer the Diàn to the Yǒusī.”
Fèng horses enter the temple gate;
Fù horses and their silks,
and great white war chariots,
do not enter the temple gate.
17.5 When the one offering Fù has delivered the message,
they sit and lay it down,
and the Bìnzhě lifts it up.
The Zhǔrén does not receive it personally.
17.6 When receiving while standing
or giving while standing, one does not sit.
Those with a naturally straightforward character may do so.
Upon first entering and declining,
one says:
“I decline.”
Upon taking the seat,
one says:
“It is well.”
To push open the door and take off one's shoes inside the room
should be done by one person only.
If a senior or elder is present, then one does not do so.
17.7 In asking about tastes, one says:
“Do you frequently eat such-and-such?”
In asking about ways and arts, one says:
“Are you practiced in such-and-such?”
“Are you good at such-and-such?”
One does not question what is personal to another,
one does not measure the people’s tools,
one does not desire the wealth of great families,
one does not criticize precious vessels.
General sweeping is called Sǎo,
sweeping before the mat is called Biàn;
when sweeping the mat, do not use a stiff broom.
When holding the dustpan, the handle should be against the breast.
17.8 Do not ask a question twice.
When asking about divination, say:
“Is it for righteousness?
Or for personal intent?”
If for righteousness, one may ask;
if for personal intent, one does not.
17.9 If a senior or elder is of a rank much higher than oneself,
one does not dare to ask their age.
At an informal audience, one does not announce the mission.
If meeting on the road,
if they see each other they face each other,
but do not ask where the other is going.
While waiting for the funeral rites to begin, one does not offer condolences alone.
When sitting in attendance, unless instructed,
one does not touch the Qín or Sè,
does not draw on the ground,
the hands do not fidget,
and one does not use a fan.
If the person is in bed, one sits to deliver the message.
When attending archery, one holds the arrows together;
when attending the game of pitch-pot, one cradles the arrows.
The winner washes the cup and requests the other to drink;
the guest does the same.
One does not compete for the score markers,
one does not advance the horses.
17.10 When holding the reins of the Jūn’s chariot, one sits.
The Púzhě carries a sword on the right,
carries the fine Suí on his back,
extends it to the front,
hangs it on the screen,
ascends using the loose Suí,
and takes the reins before walking.
17.11 Request to see, but do not request to withdraw.
At court, it is called “withdrawing”;
at informal leisure, it is called “returning”;
for military service, it is called “dismissal.”
17.12 When sitting in attendance on a Jūnzǐ,
if the Jūnzǐ yawns and stretches,
moves his Hù tablet,
polishes the pommel of his sword,
adjusts his shoes,
or asks about the time of day,
then one may request to withdraw.
17.13 One who serves a Jūn measures the task before entering service,
not entering and then measuring;
whenever begging or borrowing from others,
and when performing services for others, it is the same.
Being so,
consequently the superior has no resentment,
and the subordinate stays far from guilt.
Do not peer into private places,
do not be overly familiar with those nearby,
do not talk of old grievances,
do not show a playful countenance.
17.14 One who is a minister or subordinate
should remonstrate but not slander,
may leave but not be resentful;
praise without flattery,
remonstrate without arrogance;
if the ruler is weary, support and assist him;
if things are neglected, sweep and renew them;
this is called the service of the Shèjì.
17.15 Do not be sudden in coming,
do not be hasty in leaving,
do not profane the spirits,
do not follow what is crooked,
do not speculate on what has not yet arrived.
The Shì relies on Dé
and finds recreation in the arts;
the artisan relies on laws
and finds recreation in explanations.
Do not criticize clothing or finished vessels,
do not personally vouch for words.
The beauty of speech
is solemn and magnificent;
the beauty of the court
is dignified and soaring;
the beauty of sacrifice
is reverent and grand;
the beauty of chariots and horses
is numerous and orderly;
the beauty of the Luánhé bells
is solemn and harmonious.
17.16 When asking about the seniority of a Guójūn’s son,
if he is of age,
then one says:
“He is able to follow the affairs of the Shèjì”;
if young,
then one says:
“He is able to drive,”
or “He is not yet able to drive.”
When asking about the seniority of a Dàfū’s son,
if he is of age,
then one says:
“He is able to follow the affairs of the music masters”;
if young,
then one says:
“He is able to be corrected by the music masters,”
or “He is not yet able to be corrected by the music masters.”
When asking about the seniority of a Shì’s son,
if he is of age,
then one says:
“He is able to plow”;
if young,
then one says:
“He is able to carry firewood,”
or “He is not yet able to carry firewood.”
17.17 When holding jade or the tortoise shells and stalks, one does not hurry;
one does not hurry while on the Táng,
nor on top of the city wall.
On a war chariot, one does not bow to the crossbar;
the Jièzhě does not bow.
For a woman, on auspicious occasions,
even if there is a gift from the Jūn,
she performs the Sùbài.
When acting as the Shī,
then one does not bow with hands to the ground
but performs the Sùbài;
when acting as the host of mourning, one does not bow with hands to the ground.
Use a kudzu headband and a hemp belt.
When taking up or presenting the Zǔ, one does not sit.
17.18 Hold an empty vessel as if holding a full one;
enter an empty room as if someone were there.
Whenever sacrificing in a chamber
or on the Táng, one does not go barefoot,
though at informal banquets one may.
One never fails to eat the new crops.
17.19 When a servant is with a Jūnzǐ,
when the Jūnzǐ ascends or descends, the servant hands him the mounting strap;
when first starting to ride, the servant bows to the crossbar;
when the Jūnzǐ gets down and walks,
then the servant turns around and stands.
17.20 When riding in a secondary carriage, one bows to the crossbar;
in a standard escort carriage, one does not.
As for the secondary carriages:
for Zhūhóu, seven;
for Shàng Dàfū, five;
for Xià Dàfū, three.
The horses and the main carriage of one who has secondary carriages are not compared in age.
When looking at a Jūnzǐ’s robes,
his worn sword,
or his carriage horses,
one does not ask the price.
When using a set of four pots of wine,
bundles of dried meat,
or a dog as a gift to another,
or if offering them to a superior,
one arranges the wine and holds the dried meat to convey the message,
also saying: “A set of four pots of wine,
bundles of dried meat,
and a dog.”
If it is meat from a Dǐng,
then one carries it to convey the message.
If the game birds exceed one pair,
then one carries one pair to convey the message,
and leaves the rest.
For a dog, one holds the leash;
for a guard dog
or a hunting dog,
one hands it to the usher;
after it is received,
then one asks the dog’s name.
For an ox, one holds the nose-rope;
for a horse, one holds the bridle;
keeping both to one's right.
A servant keeps them to his left.
For a carriage, one removes the mounting strap
and holds it to convey the message.
For armor, if there is something to precede it,
then one holds that to convey the message;
if there is nothing to precede it,
then one bares the quiver and carries the helmet.
For a vessel, one holds the lid.
For a bow, one uses the left hand to fold the case and hold the grip.
For a sword, one opens the scabbard and places the cover over it,
adding the cloth bag and the sword.
Tablets (Hù), books, dried meat, straw-wrapped bundles, bows, mats, sitting mats, pillows, armrests, torches, canes, Qín, Sè, halberds with blades in cases, divining stalks, and flutes—
when holding these, the left hand is always on top.
For a knife, turn the blade away and hand over the pommel.
For a paring knife, hand over the grip.
For anything with a blade or point,
when handing it to someone, turn the blade away.
When riding in a war chariot,
exiting, the blades go first;
entering, the blades go last.
In the army, the left is the place of honor;
for the ranks, the right is the place of honor.
With guests, reverence is primary;
in sacrifices, respect is primary;
in mourning, grief is primary;
in assemblies, majesty is primary.
In military matters, think of the dangers;
conceal your intentions and prepare for contingencies.
17.21 When attending a banquet and eating with a Jūnzǐ,
start eating before him and finish after him;
do not roll the rice into balls;
do not gulp down soup;
take small mouthfuls and chew quickly;
chew thoroughly and do not make facial expressions.
The guest clears his own dishes;
if the host declines this, he stops.
17.22 The guest’s cup is placed on the left,
and his drink on the right;
the assistant’s cup, the return-toast cup,
and the assistant-host’s cup are all on the right.
17.23 When serving cooked fish, present the tail;
in winter, the belly is to the right;
in summer, the dorsal fin is to the right;
for the sacrificial portion, use the large slab of belly meat.
17.24 For all condiments (Jì),
hold them with the right hand
but place them on the left.
17.25 Assist with the ritual silks from the left;
announce the ritual words from the right.
17.26 The attendant who pours for the Shī,
is like the attendant of a ruler.
If in a carriage, he holds the reins with the left and receives the cup with the right;
he offers a libation to the left and right wheel-guards, then drinks.
17.27 For all food served on a stand (Zǔ),
the sacrifice is made from within the stand.
A Jūnzǐ does not eat the intestines of animals fed on refuse.
A young person walks fast but does not perform the ritual trot;
when raising a cup, he sits to offer the libation but stands to drink.
For every washing of a cup, one must wash one's hands.
As for the lungs of an ox or sheep,
slice them apart but do not remove the heart portion.
For all food served with soup,
do not add condiments.
When preparing scallions or shallots for a Jūnzǐ,
cut off the roots and the tips.
When serving the head,
present the snout and offer the ear as sacrifice.
For wine vessels, the one to the left of the pourer is the most honored.
When setting out wine pots, face their spouts toward the guests.
Those drinking, performing purification rites, or performing capping libations,
if they have meat-stands, they do not sit.
Before the cup has been passed around,
one does not taste the food.
17.28 The raw meat of oxen, sheep, and fish
is sliced and shredded to make Kuài;
elk and deer are made into Zū;
wild boar is made into Xuān;
both are sliced but not shredded;
muntjac is made into Bìjī;
rabbit is made into Wǎnpí;
both are sliced and shredded.
Slice scallions and shallots,
and use vinegar to soften them.
17.29 For those who have meat-stands,
when they take the sacrificial lung,
and return it,
they do not sit;
for roasted meat, it is the same.
The Shī, however, sits.
17.30 To wear clothes on one’s body
and not know their names is called being ignorant.
17.31 If someone arrives late before torches are lit,
then inform them of those already present.
The same is done when guiding the blind.
Whenever drinking wine, the host for the toast
holds a torch and carries firewood;
the guest rises and declines,
only then is it handed to another.
While holding a torch, one does not yield,
does not decline,
and does not sing.
Those washing cups, washing hands, or holding food and drink must not breathe on them;
if there is a question,
turn the head away and answer.
17.32 Sacrificing on behalf of another is called “sending blessings”;
sacrificing for oneself and sending the meal to a Jūnzǐ is called “presenting a meal”;
the Fù and Liàn sacrifices are called “reports.”
For all meals and reports to a Jūnzǐ,
the host inspects them
and hands them to the messenger to the south of the eastern steps,
facing south, bowing twice and touching the head to the ground to send them off;
when the messenger returns with the report,
the host again bows twice and touches his head to the ground.
As for the ritual portions:
for the Dàláo, nine pieces are cut from the ox’s left shoulder, arm, and lower leg;
for the Shǎoláo, seven pieces from the sheep’s left shoulder;
for the Zhìshǐ, five pieces from the pig’s left shoulder.
17.33 When the state is in decline,
then carriages are not intricately carved,
armor is not tied with colored silk cords,
food vessels are not engraved,
a Jūnzǐ does not wear silk shoes,
and horses are not fed grain regularly.
18.1 Issuing one’s thoughts as laws
and seeking out the good
is enough to gain a small reputation,
but not enough to move the masses;
drawing near to the worthy and showing consideration for those far away
is enough to move the masses,
but not enough to transform the people.
If a Jūnzǐ wishes to transform the people and establish customs,
he must do so through education!
18.2 If jade is not carved,
it does not become a vessel;
if a person does not learn,
he will not know the Dào.
Therefore, the ancient kings,
when establishing states and ruling the people,
made teaching and learning their priority.
The Yuè Mìng says:
“Think of the beginning and the end, making learning the constant rule.”
This is surely what it means!
Although there may be fine food,
if one does not eat it,
one does not know its flavor;
although there may be the ultimate Dào,
if one does not learn it,
one does not know its excellence.
Therefore, only through learning does one know one’s deficiencies;
only through teaching does one know one’s difficulties.
Knowing one’s deficiencies,
then one is able to reflect on oneself;
knowing one’s difficulties,
then one is able to strengthen oneself.
Hence it is said:
“Teaching and learning promote each other.”
The Yuè Mìng says:
“Teaching is the half of learning.”
This is surely what it means.
In the education of old,
families had a *shú*,
neighborhoods had a *xiáng*,
districts had an *xù*,
and the state capital had a *xué*.
Every year students entered the school,
and every second year their progress was examined.
In the first year, they were observed for their ability to punctuate texts and discern their goals;
in the third year, for their dedication to study and joy in companionship;
in the fifth year, for the breadth of their learning and intimacy with their teachers;
in the seventh year, for their discussions on learning and choice of friends.
This was called the Minor Achievement.
In the ninth year, they understood categories and were comprehensive in their reach,
standing firm without backsliding.
This was called the Great Achievement.
Only then were they sufficient to transform the people and change customs,
making those nearby pleased and submissive,
and those far away long for them.
This is the Way of the *Dàxué*.
The *Jì* says:
“The young of the mason-wasp constantly follow and practice it.”
This is what it means.
18.3 When teaching begins at the *Dàxué*,
wearing the *píbiàn* and offering vegetables
showed respect for the Way;
practicing the first three odes of the *Xiāoyǎ*
marked the beginning of their official life;
upon entering school, the drum was beaten for the cases to be opened,
to encourage humility in their studies;
the *xià* and *chǔ*—the two switches—
served to maintain authority and restraint;
until the *dì* sacrifice had been divined for, the sovereign did not inspect the school,
to allow the students’ will to wander freely;
the teacher would observe periodically but not speak,
to allow the students to maintain their own thoughts;
the younger students listened but did not ask questions,
so that learning did not skip over the proper order.
These seven things
are the major principles of teaching.
The *Jì* says:
“In all learning, those taking office prioritize service,
and scholars prioritize the will.”
This is what it means.
The teaching of the *Dàxué* follows the seasons;
teaching must have a formal curriculum,
and there must be a place for rest and dwelling when withdrawn.
In learning,
if one does not learn the fingering of the strings,
one cannot be at ease with the instrument;
if one does not learn the broad metaphors,
one cannot be at ease with poetry;
if one does not learn the various garments,
one cannot be at ease with ritual;
if one is not inspired by these arts,
one cannot find joy in learning.
Therefore, in the *jūnzǐ*’s approach to learning,
he treasures it in his heart,
practices it,
rests in it,
and takes leisure in it.
Because of this,
he is at peace with his learning and feels close to his teacher,
finds joy in his friends and has faith in the Way.
Hence, even when he leaves his teacher and mentors, he does not turn back from it.
The *Yuèmìng* says:
“Be reverent, humble, and strive for timely diligence,
then the cultivation will come.”
This is what it means.
18.4 Educators of today
merely hum over their writing tablets,
multiply their questions,
and talk incessantly of numbers;
they push forward without considering the student’s ease,
forcing people not to follow their own sincerity,
and teaching without fully developing their potential;
their methods are contrary to reason,
and their demands are perverse.
Because of this,
students hide their learning and resent their teachers;
they suffer through the difficulties without knowing the benefits,
and although they finish their studies,
they will surely abandon them quickly.
That teaching is not successful
is due to this!
The methods of the *Dàxué* are:
prohibiting before things arise is called prevention;
acting when the time is right is called timeliness;
applying lessons without skipping steps is called orderliness;
observing one another to improve is called mutual polishing.
These four
are the reasons why teaching flourishes.
18.5 If prohibition comes only after a thing has occurred,
there will be resistance that cannot be overcome;
if learning comes only after the time has passed,
then even with hard work, it is difficult to achieve success;
if lessons are applied randomly without order,
then there will be disorder and no cultivation;
if one learns alone without friends,
then one will be narrow-minded and ill-informed;
trivial friends go against one’s teacher;
trivial conversations waste one’s learning.
These six
are the reasons why teaching fails.
18.6 Once the *jūnzǐ* knows why teaching flourishes
and knows why teaching fails,
only then can he be a teacher for others.
Therefore, in the teaching and enlightenment of the *jūnzǐ*,
he guides but does not drag,
he strengthens but does not suppress,
and he opens the way but does not deliver the destination.
Guiding without dragging leads to harmony;
strengthening without suppressing leads to ease;
opening the way without delivering the destination leads to reflection.
Harmony, ease, and reflection—
this may be called good enlightenment.
18.7 Learners have four failings,
which the teacher must know.
When people learn,
some fail by trying to learn too much,
some fail by learning too little,
some fail by finding it too easy,
or some fail by stopping too soon.
These four
arise from the differences in their minds.
Only by knowing their minds
can one remedy their failings.
Teaching
is to grow what is good and remedy failings.
A good singer
makes people carry on his melody;
a good teacher
makes people carry on his will.
His words are concise yet thorough,
subtle yet excellent,
with few examples yet making things clear—
this may be called making them carry on the will.
18.8 The *jūnzǐ* knows the difficulty and ease of reaching the goal of learning,
and knows its beauty and ugliness;
only then can he enlighten extensively.
Being able to enlighten extensively, he can then be a teacher;
being a teacher, he can then be a leader;
being a leader, he can then be a ruler.
Therefore, being a teacher
is the means of learning to be a ruler.
Hence, one must be cautious in choosing a teacher.
The *Jì* says:
“The kings of the Three Dynasties and Four Eras only valued their teachers.”
This is what it means.
18.9 In all ways of learning,
respecting the teacher is the most difficult.
Only when the teacher is respected is the Way honored;
only when the Way is honored do the people know to respect learning.
Therefore, there are two instances where a ruler does not treat his subjects as subjects:
when he acts as the *shī*, he does not treat him as a subject;
when he acts as the teacher, he does not treat him as a subject.
According to the rites of the *Dàxué*,
even when summoned by the *Tiānzǐ*,
the teacher does not face north;
this is the way to respect the teacher.
The good learner
makes the teacher’s task easy while achieving double the results,
and attributes the success to the teacher;
the poor learner
makes the teacher toil while achieving only half the results,
and subsequently resents the teacher.
A good questioner
is like one attacking hard wood:
first hitting the easy parts,
leaving the knots for later;
after some time,
the parts come apart with a sense of pleasure.
A poor questioner does the opposite.
One who is good at answering questions
is like one striking a bell:
striking it lightly makes a small sound,
striking it hard makes a loud sound;
he waits for the questioner to be composed,
and then lets the sound ring out fully.
One who is poor at answering questions does the opposite.
These are all the ways of advancing in learning.
18.10 Learning that consists only of memorizing what is asked
is not sufficient to be a teacher.
Must one not listen to their words?
If the student is unable to ask,
only then should one speak to them;
if after speaking to them they still do not understand,
it is acceptable to let it rest.
The son of a good ironsmith
must first learn to make fur garments;
the son of a good bow-maker
must first learn to weave baskets;
one first training horses to the yoke does the opposite:
the carriage is placed in front of the horse.
The *jūnzǐ* who examines these three examples
can set his will upon learning.
18.11 Scholars of antiquity:
they compared things by their classes and grouped them by their types.
The drum does not belong to any of the five sounds,
yet the five sounds cannot be harmonious without it.
Water does not belong to any of the five colors,
yet the five colors cannot be brilliant without it.
Learning does not belong to any of the five offices,
yet the five offices cannot be well-governed without it.
The teacher does not belong to any of the five degrees of mourning dress,
yet the five degrees of mourning dress cannot be characterized by intimacy without him.
18.12 The Jūnzǐ says:
“Great virtue is not confined to one office;
the Dà Dào is not a mere tool;
great good faith does not require a formal covenant;
great timing is not uniform.
He who understands these four things
can set his will upon learning.”
When the Sān Wáng sacrificed to the rivers,
they always prioritized the Hé and put the sea last;
for one is the source,
and the other is the outlet.
This is called attending to the root.
19.1 All tones arise
from the human heart.
The movement of the human heart
is caused by external things.
Being affected by things, it moves,
and thus takes form in sounds.
When sounds respond to one another,
variations arise;
when these variations form a pattern,
it is called a melody;
when these melodies are combined for enjoyment,
and accompanied by shields, axes, feathers, and yak-tails,
it is called music.
Music is
that which melodies arise from;
its root lies in the human heart being affected by things.
Therefore, when a heart of sorrow is affected,
its sounds are sharp and fading.
When a heart of joy is affected,
its sounds are relaxed and slow.
When a heart of delight is affected,
its sounds are expansive and scattered.
When a heart of anger is affected,
its sounds are coarse and harsh.
When a heart of reverence is affected,
its sounds are upright and crisp.
When a heart of love is affected,
its sounds are harmonious and soft.
These six
are not the nature itself;
they are movements only after being affected by things.
Therefore, the former kings were careful about what affected the heart.
Thus, they used ritual to guide the will,
music to harmonize the voice,
government to unify conduct,
and punishments to prevent wickedness.
Ritual, music, punishments, and government—
their ultimate goal is one;
they are the means to unify the hearts of the people and bring forth the way of governance.
All melodies
are born in the human heart.
Emotions are moved within,
and thus take form in sounds.
When sounds form a pattern,
it is called a melody.
Therefore,
the melodies of a well-governed age are peaceful and joyful,
and its government is harmonious.
The melodies of a chaotic age are resentful and angry,
and its government is perverse.
The melodies of a dying state are sorrowful and pensive,
and its people are distressed.
The way of sounds and melodies
is connected with government.
Gōng represents the ruler,
Shāng represents the ministers,
Jué represents the people,
Zhǐ represents affairs,
Yǔ represents objects.
If these five are not in disorder,
there will be no discordant sounds.
If Gōng is disordered, then there is wildness;
the ruler is arrogant.
If Shāng is disordered, then there is crookedness;
the officials are corrupt.
If Jué is disordered, then there is anxiety;
the people are resentful.
If Zhǐ is disordered, then there is sorrow;
the affairs are toilsome.
If Yǔ is disordered, then there is peril;
resources are depleted.
If all five are disordered
and encroach upon one another,
it is called licentiousness.
In such a case,
the destruction of the state is imminent.
The music of Zhèng and Wèi
is the music of a chaotic age,
akin to licentiousness.
The music of Sāngjiān and the Pú river bank
is the music of a dying state;
its government is dissipated,
its people are adrift,
and they slander their superiors and act selfishly without restraint.
All melodies
are born from the human heart.
Music is
that which connects with the principles of human relations.
Therefore,
those who know sounds but not melodies
are birds and beasts;
those who know melodies but not music
are the common masses.
Only the Jūnzǐ is capable of knowing music.
Therefore,
one examines the sounds to know the melodies,
examines the melodies to know the music,
examines the music to know the government;
and the way of governance is complete.
Therefore,
one who does not know sounds cannot be spoken to about melodies,
one who does not know melodies cannot be spoken to about music.
To know music
is to be close to ritual.
When both ritual and music are attained,
it is called having virtue.
Virtue means attainment.
Therefore,
the pinnacle of music
is not the utmost in sound.
The ritual of the banquet
is not the utmost in flavor.
In the music of the Qīngmiào zither,
with its vermilion strings and sparse holes,
there is one singer and three who join in sighing;
there are lingering sounds.
The ritual of the Great Banquet
honors dark water and places raw fish on the stand;
the Great Broth is unseasoned;
there is a lingering flavor.
Therefore, the former kings' institution of ritual and music
was not to satisfy the desires of the mouth, stomach, ears, and eyes,
but to teach the people to balance their likes and dislikes
and return to the correctness of the human way.
Man is born still;
this is the nature given by Heaven.
Being affected by things and moving,
this is the desire of that nature.
As things arrive, knowledge is produced,
and then likes and dislikes take shape.
If likes and dislikes are not regulated within
and knowledge is tempted from without,
and one cannot reflect upon oneself,
then Tiānlǐ is extinguished.
Now, the things that affect man are infinite,
and if man's likes and dislikes have no regulation,
then as things arrive, man is transformed by things.
Man being transformed by things
means the extinguishing of Tiānlǐ and the exhaustion of human desires.
From this arise rebellious and deceitful hearts,
and licentious and chaotic deeds.
Therefore,
the strong threaten the weak,
the many oppress the few,
the clever deceive the simple,
the brave torment the timid,
the sick are not cared for,
and the old, the young, the orphaned, and the widowed lose their proper places;
this is the way to great chaos.
Therefore, the former kings instituted ritual and music
to provide regulations for man;
mourning garments and weeping
were used to regulate the period of mourning;
bells, drums, shields, and axes
were used to harmonize peace and joy;
marriage and capping ceremonies
were used to distinguish men and women;
archery and local banquets
were used to correct social interactions.
Ritual regulates the hearts of the people;
music harmonizes the sounds of the people;
government is used to implement them;
punishments are used to guard against them.
When ritual, music, punishments, and government
are all four applied and not in conflict,
then the Wáng Dào is complete.
Music serves to unify;
ritual serves to differentiate.
Through unification, there is mutual intimacy;
through differentiation, there is mutual respect.
If music prevails, there is drifting;
if ritual prevails, there is separation.
Bringing together emotions and adorning outward appearance
are the business of ritual and music.
Ritual and righteousness are established,
and then the noble and the base are graded;
the patterns of music are uniform,
and then superior and inferior are in harmony;
likes and dislikes are made manifest,
and then the worthy and the unworthy are distinguished.
Punishments forbid violence,
noble ranks promote the worthy,
and then governance is equitable.
Benevolence is used to love them,
righteousness is used to correct them;
in this way,
the governance of the people proceeds.
Music emerges from within,
ritual is created from without.
Because music emerges from within, it is tranquil;
because ritual is created from without, it is patterned.
Great music must be easy,
great ritual must be simple.
When music is perfect, there is no resentment;
when ritual is perfect, there is no contention.
Governing the world through bowing and yielding
is what is meant by ritual and music.
Violent people do not arise,
the Zhūhóu submit as guests,
weapons and armor are not put to use,
the five punishments are not employed,
the common people have no hardships,
the Tiānzǐ is not angry;
in this way,
music is pervasive.
Uniting the kinship of father and son,
clarifying the order of elders and juniors,
so that all within the four seas respect the Tiānzǐ;
in this way,
ritual is practiced.
19.2 Great music is in harmony with Heaven and Earth,
great ritual has the same rhythm as Heaven and Earth.
Because of harmony, the hundred things do not lose their place;
because of rhythm, they sacrifice to Heaven and Earth.
In the manifest realm, there are ritual and music;
in the hidden realm, there are ghosts and spirits.
In this way,
within the four seas,
respect is united and love is shared.
Ritual is what distinguishes affairs to unite respect;
music is what differentiates patterns to unite love.
The essence of ritual and music is the same,
therefore wise kings follow them in succession.
Thus affairs proceed with the times,
and names accompany achievements.
19.3 Therefore, bells, drums, pipes, and chimes,
feathers, flutes, shields, and axes
are the instruments of music.
Bending and stretching, bowing and looking up,
the positions and tracks, the slow and the fast,
are the patterns of music.
Fǔ, Guǐ, Zǔ, and Dòu vessels,
regulations and patterns,
are the instruments of ritual.
Ascending and descending, moving up and down,
circling around, exposing and covering the inner garment,
are the patterns of ritual.
Thus those who know the essence of ritual and music can create;
those who recognize the patterns of ritual and music can transmit.
To create is called Shèng,
to transmit is called Míng;
the Míng and the Shèng
refer to transmitting and creating.
19.4 Music
is the harmony of Heaven and Earth;
ritual
is the order of Heaven and Earth.
Because of harmony, the hundred things are all transformed;
because of order, the many things are all distinguished.
Music is created by Heaven,
ritual is established by Earth.
Excessive regulation leads to disorder,
excessive creation leads to violence.
Being clear about Heaven and Earth,
one can then promote ritual and music.
Discoursing on categories without error
is the essence of music;
joy, pleasure, kindness, and love
are the functions of music.
Being central, correct, and without evil
is the substance of ritual;
being solemn, respectful, reverent, and compliant
is the regulation of ritual.
As for the application of ritual and music to metal and stone,
their diffusion through sounds,
their use in ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain,
and their service to mountains, rivers, ghosts, and spirits,
these are what the people share in common.
19.5 A King creates music when achievements are accomplished,
and establishes ritual when governance is set.
Those whose achievements are great have complete music,
those whose governance is comprehensive have thorough ritual.
The dance with shields and axes is not complete music,
simply cooking and sacrificing is not universal ritual.
The Wǔdì lived in different times,
and did not follow the same music;
the Sānwáng lived in different ages,
and did not inherit the same ritual.
Excessive music leads to sorrow,
coarse ritual leads to partiality.
As for those who enrich music without sorrow
and complete ritual without partiality,
are they not only the great Shèng?
19.6 Heaven is high and Earth is low,
the ten thousand things are scattered and different,
and thus the regulations of ritual are practiced.
Flowing without ceasing,
uniting and transforming,
and thus music arises.
Spring creating and Summer growing
are Benevolence;
Autumn gathering and Winter storing
are Righteousness.
Benevolence is close to music,
Righteousness is close to ritual.
Music enriches harmony,
leading the spirits to follow Heaven;
ritual distinguishes what is appropriate,
situating the ghosts to follow Earth.
Therefore, the Shèngrén created music to respond to Heaven
and established ritual to match Earth.
When ritual and music are clear and complete,
Heaven and Earth perform their functions.
Heaven is honored and Earth is lowly,
so ruler and minister are settled.
Low and high are already displayed,
so noble and base have their positions.
Motion and stillness have constancy,
so small and great are distinguished.
Directions are grouped by kind,
things are divided into clusters,
so natures and destinies are not the same.
In Heaven, they form images,
on Earth, they form shapes;
in this way,
ritual is the distinction between Heaven and Earth.
The qi of Earth rises to align with Heaven,
the qi of Heaven descends,
Yīn and Yáng rub against each other,
Heaven and Earth vibrate against each other,
drummed by thunder and lightning,
roused by wind and rain,
moved by the four seasons,
warmed by the sun and moon,
and thus the hundred transformations arise.
In this way,
music is the harmony of Heaven and Earth.
If transformation is not timely, things do not grow;
if there is no distinction between male and female, disorder arises;
this is the nature of Heaven and Earth.
As for ritual and music, they reach to Heaven and coil around Earth,
acting through Yīn and Yáng and communicating with ghosts and spirits;
they reach the highest and farthest and measure the deep and thick.
Music manifests the Great Beginning,
and ritual resides in the completion of things.
That which manifests without ceasing is Heaven,
that which manifests without moving is Earth.
The alternation of motion and stillness
is what exists between Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, the Shèngrén speaks of "ritual and music."
19.7 Formerly,
Shùn made the five-stringed qín to sing the "Nánfēng,"
and Kuí first established music to reward the Zhūhóu.
19.8 Therefore, when the Tiānzǐ creates music,
it is to reward those among the Zhūhóu who have virtue.
When virtue is abundant and teaching is honored,
and the five grains ripen in season,
then they are rewarded with music.
Therefore, for those whose governance of the people was laborious,
the rows of their dancers were far apart;
for those whose governance of the people was easy,
the rows of their dancers were close together.
Thus, by observing their dance,
one knows their virtue;
by hearing their posthumous title,
one knows their conduct.
19.9 *Dàzhāng*
is to manifest it.
*Xiánchí*
is complete.
*Sháo*
is to continue.
*Xià*
is great.
The music of Yīn and Zhōu
is exhaustive.
The Dào of Heaven and Earth:
if cold and heat do not come at their proper times, there is illness;
if wind and rain are not regulated, there is famine.
Education
is the cold and heat of the people;
if education is not timely, it harms the age.
State affairs
are the wind and rain of the people;
if state affairs are not regulated, there is no success.
Thus, when the Former Kings created music,
they did so to govern by law;
when it is good, its performance reflects virtue.
19.10 Now, raising pigs and making wine
was not intended to cause disaster,
yet as litigation and lawsuits became more frequent,
it was the excessive flow of wine that produced the disaster.
For this reason, the Former Kings created the wine rituals:
in the ritual of a single libation,
the guest and host bow to each other a hundred times,
so that they may drink wine all day without becoming intoxicated;
this was how the Former Kings guarded against the disasters of wine.
Therefore, wine and food are used to bring people together in joy;
music is used to reflect virtue;
and ritual is used to restrain excess.
Thus, when the Former Kings had a great calamity,
they necessarily had rituals to mourn it;
when they had great blessings,
they necessarily had rituals to celebrate them with music.
The distinctions between mourning and joy
were all finalized through ritual.
As for music,
it is what the Sages delighted in,
and it can improve the hearts of the people.
Its impact on people is deep,
and its ability to shift manners and change customs
is easy;
therefore, the Former Kings emphasized its teaching.
19.11 People possess a nature of blood, breath, and consciousness,
but they have no constant state of mourning, joy, delight, or anger.
They move in response to the influence of external things,
and only then do the workings of the heart take shape.
Therefore, when low, faint, and gasping sounds arise,
the people's thoughts become sorrowful.
When easy, harmonious, slow, and relaxed sounds,
with ornate melodies and simple rhythms arise,
the people are peaceful and happy.
When coarse, harsh, violent,
vigorous, and expansive sounds arise,
the people become resolute and strong.
When upright, firm, solemn, and sincere sounds arise,
the people become respectful.
When broad, mellow, smooth, and harmonious sounds arise,
the people become compassionate and loving.
When dissolute, depraved, wild, and overflowing sounds arise,
the people become licentious and disorderly.
19.12 Therefore,
the Former Kings rooted music in the emotions and nature,
examined it through measures and numbers,
and regulated it through ritual and righteousness.
They harmonized it with the harmony of the vital breath,
and guided it with the practice of the Wǔcháng,
making the yáng not dissipate
and the yīn not become compressed,
so that the hard breath was not angry
and the soft breath was not fearful.
The four flows intersected within
and manifested outwardly,
each resting in its place without displacing the others.
Only then did they establish grades of learning,
broaden the rhythms,
and refine the embellishments,
so as to measure the depth of virtue.
They proportioned the sizes of the pitch pipes
and matched the order of beginning and end
to represent the conduct of affairs.
They caused the principles of kinship, status, age, and gender
to be clearly manifested in music;
therefore it is said:
"In music, one observes its depth."
If the soil is exhausted, then grass and trees will not grow;
if the water is troubled, then fish and turtles will not grow large;
if the vital breath decays, then living things will not flourish;
if the age is in disorder, then rituals will be perverse and music will be licentious.
Therefore, its sounds are mournful but not solemn,
or joyful but not peaceful;
they are slow and easy so as to violate the measures,
and they are dissolute so as to forget the root.
If expansive, they harbor wickedness;
if narrow, they induce desire;
they move the smooth-flowing breath
but destroy the virtue of peace and harmony.
This is why the Jūnzǐ disdains them.
19.13 Whenever depraved sounds move a person,
adverse breath responds to them;
when adverse breath takes form,
licentious music arises.
When correct sounds move a person,
obedient breath responds to them;
when obedient breath takes form,
harmonious music arises.
There is resonance between the lead and the response;
the crooked and the depraved, the straight and the upright,
each returns to its own kind;
for the principles of all things
are such that they move each other according to their categories.
Therefore,
the Jūnzǐ returns to true feelings to harmonize his will
and compares categories to perfect his conduct.
Depraved sounds and disorderly colors
do not remain in his hearing or sight;
licentious music and perverse rituals
do not touch the workings of his heart.
Lazy, slow, depraved, or perverse breath
is not present in his body,
causing his ears, eyes, nose, mouth, consciousness, and all parts of the body
to follow what is obedient and correct in practicing righteousness.
Only then does he express this in sounds,
adorn it with the qín and sè,
move with the shields and axes,
decorate with feathers and banners,
and follow with flutes and pipes.
He spreads the light of ultimate virtue,
moves the harmony of the four breaths,
so as to manifest the principles of all things.
Thus, clarity and brightness represent Heaven,
vastness and greatness represent Earth,
the beginning and end represent the four seasons,
and the circling rotations represent wind and rain.
The five colors form patterns without confusion;
the eight winds follow the pitch pipes without discord;
and the hundred measures obtain their numbers and have constancy.
Small and large complete each other;
beginning and end produce each other.
The leading and responding, the clear and the turbid,
alternately serve as the guiding thread.
Therefore, when music is performed, human relations are clarified,
ears and eyes become sharp,
blood and breath become harmonious and peaceful,
manners are shifted and customs changed,
and the whole world is at peace.
19.14 Therefore it is said:
"Music is joy."
The Jūnzǐ finds joy in attaining the Dào;
the xiǎorén finds joy in attaining his desires.
If one uses the Dào to regulate desire,
then there is joy without disorder;
if one uses desire to forget the Dào,
then there is confusion without joy.
19.15 For this reason,
the Jūnzǐ returns to true feelings to harmonize his will
and expands music to complete his education;
when music is performed,
the people turn toward the right direction,
and one can observe their virtue.
Virtue is the source of nature;
music
is the flowering of virtue.
Metal, stone, silk, and bamboo
are the instruments of music.
Poetry expresses the will;
singing chants the sounds;
and dancing moves the appearance.
These three are rooted in the heart,
and then the breath of music follows them.
Thus, when feelings are deep, the patterns are clear;
when the breath is abundant, the transformation is divine.
When harmony and obedience accumulate within and the flowering brilliance manifests without,
only music cannot be faked.
19.16 Music
is the movement of the heart;
sounds
are the images of music.
Melodic patterns and rhythms
are the ornaments of sound.
The Jūnzǐ sets the root in motion.
19.17 He takes joy in the image,
and then regulates the ornaments.
Therefore, first there are the drums to provide warning;
then three steps to show the direction;
then a restart to manifest what has passed;
and a conclusion to the disorder to regulate the return.
It is vigorous and rapid but not uprooting;
it reaches the ultimate depths but is not hidden.
He alone finds joy in his will
and never tires of the Dào;
he fully upholds the Dào
and is not private in his desires.
Thus, feelings are manifested and righteousness is established;
the music ends and virtue is honored.
The Jūnzǐ uses it to love the good,
and the xiǎorén uses it to listen for his faults.
Therefore it is said:
"In the Dào of living for the people,
music is the greatest part of it."
19.18 Music is a bestowing;
Ritual is a reciprocating.
Music
rejoices in that from which it was born;
and Ritual
returns to that from which it began.
Music manifests virtue,
Ritual reciprocates feeling and returns to the beginning.
19.19 What is called the *Dàlù*
is the carriage of the *Tiānzǐ*.
The dragon banner with nine tassels
is the ensign of the *Tiānzǐ*.
That with the blue and black border
is the precious tortoise-shell of the *Tiānzǐ*.
Following these with herds of cattle and sheep
is the means by which to present gifts to the *Zhūhóu*.
19.20 Music is
that in the feelings which cannot be changed.
Ritual is
that in the principles which cannot be altered.
Music unifies the similar,
Ritual distinguishes the different.
The theory of Ritual and Music
governs human feelings.
19.21 Exhausting the source and knowing the transformations
is the essence of Music;
manifesting sincerity and removing falsehood
is the constant principle of Ritual.
Ritual and Music accord with the feelings of Heaven and Earth,
reach the virtue of the divine and bright,
bring down and raise up the spirits of the high and low,
and give form to the essential and the coarse,
presiding over the regulations between father and son, ruler and minister.
19.22 Therefore,
when the Great Man initiates Ritual and Music,
Heaven and Earth will manifest for him.
Heaven and Earth harmonize and unite,
*Yīnyáng* find each other,
warming and nourishing all things;
thereafter the grasses and trees flourish,
the buds and sprouts break through,
the feathered wings flutter,
horns and antlers grow,
hibernating insects awaken,
the feathered ones brood and hatch,
the furry ones conceive and suckle,
those born from the womb do not miscarry,
and those born from eggs do not break,
and thus the Way of Music is returned to.
19.23 Music
is not merely the *Huángzhōng*, *Dàlǚ*, strings, singing, shields, or battle-axes;
these are the minor details of music,
and therefore youths dance to them.
Spreading mats,
arranging vessels and stands,
lining up baskets and bowls,
and the ritual of ascending and descending
are the minor details of Ritual,
and therefore officials oversee them.
The *Yuèshī* is clear about the sounds and poems,
so he faces north and plays the strings;
