the *Zōng* and *Zhù* are clear about the rituals of the ancestral temple,
so they stand behind the *Shī*;
the *Shāngzhù* is clear about funeral rituals,
so he stands behind the chief mourner.
Therefore,
virtue being perfected is superior,
skill being perfected is inferior;
conduct being perfected comes first,
affairs being perfected come after.
Therefore, the former kings had the superior and the inferior,
the first and the last,
and thereafter they could establish systems for all under Heaven.
19.24 Marquis *Wén* of *Wèi* asked *Zǐxià*, saying:
"When I wear my cap and robes and listen to ancient music,
I only fear I will fall asleep;
but when I listen to the sounds of *Zhèng* and *Wèi*,
I do not know weariness.
I venture to ask,
why is ancient music like that?
And why is new music like this?"
*Zǐxià* replied:
"Now, as for ancient music,
the movements forward and backward are in unison,
it is harmonious, correct, and expansive.
The strings, gourds, pipes, and reeds
meet at the beat of the hand-drum and drum.
It begins the performance with refinement,
and concludes the movement with military spirit,
regulating the conclusion with the *Xiàng*,
and signaling the pace with the *Yǎ*.
Thereupon the superior man speaks,
and discourses on antiquity,
cultivating himself and his family,
and bringing peace to all under Heaven.
This is the manifestation of ancient music.
19.25 Now, as for new music,
the movements forward and backward are stooped and bent,
the perverse sounds are excessive,
drowning the listener without stopping;
and with actors and dwarves,
monkeys, and mixed men and women,
the distinction between father and son is lost.
When the music ends, one cannot speak,
nor discourse on antiquity.
This is the manifestation of new music.
Now, what you ask about is music,
but what you love are sounds!
For music
is close to sound, but not the same."
Marquis *Wén* said:
"I venture to ask how so?"
*Zǐxià* replied:
"In antiquity,
Heaven and Earth were in accord and the four seasons were appropriate,
the people had virtue and the five grains flourished,
diseases did not arise and there were no ominous portents;
this was called the Great Accord.
Thereafter the sages established the roles of father and son, ruler and minister,
to serve as the guiding principles.
Once the principles were correct,
all under Heaven was greatly settled.
When all under Heaven was greatly settled,
they then rectified the *Liùlǜ*,
harmonized the five tones,
and sang the *Shī* and *Sòng* to stringed instruments.
These are called the tones of virtue;
the tones of virtue are called music.
The *Shī* says:
'Solemn is his virtuous sound,
his virtue is able to be bright.
He can be bright and can distinguish,
he can be a leader and can be a ruler,
ruling this great state;
he can be compliant and can make others compliant,
like *Wénwáng*,
his virtue has nothing to regret.
Having received the blessings of *Dì*,
they are extended to his grandsons and sons.'
This is what is meant.
Now, what you love,
is it not the drowning sounds?"
Marquis *Wén* said:
"I venture to ask, from where do drowning sounds come?"
*Zǐxià* replied:
"The sounds of *Zhèng* are fond of excess and debauch the will;
the sounds of *Sòng* are of beautiful women and drown the will;
the sounds of *Wèi* are rapid and frantic and vex the will;
the sounds of *Qí* are arrogant, depraved, and haughty and swell the will.
These four are all excessive in sensuality
and harmful to virtue,
and for this reason, they are not used in sacrifices.
The *Shī* says:
'Solemn and harmonious they sing in unison,
the ancestors listen to this.'
Now, *Sùsù*
is reverence;
*Yōngyōng*
is harmony.
With reverence and harmony,
what task cannot be accomplished?
He who is the ruler of men
should merely be careful about what he likes and dislikes.
If the ruler likes something,
the ministers will do it.
If those above practice it,
the people will follow it.
The *Shī* says:
'To lead the people is very easy.'
This is what is meant.
Thereafter,
the sages made the *Táo*, *Gǔ*, *Qiāng*, *Jié*, *Xūn*, and *Chí*;
these six are the sounds of the tones of virtue.
Then the bells, chimes, reed organs, and zithers were used to harmonize them,
and shields, battle-axes, ox-tails, and pheasant feathers were used to dance to them.
This is the means by which to sacrifice in the temples of the former kings,
the means for the ceremonies of offering, pledging, and toasting,
the means by which the official ranks of the noble and the mean each find their propriety,
and the means by which to show later generations the order of honored and humble, old and young.
The sound of the bells is resonant;
resonance is used to establish a signal;
a signal is used to establish resolve;
resolve is used to establish military prowess.
When the superior man hears the sound of the bell,
he thinks of his military officials.
The sound of the stone chimes is sharp;
sharpness is used to establish distinction;
distinction is used to lead one to die for a cause.
When the superior man hears the sound of the chimes,
he thinks of the officials who would die at the borders.
The sound of the silk strings is mournful;
mournfulness is used to establish integrity;
integrity is used to establish the will.
When the superior man hears the sound of the *Qín* and *Sè*,
he thinks of officials of righteous will.
The sound of the bamboo pipes is overflowing;
overflowing is used to establish an assembly;
the assembly is used to gather the masses.
When the superior man hears the sounds of the yú, sheng, xiāo, and guǎn,
he thinks of ministers who gather and accumulate resources.
The sound of the drum and kettle-drum is clamorous;
being clamorous, it arouses to action;
arousing to action, it advances the multitude.
When the superior man hears the sound of the drum and kettle-drum,
he thinks of ministers who are generals and commanders.
When the superior man listens to music,
it is not merely to hear the clanging and tinkling;
he also has something that he associates with it."
Móujiǎ was sitting in attendance upon Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ spoke with him, and when the conversation reached the subject of music,
he said:
"In the performance of the *Wǔ*, the period of preparation and vigilance lasts a long time;
why is this?"
He replied:
"It is because of the concern of not gaining the support of the multitude."
"The singing is sighed forth,
the sounds are prolonged and flowing—
why is this?"
He replied:
"It is because of the fear of not being equal to the task."
"The brandishing of weapons and the stamping of feet occur early;
why is this?"
He replied:
"It is to be timely for the campaign."
"In the *Wǔ*, the dancers kneel, extending the right knee and touching the ground with the left;
why is this?"
He replied:
"That is not the kneeling posture of the *Wǔ*."
"The sounds are excessive and reach the Shāng note;
why is this?"
He replied:
"Those are not the sounds of the *Wǔ*."
The Master said:
"If they are not the sounds of the *Wǔ*,
then what sounds are they?"
He replied:
"The officials in charge have lost the tradition.
If the officials had not lost the tradition,
then the will of Wǔwáng would have been neglected."
The Master said:
"Indeed!
What Qiū heard from Cháng Hóng
is exactly as you have said."
Bīn Móujiǎ rose,
left his mat, and asked:
"I have heard your instruction regarding the long period of preparation and vigilance in the *Wǔ*;
I have already heard your command.
I venture to ask,
why does it proceed so slowly and continue for so long—
why is this?"
The Master said:
"Sit down!
I will tell you.
Music
symbolizes achievements.
Grasping the shields and standing like a mountain
represents the deeds of Wǔwáng.
The brandishing of weapons and the stamping of feet
represents the will of Tàigōng.
When the *Wǔ* concludes and all kneel,
it represents the governance of Zhōu and Shào.
Moreover, in the *Wǔ*,
the first movement represents the march to the north;
the second movement represents the destruction of Shāng.
The third movement represents the turn to the south;
the fourth movement represents the marking of the borders of the southern states;
the fifth movement represents the division with Zhōugōng on the left and Shàogōng on the right;
the sixth movement represents returning to the original positions
to pay homage to the Son of Heaven.
The shaking of shields on both sides and the fourfold striking
displays great majesty throughout the Middle Kingdom.
Advancing in divided files
shows that the work was quickly accomplished.
Standing for a long time in their positions
is to wait for the arrival of the feudal lords.
Have you alone not heard the account of Mùyě?
When Wǔwáng conquered Yīn,
he overthrew Shāng.
Even before getting down from his carriage,
he enfeoffed the descendants of Huángdì in Jì,
enfeoffed the descendants of Dìyáo in Zhù,
and enfeoffed the descendants of Dìshùn in Chén.
After getting down from his carriage, he enfeoffed the descendants of the Xiàhòushì in Qǐ
and placed the descendants of Yīn in Sòng.
He raised a mound over the grave of Prince Bǐgān,
released Jīzǐ from prison,
and restored Shāng Róng to his position.
The common people were relieved from heavy administration,
and the various officials had their emoluments doubled.
He crossed the River and went west;
his horses
were released on the sunny side of Huáshān
and were never ridden again;
his oxen
were released in the wilds of Táolín
and were never used for pulling again.
The chariots and armor were smeared with blood and stored in the armories,
never to be used again.
Shields and spears were inverted
and wrapped in tiger skins;
the generals and commanders
were made feudal lords;
it was called
'Jiàn Gāo'.
Only then
did the world know that Wǔwáng would not use weapons again.
He disbanded the army and practiced archery in the suburbs;
on the left they shot to the rhythm of 'Líshǒu',
on the right they shot to the rhythm of 'Zōuyú',
and archery aimed at piercing leather targets ceased.
Wearing ritual robes and caps and carrying tablets in their belts,
the guards of the royal escort laid aside their swords.
He sacrificed in the Míngtáng, and the people learned filial piety.
He held audiences,
and then the feudal lords knew how to be subjects;
he plowed the ritual field,
and then the feudal lords knew how to show respect.
These five things
are the great lessons for the world.
He hosted the Three Elders and Five Experienced Ones in the Great School;
the Son of Heaven bared his arm and cut the sacrificial meat;
he held the sauce and served it;
he held the cup and offered the wine;
wearing his ceremonial cap, he grasped the shield;
this was to teach the feudal lords fraternal duty.
In this way,
the way of Zhōu reached everywhere,
and ritual and music were spread and exchanged.
Then, for the performance of the *Wǔ* to take a long time,
is it not appropriate?"
The superior man says:
"Ritual and music must not for a moment be absent from one's person.
By applying music to govern the heart,
a heart that is easy, straightforward, gentle, and sincere will naturally arise.
When an easy, straightforward, gentle, and sincere heart arises, there is joy;
with joy comes peace;
with peace comes endurance;
with endurance comes the heavenly;
with the heavenly comes the divine.
The heavenly is trusted without speaking;
the divine is majestic without anger;
this is the effect of applying music to govern the heart.
By applying ritual to govern the person, one becomes grave and respectful;
being grave and respectful, one has dignified majesty.
If for a moment there is no harmony or joy in the heart,
then a base and deceitful heart will enter.
If for a moment the outward appearance is not grave or respectful,
then a heart of levity and disrespect
will enter.
Therefore, music
is what moves within;
ritual
is what moves without.
Music represents ultimate harmony;
ritual represents ultimate compliance.
When there is harmony within and compliance without,
the people look at the countenance
and do not contend with it;
they observe the appearance,
and the people do not give way to levity or disrespect.
Thus, when the radiance of virtue moves within,
the people all listen and obey;
when principle is manifested without,
the people all follow and comply.
Therefore it is said:
'By perfecting the way of ritual and music
and applying them
to the world,
nothing will be difficult.'
Music
is what moves within;
ritual
is what moves without.
Therefore, ritual prioritizes restraint;
music prioritizes fullness.
Ritual restrains but advances,
taking advancement as its refinement;
music is full but returns,
taking the return as its refinement.
If ritual restrains but does not advance, it withers;
if music is full but does not return, it becomes unrestrained.
Therefore, ritual has reciprocity and music has a return.
When ritual achieves reciprocity, there is joy;
when music achieves its return, there is peace.
The reciprocity of ritual
and the return of music
are one in their meaning.
Music is joy,
something that human emotion cannot be without.
Joy must be expressed in sounds
and take form in movement and stillness;
this is the way of man.
Sounds, movements, and stillness—
the variations in the art of manifesting nature
are all contained herein.
Therefore, humans cannot endure a lack of music;
music cannot endure being without form;
if it has form but is not guided by the Way,
it cannot endure without falling into chaos.
19.27 The ancient kings were ashamed of such chaos,
so they established the sounds of the *Yǎ* and *Sòng* to guide it,
making the sounds enjoyable enough without being dissolute,
making the lyrics meaningful enough without ceasing,
and making the modulations—the complex and simple, the sharp and full, and the rhythms—
sufficient only to move the good hearts of people.
They did not allow dissipated minds or depraved airs to come into contact with it;
this was the method by which the ancient kings established music.
19.28 Therefore, when music is performed in the ancestral temple,
and the ruler and ministers, high and low, listen to it together,
none fail to be harmonious and respectful;
when in the presence of clan elders and in the local districts,
the old and young listen to it together,
and none fail to be harmonious and compliant;
when within the inner gates of the home,
fathers and sons, elder and younger brothers listen to it together,
and none fail to be harmonious and affectionate.
Thus, music
scrutinizes the unity to determine harmony,
and compares different things to adorn the measures;
rhythms are joined to form the pattern.
It is the means to harmonize fathers and sons, rulers and ministers,
and to bring the myriad people into close affection;
this was the method by which the ancient kings established music.
Thus, when one hears the sounds of the *Yǎ* and *Sòng*,
one’s will and intentions become broad;
when one wields the shields and axes,
and practices the bowing, rising, bending, and stretching,
one’s appearance and demeanor become dignified;
when one follows the positions and steps,
and matches the rhythms,
the ranks and files become orderly,
and the advances and retreats become uniform.
Therefore, music is
the mandate of Heaven and Earth,
the guideline of central harmony,
and that which human emotions cannot avoid.
Now, music
is that with which the ancient kings adorned their joy,
while armies and executioner's axes
were that with which the ancient kings adorned their anger.
Therefore, the joy and anger of the ancient kings
both found their proper counterparts.
When they were joyful, the world harmonized with them;
when they were angry, the violent and rebellious feared them.
In the Way of the ancient kings,
ritual and music may be called flourishing.
19.29 Zǐgàn saw Shī Yǐ and questioned him,
saying:
“I, Cì, have heard that sounds and songs each have their suitability.
For someone like me,
what song is suitable?”
Shī Yǐ said:
“I, Yǐ, am but a lowly musician;
how am I worthy to be asked about what is suitable?
Let me recite what I have heard,
and you, sir, may decide for yourself.
One who is loving should sing the *Shāng*;
one who is gentle and kind yet capable of decisiveness should sing the *Qí*.
Now, singing
is a matter of straightening oneself and displaying virtue.
When one moves oneself, Heaven and Earth respond,
the four seasons harmonize,
the stars and planets follow their order,
and the myriad things are nourished.
Thus, the *Shāng* mode
is the legacy sound of the *Wǔdì*.
One who is broad-minded and quiet,
gentle and upright, should sing the *Sòng*.
One who is vast and quiet,
perceptive and trustworthy, should sing the *Dà Yǎ*.
One who is respectful, frugal, and loves ritual
should sing the *Xiǎo Yǎ*.
One who is upright and quiet,
incorruptible and humble, should sing the *Fēng*.
One who is uninhibited, straightforward, and compassionate.”
These were the legacy sounds of the *Shāng*;
the people of *Shāng* recognized them,
so they are called *Shāng*.
The *Qí* mode
is the legacy sound of the *Sāndài*;
the people of *Qí* recognized it,
so they are called *Qí*.
One who understands the notes of *Shāng*
will be frequently decisive when facing affairs;
one who understands the notes of *Qí*
will yield when seeing personal gain.
Being frequently decisive when facing affairs
is courage;
yielding when seeing personal gain
is righteousness.
If one possesses courage and righteousness,
what other than singing can preserve these?
Therefore, in singing,
the high notes are like things being lifted up,
the low notes are like things falling down,
the turns are like something being broken,
the stops are like withered wood,
the angular movements match the carpenter's square,
the curved movements match the hook,
and the notes follow one another in a continuous line like a string of pearls.
Thus, as for what 'singing' means,
it is the prolonging of speech.
Being pleased with something,
one speaks of it;
when speaking of it is not enough,
one prolongs the speech;
when prolonging the speech is not enough,
one sighs and groans it;
when sighing and groaning it is not enough,
unconsciously, the hands begin to dance it,
and the feet begin to stomp it.”
Zǐgòng questioned him about music.
20.1 If a feudal lord dies in a guest house while traveling,
then the ritual of recalling the soul
is performed as it would be in his own state.
If he dies on the road,
they climb onto the left hub of the carriage he was riding,
and use his hand-strap to recall the soul.
His hearse-curtain has a fringe,
with black cloth for the lower hangings and white brocade for the roof-cover as they travel.
When they reach the temple gate,
they do not tear down the wall,
but enter and go straight to the place of the lying-in-state,
and only the hearse-curtain is removed outside the temple gate.
20.2 If a Great Officer or an officer dies on the road,
they climb onto the left hub of the carriage he was riding,
and use his hand-strap to recall the soul.
If he dies in a guest house,
then the ritual of recalling the soul
is performed as it would be at home.
A Great Officer uses plain cloth for the hearse-curtain as they travel;
when they reach his home, the hearse-curtain is removed,
he is placed on a low-wheeled hearse,
which enters through the gate,
stopping at the foot of the eastern steps where the carriage is removed,
he is lifted up the eastern steps,
and taken up to the place of the lying-in-state.
For an officer's hearse-curtain,
reed mats are used for the roof-cover,
and rush mats are used for the lower hangings.
20.3 In all cases of reporting a death to one's ruler,
one says:
“Your ruler’s servant So-and-so has died.”
For parents, a wife, or the eldest son,
one says:
“The so-and-so of your ruler’s servant So-and-so has died.”
When a ruler reports a death to the ruler of another state,
he says:
“Our humble ruler has lost his life,
and we venture to inform your officials.”
For the ruler's wife,
he says:
“Our humble lady has lost her life.”
For the death of the Crown Prince,
he says:
“Our humble ruler’s legitimate son So-and-so has died.”
When a Great Officer reports a death within the same state:
to a peer,
he says:
“So-and-so has lost his life”;
when reporting to an officer,
he also says:
“So-and-so has lost his life.”
When reporting to the ruler of another state,
he says:
“Your ruler’s external servant, our Great Officer So-and-so, has died.”
When reporting to a peer in another state,
he says:
“Your Honor’s external humble associate, our Great Officer
So-and-so, has lost his life,
and has sent So-and-so to report the facts.”
When reporting to an officer in another state,
he also says:
“Your Honor’s external humble associate, our Great Officer So-and-so, has lost his life,
and has sent So-and-so to report the facts.”
When an officer reports a death within the same state to a Great Officer,
he says:
“So-and-so has died.”
When reporting to another officer,
he also says:
“So-and-so has died.”
When reporting to the ruler of another state,
he says:
“Your ruler’s external servant So-and-so has died.”
When reporting to a Great Officer in another state,
he says:
“Your Honor’s external humble associate So-and-so has died.”
When reporting to an officer in another state,
he also says:
“Your Honor’s external humble associate So-and-so has died.”
A Dàfū lodges in the public shed to complete the mourning period;
a Shì returns home after the anniversary sacrifice.
A Shì lodges in the public shed,
while a Dàfū stays in a mourning hut,
and a Shì stays in a whitewashed room.
A Dàfū’s mourning for his parents or brothers who have not become Dàfū
follows the mourning dress of a Shì.
A Shì’s mourning for his parents or brothers who have become Dàfū
follows the mourning dress of a Shì.
The legitimate son of a Dàfū
wears the mourning dress of a Dàfū.
If a concubine-born son of a Dàfū becomes a Dàfū,
then for his parents he wears the mourning dress of a Dàfū;
however, his position
is ranked with those who have not become Dàfū.
If the son of a Shì becomes a Dàfū,
then his parents cannot preside over the sacrifice;
they make their son preside over it.
If there is no son,
then a successor is appointed for him.
When a Dàfū divines for the burial site and the day of burial,
the officials wear hemp garments, cloth mourning coats, and cloth belts,
along with mourning shoes,
and a black cloth cap without tassels;
the interpreter wears a Píbiàn.
If divining by yarrow stalks,
then the scribe wears a Liàn cap and a long robe to perform the divination.
The interpreter wears court dress.
In the funeral of a Dàfū,
after the horses have been presented.
Those who present the horses
wail and leap;
when they exit,
the offerings are then wrapped and the inventory of gifts is read.
In the funeral of a Dàfū,
the Dàzōngrén assists,
the Xiǎozōngrén commands the tortoise,
and the Bǔrén prepares the tortoise.
The Nèizǐ wears a Jūyī and
a Bāoyī,
with white gauze.
A Lower Dàfū wears a Zhǎnyī;
the rest is like a Shì.
For the rite of summoning the soul,
a Zhūhóu uses a Bāoyī, sacrificial robes,
and Juébiàn robes.
The Fūrén wears a Shuìyī and Yúdí;
for the Dí and Shuìyī, white gauze is used.
In summoning the soul, they ascend from the west.
A Dàfū does not use the embroidered silk
that belongs beneath the canopy.
A Dàfū is attached to a Shì;
a Shì is not attached to a Dàfū,
but is attached to a brother of a Dàfū.
If there are no brothers,
then he follows the Zhāomù order.
Even if the paternal grandparents are alive,
it is the same.
A wife is attached to the consort of the person her husband is attached to;
if there is no such consort,
then she also follows the consort in the Zhāomù order.
A concubine is attached to a concubine of the grandfather's generation;
if there is no such concubine,
then she also follows the concubine in the Zhāomù order.
A male attached to his paternal grandfather is matched with him;
a female attached to her paternal grandmother
is not matched.
A Gōngzǐ is attached to a Gōngzǐ.
When a ruler dies,
the heir apparent is called "Zǐ,"
and is treated as if he were the ruler.
When one is wearing the Liàn cap of the three-year mourning,
if there is a death requiring Dàgōng mourning, one changes to hemp;
only the staff and shoes are not changed.
When in mourning for parents,
if one is wearing the Gōngcuī coat
and an infant brother who died young is to be attached, one wears the Liàn cap.
When attached as one who died young,
he is addressed as "Yángtóng Mǒufǔ";
he is not called by name,
for he is now a spirit.
In all cases of living in different places,
upon first hearing of a brother's death,
only wailing in response
is sufficient.
Initially, hemp is worn
with a loose belt and fillet.
If one has not yet worn hemp and hurries to the funeral,
and arrives before the chief mourner has finished the fillet:
distant relatives
finish it together with the chief mourner;
near relatives
complete the full number of days for the hemp, belt, and fillet.
In presiding over the mourning for a concubine,
from the initial attachment to the Liàn and Xiáng sacrifices,
the chief mourner always makes her son preside.
Her encoffining and sacrifices
are not held in the main hall.
A ruler does not touch the bodies of servants or concubines.
When the principal wife dies,
the concubines wear mourning for her kin.
If a concubine acts in place of the principal wife,
she does not wear mourning for the kin of the previous principal wife.
Upon hearing of the death of a brother
for whom Dàgōng or higher mourning is due,
one wails upon seeing the deceased's village.
If one goes to join a brother's funeral procession but does not arrive in time,
and meets the chief mourner on the road,
then one follows him to the grave.
In all cases of presiding over a brother's mourning,
even if he is a distant relative, one performs the repose sacrifice for him.
Whenever the mourning period is not yet finished
and there is a visitor offering condolences,
one takes the proper position, wails, bows, and leaps.
When a Dàfū wails for another Dàfū,
he wears the Biàn with a fillet;
when a Dàfū attends an encoffining,
he also wears the Biàn with a fillet.
If a Dàfū is in the stage of wearing kudzu for personal mourning,
then for the light mourning of a brother,
he wears the Biàn with a fillet.
If a staff is used for an eldest son,
then his son does not take his position with a staff.
For a wife,
if the parents are alive,
the husband does not use a staff
and does not touch his forehead to the ground.
If the mother is alive,
he does not touch his forehead to the ground.
For those who touch their forehead to the ground,
they bow when receiving funeral gifts.
If one leaves a Zhūhóu to serve a Dàfū,
one does not go back to wear mourning for the former lord.
If one leaves a Dàfū to serve a Zhūhóu,
one does not go back to wear mourning.
The mourning cap has its strings attached
to distinguish between auspicious and inauspicious.
The Liàn cap of the three-year mourning
also has strings attached;
it is sewn on the right;
for Xiǎogōng and below, it is on the left.
The Sī mourning cap has variegated tassels.
For Dàgōng and above, the belt is loose.
Court dress is of fifteen Shēng fineness;
if half of the threads are removed, it is Sī cloth;
if ash is added,
it becomes Xī cloth.
When Zhūhóu send funeral shrouds to one another,
they use the secondary carriage and sacrificial robes.
The primary carriage and Bāoyī
are not used for shrouds.
The number of sent carriages corresponds to the number of sacrificial animals.
The hearse-canopy is of coarse cloth;
it has insignia on four sides,
placed at the four corners.
Provisions are carried;
Yǒuzǐ said:
"This is not in accordance with ritual.
Mourning offerings
consist of dried meat and mince only."
In sacrifices, one is called "Filial Son" or "Filial Grandson."
In mourning, one is called "Grieving Son" or "Grieving Grandson."
For the formal mourning robe
and the mourning carriage,
there are no hierarchical distinctions.
The great white cap
and the black cloth cap
both have no tassels.
Only after the Wěiwǔ, Xuán, and Gǎo caps are there tassels.
A Dàfū wears a Miǎn when sacrificing at the Duke's court,
and a Biàn when sacrificing at his own home.
A Shì wears a Biàn when sacrificing at the Duke's court,
and a cap when sacrificing at his own home.
Since a Shì wears a Biàn for the personal greeting of his bride,
then
it is acceptable for a Shì to wear a Biàn when sacrificing at his own home.
For the fragrant wine, the mortar is made of Jū wood,
and the pestle is of Wú wood.
The ladle is made of mulberry,
three feet long;
some say five feet.
The fork is made of mulberry,
three feet long,
with its handle and end shaved.
For the Lǜyì banners,
Zhūhóu and Dàfū both use five colors;
a Shì uses two colors.
The sweet wine
is rice wine.
The jars, vases, baskets, and beams
are placed in the visible spaces
and then inserted.
The spirit pole
is buried after the repose sacrifice.
20.16 Generally, for a woman,
she follows the rank of her husband.
At the minor dressing, the major dressing, and the opening of the coffin,
she bows to all visitors in turn.
20.17 During the morning and evening wailing,
no curtain is used.
When there is no coffin, no curtain is used.
20.18 If the Jūn waits until the body is on the carriage to offer condolences,
then the host bows facing east,
and to the right of the gate, facing north, they leap in grief.
He goes out to wait for the Jūn,
and only after returning does he perform the offering.
20.19 At the dressing of Zǐgāo:
the raw silk robe and skirt, the black silk robe, and the red-bordered robe were treated as one set;
one white ceremonial robe;
one skin cap robe;
one sparrow-colored cap robe;
one dark-crown robe.
Zēngzǐ said:
"One should not dress a man in women's clothing."
20.20 If one dies while on a mission for the Jūn, at a public hostel
the soul is called back;
at a private hostel, the soul is not called back.
Public hostels
are the Jūn's palace and places established by the Gōng.
Private hostels
are the homes of the Qīng, Dàfū, and those below.
20.21 For a Gōng, there are seven leaps,
for a Dàfū, five leaps,
with the women positioned in between;
for a Shì, three leaps,
and the women are also in between.
For a Gōng's dressing:
one ceremonial robe with curled patterns,
one dark ceremonial robe,
one court robe,
one white pleated skirt,
one light red skirt,
two sparrow-colored cap robes,
one dark-crown robe,
one long ceremonial robe.
A vermilion and green sash,
with a large sash added on top.
For the minor dressing, the circular mourning band
is the same for the Gōng, Dàfū, and Shì.
When the Gōng observes the major dressing,
the Gōng ascends,
the Shāngzhù spreads the mat,
and then the dressing is performed.
The gifts from the people of Lǔ:
three dark and two light red pieces of silk,
one foot wide,
and the length of the full width of the cloth.
The condoler takes his position to the west of the gate,
facing east;
his attendants are to his southeast,
facing north with the highest-ranking on the west,
to the west of the gate.
The host orphan faces west.
The Xiàngzhě receives the command and says:
"The orphan So-and-so has sent So-and-so to request your business."
The guest says:
"My unworthy Jūn has sent me; what a misfortune!";
the Xiàngzhě enters to report,
and comes out saying:
"The orphan So-and-so is waiting."
The condoler enters,
and the host ascends the hall,
facing west.
The condoler ascends from the western steps,
facing east,
and delivers the message, saying:
"My unworthy Jūn has heard of your Jūn's mourning,
my unworthy Jūn has sent me;
what a misfortune!"
The son bows and touches his forehead to the ground,
and the condoler descends,
returning to his position.
The one presenting the mouth-gem holds the Bì to deliver the message, saying:
"My unworthy Jūn has sent me to provide the mouth-gem."
The Xiàngzhě enters to report,
and comes out saying:
"The orphan So-and-so is waiting."
The one presenting the mouth-gem enters,
ascends the hall,
and delivers the message.
The son bows twice and touches his forehead to the ground.
The one presenting the mouth-gem sits and places it to the southeast of the coffin,
where there is a reed mat;
after the burial,
a cattail mat is used.
He descends,
exits,
and returns to his position.
The Zǎifū in court dress
and mourning shoes ascends from the western steps,
facing west,
sits to take the Bì,
descends from the western steps, and goes east.
The presenter of grave-clothes says:
"My unworthy Jūn has sent me to present grave-clothes."
The Xiàngzhě enters to report,
and comes out saying:
"The orphan So-and-so is waiting."
The presenter of grave-clothes holds the ceremonial robes:
holding the collar with the left hand
and the waist with the right; he enters,
ascends the hall and delivers the message, saying:
"My unworthy Jūn has sent me to present grave-clothes."
The son bows and touches his forehead to the ground.
He places the clothes to the east of the coffin.
The presenter of grave-clothes descends,
receives the sparrow-colored cap robe at the inner eaves of the gate,
delivers the message,
and the son bows and touches his forehead to the ground,
as before.
He receives the skin-cap robe in the courtyard,
receives the court dress at the western steps,
and receives the dark ceremonial robe at the hall,
delivers the message,
and the son bows and touches his forehead to the ground,
all as before.
The presenter of grave-clothes descends,
exits,
and returns to his position.
Five Zǎifū
lift them and go east.
They descend from the western steps.
Those lifting also face west.
The chief attendant presents funeral gifts:
holding the Guī to deliver the message,
saying:
"My unworthy Jūn has sent me to present funeral gifts."
The Xiàngzhě enters to report,
and returns with the message:
"The orphan So-and-so is waiting."
Four yellow horses and
a Dàlù are displayed in the courtyard,
with the shafts pointing north.
He holds the Guī to deliver the message.
The guest's messenger comes from below,
passing to the west of the Dàlù.
The son bows and touches his forehead to the ground,
and he sits and places it at the southeast corner of the coffin.
The Zǎi lifts it and goes east.
Whenever a message is delivered,
it is delivered facing the coffin,
and the son bows and touches his forehead to the ground.
He faces west and sits
to place it down.
The Zǎi lifts the Bì and Guī,
and the Zǎifū lift the grave-clothes,
ascending from the western steps;
they face west,
sit to take them,
and descend from the western steps.
The presenter of funeral gifts exits
and returns to his position outside the gate.
The chief guest comes to mourn,
saying:
"My unworthy Jūn has duties at the ancestral temple,
and cannot attend the service in person;
he has sent a Jièlǎo So-and-so to assist in holding the ropes."
The Xiàngzhě returns with the message,
saying:
"The orphan So-and-so is waiting."
The mourner enters on the right of the gate,
and his attendants all follow him,
standing to his left, with the highest-ranking on the east.
The Zōngrén brings in the guest,
ascends,
and receives instructions from the Jūn;
he descends and says:
"The orphan dares to decline the honor of your presence,
and requests that you return to your position."
The guest replies:
"My unworthy Jūn commanded
that I not be treated as a guest;
I dare to decline."
The Zōngrén returns with the message, saying:
"The orphan dares to firmly decline the honor of your presence,
and requests that you return to your position."
The guest replies:
"My unworthy Jūn commanded
that I not be treated as a guest;
I dare to firmly decline."
The Zōngrén returns with the message, saying:
"The orphan dares to firmly decline the honor of your presence,
and requests that you return to your position."
The guest replies:
"My unworthy Jūn commanded
that his servant So-and-so
not be treated as a guest;
and so I dared to firmly decline.
Having firmly declined without obtaining permission,
I dare not but respectfully obey."
The guest stands to the west of the door,
and the assistant stands to his left,
with the east being the superior position.
The Gū descends from the Zuòjiē,
bows to him,
ascends, wails,
and performs the alternating leaping with the guest three times.
The guest departs,
and he escorts him outside the door,
where he bows and prostrates his forehead to the ground.
20.22 When there is mourning for the ruler in one’s state,
one does not dare receive condolences.
20.23 The Wàizōng stands in the chamber facing south,
the Xiǎochén spreads the mat,
and the Shāngzhù spreads the binding cords, the inner shroud, and the outer shroud.
The Shì wash their hands at the north of the basin,
lift and move the corpse onto the shrouds,
and when the dressing is completed,
the Zǎi announces it,
and the son leans over the body and leaps.
The wife sits facing east,
leans over it, rises, and leaps.
There are three things in the mourning for a Shì that are the same as for the Tiānzǐ:
the burning of torches throughout the night,
the use of men to carry the carriage,
and occupying the whole road while proceeding.
21.1 During the mourning for a father,
if the mother dies before that mourning has ended,
when removing the mourning for the father,
one wears the garments for that removal.
After the ceremony is finished,
one returns to the mourning garments for the mother.
21.2 Even in the mourning for paternal uncles or brothers,
if it coincides with the mourning for parents,
when removing the mourning for the paternal uncles or brothers,
one wears the garments for the removal of that mourning.
After the ceremony is finished,
one returns to the mourning garments for the parents.
In the case of a three-year mourning,
after the Jǐng ceremony has been performed,
both the Liàn and Xiáng sacrifices are carried out.
If a grandfather dies,
and before the Liàn and Xiáng sacrifices a grandson also dies,
he is still attached to the grandfather in the ritual.
21.3 When there is a coffin in the hall,
and one hears of mourning elsewhere,
one wails for it in another room.
One enters to make an offering,
and after the offering is finished,
one goes out,
changes garments and takes his place,
following the ritual as when first taking the place.
21.4 When a Dàfū or Shì is about to participate in a sacrifice for the Gōng,
and after having inspected the washing of the vessels,
his father or mother dies,
he still participates in the sacrifice,
but stays in a different building.
After the sacrifice is finished,
he takes off his robes, goes outside the gate of the Gōng,
wails, and then returns home.
In other matters,
he follows the ritual for rushing to a funeral.
If he had not yet inspected the washing,
he sends someone to inform the Gōng.
When the messenger returns,
he then begins to wail.
In the case of mourning for paternal uncles, brothers, paternal aunts, or sisters,
if the fast has already been observed,
then he participates in the sacrifice.
After the ceremony is finished,
he goes out of the Gōng’s gate,
takes off his robes, and then returns home.
In other matters, he follows the ritual for rushing to a funeral;
if they lived in the same palace,
then he stays in a different building.
21.5 Zēngzǐ asked,
“If a Qīng or Dàfū is to act as the Shī for the Gōng,
and has received the instruction for fasting,
but then there is an internal mourning of the Zīcuī degree,
what should be done?”
Kǒngzǐ said,
“To go out and lodge in the palace of the Gōng to await the ceremony
is the ritual.”
Kǒngzǐ said,
“When the Shī comes forth wearing the Biànmiǎn,
the Qīng, Dàfū, and Shì must all dismount for him.
The Shī must bow over the crossbar, and he must have outriders in front.”
21.6 During the mourning for one’s parents,
when about to perform a sacrifice,
a brother dies;
the sacrifice is performed after the encoffining.
If they live in the same palace,
even for a servant or concubine,
the sacrifice is performed only after the burial.
During the sacrifice,
the host’s ascending and descending are done with Sǎnděng,
and the attendants also use Sǎnděng.
This is the case even for the Yú and Fù sacrifices.
21.7 From the feudal lords down to the Shì,
at the Xiǎoxiáng sacrifice,
the host tastes the wine when it is returned to him;
the guests and brothers
all sip it.
At the Dàxiáng:
the host sips it,
and the guests and brothers may all drink it
— that is permissible.
21.8 Whenever anyone assists at a mourning sacrifice,
he informs the guests to perform the offerings but does not eat.
Zǐgòng asked about mourning,
and the Master said,
“Respect is paramount,
grief comes next,
and emaciation is the lowest.
The expression of the face should match the feelings;
the appearance of sorrow should match the garments.”
“I beg to ask about the mourning for brothers.”
The Master said,
“In the mourning for brothers,
the rules are preserved in the records.”
A superior man does not deprive others of their mourning,
nor can he be deprived of his own mourning.
Kǒngzǐ said,
“Shǎolián and Dàlián were good at observing mourning;
for three days they were not negligent,
for three months they did not slacken,
for a year they were sorrowful,
and for three years they were grieved.
They were sons of the Dōngyí.”
21.9 During the three-year mourning,
one speaks but does not discourse,
and one responds but does not ask questions.
In the mourning hut
or in the unplastered room,
one does not sit with others.
While in the unplastered room,
unless it is the time to see his mother,
he does not enter the door.
Those wearing the Shūcuī mourning all live in the unplastered room and not in the hut.
The mourning hut
is for the most solemn mourning.
21.10 A wife’s mourning for her husband’s uncles and their wives is the same as his;
paternal aunts and sisters’ mourning is the same as for brothers;
and mourning for those who died at the ages of the eldest, middle, or youngest Shāng is the same as for an adult.
21.11 Mourning for parents is removed outside the house,
while mourning for brothers is removed inside the house.
21.12 The mourning for the ruler’s mother and his wife
is compared to that for one’s own brothers.
If the grief shows in one’s expression,
one also does not eat or drink.
21.13 Outside of the mourning for which one wears the Miǎn,
when walking on the road,
if he sees someone resembling the deceased, his eyes look startled;
if he hears the name, his heart is startled.
When offering condolences for the dead or inquiring about the sick,
his expression and look of sorrow must be different from others.
Only after being like this
can one observe the three-year mourning.
As for the rest,
one simply follows the regular way,
and that is it.
21.14 At the Xiáng sacrifice,
when the host is to remove his mourning,
the time is fixed on the preceding evening;
in the morning he wears his sacrificial robes.
For the Xiáng sacrifice itself, he wears the mourning garments used previously.
Zǐyóu said,
“After the Xiáng sacrifice,
even those who should not wear Gǎo must wear it,
and only then return to their regular garments.”
When one should bare the shoulder,
if a Dàfū arrives,
even if it is the time for leaping,
he stops the leaping and bows to him,
then returns to complete the proper number of leaps,
and then puts on the upper garment.
In the case of a Shì,
after completing the ceremony and the leaping,
he puts on the garment and then bows to him,
without needing to redo the leaping.
At the Yú sacrifice for an upper Dàfū,
a Shǎoláo is used.
When the wailing ends and the ceremony is completed,
and at the Fù sacrifice,
a Dàláo is used in both cases.
At the Yú sacrifice for a lower Dàfū,
a single victim is used.
When the wailing ends and the ceremony is completed,
and at the Fù sacrifice,
a Shǎoláo is used in both cases.
21.15 When the Zhù announces the divination for burial and the Yú sacrifice,
the sons and grandsons are called “the grieving ones,”
a husband is called “Nǎi,”
a brother is called by his name,
and when divining for the burial of a brother, he is called “Bózǐ Mǒu.”
21.16 In ancient times,
both the noble and the lowly used a staff.
When Shūsūn Wǔshū went to court,
he saw a wheelwright using his staff to pass through a hub and turn the wheel;
from then on,
only those with a rank of nobility used a staff.
21.17 Cutting a hole in the face-cloth to feed the deceased
was first done by Gōngyáng Jiǎ.
21.18 What is the shroud?
It is that which is used to cover the body.
From the dressing of the corpse to the minor dressing,
if the shroud is not set, the form of the body would be visible;
therefore, the shroud is set after the dressing.
21.19 Someone asked Zēngzǐ, saying:
"Since the funeral offerings have been sent and the leftovers wrapped up,
is it like wrapping up the leftovers after a meal?
When a superior man has finished a meal,
does he wrap up the leftovers?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"Have you, sir, not seen the Great Sacrifice?
At the Great Sacrifice,
when the feast is over,
the meat of the three victims on the stands is rolled up and taken to the guest's lodging.
To treat one's parents as guests
is an expression of grief!
Have you not seen the Great Sacrifice?"
21.20 If it is not a mourning for one's own relative,
it consists of inquiring and giving gifts.
21.21 In the three-year mourning,
one bows in the mourning fashion;
in a mourning of less than three years,
one bows in the auspicious fashion.
In the three-year mourning,
if someone sends wine or meat,
one receives it but must decline it three times.
The host receives it wearing the mourning sackcloth and headband.
If it is by the ruler's command,
then one does not dare to decline,
but receives it and offers it to the deceased.
A mourner does not send gifts to others;
if others send gifts to him,
even if it is wine or meat,
he receives it.
For cousins and those below them,
after the final wailing is over,
it is permissible to send gifts to others.
Xiànzǐ said:
"The three-year mourning
is like being cut down.
The one-year mourning
is like being pared."
In the one-year mourning,
the liàn sacrifice is in the eleventh month,
the xiáng sacrifice in the thirteenth month,
and the dàn sacrifice in the fifteenth month.
In the three-year mourning,
even in the gōngshuāi mourning, one does not pay condolence visits;
this applies from the feudal lords down to the officers.
If one has a mourning obligation and is going to wail for someone,
then one wears the appropriate mourning dress and goes.
After the liàn sacrifice, one may pay condolence visits.
After the burial,
those in dàgōng mourning may pay condolences,
wail, and then withdraw,
without staying to attend to the affairs of the ceremony.
In the one-year mourning,
before the burial,
when paying condolences to a fellow villager,
one wails and then withdraws,
without staying to attend to the affairs.
One in gōngshuāi mourning paying condolences
stays for the affairs but does not manage them.
Those in xiǎogōng or sī mourning
manage the affairs but do not participate in the formal rites.
21.22 Those who come to help
withdraw after the coffin has left the palace.
Those who come to bow
withdraw after reaching the place of mourning.
Those who come to inquire
withdraw after the grave is filled.
Those who come to see the mourner
withdraw after the return wailing.
Friends
withdraw after the yú and attached sacrifices.
21.23 Paying condolences
does not mean following the host.
Those of forty years old hold the ropes of the hearse;
those of the village who are fifty follow the return wailing;
those who are forty wait until the grave is filled.
21.24 Although the mourning food is poor, one must eat enough to satisfy hunger;
to be so hungry as to fail in one's duties
is contrary to the rites;
to be so full as to forget one's grief
is also contrary to the rites.
If the vision is not clear,
the hearing not sharp,
the gait not steady,
and one is unaware of grief,
the superior man considers this an illness.
Therefore, if one is ill, one may drink wine and eat meat;
at fifty, one should not reach the state of extreme emaciation;
at sixty, one should not be emaciated;
at seventy, one drinks wine and eats meat;
all these are to prevent death from over-mourning.
21.25 If one is in mourning
and people invite him to a meal,
he does not go.
For those in dàgōng mourning and below,
after the burial,
if one goes to others
and they offer food,
if they are of his kin, he eats;
if they are not of his kin, he does not eat.
In gōngshuāi mourning, one eats vegetables and fruit,
and drinks water,
without salt or pickles.
If one cannot eat the food,
salt and pickles are permissible.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If the body has sores, one bathes;
if the head has a wound, one washes it;
if one is ill, one drinks wine and eats meat.
To become emaciated to the point of illness
is something a superior man does not do.
To die from emaciation
is what a superior man calls being without a son."
21.26 Except when following the coffin or at the return wailing,
one does not wear the head-band on the road.
21.27 In all mourning,
for xiǎogōng and above,
except for the yú, attached, liàn, and xiáng sacrifices,
one does not bathe the body or wash the head.
21.28 In the mourning of coarse hemp,
after the burial,
if people request to see him,
he sees them;
but he does not request to see others.
In xiǎogōng mourning,
it is permissible to request to see others.
In dàgōng mourning, one does not carry a ritual gift.
Only in the mourning for parents
does one see people without wiping away tears and weeping.
21.29 In the three-year mourning,
one returns to government business after the xiáng sacrifice;
in the one-year mourning,
after the final wailing;
in the nine-month mourning,
after the burial;
in the xiǎogōng or sī mourning,
after the encoffining.
Zēng Shēn asked Zēngzǐ, saying:
"Is there a regular sound for wailing for parents?"
He said:
"When an infant loses its mother on the road,
what regular sound is there?"
After the final wailing, the name taboo is observed.
Paternal grandparents and brothers,
elder and younger paternal uncles,
paternal aunts and sisters.
A son shares the same name taboos as his father.
The mother's name taboo
is observed within the house.
The wife's name taboo
is not mentioned by her side;
if one has the same name as a second cousin, it is tabooed.
When capping one who is in mourning,
even in the three-year mourning,
it is permissible.
After being capped in the mourning shed,
one enters to wail and leap;
three intervals of three leaps,
and then one goes out.
At the end of the dàgōng mourning,
one may cap one's son
or give one's daughter in marriage.
A father,
at the end of the dàgōng mourning,
may cap his son,
give his daughter in marriage,
or take a wife for his son.
For oneself,
even in xiǎogōng mourning,
after the final wailing,
one may be capped
or take a wife;
however, in the xiǎogōng mourning for a child who died young,
it is not permissible.
21.30 In all cases of wearing the cap and headband,
the mourning garment should have wide sleeves.
If the father is in mourning,
the son does not participate in music within the house.
If the mother is in mourning,
if the sound of music can be heard, it is not performed.
If the wife is in mourning,
music is not performed by her side.
When the dàgōng mourning is approaching,
one puts away the zither and lute.
When the xiǎogōng mourning arrives,
music is not discontinued.
21.31 As for father's sisters and one’s own sisters,
if their husbands die,
and there are no brothers in the husband’s clan,
a member of the husband’s lineage shall preside over the funeral.
As for the wife’s clan,
even if they are close relatives, they do not preside.
If the husband has no lineage members,
then the families in front and behind,
or the families to the east and west shall preside;
if there are none,
then the *Lǐyǐn* shall preside over it.
Some say:
He presides over it,
and attaches the ceremony to the husband’s clan.
21.32 Those wearing hemp mourning garments do not wear the ceremonial sash;
those holding ritual jade do not wear hemp.
Hemp is not added over colored garments.
21.33 If the state forbids wailing,
then it stops; but for the morning and evening offerings,
taking one’s position proceeds according to the usual practice.
A child wailing does not use the rhythmic *yǐ* sound,
does not leap,
does not use a staff,
does not wear straw sandals,
and does not live in a mourning hut.
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"For an elder aunt or a younger aunt
in *shūsuāi* mourning,
the leaping should not leave the ground.
for the *dàgōng* mourning of a father’s sister or one's own sister,
the leaping should leave the ground.
If one knows this,
they follow the ritual patterns!
They follow the ritual patterns!"
21.34 When the mother of *Shì Liǔ* died,
the ritual assistant stood on the left.
When *Shì Liǔ* died,
his disciples assisted from the right.
Assisting from the right
was done by the disciples of *Shì Liǔ*.
21.35 For the *Tiānzǐ*’s mouth-stuffing,
nine cowries are used;
for a *Zhūhóu*, seven;
for a *Dàfū*, five;
for a *Shì*, three.
A *Shì* is buried after three months,
and in that month the final wailing occurs;
a *Dàfū* is buried after three months,
and the final wailing is in the fifth month;
a *Zhūhóu* is buried after five months,
and the final wailing is in the seventh month.
For a *Shì*, there are three *yú* sacrifices;
for a *Dàfū*, five;
for a *Zhūhóu*, seven.
When a *Zhūhóu* sends someone to offer condolences,
the sequence is:
putting grain in the mouth, presenting burial clothes, presenting carriage and horses, and visiting to wail;
these are all completed on the same day,
the sequence being as such.
When a *Qīng Dàfū* is ill,
the ruler inquires after him without limit;
for a *Shì*, he inquires once.
For a *Qīng Dàfū*, the ruler
does not eat meat until the burial,
and does not have music performed until the final wailing;
for a *Shì*,
he does not have music performed until the encoffinment.
21.36 When raising the coffin to its place,
for a *Zhūhóu*, five hundred men hold the ropes,
with four ropes,
all holding gags in their mouths.
The *Sīmǎ* holds a bell,
with eight men on the left
and eight on the right;
the *Jiàngrén* holds a feathered fan to guide the coffin.
For the funeral of a *Dàfū*,
when raising the coffin to its place,
three hundred men hold the ropes,
and those holding bells
are four on each side,
and the coffin is guided with cogon grass.
21.37 *Kǒngzǐ* said:
"*Guǎn Zhòng* had engraved ritual food containers and red cap-strings,
a screen at his gate and a stand for inverted cups,
mountain-shaped capitals and duckweed-patterned king-posts.
He was a worthy *Dàfū*,
but it is difficult for him to be an example for those above.
*Yàn Píngzhòng* sacrificed to his ancestors.
The shoulder of a pig did not even cover the sacrificial vessel.
He was a worthy *Dàfū*,
but it is difficult for him to be an example for those below.
A gentleman should not usurp the rank of those above,
nor press upon those below."
21.38 A woman does not cross the border to offer condolences unless it is for a three-year mourning period.
If it is for a three-year mourning,
then the *Jūnfūrén* returns to her native state.
When the *Fūrén* returns,
she uses the ritual for a *Zhūhóu* offering condolences;
the way she is received
is the same as how a *Zhūhóu* is received.
When the *Fūrén* arrives,
she enters through the side gate,
and ascends by the side steps,
while the ruler stands at the *Zuò*.
All other things are done according to the ritual for rushing to a funeral.
21.39 An elder brother’s wife does not comfort a younger brother-in-law,
and a younger brother-in-law does not comfort an elder brother’s wife.
A gentleman has three worries:
when he has not heard of something,
he worries he might not get to hear it;
once he has heard it,
he worries he might not get to study it;
once he has studied it,
he worries he might not be able to practice it.
A gentleman has five shames:
to occupy a position
without having the proper words,
a gentleman is ashamed of this.
To have the words
but not the actions,
a gentleman is ashamed of this.
To have gained something and then lost it,
a gentleman is ashamed of this.
To have surplus land but insufficient people,
a gentleman is ashamed of this.
When numbers are equal but the enemy is twice as strong,
a gentleman is ashamed of this.
21.40 *Kǒngzǐ* said:
"In years of famine, use inferior horses.
For sacrifices,
use the lower-grade animals."
21.41 At the funeral of *Xù Yóu*,
Duke *Āi* sent *Rú Bēi* to *Kǒngzǐ* to study
the "Funeral Rites for Officers,"
and thus the *Shì Sàng Lǐ* was written down.
21.42 *Zǐgòng* was watching the *Zhà* festival.
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"*Cì*, are you enjoying this?"
He replied:
"The people of the whole state act as if they are mad;
*Cì* does not yet see the joy in it!"
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"A hundred days of toil for the *Zhà* festival,
and one day of bounty;
this is not something you understand.
To keep the bowstring taut without ever relaxing it
was something even Kings *Wén* and *Wǔ* could not do;
to keep it relaxed without ever tightening it
was something even Kings *Wén* and *Wǔ* would not do.
Now tightening and now relaxing—
that is the Way of Kings *Wén* and *Wǔ*."
21.43 *Mèng Xiànzǐ* said:
"When the solstice arrives in the first month,
one may have service for the Lord on High;
when the solstice arrives in the seventh month,
one may have service for the ancestors."
Performing the *Dì* sacrifice in the seventh month
was started by *Xiànzǐ*.
21.44 The practice of the *Fūrén* not being appointed by the *Tiānzǐ*
began with Duke *Zhāo* of *Lǔ*.
21.45 The *Wàizōng* mourn for the ruler and the *Fūrén*
in the same way as the *Nèizōng*.
21.46 When the stables burned,
*Kǒngzǐ* bowed to the people of the village who came because of the fire.
In bowing to them,
he bowed once to a *Shì*
and twice to a *Dàfū*.
This is also the way of offering mutual condolences.
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"When *Guǎn Zhòng* encountered some robbers,
he selected two men from among them,
and his lord made them state officials,
saying:
'Those with whom they associated were depraved,
but they themselves are capable men!'
When *Guǎn Zhòng* died,
Duke *Huán* made others wear mourning for him.
The practice of those in the service of a *Dàfū* wearing mourning for him
began with *Guǎn Zhòng*;
there was an order from the ruler to that effect."
21.47 If one mentions the ruler’s taboo name by mistake,
one should stand up.
If one’s own name is the same as the ruler’s taboo name,
one should use their courtesy name.
21.48 In internal disorder, he does not participate;
from external threats, he does not flee.
21.49 Regarding ritual assistance,
the tablet for the grand envoy is called a *Guī*.
For a *Gōng*, it is nine inches long;
for a *Hóu* or *Bó*, seven inches;
for a *Zǐ* or *Nán*, five inches.
The width is three inches,
and the thickness is half an inch.
It is tapered at the top,
for an inch and a half on both left and right;
it is made of jade.
The pendants have three colors and six grades.
Āi Gōng asked Zǐ Gāo:
"To what rank does your stipend correspond?"
He replied:
"It is that of an inferior officer under Wén Gōng."
21.50 When an ancestral temple is completed, it is consecrated with blood.
The ritual for this:
The Zhù, the Zōngrén, the Zǎifū, and the Yōngrén
all wear the sparrow-colored cap and dark robes with borders.
The Yōngrén wipes the sheep,
the Zōngrén inspects it,
the Zǎifū faces north
south of the stone pillar,
with the east as the place of honor.
The Yōngrén lifts the sheep
and ascends the roof from the middle;
at the center of the roof, facing south,
he slits the sheep's throat,
letting the blood flow down the front,
and then descends.
For the gate and the side-chambers,
they both use chickens.
The gate is first, then the side-chambers.
The smearing of blood
is all done below the eaves.
In slitting the chickens,
at the gate they are directly at the gate,
and for the side-chambers, in the middle of the chamber.
The officers all stand facing the chamber;
while at the gate, the officers are directly at the gate facing north.
When the ceremony is finished,
the Zōngrén announces the completion of the service,
and they all withdraw.
They report the fulfillment of the mission to the ruler, saying:
"The service of consecrating such-and-such temple is completed."
They report the fulfillment of the mission at the private apartments,
where the ruler faces south inside the gate, wearing court dress.
Once the report is made,
they then withdraw.
When the Lùqǐn is completed,
it is inaugurated with a feast but not consecrated with blood.
The consecration of a building
is the way to commune with the spiritual intelligences.
For all the vessels of the ancestral temple,
those that are named
when completed, are consecrated with a young boar.
21.51 When a feudal lord divorces his wife,
until she reaches her own state,
she travels with the ceremonies of a ruler's wife;
when she arrives,
she enters as a ruler's wife.
The messenger delivers the message, saying:
"My unworthy ruler, not being clever enough,
was unable to follow her in serving the Altars of Soil and Grain and the ancestral temple.
He has sent me, his servant [Name],
to venture to inform your officers."
The host replies:
"My ruler indeed previously excused her for her 'lack of instruction,'
my ruler dares not but respectfully wait to receive your command."
The officials arrange the vessels and utensils;
the host's officials likewise receive them officially.
When a wife is divorced,
the husband sends someone to escort her, saying:
"I, [Name], not being clever enough,
was unable to follow her in providing the sacrificial grain,
and have sent [Name] to venture to inform your attendants."
The host replies:
"My child was unworthy,
she does not dare to avoid your punishment,
I dare not but respectfully wait to receive your command."
The messenger withdraws,
and the host bows as he sees him off.
If the father-in-law is alive,
then he refers to the father-in-law.
If the father-in-law is deceased,
then he refers to the husband's elder brother.
If there is no elder brother,
then he refers to the husband.
The host's words say:
"My child [Name] was unworthy."
In the case of an aunt, an elder sister, or a younger sister,
they are also referred to accordingly.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I ate at the Shǎoshī clan's and was satisfied;
the Shǎoshī clan fed me according to the rites.
When I made an offering,
I rose and said in excuse:
'This coarse food is not sufficient for an offering.'
When I performed the final meal,
I rose and said in excuse:
'This is coarse food,
I do not dare to let it cause you distress.'"
The presentation of ritual silk consists of one bundle:
a bundle is five pairs,
a pair is five xún.
When the bride is presented to her father-in-law and mother-in-law,
the brothers, aunts, and sisters
all stand below the hall,
facing west, with the north as the place of honor;
this is her presentation to them.
When she is presented to her uncles,
she goes to each of their private apartments.
Even if a girl is not yet betrothed,
at the age of twenty she receives the hairpin,
she is given the ritual ceremony,
and the women perform the ceremony for her.
For an informal gathering, she does her hair in curls.
21.52 The knee-cover
is three feet long,
two feet wide at the bottom,
and one foot wide at the top.
The junction is five inches from the top,
with a six-inch border of sparrow-colored leather,
not reaching the bottom by five inches.
The binding is of white silk,
and the piping is of five colors.
22.1 In case of serious illness,
both the outside and inside are swept.
22.2 A ruler or Great Officer removes the suspended musical instruments,
and an officer removes the qín and sè zithers.
The patient lies in the private apartment with his head to the east, under the north window.
The bed is removed.
His everyday clothes are removed,
and new clothes are put on him,
with one person for each limb.
Men and women change their dress.
Fine floss is placed to wait for the breath to cease.
A man should not die in the hands of women,
and a woman should not die in the hands of men.
22.3 The ruler and his wife die in the Lùqǐn,
a Great Officer and his primary wife die in their principal apartment;
a secondary wife who has not been commissioned
dies in a lower room.
The body is then moved to the principal apartment;
an officer and his wife both die in their principal apartment.
22.4 For the rite of recalling the soul,
if there are forests and foothills,
then the Yúrén sets up the ladder;
if there are no forests or foothills,
then the Dí person sets up the ladder.
22.5 The Xiǎochén performs the recalling of the soul;
the one who recalls the soul wears court dress.
For a ruler, he uses the embroidered robe,
for his wife, the qūdí robe;
for a Great Officer, the dark robe with red lining,
for a secondary wife, the zhǎnyī robe;
for an officer, the sparrow-colored cap,
for an officer's wife, the shuìyī robe.
They all ascend from the eastern wing,
stand on the middle of the roof astride the ridge,
face north and call out three times,
roll up the robe and throw it down in front,
where the Sīfú receives it,
and then he descends from the northwestern wing.
If he was a guest,
the soul is recalled at a public hostel,
but not at a private hostel;
if he was in the open country,
then they ascend the left wheel-hub of his carriage to recall the soul.
The robe used for recalling the soul is not used to dress the corpse,
nor is it used for the encoffining.
In recalling the soul of a woman,
the embroidered border is not used.
In all cases of recalling the soul,
for a man, his name is called,
for a woman, her style name is called.
Only wailing precedes the recalling of the soul;
the soul is recalled, and then the matters concerning the dead are proceeded with.
22.6 When death has just occurred,
the chief mourner moans,
the brothers wail,
and the women wail and leap.
Once the body has been laid out straight,
the son sits on the east,
the Ministers, Great Officers, paternal uncles, brothers, and other sons and nephews stand on the east,
the officials and common officers wail below the hall, facing north;
the ruler's wife sits on the west,
the internal titled ladies, aunts, sisters, and daughters stand on the west,
the external titled ladies lead the external female relatives to wail on the hall, facing north.
22.7 In the funeral rites for a Great Officer,
the chief mourner sits on the east,
the mistress of the house sits on the west;
if there are titled men or ladies present, they sit,
otherwise they all stand.
In the funeral rites for an officer,
the chief mourner, paternal uncles, brothers, and other sons and nephews all sit on the east,
the mistress of the house, aunts, sisters, and daughters all sit on the west.
Whenever they wail for the corpse in the chamber,
the chief mourner supports the shroud with both hands while wailing.
22.8 In the funeral rites for a ruler,
before the minor encoffining,
he goes out to receive a refugee prince or a state guest;
in the funeral rites for a Great Officer,
before the minor encoffining,
he goes out to receive a message from the ruler;
in the funeral rites for an officer,
he goes out for a Great Officer at a time not during the encoffining.
22.9 Whenever the host goes out:
he goes barefoot, tucks in the front of his robe, beats his breast,
and descends by the western steps.
When the Jūn bows to a Jìgōng or a state guest at their positions;
or when a Dàfū receives a command from the Jūn,
he meets the messenger outside the chamber gate;
the messenger ascends the hall to deliver the command,
and the host bows below;
when a Shì has a Dàfū come in person to offer condolences,
he wails with him
but does not meet him outside the gate.
22.10 A Fūrén goes out for the wife of a Jìgōng;
a Mìngfù goes out for a command from the Fūrén;
if the wife of a Shì is not yet due to be present for the dressing of the corpse,
she goes out for a Mìngfù.
22.11 At the minor dressing:
the host takes his position inside the door,
the Zhǔfù faces east,
and then the dressing is performed.
When the dressing is finished,
the host leans over the body and leaps,
and the Zhǔfù does the same.
The host bares his shoulder and removes his hair ornaments,
binding his hair with hemp;
the women wear the mourning coiffure
and put on their hemp girdles in the inner room.
22.12 The curtain is removed,
and the men and women support the corpse as it is moved to the couch in the hall,
then they descend and bow.
22.13 The Jūn bows to a Jìgōng and state guests;
the Dàfū and Shì bow to the Qīng and Dàfū at their positions,
and bow thrice beside the Shì;
the Dàfū also bows to the wife of a Jìgōng on the hall;
the Nèizǐ
and the wife of a Shì bow individually to
Mìngfù,
and bow generally to the many guests on the hall.
The host takes his position,
puts on his upper garment, girdle, and headband, and leaps.
—In mourning for a mother,
he takes his position and wears the headband,
and then makes the offering.
Condolence-givers put on their fur robes,
add the cap-band, girdle, and headband,
and leap alternately with the host.
22.14 At the mourning for a Jūn,
the Yúrén bring out wood and horns,
the Dí people bring out water-jars,
the Yōngrén bring out tripods,
the Sīmǎ hangs them up,
and then officials take turns wailing;
for a Dàfū, officials take turns wailing,
but the water-jars are not hung;
for a Shì, the wailing is not done by officials in turn.
For a Jūn, there are two candles on the hall
and two below;
for a Dàfū, one candle on the hall
and two below;
for a Shì, one candle on the hall
and one below.
22.15 When the guests depart, the curtain is removed.
22.16 Wailing for the corpse in the hall:
the host is on the eastern side,
those coming from outside are on the western side,
and all the women face south.
22.17 Women meeting or seeing off guests do not descend from the hall;
if they descend from the hall, they do not wail.
When men go out of the chamber gate,
they do not wail when they see people.
If there is no Zhǔfù,
then the male host bows to female guests inside the chamber gate;
if there is no male host,
then the Zhǔfù bows to male guests below the eastern steps.
If the son is young,
he is held while wearing mourning hemp,
and another person bows for him;
if the successor is absent,
then one who holds rank makes the excuses,
and for one who holds no rank,
another person bows for him.
If he is within the borders, they wait for him;
if he is outside the borders, then the encoffining and burial may proceed.
In mourning, there may be no successor,
but there is never a time without a master of ceremonies.
22.18 At the mourning for a Jūn:
on the third day,
the son and the Fūrén use staffs;
on the fifth day, after the encoffining,
staffs are given to the Dàfū and Shìfù.
The son and Dàfū use their staffs outside the chamber gate
but carry them horizontally inside the chamber gate;
the Fūrén and Shìfù use their staffs while in their mourning sheds,
but when they take their positions, they have someone else hold them.
If the son receives a Royal command, he puts away the staff;
for the command of a state Jūn, he carries it horizontally;
when listening to divination or performing duties for the corpse, he puts away the staff.
A Dàfū carries the staff horizontally at the Jūn’s place,
but uses it at another Dàfū’s place.
22.19 At the mourning for a Dàfū:
on the morning of the third day, after the encoffining,
the host, the Zhǔfù, and the Shìlǎo all use staffs.
If a Dàfū receives a command from the Jūn, he puts away the staff;
for a Dàfū’s command, he carries it horizontally;
the Nèizǐ, for the command of the Fūrén, puts away the staff;
for the command of a Shìfù, she hands her staff to someone else.
22.20 At the mourning for a Shì:
the encoffining is on the second day;
on the morning of the third day,
the host uses a staff,
and all the women use staffs.
Regarding commands from the Jūn or Fūrén, they act as the Dàfū;
regarding commands from a Dàfū or Shìfù, they act as the Dàfū.
All the sons use staffs,
but they do not use them when taking their positions.
When Dàfū and Shì wail at the encoffining, they use staffs;
when wailing at the coffin, they carry them horizontally.
Those who discard their staffs
should break them and discard them in a secluded place.
22.21 A Jūn has a large basin set with ice in it;
a Dàfū has a shallow basin set with ice in it;
a Shì has two earthenware basins without ice.
A couch is set with a bamboo mat
and a pillow.
One couch is for the mouth-filling ceremony,
one couch is for the dressing,
and when the corpse is moved to the hall, there is yet another couch—
all have pillows—
this is the same for the Jūn, Dàfū, and Shì.
22.22 Upon death,
the corpse is moved to the couch,
and covered with the dressing quilt;
the clothes worn at death are removed.
The Xiǎochén props the teeth open with a horn ladle
and secures the feet using a low stool,
which is the same for the Jūn, Dàfū, and Shì.
22.23 The Guǎnrén draws water,
not untying the rope but coiling it up;
having reached the top of the steps, he does not enter the hall,
but hands it to the attendants;
the attendants enter to wash the body:
four Xiǎochén hold up the quilt,
while two attendants wash the body.
A basin is used for the washing water,
and a ladle is used for pouring water.
Fine linen is used for washing,
and the drying is done with a bathing robe,
as on ordinary days; the Xiǎochén clips the toenails,
and the remaining washing water is discarded in a pit.
At the mourning for a mother,
the female attendants hold the quilt and wash her.
22.24 The Guǎnrén draws water,
hands it to the attendants,
and the attendants prepare the hair-washing water on the hall.
—For a Jūn, the hair is washed with water from fine millet;
for a Dàfū, with water from broomcorn millet;
for a Shì, with water from fine millet.
The Diànrén makes a furnace under the western wall;
the Táorén brings out the ritual tripods;
the Guǎnrén receives the hair-washing water
and boils it.
The Diànrén takes firewood from the screened area in the northwest of the ancestral temple that was being removed,
and uses it for the fire.
The Guǎnrén hands the hair-washing water to the attendants,
and they wash the hair.
An earthenware basin is used for the hair-washing,
and a cloth is used for drying, as on ordinary days;
the Xiǎochén clips the fingernails and trims the beard,
and the discarded water and clippings are thrown into the pit.
22.25 At the mourning for a Jūn,
the son, Dàfū, Gōngzǐ, and Zhòngshì all do not eat for three days.
The son, Dàfū, and Gōngzǐ eat congee.
They bring in the supplies:
one handful of rice in the morning,
and one handful of rice in the evening;
they eat without a fixed number of meals.
Shì eat coarse food and drink water,
eating without a fixed number of meals.
The Fūrén, Shìfù, and the various wives all eat coarse food and drink water,
eating without a fixed number of meals.
22.26 At the mourning for a Dàfū,
the host, Shìlǎo, and Zǐxìng all eat congee;
the Zhòngshì eat coarse food and drink water;
the wives and concubines eat coarse food and drink water.
For a Shì, it is the same.
22.27 After the burial,
the host eats coarse food and drinks water,
and does not eat vegetables or fruit;
the women do the same,
—which is the same for the Jūn, Dàfū, and Shì.
After the Liàn sacrifice, they eat vegetables and fruit;
after the Xiáng sacrifice, they eat meat.
22.28 When eating congee from a shèng-vessel, they do not wash their hands;
when eating from a basket, they wash their hands.
When eating vegetables, they use vinegar and sauce.
When they first begin to eat meat, they first eat dried meat;
when they first begin to drink wine, they first drink sweet wine.
22.29 For the one-year mourning period (*Qī zhī sāng*),
one does not eat for three meals;
when eating:
one has coarse grain and water to drink,
and does not eat vegetables or fruit.
After three months, once the burial is completed,
one may eat meat and drink wine.
For the duration of the one-year mourning,
one does not eat meat
and does not drink wine,
when mourning for a mother while the father is alive,
or when mourning for a wife.
For the nine-month mourning period (*Jiǔyuè zhī sāng*),
eating and drinking are the same as for the one-year mourning;
when eating meat and drinking wine,
one does not join others in making music.
22.30 For the five-month and three-month mourning periods,
skipping one meal, or even two meals, is permissible.
Until the burial,
even though one eats meat and drinks wine,
one does not join others in making music.
For an aunt (*Shùmǔ*), a senior aunt (*Shìmǔ*),
a former lord (*Gùzhǔ*), or the head of the lineage (*Zōngzǐ*),
one may eat meat and drink wine.
If one cannot eat gruel,
flavoring it with vegetables is permissible;
if one is ill,
eating meat and drinking wine is permissible.
At fifty, one does not complete the full rigors of mourning;
at seventy, only the mourning garments of sackcloth (*Cuīmá*) are kept on the body.
22.31 After the burial,
if the *Jūn* provides food,
then eat it;
if a *Dàfū* or a friend of one’s father provides food,
then eat it.
One does not avoid fine grain or meat,
but if there is wine or sweet wine, one should decline it.
22.32 The Lesser Shrouding (*Xiǎoliǎn*) is performed inside the door,
and the Greater Shrouding (*Dàliǎn*) is performed at the eastern steps (*Zuò*).
The *Jūn* uses a bamboo mat,
the *Dàfū* uses a bulrush mat,
and the *Shì* uses a reed mat.
22.33 For the Lesser Shrouding:
the cloth for the bindings (*Jiǎo*),
one vertical
and three horizontal.
The *Jūn* uses a brocade quilt,
the *Dàfū* a white silk quilt,
and the *Shì* a black silk quilt—
each consists of one.
There are nineteen sets of clothes;
the *Jūn* displays the clothes at the east of the wall (*Xù*);
the *Dàfū* and *Shì* display the clothes in the chamber (*Fáng*);
all have the collars facing west, with the north as the highest position;
the bindings and the inner shroud (*Jǐn*) are not included in the count.
23.1 For the Greater Shrouding:
use cloth for the bindings,
three vertical
and five horizontal;
use a cloth inner shroud and two quilts—
these are the same for the *Jūn*, *Dàfū*, and *Shì*.
The *Jūn* displays the clothes in the courtyard,
one hundred sets,
with collars facing north and the west as the highest position;
the *Dàfū* displays the clothes at the east of the wall,
fifty sets,
with collars facing west and the south as the highest position;
the *Shì* displays the clothes at the east of the wall,
thirty sets,
with collars facing west and the south as the highest position.
The bindings and inner shroud are like court robes (*Cháofú*);
for the bindings, one width of cloth is divided into three,
not hemmed;
the inner shroud consists of five widths,
without ribbons (*Dǎn*).
23.2 For the clothes of the Lesser Shrouding,
the sacrificial robes are not put on upside down.
The *Jūn* does not use funeral gifts (*Suì*);
for the *Dàfū* and *Shì*, all the sacrificial robes of the host are used;
clothes from relatives
are received but not included in the immediate display.
For the Lesser Shrouding,
the *Jūn*, *Dàfū*, and *Shì* all use lined clothes and lined quilts;
for the Greater Shrouding,
the sacrificial robes for the *Jūn*, *Dàfū*, and *Shì* are without fixed number;
the *Jūn* uses quilted clothes and quilted quilts;
the *Dàfū* and *Shì* follow the same rules as for the Lesser Shrouding.
23.3 A gown (*Páo*) must have an outer garment;
it is not a single layer.
A robe must have a lower garment (*Sháng*);
these together are called one set.
23.4 All those displaying the clothes
place them in chests;
those taking the clothes also use chests.
Ascending and descending are done by the western steps.
In all displays of clothes, they are not folded;
unless they are of various colors, they are not brought in;
fine linen, coarse linen, and ramie are not brought in.
23.5 All who shroud bare their shoulders (*Tǎn*);
those who move the body wear their garments normally (*Xí*).
For the mourning of a *Jūn*,
the *Dàxū* performs the shrouding,
and the *Zhòngxū* assist him;
