for the mourning of a *Dàfū*,
the *Dàxū* supervises,
and the *Zhòngxū* perform the shrouding;
for the mourning of a *Shì*,
the *Xū* supervise,
and the *Shì* perform the shrouding.
23.6 In the Lesser and Greater Shroudings,
the sacrificial robes are not put on upside down;
all are lapped to the left,
and the bindings are tied without a bow.
23.7 Those who shroud must wail once they have finished.
A *Shì* who joins in the service performs the shrouding,
and because he shrouded, he skips one meal.
There are six people for the shrouding.
23.8 For the *Jūn*, a brocade head-shroud (*Mào*) with an ax-patterned border (*Fǔshài*),
with seven ties on the sides;
for the *Dàfū*, a dark silk head-shroud with an ax-patterned border,
with five ties on the sides;
for the *Shì*, a black silk head-shroud with a red border (*Chēngshài*),
with three ties on the sides.
For all head-shrouds, the main part is equal in length to the hands;
the border is three feet long.
From the Lesser Shrouding onwards, the corpse-quilt (*Yíqīn*) is used;
the *Yíqīn* has its main part and border,
and its cut is like the head-shroud.
23.9 When the *Jūn* is about to have the Greater Shrouding,
the son wears the cap and mourning headband (*Biànzhī*),
taking his position at the end of the wall.
The *Qīng* and *Dàfū* take their positions at the edge of the hall, west of the pillars,
facing north with the east as the highest position;
the father and elder brothers are below the hall facing north;
the *Fūrén* and the *Mìngfù* are to the west of the body facing east;
the *Wàizōng* are in the chamber facing south.
The *Xiǎochén* spread the mats;
the *Shāngzhù* spread the bindings, inner shroud, quilts, and clothes;
the *Shì* wash their hands in the basin
above; the *Shì* lift and move the body onto the shrouding.
When the shrouding is finished,
the *Zǎi* announces it;
the son leans over the body and leaps (*Yǒng*);
the *Fūrén* facing east does the same.
23.10 For the mourning of a *Dàfū*,
when about to have the Greater Shrouding,
once the bindings, inner shroud, quilts, and clothes are spread,
the *Jūn* arrives, and the host meets him,
first entering and standing to the right of the gate.
The *Wū* stops outside the gate;
the *Jūn* offers the vegetable sacrifice (*Shìcài*).
The *Zhù* enters first and ascends to the hall;
the *Jūn* takes his position at the end of the wall.
The *Qīng* and *Dàfū* take their positions at the edge of the hall, west of the pillars,
facing north with the east as the highest position;
the host is outside the chamber facing south;
the *Zhǔfù* is to the west of the body facing east.
They move the body and finish the shrouding;
the *Zǎi* announces it;
the host descends
and faces north below the hall;
the *Jūn* strokes the body to comfort him;
the host bows and touches his forehead to the ground (*Kē sǎng*).
The *Jūn* descends; the host ascends and leans over the body;
he commands the *Zhǔfù* to lean over the body.
23.11 For the mourning of a *Shì*,
when about to have the Greater Shrouding,
the *Jūn* is not present;
the rest of the ritual is the same as for a *Dàfū*.
When spreading the bindings and inner shroud, they leap;
when spreading the quilts, they leap;
when spreading the clothes, they leap;
when moving the body, they leap;
when wrapping the clothes, they leap;
when wrapping the quilts, they leap;
when wrapping the bindings and inner shroud, they leap.
23.13 The *Jūn* strokes the body of a *Dàfū*
and the internal *Mìngfù*;
the *Dàfū* strokes the *Shìlǎo*
and the younger sisters and cousins of his wife (*Dié dì*).
The *Jūn* and *Dàfū* lean over their father, mother, wife, and eldest son,
but they do not lean over concubine-born sons (*Shùzǐ*);
the *Shì* leans over his father, mother, wife, eldest son, and concubine-born sons.
If a concubine-born son has a son of his own,
then the parents do not lean over his body.
For all those leaning over a body,
the parents go first,
and the wife and children follow.
For a *Jūn* toward a minister, he strokes the body;
for parents toward a child, they hold the body;
for a child toward parents, they lean over the body;
for a daughter-in-law toward parents-in-law (*Jiù gū*), she supports the body;
for parents-in-law toward a daughter-in-law, they stroke the body;
for a wife toward a husband, she clings to him (*Jū*);
for a husband toward a wife or toward brothers, he holds them.
One does not lean over a body in the presence of the *Jūn*.
Whenever leaning over a body,
one must leap upon rising.
23.14 During mourning for parents,
one stays in a lean-to hut that is not plastered.
One sleeps on a straw mat and pillows on a clod of earth.
Unless it is a matter of the mourning, one does not speak.
For a *Jūn*, a house is built to enclose the hut.
For *Dàfū* and *Shì*, it is screened with plain cloth.
23.15 After the burial, a pillar and lintel are added.
The hut is plastered, but not on the prominent parts.
*Jūn*, *Dàfū*, and *Shì* all have it enclosed as a house.
23.16 For all those who are not the eldest son,
from the time before the burial, they build their hut in a concealed place.
23.17 After the burial,
when standing with others:
a *Jūn* speaks of the *Wáng*’s affairs,
but does not speak of the state’s affairs.
*Dàfū* and *Shì* speak of public affairs,
but do not speak of family affairs.
23.18 After a *Jūn* is buried,
the *Wáng*’s administration enters the state.
After the wailing has ended, he attends to the *Wáng*’s affairs.
After *Dàfū* and *Shì* are buried,
public administration enters the family.
After the wailing has ended,
wearing the *biàn* cap, *dié* headband, and *dài* sash,
they do not avoid military affairs.
23.19 After the *liàn* sacrifice,
one stays in a white-washed room
and does not live with others.
A *Jūn* deliberates on state administration,
while *Dàfū* and *Shì* deliberate on family affairs.
After the *xiáng* sacrifice,
the room is blackened and white-washed.
After the *xiáng* sacrifice, there is no wailing outside the house.
After the *dàn* sacrifice, there is no wailing inside the house,
because music has resumed.
23.20 After the *dàn* sacrifice, one may resume sexual relations.
After the *jí* sacrifice, one returns to the regular bedchamber.
For a year, one stays in the hut.
Those who do not have intercourse with those of the inner quarters throughout the mourning
are a son whose father is alive, mourning for his mother or his wife.
For those in *zī cuī* for one year,
or in *dà gōng* with hempen mourning for nine months,
they all do not have intercourse with those of the inner quarters for three months.
Women do not stay in the hut,
and do not sleep on straw.
When mourning for parents,
they return home after the *liàn* sacrifice.
For one year or nine months of mourning,
they return home after the burial.
23.21 During the mourning for a *Gōng*,
*Dàfū* wait until the *liàn* sacrifice to return home,
and *Shì* return after the wailing has ended.
23.22 For *Dàfū* and *Shì*, when mourning for their parents,
they return home after the *liàn* sacrifice.
On the first day of the month and on the anniversary of the death,
they return to wail at the ancestral home.
For the mourning of uncles and brothers,
they return home after the wailing has ended.
23.23 A father does not stay in a mourning shed for a son,
nor does an elder brother for a younger brother.
23.24 For a *Dàfū*
or a *shì fù*, the *Jūn* attends the great dressing.
If a special favor is granted,
he attends the minor dressing.
23.25 For an *wài mìng fù*,
the *Jūn* arrives after the cover has been placed on the coffin.
For a *Shì*,
he goes after the encoffining.
If a special favor is granted,
he attends the great dressing.
The *Fū rén* attends the great dressing
for a *shì fù*.
If a special favor is granted,
she attends the minor dressing.
For other wives,
if a special favor is granted,
she attends the great dressing.
For *Dàfū* and *wài mìng fù*,
she goes after the encoffining.
When a *Jūn* is to go after the encoffining of a *Dàfū* or *Shì*,
he sends someone to warn them.
The host prepares the rites for the *yīn diàn* offering
and waits outside the gate.
Upon seeing the horse’s head,
the host first enters and stands to the right of the gate.
The *wū* shaman stops outside the gate,
and the *zhù* invoker takes his place to lead.
The *Jūn* performs the *shì cài* offering inside the gate.
The *zhù* first ascends by the eastern steps
and stands with his back to the wall, facing south.
The *Jūn* takes his position on the eastern steps.
Two *xiǎo chén* stand in front holding halberds,
and two stand behind.
The *bìn zhě* advances,
and the host performs the *bài qǐ sǎng* bow.
The *Jūn* speaks words of consolation.
Looking at the *zhù*, he performs the *yǒng* leaping,
and the host leaps.
23.26 For a *Dàfū*, the offering may then be made.
For a *Shì*, the host goes out to wait outside the gate;
being commanded to return for the offering,
he then returns for the offering.
When the offering is finished,
the host first waits outside the gate.
When the *Jūn* withdraws,
the host escorts him outside the gate
and performs the *bài qǐ sǎng* bow.
When a *Dàfū* is ill, the *Jūn*
inquires about him three times.
During the encoffining stage,
the *Jūn* goes there three times.
When a *Shì* is ill,
he inquires once.
During the encoffining stage,
he goes once.
23.27 When the *Jūn* comes to condole, the mourner resumes the encoffining clothes.
23.28 When the *Fū rén* condoles a *Dàfū* or *Shì*,
the host goes out to meet her outside the gate.
Seeing the horse’s head,
he first enters and stands to the right of the gate.
The *Fū rén* enters
and ascends the hall to take her position.
The *zhǔ fù* descends by the western steps
and performs the *bài qǐ sǎng* bow below.
The *Fū rén* looks at the *shì zǐ* and leaps.
The offering is made according to the rites for the *Jūn*’s arrival.
When the *Fū rén* withdraws,
the *zhǔ fù* escorts her inside the gate
and performs the *bài qǐ sǎng* bow.
The host escorts her outside the great gate
but does not bow.
23.29 For a *Dàfū*, the *Jūn* does not meet him outside the gate.
He enters and takes his position below the hall.
The host faces north,
the other hosts face south,
and the women take their positions in the room.
If there is a command from the *Jūn*,
a command for a *mìng fū* or *mìng fù*,
or guests from the four neighbors,
their *Jūn* bows after the host.
23.30 When the *Jūn* condoles,
he leaps only after seeing the corpse or the coffin.
23.31 If a *Dàfū* or *Shì* goes when the *Jūn* has not warned them,
they do not prepare the *yīn diàn* offering.
After the *Jūn* withdraws, they must make an offering.
23.32 The *Jūn*’s outer coffin is eight inches thick,
the inner coffin six inches,
and the *bèi* innermost coffin four inches.
For an upper *Dàfū*, the outer coffin is eight inches,
and the inner coffin six inches.
For a lower *Dàfū*, the outer coffin is six inches,
and the inner coffin four inches.
For a *Shì*, the coffin is six inches.
23.33 For a *Jūn*’s coffin lining, red and green are used,
with pins of various metals.
For a *Dàfū*, the coffin lining uses black and green,
with pins of ox-bone.
For a *Shì*, green is not used.
23.34 The *Jūn*’s coffin lid is lacquered,
with three tenons and three bands.
For a *Dàfū*, the lid is lacquered,
with two tenons and two bands.
For a *Shì*, the lid is not lacquered,
with two tenons and two bands.
23.35 For a *Jūn* and *Dàfū*, the hair and nail clippings
are placed in a green bag.
A *Shì* buries them.
23.36 For the encoffining of a *Jūn*, a *chún* hearse is used,
with rafters built up to the top,
and the whole structure is plastered.
For a *Dàfū*, the encoffining uses a canopy,
with rafters placed against the western wall,
and the plastering does not reach the coffin.
For a *Shì*, the encoffining shows the tenons,
and the plaster is on the top. It is then curtained.
23.37 For the parched grain,
a *Jūn* has four kinds in eight baskets.
A *Dàfū* has three kinds in six baskets.
A *Shì* has two kinds in four baskets.
Fish and dried meat are added to them.
23.38 In decorating the coffin:
a *Jūn* has dragon-patterned curtains,
three pools,
and fluttering ornaments.
An ax-patterned cover,
with three rows of fire patterns
and three rows of ax patterns.
A white silk cloth
with a fake cover added.
Six dark red ribbons.
The *qí* ornament
has five colors and five shells.
Two ax-patterned fans,
two symbol-patterned fans,
and two painted fans,
all topped with *guī* jade tablets.
The leaping fish brush the ornamental hangings.
For a *Jūn*, the head-pieces are six and of crimson;
the side-hangings are also six and of crimson.
For a *Dàfū*, the curtains are painted, there are two ornamental hangings,
and they do not wave about.
The top covering is painted,
with three rows of fire patterns
and three rows of axe patterns.
The coffin-cover is of plain white brocade.
There are two crimson ribbons
and two black ribbons.
The borders have three colors and three cowrie shells.
There are two fans with axe patterns
and two painted fans,
all of which have silken tassels on top.
The leaping fish brush the ornamental hangings.
For a *Dàfū*, the front head-piece is crimson and the rear is black;
the side-hangings are also like this.
For a *Shì*, the curtains and top covering are of plain cloth;
there is one ornamental hanging,
with white and blue ribbons.
There are two crimson ribbons
and two dark ribbons.
The borders
have three colors and one cowrie shell.
There are two painted fans,
all of which have silken tassels on top.
For a *Shì*, the front head-piece is crimson and the rear is dark;
the two side-hangings are of crimson.
23.39 For the burial of a *Jūn*, a *chūn* hearse is used,
with four ropes and two pillars;
to direct the coffin, feather banners are used.
For the burial of a *Dàfū*, a *chūn* hearse is used,
with two ropes and two pillars;
to direct the coffin, bundles of thatch are used.
For the burial of a *Shì*, a state carriage is used,
with two ropes and no pillars;
until leaving the palace,
hempen cloth is used to direct the coffin.
23.40 Regarding the lowering into the grave,
use the ropes, remove the pillars, and carry the pull-ropes on the shoulders.
For a *Jūn*, the ropes are passed over a horizontal beam;
for a *Dàfū* and a *Shì*, they use a transverse piece.
For a *Jūn*, it is ordered that there be no noise,
and the burial proceeds by the beating of drums.
For a *Dàfū*, it is ordered that there be no wailing.
For a *Shì*, those who wail stop one another.
23.41 A *Jūn* uses pine for the outer coffin.
A *Dàfū* uses cypress for the outer coffin.
A *Shì* uses various woods for the outer coffin.
23.42 Between the inner and outer coffins,
for a *Jūn*, there is room for a liturgist;
for a *Dàfū*, there is room for a vase;
for a *Shì*, there is room for a jar.
23.43 A *Jūn* has the outer coffin lined and uses baskets for the *Yú* sacrifice.
A *Dàfū* does not have the outer coffin lined.
A *Shì* does not use baskets for the *Yú* sacrifice.
24.1 The Law of Sacrifices:
The house of *Yǒu Yú Shì* performed the *dì* sacrifice to *Huáng Dì* and the *jiāo* sacrifice to *Kù*;
they honored *Zhuānxū* as the Founder and *Yáo* as the Ancestor.
The house of *Xià Hòu Shì* also performed the *dì* sacrifice to *Huáng Dì* and the *jiāo* sacrifice to *Gǔn*;
they honored *Zhuānxū* as the Founder and *Yǔ* as the Ancestor.
The people of *Yīn* performed the *dì* sacrifice to *Kù* and the *jiāo* sacrifice to *Míng*;
they honored *Xiè* as the Founder and *Tāng* as the Ancestor.
The people of *Zhōu* performed the *dì* sacrifice to *Kù* and the *jiāo* sacrifice to *Jì*;
they honored *Wén Wáng* as the Founder and *Wǔ Wáng* as the Ancestor.
24.2 Burning firewood on the *Tài Tán*
is to sacrifice to Heaven.
Burying victims in the *Tài Zhé*
is to sacrifice to Earth.
They use a red
calf.
Burying a lesser victim at the *Tài Zhāo*
is to sacrifice to the Seasons.
Making offerings near the pit and the altar
is to sacrifice to Cold and Heat.
At the *Wáng Gōng*,
they sacrifice to the Sun.
At the *Yè Míng*,
they sacrifice to the Moon.
At the *Yōu Zōng*,
they sacrifice to the Stars.
At the *Yú Zōng*,
they sacrifice to Water and Drought.
At the four pits and altars,
they sacrifice to the Four Quarters.
Mountains, forests, rivers, valleys, and hills
that can produce clouds and make wind and rain,
or manifest strange phenomena, are all called *Shén*.
He who possesses the world
sacrifices to all the spirits.
The *Zhūhóu*
sacrifice to those within their territories,
but not to those outside them.
24.4 Generally, everything born between Heaven and Earth
is called *mìng*.
When the myriad things die,
it is called *zhé*.
When a person dies,
it is called *guǐ*.
This has not changed for five generations.
What the seven generations have changed and established
are the *dì*, *jiāo*, *zōng*, and *zǔ* sacrifices;
the rest has not changed.
24.5 When there is a *Wáng* in the world,
he divides the land and establishes states,
sets up capitals and establishes cities,
and sets up temples, distant temples, altars, and level grounds to sacrifice to them,
thus establishing the numbers based on closeness or distance of kinship.
Therefore:
The *Wáng* establishes seven temples,
one altar, and one level ground:
called the *Kǎo Miào*,
called the *Wáng Kǎo Miào*,
called the *Huáng Kǎo Miào*,
called the *Xiǎn Kǎo Miào*,
called the *Zǔ Kǎo Miào*;
all are sacrificed to monthly.
Distant temples become *tiāo*;
there are two *tiāo*,
where sacrifices are made only in the *xiǎng* and *cháng* seasons.
When removed from the *tiāo*, they become an altar.
When removed from the altar, they become a level ground.
At the altar and level ground,
they are sacrificed to when there is a prayer;
when there is no prayer,
they cease.
Beyond the level ground, they are called *guǐ*.
The *Zhūhóu* establish five temples,
one altar, and one level ground:
called the *Kǎo Miào*,
called the *Wáng Kǎo Miào*,
called the *Huáng Kǎo Miào*,
all are sacrificed to monthly;
the *Xiǎn Kǎo Miào*
and the *Zǔ Kǎo Miào*
are sacrificed to only in the *xiǎng* and *cháng* seasons.
When removed from the high ancestor, they become an altar.
When removed from the altar, they become a level ground.
At the altar and level ground,
they are sacrificed to when there is a prayer;
when there is no prayer,
they cease.
Beyond the level ground, they become *guǐ*.
A *Dàfū* establishes three temples
and two altars:
called the *Kǎo Miào*,
called the *Wáng Kǎo Miào*,
called the *Huáng Kǎo Miào*;
sacrifices are made only in the *xiǎng* and *cháng* seasons.
For the *Xiǎn Kǎo* and *Zǔ Kǎo*, there are no temples;
when there is a prayer,
an altar is made to sacrifice to them.
Beyond the altar, they become *guǐ*.
An *Shìshì* has two temples
and one altar:
called the *Kǎo Miào*,
called the *Wáng Kǎo Miào*;
sacrifices are made only in the *xiǎng* and *cháng* seasons.
For the *Xiǎn Kǎo*, there is no temple;
when there is a prayer,
an altar is made to sacrifice to him.
Beyond the altar, they become *guǐ*.
A *Guānshī* has one temple:
called the *Kǎo Miào*.
The *Wáng Kǎo* has no temple but is sacrificed to;
beyond the *Wáng Kǎo*, they become *guǐ*.
*Shùshì* and *Shùrén* have no temples;
when they die, they are called *guǐ*.
24.6 The *Wáng* establishes an altar for all the people,
called the *Dà Shè*.
The *Wáng* establishes an altar for himself,
called the *Wáng Shè*.
A *Zhūhóu* establishes an altar for the people of his state,
called the *Guó Shè*.
A *Zhūhóu* establishes an altar for himself,
called the *Hóu Shè*.
From the *Dàfū* downwards,
they establish an altar in groups, called the *Zhì Shè*.
24.7 The *Wáng* establishes seven sacrifices for all the people:
called *Sīmìng*,
called *Zhōngliù*,
called *Guómén*,
called *Guóháng*,
called *Tàilì*,
called *Hù*,
called *Zào*.
The *Wáng* establishes seven sacrifices for himself.
A *Zhūhóu* establishes five sacrifices for the state:
called *Sīmìng*,
called *Zhōngliù*,
called *Guómén*,
called *Guóháng*,
called *Gōnglì*.
A *Zhūhóu* establishes five sacrifices for himself.
The Dàfū establish three sacrifices:
called the Zúlì,
called the Mén,
and called the Xíng.
The Shìshì establish two sacrifices:
called the Mén
and called the Xíng.
The Shùshì and
Shùrén
establish one sacrifice:
either establishing the Hù
or establishing the Zào.
24.8 The Wáng sacrifices downward to five Shāng:
the Shìzǐ,
the Shìsūn,
the Shìcéngsūn,
the Shìxuánsūn,
and the Shìláisūn.
The Zhūhóu sacrifice downward to three;
the Dàfū sacrifice downward to two;
for the Shìshì and the Shùrén,
they sacrifice to a son and then stop.
24.9 As for the Shèngwáng's institution of sacrifices:
if laws were bestowed upon the people,
then they are sacrificed to;
if one died in diligent service to affairs,
then they are sacrificed to;
if one stabilized the state through labor,
then they are sacrificed to;
if one could ward off great disasters,
then they are sacrificed to;
if one could defend against great calamities,
then they are sacrificed to.
Therefore,
when Lìshānshì possessed the world,
his son was called Nóng,
who was able to cultivate the hundred grains;
when the Xià declined,
Zhōu Qì succeeded him,
and thus he is sacrificed to as Jì.
When Gònggōngshì dominated the Jiǔzhōu,
his son was called Hòutǔ,
who was able to level the Jiǔzhōu,
and thus he is sacrificed to as Shè.
Dì Kù was able to order the stars and constellations to provide guidance to the masses;
Yáo was able to distribute rewards and apply punishments fairly to conclude matters with righteousness;
Shùn was diligent in various affairs and died in the wilderness.
Gǔn dammed the floodwaters and was executed;
Yǔ was able to complete the work of Gǔn.
Huángdì corrected the names of the hundred things to clarify shared resources for the people;
Zhuānxū was able to carry this on.
Xiè served as Sītú and the people were perfected;
Míng was diligent in his office and died in the water.
Tāng governed the people with leniency and removed their oppression;
Wénwáng governed through civil culture;
Wǔwáng through military merit
removed the disasters of the people.
These are all those who had meritorious achievements for the people.
As for the sun, moon, stars, and constellations,
they are what the people look up to;
the mountains, forests, rivers, valleys, hills, and mounds
are where the people obtain their resources for use.
If they are not of these kinds,
they are not included in the sacrificial canons.
25.1 Sacrifices should not be frequent;
frequency leads to weariness;
weariness leads to a lack of respect.
Sacrifices should not be infrequent;
infrequency leads to negligence;
negligence leads to forgetting.
Therefore,
the Jūnzǐ accords with the Way of Heaven:
the Dì sacrifice in spring and the Cháng sacrifice in autumn.
When the frost and dew have fallen,
the Jūnzǐ treads upon them
and must feel a sense of sorrow;
it is not the cold that is meant.
In spring,
when the rain and dew have moistened the ground,
the Jūnzǐ treads upon them
and must feel a sense of apprehension,
as if about to see the deceased.
Music is used to welcome their coming,
and grief is used to send off their departure;
thus there is music at the Dì sacrifice
but no music at the Cháng sacrifice.
25.2 Perfected fasting is conducted within;
external fasting is conducted without.
During the days of fasting:
one thinks of their dwelling,
thinks of their laughter and speech,
thinks of their will and intentions,
thinks of what they enjoyed,
and thinks of what they relished.
After fasting for three days,
one will see those for whom the fasting is performed.
25.3 On the day of sacrifice:
entering the chamber,
one must dimly see them in their place;
circling and exiting the door,
one must reverently hear the sound of their appearance;
going out the door to listen,
one must sighingly hear the sound of their sighs.
25.4 Therefore,
in the filial piety of the former kings:
the countenance was not forgotten by the eyes,
the voice did not cease in the ears,
and the heart's will and desires were not forgotten in the mind.
By perfecting love, they are preserved;
by perfecting sincerity, they become manifest.
If they are manifest and preserved and not forgotten in the mind,
how could one not be respectful?
25.5 When parents are alive, the Jūnzǐ serves them with respect;
when they are dead, he offers sacrifices with respect,
thinking of never bringing disgrace to them throughout his life.
The Jūnzǐ has a lifelong mourning,
which refers to the anniversary of their death.
On the anniversary of a death, one does not attend to business;
this is not because it is inauspicious.
It means that on that day,
the mind is focused on a certain destination,
and one does not dare to pursue one's own private affairs.
25.6 Only a Sage can feast the Emperor of Heaven,
and only a filial son can feast his parents.
"Xiǎng" (to feast)
means "Xiàng" (to turn toward).
Only after turning toward them
can one then feast them.
Therefore,
the filial son approaches the Shī without feeling ashamed.
The Jūn leads the victim,
and the Fūrén places the wine vessel.
The Jūn presents the offering to the Shī,
and the Fūrén presents the Dòu.
The Qīng and Dàfū assist the Jūn,
and the Mìngfù assist the Fūrén.
How focused and grave is their respect!
How joyful is their loyalty!
How earnest is their desire for the spirits to feast upon the offering!
25.7 When Wénwáng sacrificed:
he served the dead as he served the living;
he thought of the dead as if he did not wish to go on living himself.
On the anniversary of a death, he was surely grieved;
when mentioning the taboo name, it was as if he saw his parent.
The loyalty of his sacrifice:
it was like seeing what his parents loved,
like the desire for beauty;
was this not Wénwáng?
The Shī says:
"From dawn I could not sleep,
cherishing the memory of those two persons."
This refers to Wénwáng.
On the day after the sacrifice,
from dawn he could not sleep;
having feasted them and brought them near,
he followed it by thinking of them again.
On the day of the sacrifice,
joy and grief are equal halves;
there must be joy in feasting them,
but when they have come, there must be grief.
25.8 When Zhòngní performed the Cháng sacrifice,
he held the offering and advanced;
his approach was sincere,
and his steps were quick and frequent.
After the sacrifice,
Zǐgòng asked:
"When you speak of sacrifice,
you describe it as Jǐjǐ and Qīqī;
but in your sacrifice today,
there was no Jǐjǐ or Qīqī.
Why is this?"
The Master said:
"Jǐjǐ
is an appearance of distance;
Qīqī
is an appearance of self-reflection.
If one maintains an appearance of distance
or an appearance of self-reflection,
how could one reach and commune with the spiritual intelligences?
How could there be such Jǐjǐ and Qīqī?
When the food is returned,
the music is completed,
the offerings and stands are presented,
the rites and music are in order,
and the various officials are in place—
then the Jūnzǐ attains that Jǐjǐ and Qīqī.
How could there be any sense of the ethereal or indistinct then?
Truly, words
are not limited to a single aspect;
each has its proper application."
25.9 When a filial son is about to sacrifice,
he must not fail to plan and prepare his affairs beforehand;
when the time arrives and the items are gathered,
he must not fail to be fully prepared;
he maintains an empty and focused mind to manage the ceremony.
25.10 Once the rooms are repaired,
the walls and roofs are set in order,
and the various items are ready,
the husband and wife fast, bathe,
and put on their finest robes.
They respectfully carry them forward and present them,
with a look of profound reverence
and deep attachment,
as if they cannot bear the weight,
as if they were about to lose them;
this is because their heart of filial respect has reached its peak!
They present the offerings in stands and on trays,
arrange the rituals and music in order,
prepare the various officials,
and respectfully carry them forward and present them.
25.11 Then
they express their will and intentions,
and in their state of ethereal abstraction they commune with the *shénmíng*,
hoping that perhaps they will partake of the offerings.
"Hoping that perhaps they will partake"
is the aim of the filial son.
25.12 In the sacrifice of a filial son,
he exerts his utmost sincerity and is sincere,
he exerts his utmost faith and is faithful,
he exerts his utmost respect and is respectful,
and he performs the rituals to the utmost without error.
Advancing and retreating, he must be respectful,
as if personally listening to a command,
as if someone were directing him.
25.13 The sacrifice of a filial son
can be known:
when he stands,
he is respectful and bent;
when he advances,
he is respectful and pleasant;
when he presents the offerings,
he is respectful and earnest;
when he retreats and stands,
it is as if he were about to receive a command;
after the removal of the offerings and his retreat,
the expression of respect and fasting does not leave his face.
In the sacrifice of a filial son,
to stand without bending
is to be stiff;
to advance without a pleasant look
is to be distant;
to present offerings without earnestness
is to lack love;
to retreat and stand without appearing to receive a command
is to be arrogant;
after the removal of the offerings and retreating,
to lack the expression of respect and fasting
is to forget the root.
Sacrificing in this way,
one has failed.
25.14 A filial son who possesses deep love
will surely have a harmonious air;
he who has a harmonious air
will surely have a pleasant expression;
he who has a pleasant expression
will surely have a gentle countenance.
A filial son holds the offerings as if holding jade,
or as if carrying a full vessel,
with a look of profound reverence and deep attachment,
as if he cannot bear the weight,
as if he were about to lose it.
Stern majesty and solemn gravity
are not the means for serving parents;
they belong to the way of a fully-grown person.
25.15 There were five means by which the former kings governed the world:
honoring those with virtue,
honoring the noble,
honoring the aged,
respecting the elderly,
and being kind to the young.
These five
were the means by which the former kings settled the world.
Why did they honor those with virtue?
Because they are close to the *Dào*.
Why did they honor the noble?
Because they are close to the ruler.
Why did they honor the aged?
Because they are close to one's parents.
Why did they respect the elderly?
Because they are close to one's elder brothers.
Why were they kind to the young?
Because they are close to one's children.
Therefore,
perfect filial piety is close to the way of a King,
and perfect fraternal respect is close to the way of a Hegemon.
Perfect filial piety is close to the way of a King:
even the Son of Heaven
must have a father;
perfect fraternal respect is close to the way of a Hegemon:
even the feudal lords
must have elder brothers.
The teachings of the former kings
were followed and not changed;
this is how they guided the world, the states, and the families.
25.16 *Zǐ* said:
"Establishing love begins with one's parents;
this teaches the people to be harmonious.
Establishing education begins with the elderly;
this teaches the people to be obedient.
When taught with kindness and harmony,
the people value having parents;
when taught to respect the elderly,
the people value following orders.
Using filial piety to serve parents
and obedience to listen to commands,
when applied throughout the world,
there is nowhere it will not be effective."
25.17 At the *Jiāo* sacrifice,
those in mourning do not dare to wail,
and those in funeral clothes do not dare to enter the city gates;
this is the height of respect.
25.18 On the day of sacrifice,
the ruler leads the victim,
the *Mù* respond to the ruler,
and the ministers and grand masters follow in order.
Having entered the temple gate,
they tether it to the stone pillar;
the ministers and grand masters bare their shoulders,
and the hair of the ox's ear is prioritized;
they use the *luán* knife to cut it open,
take the blood and the fat from the caul,
and then they retire.
They perform the seared-meat sacrifice,
and after sacrificing the raw meat they retire;
this is the height of respect.
25.19 The *Jiāo* sacrifice
is a great recompense to Heaven and takes the Sun as the primary object,
accompanied by the Moon.
The *Xiàhòu* clan sacrificed during the darkness,
the *Yīn* people sacrificed during the daylight,
and the *Zhōu* people sacrificed to the Sun
from morning until dark.
25.20 They sacrifice to the Sun on an altar
and to the Moon in a pit,
to distinguish between the dark and the light,
and to regulate the high and the low.
25.21 They sacrifice to the Sun in the east
and to the Moon in the west,
to distinguish between the outer and the inner,
and to set their positions correctly.
25.22 The Sun rises in the east,
and the Moon is born in the west.
*Yīn* and *yáng*, long and short,
follow each other in cycles of end and beginning,
thereby bringing harmony to the world.
25.23 The rituals of the world
lead to returning to the beginning,
lead to the *guǐshén*,
lead to the proper use of things,
lead to righteousness,
and lead to yielding.
Returning to the beginning
is to strengthen the root;
serving the *guǐshén*
is to honor those above;
the use of things
is to establish the norms for the people;
righteousness
ensures that high and low do not conflict;
yielding
is to remove contention.
Combining these five
to govern the rituals of the world,
even if there is perversion or evil,
those that cannot be governed will be few.
25.24 *Zǎiwǒ* said:
"I have heard the names of *guǐ* and *shén*,
but I do not know what they mean."
*Zǐ* said:
"The *qì*
is the abundance of the *shén*;
the *pò*
is the abundance of the *guǐ*;
to unite the *guǐ* and the *shén*
is the height of teaching."
25.25 All living things must die,
and in death, they must return to the earth:
this is called *guǐ*.
The bones and flesh decay below,
becoming the soil of the fields.
25.26 Their *qì* ascends and radiates above,
becoming the bright brilliance,
The fragrance of incense
and the feeling of sorrow
are the essence of the hundred things
and the manifestation of the spirits.
25.27 Following the essence of things,
they established the ultimate standards,
clearly defining the mandates for ghosts and spirits,
to serve as laws for the Qiánshǒu.
The masses were thus filled with awe,
and the myriad people were thus submissive.
25.28 The sages considered this insufficient,
so they built halls and rooms,
and established the Zōng and Tiáo ancestral shrines,
to distinguish between relatives and strangers, the distant and the near,
teaching the people to return to antiquity and revert to the beginning,
so they would not forget where they originated.
The submission of the masses stems from this;
therefore, they are obedient and swift to act.
25.29 Once these two ends were established,
they responded with two rituals.
They established the morning service,
burning the fat of Shān and the fragrance of Xiāng,
showing the light of the Xiāo plant,
to recompense the qì.
This teaches the masses to return to the beginning.
They offered Shǔ and Jì grains,
and presented the liver, lungs, head, and heart,
shown between jars of Wǔ,
supplemented with Yùchàng wine,
to recompense the pò.
This teaches the people to love one another,
and for superiors and inferiors to use sincere emotion;
this is the height of ritual.
25.30 The Jūnzǐ returns to antiquity and reverts to the beginning,
not forgetting where he originated;
thus he expresses his respect,
gives vent to his feelings,
and exerts all his strength in service,
to recompense his parents,
not daring to leave anything undone.
25.31 Therefore,
in the past,
the Tiānzǐ had a ritual field of a thousand mǔ,
wearing a ceremonial cap with a Zhūhóng,
and personally holding the Lěi plow.
The Zhūhóu had a ritual field of a hundred mǔ,
wearing a ceremonial cap with a Qīnghóng,
and personally holding the Lěi plow,
to serve Heaven, Earth, mountains, rivers, the Shèjì, and the Xiāngǔ,
providing the Lǐ, Lào, and Zīshèng offerings;
from these fields they took them,
which is the height of respect.
25.32 In ancient times,
the Tiānzǐ and Zhūhóu necessarily had officials to raise animals;
when the seasons arrived,
they would perform Qíjiè and bathe, then personally go to inspect them.
The Xī, Quán, and sacrificial animals
had to be taken from there;
this is the height of respect.
The ruler would call for the ox,
bring it in and inspect it,
select it by its hair and perform divination;
if it was Jí,
only then would they raise it.
The ruler wore a Píbàn and Sùjī;
on the first of the month
and the middle of the month,
the ruler would inspect the animals,
showing his exertion of effort;
this is the height of Xiào.
25.33 In ancient times, the Tiānzǐ and Zhūhóu
necessarily had public mulberry trees and silkworm rooms,
built near a river.
They built the chambers, eight feet and three inches high,
with thorn walls and closed to the outside.
On the morning of the great dawn,
the ruler wore a Píbàn and Sùjī,
and divined for the Jí among the Fūren and Shìfù of the three palaces,
sending them into the silkworm rooms to tend to the silkworms,
carrying the seeds to be washed in the river;
they gathered leaves from the public mulberry trees,
dried them in the wind to feed the worms.
When the year was completed,
the Shìfù finished the silk work,
presented the cocoons to the ruler,
and then offered the cocoons to the Fūren.
The Fūren would say,
"Is this what will be used for the ruler's robes?"
She then wore the Fù and Huī to receive them,
and performed a ritual with a Shǎoláo.
Those who offered cocoons in ancient times,
did they not generally follow this?
On an auspicious day,
the Fūren would reel the silk,
dipping her hands into the basin three times,
then distributed it to the Jí among the Fūren and Shìfù of the three palaces
to have them reel it;
then they dyed it Zhū and Lǜ,
and dyed it Xuán and Huáng,
to make the Fǔfú and other patterns.
When the robes were finished,
the ruler wore them to sacrifice to the Xiānwáng and Xiāngōng;
this is the height of respect.
25.34 The Jūnzǐ said,
"Ritual and music cannot for a moment be removed from the person.
Using music to regulate the heart,
then a mind of Yìzhí and Ziliàng
will naturally arise.
When the mind of Yìzhí and Ziliàng arises, there is joy;
with joy comes peace;
with peace comes endurance;
with endurance comes the Way of Tiān;
with Tiān comes the Shén.
Tiān is believed without speaking;
Shén is awe-inspiring without anger.
This is using music to regulate the heart.
Using ritual to regulate the person leads to Zhuāngjìng;
Zhuāngjìng leads to solemn majesty.
If the heart is for a moment without harmony and joy,
then a base and deceitful mind will enter it;
if the outward appearance is for a moment without Zhuāng and respect,
then a mind of neglect and ease will enter it.
Therefore, music
is what moves within;
ritual
is what moves without.
Music reaches the height of harmony;
ritual reaches the height of compliance.
With internal harmony and external compliance,
the people look upon one's countenance and do not contend;
they observe one's appearance
and the masses do not develop neglect or ease.
Thus, when the radiance of virtue moves within,
the people all listen and obey;
when principle is manifest without,
the masses all follow and comply.
Therefore it is said:
'Attain the way of ritual and music,
and the world will be filled with them;
to take them up and apply them is without difficulty.'
Music
is what moves within;
ritual
is what moves without.
Ritual prioritizes diminishing,
while music prioritizes fullness.
Ritual diminishes yet advances,
and this advancement constitutes its refinement;
music is full yet returns,
and this return constitutes its refinement.
If ritual diminishes without advancing, it withers;
if music is full without returning, it becomes dissipated.
Therefore, ritual has its recompense and music has its return.
When ritual finds its recompense, there is joy;
when music finds its return, there is peace.
The recompense of ritual
and the return of music
have the same significance."
25.35 Zéngzǐ said,
"There are three levels of Xiào:
the highest Xiào is to honor one's parents;
the next is not to disgrace them;
the lowest is to be able to support them."
Gōngmíng Yí asked Zéngzǐ,
"Can you, Master, be considered filial?"
Zéngzǐ said,
"What kind of words are these?
What kind of words are these?
What the Jūnzǐ calls Xiào
is to anticipate their thoughts and carry out their will,
and to lead one's parents toward the Way.
I, Shēn,
am merely one who provides support!
How can I be considered filial?"
Zéngzǐ said,
"The body
is the legacy of one's parents.
In conducting oneself with the legacy of one's parents,
how can one dare not be respectful?
To live without dignity
is not Xiào;
to serve one's ruler without Zhōng
is not Xiào;
to hold office without respect
is not Xiào;
to be untrustworthy to friends
is not Xiào;
to lack courage in battle
is not Xiào.
If these five are not fulfilled,
disaster will reach one's parents;
how can one dare not be respectful?"
Boiling, cooking, animal sacrifices, and fragrant offerings,
which are tasted and then presented,
are not filial piety;
they are merely nourishment.
What the Jūnzǐ calls filial piety
is when the people of the nation praise him with admiration, saying:
"How fortunate to have a son
such as this!"
That is what is called filial piety.
The fundamental teaching for the masses is called filial piety,
and its practice is called nourishment.
Nourishment
is possible,
but respect is difficult;
respect
is possible,
but peace of mind is difficult;
peace of mind
is possible,
but consistency until the end is difficult.
Once the parents have passed away,
to be cautious in one's personal conduct
so as not to leave an evil reputation for one's parents—
this can be called being able to maintain it to the end.
As for benevolence,
it is being benevolent in this;
as for ritual,
it is the practice of this;
as for righteousness,
it is the appropriateness of this;
as for trustworthiness,
it is the belief in this;
as for strength,
it is being strong in this.
Joy naturally arises from following this;
punishment naturally arises from opposing this.
Zèngzǐ said:
"As for filial piety,
when established, it fills Heaven and Earth;
when spread, it traverses the Four Seas;
when applied to future generations, it knows no morning or evening;
when extended to the Eastern Sea, it is the standard;
when extended to the Western Sea, it is the standard;
when extended to the Southern Sea, it is the standard;
when extended to the Northern Sea, it is the standard.
The Shī says:
'From the west and from the east, from the south and from the north,
none thought of not submitting.'
This is what it means."
Zèngzǐ said:
"Trees are felled according to the season,
and animals are killed according to the season.
The Fūzǐ said:
'To cut down a single tree,
or to kill a single animal,
not according to its proper season,
is not filial piety.'
Filial piety has three levels:
minor filial piety uses physical effort,
intermediate filial piety uses merit,
and great filial piety is never exhausted.
To think of parental love and forget one's own toil
can be called using physical effort.
To honor benevolence
and be at peace with righteousness
can be called using merit.
To provide benefits broadly and prepare all things,
can be called being never exhausted.
If parents love him,
he rejoices and does not forget it;
if parents dislike him,
he is fearful but without resentment;
if parents have faults,
he remonstrates but does not oppose them;
once parents have passed away,
he must seek the grain of a benevolent person to sacrifice to them.
This is called the completion of ritual."
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn descended from the hall and injured his foot.
For several months he did not go out,
and he still had a look of worry.
His disciples said:
"The Master's foot is healed;
for several months you have not gone out,
and you still have a look of worry,
why is this?"
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn said:
"How good is your question!
How good is your question!
I heard from Zèngzǐ,
and Zèngzǐ heard from the Fūzǐ, who said:
'Of all that Heaven produces
and Earth nourishes,
none is greater than man.
Parents give birth to the child whole,
and the child returns the body whole—
this can be called filial piety.
Not to injure the limbs
and not to disgrace the person
can be called wholeness.
Therefore, a Jūnzǐ does not dare to forget filial piety for even a single step.'
Now I have forgotten the Way of filial piety,
and that is why I have a look of worry.
With every step, one does not dare to forget one's parents;
with every word, one does not dare to forget one's parents.
With every step, one does not dare to forget one's parents;
for this reason, one walks the main road and not a shortcut,
and uses a boat rather than swimming,
not daring to risk the body inherited from one's parents.
With every word, one does not dare to forget one's parents;
for this reason, evil words do not come from the mouth,
and angry words do not reach one's person.
Not disgracing one's person
and not shaming one's parents
can be called filial piety."
In the past,
the Yǒuyú Shì valued virtue and honored age;
the Xiàhòu Shì valued rank and honored age;
the Yīn people valued wealth and honored age;
the Zhōu people valued kinship and honored age.
Yú, Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu
were the eras of the world's great kings,
and none of them neglected old age.
The honoring of age in the world
has been established for a long time;
it is second only to serving one's parents.
For this reason,
in the court, those of the same rank honor age.
At seventy, one may use a staff in the court;
if the ruler asks a question, the person is seated on a mat.
At eighty, one does not wait for the court session;
if the ruler asks a question, he goes to the person;
and thus brotherly respect reaches the court.
When walking on the road,
do not walk shoulder to shoulder,
but follow behind or to the side.
When seeing an elder,
carriages and pedestrians give way;
those with grey hair do not carry burdens on the road,
and thus brotherly respect reaches the road.
Dwelling in the village, rank according to age,
so the old and the poor are not neglected,
the strong do not offend the weak,
and the many do not oppress the few;
and thus brotherly respect reaches the neighborhoods.
According to the ancient Way,
at fifty, one does not perform labor in the fields;
the distribution of game is prioritized for the elders,
and thus brotherly respect reaches the hunts.
In the military ranks,
those of the same rank honor age,
and thus brotherly respect reaches the army.
When filial piety and brotherly respect are expressed in the court,
practiced on the road,
reach the neighborhoods,
extend to the hunts,
and are followed in the army,
the people will die for righteousness
and not dare to violate it.
Sacrificing in the Míngtáng
is how the feudal lords are taught filial piety;
feeding the Sānlǎo and Wǔgēng at the Dàxué
is how the feudal lords are taught brotherly respect.
Sacrificing to the former sages at the Xīxué
is how the feudal lords are taught virtue;
plowing the ritual field
is how the feudal lords are taught nourishment;
holding court audiences
is how the feudal lords are taught the duty of subjects.
These five
are the great teachings of the world.
When feeding the Sānlǎo and Wǔgēng at the Dàxué,
the Tiānzǐ bares his arm to carve the victim,
holds the sauce to offer it,
and holds the cup for the ritual rinse,
wearing his crown and holding the shield;
this is how the feudal lords are taught brotherly respect.
For this reason,
when there is honor for age in the village,
and the old and poor are not neglected,
the strong do not offend the weak, and the many do not oppress the few,
this comes from the Dàxué.
The Tiānzǐ established four schools;
when entering the school,
the Tàizǐ follows the order of age.
When the Tiānzǐ tours the borders,
the feudal lords wait at the boundary.
The Tiānzǐ first meets those who are a hundred years old.
When those of eighty or ninety years travel east,
those traveling west dare not pass them;
when they travel west,
those traveling east dare not pass them.
If one wishes to discuss administration,
it is appropriate for the ruler to go to them.
25.45 One commission ranks by age in the village,
two commissions rank by age in the clan,
and three commissions mean one is no longer ranked by age;
if there are those of seventy years in the clan,
one does not dare to precede them.
Those of seventy years
do not enter the court unless there is a major cause;
if there is a major cause and they enter,
the ruler must bow and yield to them,
and only after that attend to those with official rank.
25.46 When the Tiānzǐ has something good,
he yields the virtue to Heaven;
when the Zhūhóu have something good,
they attribute it to the Tiānzǐ;
when the Qīng Dàfū have something good,
they present it to the Zhūhóu;
when the Shì or commoners have something good,
they trace its root to their parents
and present it to the elders;
emoluments, ranks, rewards, and honors
are completed in the Zōngmiào;
this is to show compliance.
Formerly,
the Shèng Rén established the conditions of Yīn and Yáng and Heaven and Earth,
and set them up as the Yì.
The diviner of the Yì holds the tortoise shell facing south,
while the Tiānzǐ, in ceremonial robes and cap, faces north;
although he has a mind of clear wisdom,
he must proceed to have his will determined therein.
This shows he does not dare to act solely on his own,
in order to honor Heaven.
When there is good, credit is given to others;
when there is a fault, it is attributed to oneself.
This teaches not to be boastful so as to honor the worthy.
25.47 When a filial son is about to perform sacrifice,
he must have a purified and solemn mind to plan the matter,
to prepare the garments and offerings,
to repair the halls and chambers,
and to manage the hundred tasks.
When the day of sacrifice arrives,
his countenance must be gentle,
his gait must be apprehensive,
as if fearing he might not reach the object of his love.
When he presents the offerings,
his appearance must be gentle,
his body must be bent,
as if he were speaking to them but had not yet received a response.
After those who kept the vigil all depart,
he stands humble, quiet, and composed,
as if he were about to no longer see them.
After the sacrifice,
he is cheerful and at ease,
as if they were about to enter again.
For this reason,
sincerity and goodness do not leave his person,
ears and eyes do not stray from his heart,
and thoughts do not stray from his parents.
Knotted in the heart,
manifested in the expression,
he examines them through his methods;
this is the will of a filial son.
25.48 In establishing the divine positions of the state,
to the right are the Shèjì,
and to the left is the Zōngmiào.
26.1 In all ways of governing people,
none is more urgent than Lǐ.
Of the five canons of Lǐ,
none is weightier than sacrifice.
Sacrifice
is not something that comes from the outside;
it comes from within, born in the heart;
the heart is moved and expresses it through Lǐ.
For this reason,
only the worthy can fully realize the meaning of sacrifice.
26.2 When a worthy person sacrifices,
they will surely receive blessings.
These are not what the world calls blessings.
Blessing
means completeness;
completeness
is the name for a hundred forms of compliance.
That which has nothing it does not comply with
is called completeness.
This means
being fully exhausted within oneself
and complying with the Dào externally.
A loyal minister serves his ruler,
and a filial son serves his parents;
their root is the same.
Above, they comply with the Guǐshén;
externally, they comply with the ruler and elders;
internally, they are filial to their parents.
Such is what is called completeness.
Only the worthy can attain completeness,
and only after attaining completeness can they sacrifice.
For this reason,
in the sacrifice of a worthy person:
they bring forth their sincerity and good faith
along with their loyalty and reverence;
they present offerings,
guide them with Lǐ,
soothe them with music,
and harmonize them with the seasons.
They merely offer these clearly
and do not seek anything for themselves.
This is the heart of a filial son.
Sacrifice
is the means to continue the nourishment and sustain the filiality of the departed.
Filiality means nourishment.
Complying with the Dào
and not going against human relations—
this is what is called nourishment.
26.3 For this reason,
when a filial son serves his parents,
there are three ways:
while they are alive, he nourishes them;
when they pass away, he mourns them;
and when mourning is finished, he sacrifices to them.
In nourishment, one observes his compliance;
in mourning, one observes his grief;
and in sacrifice, one observes his reverence and timeliness.
Fulfilling these three ways
is the conduct of a filial son.
26.4 Having exhausted oneself within
and also seeking assistance from without—
this is the Hūnlǐ.
Therefore, the words of a state ruler when taking a wife are:
"I request your precious daughter
to share with me my humble state
and serve the Zōngmiào and Shèjì."
This is the basis of seeking assistance.
In sacrifice,
the husband and wife must attend to it personally,
so as to complete the roles of the external and internal;
when the roles are complete, the preparations are complete.
Pickles from water plants,
sauces from land products—
small items are complete;
meat-stands of the three sacrificial animals,
contents of the eight Guǐ-vessels—
fine items are complete;
rarities of insects,
fruits of trees and plants—
things of Yīn and Yáng are complete.
26.5 Whatever Heaven produces
and Earth grows,
if it can be presented,
none is not present,
to show the exhaustion of all things.
Externally, exhausting all things;
internally, exhausting one's will—
this is the heart of sacrifice.
For this reason,
the Tiānzǐ personally plows in the southern suburbs
to provide the sacrificial grain;
the Queen raises silkworms in the northern suburbs
to provide the sacrificial robes.
The Zhūhóu plow in the eastern suburbs
also to provide the sacrificial grain;
the consort raises silkworms in the northern suburbs
to provide the ceremonial caps and robes.
It is not that the Tiānzǐ and Zhūhóu have no one to plow for them,
nor that the Queen and consort have no one to raise silkworms for them;
they personally offer their sincerity and good faith.
Sincerity and good faith are called "exhaustion,"
and exhaustion is called "reverence."
Only after reverence is exhausted can one serve the Shénmíng;
this is the way of sacrifice.
26.6 When the time for sacrifice approaches,
the Jūnzǐ then performs Zhāi.
Zhāi means "evenness."
It is the leveling of what is uneven to achieve evenness.
Thus, unless there is a great matter
or an occasion of reverence,
the Jūnzǐ does not perform Zhāi.
When not in Zhāi, there is no defense against external things
and no end to desires.
When about to perform Zhāi,
he guards against heterodox things,
puts an end to his desires,
and his ears do not listen to music.
Therefore, the record says:
"One who is in Zhāi does not have music,"
meaning he does not dare to scatter his will.
His heart does not think casually;
it must rely on the Dào;
his hands and feet do not move casually;
they must rely on Lǐ.
Therefore, in the Zhāi of a Jūnzǐ,
he focuses on achieving the virtue of pure brightness.
Thus, he has seven days of general purification to settle it,
and three days of intensive purification to bring it to evenness.
This settling is called Zhāi.
Zhāi
is the height of pure brightness,
after which one can communicate with the Shénmíng.
Therefore,
eleven days before the appointed time,
the Gōngzǎi gives notice to the Fūrén.
The Fūrén also undergoes the loose fasting for seven days
and the intense fasting for three days.
The Jūn undergoes the intense fasting in the outer apartments,
and the Fūrén undergoes the intense fasting in the inner apartments;
only after this do they meet in the Tàimiào.
The Jūn, in his dark-colored robes and ceremonial cap, stands at the eastern steps;
the Fūrén, with her head-dress and pheasant-adorned robe, stands in the eastern chamber.
The Jūn holds the guī-handled ladle to perform the libation for the Shī;
the Dàzōng holds the zhāng-handled ladle for the second libation.
When welcoming the victim animal,
the Jūn holds the leading rope;
the Qīng and Dàfū follow;
the Shì hold the fodder.
The Zōngfù follow holding the àng-vessels, and the Fūrén presents the cleansing water.
The Jūn holds the bell-adorned knife
to present the meat for tasting;
the Fūrén presents the dòu-vessels.
This is what is called
"husband and wife personally performing it."
26.7 When it comes time for the dance,
the Jūn holds the shield and battle-axe
and takes his position in the dance.
The Jūn is the leader on the east;
wearing his ceremonial cap and grasping the shield,
he leads his various ministers
to entertain the August Shī.
Therefore, in the sacrifice of the Tiānzǐ,
he rejoices with all under heaven;
in the sacrifice of a Zhūhóu,
he rejoices with all within his borders.
Wearing the ceremonial cap and grasping the shield,
leading his various ministers
to entertain the August Shī—
this is the meaning of rejoicing with all within the borders.
26.8 In sacrifice there are three most important things:
among the various offerings,
none is more important than the libation;
among sounds, none is more important than the singing in the hall;
among dances, none is more important than the "Wǔ Sù Yè";
this is the way of Zhōu.
These three ways
are what draw from the external
to enhance the intent of the Jūnzǐ;
thus they advance or retreat with the intent.
If the intent is slight, then they are also slight;
if the intent is heavy, then they are also heavy.
To have a slight intent and seek weight from the external—
even a Shèngrén could not achieve this.
Therefore, when the Jūnzǐ sacrifices,
he must personally exert himself to the utmost;
this is how he makes the weightiness clear.
Guiding by means of ritual
to serve the three most important things
and presenting them to the August Shī—
this is the way of the Shèngrén.
26.9 Now, in sacrifice there is the jùn;
the jùn
is the conclusion of the sacrifice,
and it must be understood.
Therefore
the people of old had a saying:
"A good ending is like the beginning."
The jùn is just that.
Therefore
the Jūnzǐ of old said:
"The Shī also partakes of the leftovers of the Guǐshén."
This is a technique of benevolence;
through it one can observe the governance.
Therefore
when the Shī rises,
the Jūn and four Qīng partake of the leftovers.
The Jūn rises,
and six Dàfū partake.
The ministers partake of the Jūn's leftovers.
The Dàfū rise,
and eight Shì partake.
The lowly partake of the leftovers of the noble.
The Shì rise,
and each takes his vessels to go out,
arranging them below the hall.
The Bǎiguān come forward
and remove them;
the inferiors partake of the leftovers of the superiors.
In the general way of partaking of leftovers,
with every change the number of people increases;
this is how the ranks of noble and lowly are distinguished
and how the image of bestowing benevolence is raised.
Therefore
by the four guǐ-vessels of millet, one sees the cultivation within the temple.
What is within the temple
is the image of what is within the borders.
Sacrifice
is the greatest of bounties.
Therefore
if there is a great bounty above,
then the benefit will surely reach those below;
it is only a matter of the superior being first and the inferior being second.
It is not that the superior accumulates heavily while there are freezing and starving people below.
Therefore, when there is a great bounty above,
then every person among the people waits in the lower stream,
knowing that the benefit will surely arrive;
this is seen through the jùn.
Thus it is said:
"Through it, one can observe the governance."
26.10 Now, sacrifice as a thing is great;
its mobilization of things is complete.
Being complete through compliance,
is it not the root of teaching?
Therefore
in the teaching of the Jūnzǐ,
externally he teaches to honor one's ruler and elders,
and internally he teaches to be filial to one's parents.
Therefore
when an enlightened ruler is above,
the various ministers are submissive and obedient;
when he reverently serves the Zōngmiào and Shèjì,
then the descendants are compliant and filial.
When its way is exhausted
and its meaning is rectified,
then teaching is born from it.
Therefore, when the Jūnzǐ serves his ruler,
he must act personally.
That which he finds uneasy in his superiors,
he does not use in employing his inferiors.
That which he dislikes in his inferiors,
he does not use in serving his superiors.
To blame others
while doing it oneself
is not the way of teaching.
Therefore, in the teaching of the Jūnzǐ,
he must proceed from the root.
Of the ultimate of such compliance,
is sacrifice not it?
Thus it is said:
"Sacrifice
is the root of teaching."
26.11 Now, in sacrifice there are ten relationships:
in it one sees the way of serving the Guǐshén;
one sees the righteousness between ruler and minister;
one sees the relationship between father and son;
one sees the ranks of noble and lowly;
one sees the gradations of kinship;
one sees the bestowal of rank and reward;
one sees the distinction between husband and wife;
one sees the impartiality of governance;
one sees the order of elders and juniors;
one sees the interaction between those above and those below.
These are called the ten relationships.
26.12 Spreading the mats and setting out the common stools
is to provide a place for the spirits to rest.
Invoking and praying in the inner chamber
and then going out to the Bāng gate—
this is the way of interacting with the Shénmíng.
26.13 The Jūn welcomes the victim animal but does not welcome the Shī;
this is to avoid ambiguity.
When the Shī is outside the temple gate,
he might be mistaken for a minister;
once inside the temple, he fully takes the role of the ruler.
When the Jūn is outside the temple gate, he might be mistaken for the ruler;
once he enters the temple gate, he fully takes the role of a minister
and a son.
Therefore
his not going out
clarifies the righteousness of Jūn and minister.
26.14 In the way of sacrifice,
a grandson acts as the Shī for his grandfather.
The one appointed as the Shī
is of the generation of a son to the sacrificer;
the father faces north to serve him,
which is the way to clarify the duty of a son serving his father.
This is the relationship of father and son.
26.15 After the Shī has drunk five times,
the Jūn washes the jade cup and offers it to the Qīng;
after the Shī has drunk seven times,
he uses a cup of yáo-jade to offer to the Dàfū;
after the Shī has drunk nine times,
he uses a sǎn-cup to offer to the Shì
and the various officials.
This clarifies the ranks of the honored and the humble.
26.16 Now, in sacrifice there are the Zhāomù.
The Zhāomù
are the means to distinguish the order of father and son, distant and near, old and young, close and distant relatives, without confusion.
Therefore
when there is a service in the Tàimiào,
then all the members of the Zhāo and Mù lines are present
and do not lose their proper order.
This is called the gradation of kinship.
26.17 In ancient times,
an enlightened ruler ennobled the virtuous and rewarded the meritorious with stipends;
he would certainly bestow these ranks and stipends in the Tàimiào,
showing that he did not dare to act solely on his own authority.
Therefore, on the day of the sacrifice,
at the single offering,
the Lord descends and stands to the south of the eastern steps,
facing south.
The one receiving an appointment faces north.
The Scribe, from the Lord’s right, holds the tablets and conveys the command.
The appointee bows twice and touches his head to the ground,
receives the document to return home,
and performs a lay-offering in his own ancestral temple.
This is the implementation of rank and reward.
26.18 The Lord, in his ceremonial cap and robes, stands at the eastern steps;
the Lady, in her ceremonial hairpiece and robe, stands in the eastern chamber.
The Lady presents the *dòu* vessel, holding it by the stem;
she holds the sweet wine and hands it to the one holding the vessel-stand.
When the Personator returns the toast to the Lady, he holds the handle;
when the Lady receives it from the Personator, she holds the foot.
Thus husband and wife hand items to each other,
but do not occupy the same place,
and in returning the toast, they must change the cup.
This clarifies the distinction between husband and wife.
26.19 Whenever preparing the *zǔ* stands,
the bones are the primary focus.
Bones have ranks of noble and low;
the people of Yīn valued the thigh bone,
the people of Zhōu valued the shoulder bone,
and in all cases, the front is more noble than the back.
The *zǔ* stands
are for clarifying that the sacrifice must involve the sharing of favor.
Therefore,
the noble take the noble bones,
and the low take the low bones.
The noble do not take a double portion,
and the low are not left empty,
showing equality.
When favor is equal, government is implemented;
when government is implemented, affairs are completed;
when affairs are completed, merit is established.
How merit is established
is something one must understand.
The *zǔ* stands
are for clarifying that favor must be equal.
Those who are good at governing act in this way;
therefore it is said:
"One sees the equality of government affairs therein."
26.20 Whenever bestowing the cup,
the *Zhāo* lineage forms one group,
and the *Mù* lineage forms another.
The *Zhāo* are ranked by age among the *Zhāo*,
and the *Mù* are ranked by age among the *Mù*;
all the various officials are also ranked by age.
This is what is called order between elders and juniors.
26.21 In the sacrifice, there is the giving of remains to the attendants, butchers, musicians, and gatekeepers;
this is the way of showing favor to those below.
Only a lord of virtue is able to do this,
having clarity enough to see them
and benevolence enough to give to them.
To "give" means to grant;
it is being able to give one's leftovers to those below.
The *huī*
are the lowest of the cleaning officials;
the *bāo*
are the lowest of the meat-handling officials;
the *zhái*
are the lowest of the music officials;
the *hūn*
are the lowest of the gatekeeping officials.
In ancient times, criminals were not made to guard the gates;
these four types of guards
are the lowest of officials.
The Personator is the most honorable;
to use what the most honorable has finished at the end of the sacrifice,
and not forget the most lowly,
but give them the leftovers—
for this reason,
when an enlightened lord is on high,
then among the people within the borders there are none who are freezing or starving.
This is called the connection between upper and lower.
26.22 All sacrifices occur in the four seasons:
the spring sacrifice is called *Yuè*,
the summer sacrifice is called *Dì*,
the autumn sacrifice is called *Cháng*,
the winter sacrifice is called *Zhēng*.
*Yuè* and *Dì*
represent the meaning of *Yáng*;
*Cháng* and *Zhēng*
represent the meaning of *Yīn*.
*Dì*
is the peak of *Yáng*;
*Cháng*
is the peak of *Yīn*.
Therefore it is said: "Nothing is more important than the *Dì* and *Cháng*."
In ancient times, during the *Dì*,
cups were distributed and robes were bestowed,
following the meaning of *Yáng*;
during the *Cháng*,
lands and settlements were assigned
and the autumn administrative orders were issued,
following the meaning of *Yīn*.
Thus the record says:
"On the day of the *Cháng* sacrifice,
open the public stores
to show rewards";
those who mow grass prematurely are punished with ink branding;
until the autumn orders are issued,
the people do not dare to mow the grass.
Therefore it is said:
"The meaning of the *Dì* and *Cháng* is great indeed.
It is the root of governing a state
and must be understood."
He who understands its meaning
is the lord;
he who is capable of performing the tasks
is the minister.
If the meaning is not understood,
one's role as lord of men is incomplete;
if the tasks cannot be performed,
one's role as minister is incomplete.
Now, "meaning"
is that which aids the will;
it is the manifestation of all virtues.
Therefore,
those whose virtue is abundant
have a profound will;
those whose will is profound
have a manifest sense of duty;
those whose sense of duty is manifest
are reverent in their sacrifices.
When the sacrifice is reverent,
then among the descendants within the borders, none dare to be irreverent.
Therefore,
when a superior man performs a sacrifice,
he must personally attend to it;
if there is a reason he cannot,
then it is acceptable to send someone else.
Even if someone else is sent,
the lord does not lose the meaning of it
because the lord understands its meaning.
Those whose virtue is thin
have a light will;
they are doubtful about the meaning
yet seek to sacrifice;
to require them to be reverent
is impossible.
If one sacrifices without reverence,
how can one be the father and mother of the people?
26.23 Now, the tripods have inscriptions.
An inscription
is a self-naming.
One names oneself
to praise and spread the beauty of one's ancestors
and to make it clearly known to future generations.
Among ancestors,
there are none who do not have good points
and none who do not have bad points.
The principle of the inscription
is to praise the good and not the bad—
this is the heart of a filial son or grandson.
Only the worthy can do this.
An inscription
records and praises the ancestors' virtues and goodness,
their achievements, merits, rewards, and reputation,
displaying them to the world;
and by carving them on sacrificial vessels,
one establishes one's own name
in order to sacrifice to one's ancestors.
To manifest and spread the ancestors' name
is to honor filial piety.
To compare one's own actions to theirs
is to be in accord.
To show it clearly to future generations
is to provide instruction.
As for inscriptions,
with a single praise, those above and below all benefit.
Therefore, when a superior man observes an inscription,
he admires what is praised
and he also admires what was done to deserve it.
For the one who made it,
his clarity was enough to see it,
his benevolence was enough to give of it,
and his wisdom was enough to benefit from it—
he can be called worthy.
Being worthy and yet not boastful
can be called respectful.
Thus the inscription on the tripod of Kǒng Kuī of Wèi says:
"In the sixth month, on the day of Dīnghài,
the Duke went to the Great Temple."
The Duke said:
"Uncle!
Your ancestor Zhuāng Shú
assisted Chéng Gōng.
Chéng Gōng then commanded Zhuāng Shú
to follow him through the hardships in Hànyáng
and to establish the palace in Zōngzhōu,
rushing about without tire.
He assisted and gave aid to Xiàn Gōng.
Xiàn Gōng then commanded Chéng Shú
to continue in the service of your ancestors."
Your deceased father Wénshū,
revived the old aspirations,
acting as a leader to the auspicious officers,
personally caring for the state of Wèi,
and was diligent in the service of the ruling house,
untiring day and night,
so that the people all said:
“How excellent!”
The Duke said:
“Uncle!
I give you this inscription,
so that you may continue your father’s service.”
Kuī bowed his head to the ground and said:
“In response, I shall extol this grace and make it known,
diligently following the great command
and applying it to this sacrificial tripod.”
This is the inscription on the tripod of Kǒng Kuī of Wèi.
The gentlemen of old
discussed and composed accounts of the virtues of their ancestors
to make them clearly known to later generations.
They compared themselves to them
and thereby added weight to their state and family
in this manner.
As for descendants who guard the ancestral temple and the altars of land and grain,
if their ancestors had no virtues but they praise them,
this is falsehood;
if they have virtues but the descendants do not know them,
this is lack of intelligence;
if they know them but do not pass them on,
this is lack of benevolence.
These three things
are what a gentleman is ashamed of.
26.24 Long ago,
Zhōugōng Dàn performed meritorious service for the world.
After Zhōugōng died,
Chéngwáng and Kāngwáng remembered the reasons for Zhōugōng’s meritorious service
and wished to honor the state of Lǔ;
therefore they granted it the privilege of the great sacrifices.
The external sacrifices
were the Jiāo and Shè sacrifices;
the internal sacrifices
were the great Cháng and Dì sacrifices.
In the great Cháng and Dì sacrifices,
they sang the “Qīng Miào” on the terrace,
and below they played on the pipes
the “Xiàng” music;
with red shields and jade axes,
they performed the “Dà Wǔ” dance;
with eight rows of dancers,
they performed the “Dà Xià” dance;
this was the music of the Son of Heaven.
To give peace to Zhōugōng,
it was thus granted to Lǔ.
His descendants continued it,
without ceasing until now,
by which they make clear the virtue of Zhōugōng
and also add weight to their state.
27.1 Kǒngzǐ said:
“Entering a state,
its teachings can be known.
If the people are
gentle, kind, and deep,
it is the teaching of the Shī;
if they are insightful and far-reaching in knowledge,
it is the teaching of the Shū;
if they are broad-minded and easy-going yet good,
it is the teaching of the Yuè;
if they are pure, quiet, and subtle,
it is the teaching of the Yì;
if they are respectful, frugal, serious, and reverent,
it is the teaching of the Lǐ;
if they are skillful in phrasing and comparing events,
it is the teaching of the Chūn Qiū.
Therefore, the failure of the Shī is
foolishness;
the failure of the Shū is
deceit;
the failure of the Yuè is
extravagance;
the failure of the Yì is
harmfulness;
the failure of the Lǐ is
troublesomeness;
the failure of the Chūn Qiū is
disorder.
If the people are
gentle, kind, and deep, yet not foolish,
then they are deep in the Shī.
If they are insightful and far-reaching in knowledge, yet not deceitful,
then they are deep in the Shū.
If they are broad-minded and easy-going yet good, and not extravagant,
then they are deep in the Yuè.
If they are pure, quiet, and subtle, yet not harmful,
then they are deep in the Yì.
If they are respectful, frugal, serious, and reverent, yet not troublesome,
then they are deep in the Lǐ.
If they are skillful in phrasing and comparing events, yet not creating disorder,
then they are deep in the Chūn Qiū.”
27.2 The Son of Heaven
forms a triad with Heaven and Earth.
Thus his virtue matches Heaven and Earth,
he benefits all things simultaneously,
and his brightness is equal to the sun and moon,
his light shining over the four seas without leaving out the minute.
When in the court,
he speaks of the order of benevolence, sagacity, ritual, and righteousness;
when at leisure,
he listens to the sounds of the Yǎ and Sòng;
when walking,
there is the sound of pendant jade rings;
when ascending his carriage,
there is the sound of the carriage bells.
In his living there is ritual,
in his movements there is measure,
the various officials attain what is appropriate,
and all matters attain their order.
The Shī says:
“The virtuous gentleman,
his demeanor does not err.
His demeanor does not err,
rectifying the four states.”
This is what is meant.
When he issues commands and orders and the people are pleased,
it is called harmony.
When superior and inferior are close to each other,
it is called benevolence.
When the people obtain what they desire without seeking it,
it is called trustworthiness.
Removing what is harmful to Heaven and Earth
is called righteousness.
Righteousness and trustworthiness,
harmony and benevolence,
are the tools of a hegemon or a king.
If one has the intention to rule the people but lacks these tools,
it will not be accomplished.
27.3 Ritual is to the rectification of a state
what a balance is to weight,
what a plumb line is to crookedness and straightness,
and what a compass and square are to squareness and roundness.
Therefore,
if the balance is truly suspended,
one cannot be deceived about weight;
if the plumb line is truly laid out,
one cannot be deceived about crookedness and straightness;
if the compass and square are truly set up,
one cannot be deceived about squareness and roundness;
if the gentleman examines ritual,
he cannot be deceived by wickedness or craftiness.
For this reason,
praising ritual and following ritual
makes one a scholar of principle;
not praising ritual and not following ritual
makes one a commoner without principle.
It is the way of reverence and yielding.
Therefore, using it to serve the ancestral temple, there is reverence;
using it to enter the court,
the noble and the base have their positions;
using it to manage the household,
father and son are close, and brothers are in harmony;
using it to manage the village,
the old and the young have their order.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“For securing those above and governing the people,
nothing is better than ritual.”
This is what is meant.
27.4 Therefore, the ritual of court audiences
is how the righteousness between ruler and minister is made clear.
The ritual of diplomatic visits
is how the feudal lords are made to respect one another.
The ritual of mourning and sacrifice
is how the kindness of ministers and sons is made clear.
The ritual of the village drinking ceremony
is how the order between old and young is made clear.
The ritual of marriage
is how the distinction between men and women is made clear.
Now, ritual
stops disorder where it arises,
just as a dike stops water from where it flows.
Therefore, those who think an old dike is of no use and destroy it
will surely suffer damage from water;
those who think old rituals are of no use and discard them
will surely suffer the calamity of disorder.
27.5 Therefore, if the ritual of marriage is abandoned,
the way of husband and wife becomes bitter,
and the crimes of debauchery and depravity will be many.
If the ritual of the village drinking ceremony is abandoned,
the order between old and young is lost,
and litigations regarding disputes and fights will be frequent.
If the ritual of mourning and sacrifice is abandoned,
the kindness of ministers and sons becomes thin,
and those who turn their backs on the dead or forget their ancestors will be many.
If the rituals of diplomatic visits and court audiences are abandoned,
the positions of ruler and minister are lost,
the conduct of the feudal lords becomes evil,
and the ruin of rebellion and invasion will arise.
27.6 Therefore, the edifying influence of Lǐ is subtle;
it stops evil before it takes shape,
causing people daily to move toward goodness and stay far from crime without being aware of it.
This is why the former kings held it in high esteem.
The Yì states:
"The Jūnzǐ is careful at the beginning;
a discrepancy as small as a hair's breadth
leads to an error of a thousand lǐ."
This is what is meant.
28.1 Āigōng asked Kǒngzǐ:
"What is the Great Lǐ like?
When the Jūnzǐ speaks of Lǐ,
why is it held in such high honor?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I, Qiū, am a person of small standing,
not sufficient to know Lǐ."
The Ruler said:
"No!
Sir, please speak of it."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I, Qiū, have heard that,
of all that by which the people live,
Lǐ is the greatest.
Without Lǐ, there is no way to regulate the service to the spirits of Heaven and Earth;
without Lǐ, there is no way to distinguish the positions of ruler and subject, superior and inferior, or elder and younger;
without Lǐ, there is no way to differentiate the intimacy between male and female, father and son, or brother and brother,
or the relations of marriage and the degrees of kinship;
the Jūnzǐ therefore regards this with respect and honor.
Then, using what he is capable of, he teaches the common people,
without neglecting their gatherings and regulations.
When affairs are accomplished,
