he then manages the carvings, patterns, and ceremonial embroidery to pass down.
When things are in order,
he then discusses the durations of mourning,
prepares the dǐng and zǔ vessels,
sets out the pork and dried meat,
repairs the ancestral temples,
respectfully performs sacrifices at the seasonal times,
and orders the lineage.
He rests content in his dwelling,
moderates and makes plain his clothing,
lives in a modest palace,
drives a carriage without ornate carvings,
uses vessels without engraved patterns,
and eats food without a variety of flavors,
so as to share the benefits with the people.
Such was the practice of Lǐ by the Jūnzǐ of old."
The Duke said:
"Why do the Jūnzǐ of today
not practice it?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The Jūnzǐ of today
are insatiable in their love for material gains,
tireless in their indulgence in vice,
dissolute, lazy, arrogant, and contemptuous,
insistently exhausting the people,
and opposing the masses to attack those who possess the Way;
seeking to satisfy their desires,
they do not act in accordance with what is proper.
Formerly, those who employed the people led from the front;
today, those who employ the people drive from the back.
The Jūnzǐ of today
do not practice Lǐ."
28.2 Kǒngzǐ was in attendance and sitting with Āigōng.
Āigōng said:
"May I ask what is the greatest in the Way of Man?"
Kǒngzǐ changed his expression solemnly and replied:
"That your Lordship mentions this
is a blessing for the common people!
How could I, your servant, dare not to reply without hesitation?
In the Way of Man,
government is the greatest."
The Duke said:
"May I ask what is meant by government?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"Government is correctness.
If the ruler acts with correctness,
then the people will follow the government.
What the ruler does,
the people will follow.
What the ruler does not do,
what should the people follow?"
The Duke said:
"May I ask how to conduct government?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"Distinguish between husband and wife,
foster intimacy between father and son,
and maintain gravity between ruler and subject.
If these three are correct,
then all things will follow."
The Duke said:
"Although I am unworthy,
I wish to hear how to practice the Way of these three sayings;
may I hear it?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"In the government of the ancients,
loving the people was the greatest.
For the management of loving the people,
Lǐ is the greatest.
For the management of Lǐ,
respect is the greatest.
The peak of respect
is the Great Marriage.
The Great Marriage is the peak!
Since the Great Marriage is the peak,
wearing the ceremonial cap and personally welcoming the bride
is to show personal affection for her.
Personally showing affection for her
is the act of intimacy.
Therefore,
the Jūnzǐ promotes respect to foster intimacy;
if respect is abandoned,
then intimacy is discarded.
Without love, there is no intimacy;
without respect, there is no correctness.
Are not love and respect
the foundation of government?"
The Duke said:
"I wish to say something
on this.
Wearing the ceremonial cap and personally welcoming the bride,
is that not too much?"
Kǒngzǐ changed his expression solemnly and replied:
"To unite the friendship of two families,
to continue the line of former sages,
and to act as the lord of Heaven, Earth, the Ancestral Temple, and the Shèjì—
how can you say it is too much?"
The Duke said:
"I am indeed dull!
If I were not dull,
how could I hear such words?
I wished to ask
but did not find the right words;
please proceed a bit further!"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If Heaven and Earth do not unite,
the myriad things are not born.
The Great Marriage
is the succession for ten thousand generations;
how can you say it is too much!"
Kǒngzǐ then said:
"Internally, by managing the rituals of the ancestral temple,
one is sufficient to match the spiritual brilliance of Heaven and Earth;
externally, by managing the rituals of upright speech,
one is sufficient to establish respect between superiors and inferiors.
When things are shameful,
one is sufficient to correct them;
when the state is in shame,
one is sufficient to revive it.
In conducting government, Lǐ comes first;
is not Lǐ
the foundation of government?"
Kǒngzǐ then said:
"In the government of the enlightened kings of the Sāndài,
they necessarily respected their wives and children;
there is a way
in this.
The wife
is the mistress of the kin;
how dare one not respect her?
The child
is the successor of the kin;
how dare one not respect him?
A Jūnzǐ leaves nothing unrespected.
Regarding respect,
respecting one's own person is the greatest.
One's own person
is a branch of one's kin;
how dare one not respect it?
To be unable to respect one's own person
is to harm one's kin;
to harm one's kin
is to harm one's root;
to harm one's root
means the branches will follow and perish.
These three
are the models for the common people.
From one's own person to other persons,
from one's own child to other children,
from one's own consort to other consorts;
if a ruler practices these three,
then his influence will pervade the world;
this was the Way of Dàwáng.
In this way,
the state and the family will be in harmony."
28.3 The Duke said:
"May I ask what is meant by respecting one's own person?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"If a Jūnzǐ errs in speech,
then the people will take it as a model for their rhetoric;
if he errs in action,
then the people will take it as a model for their conduct.
If the Jūnzǐ's speech does not exceed proper rhetoric
and his actions do not exceed proper conduct,
then the people, without being ordered, will be respectful and reverent.
In this way,
one is able to respect one's own person;
by being able to respect one's own person,
one is then able to fulfill one's duty to one's kin."
28.4 The Gōng said:
"May I ask what is meant by 'perfecting one's parents'?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"As for the Jūnzǐ,
he is a name perfected by people.
When the common people attribute this name to him,
they call him 'the son of a Jūnzǐ'.
This causes his parents to be regarded as Jūnzǐ;
this is what is meant by 'perfecting the name of one's parents'!"
Kǒngzǐ then said:
"In the governance of antiquity,
loving people was the greatest priority.
If one cannot love people,
one cannot preserve one's person.
If one cannot preserve one's person,
one cannot settle the land.
If one cannot settle the land,
one cannot delight in Tiān.
If one cannot delight in Tiān,
one cannot perfect one's person."
28.5 The Gōng said:
"May I ask what is meant by 'perfecting the person'?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"It is to not exceed proper measure in things."
28.6 The Gōng said:
"May I ask why the Jūnzǐ values the Tiāndào?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"He values its 'ceaselessness'.
Like the sun and moon following each other from east to west without ceasing,
this is the Tiāndào;
it does not close off its perpetuity.
This is the Tiāndào;
acting through non-action so that things are completed,
this is the Tiāndào;
having completed them and then shining brightly,
this is the Tiāndào."
28.7 The Gōng said:
"I am dull and ignorant.
I am fortunate to trouble you to record this in my heart."
Kǒngzǐ, startled, moved off his mat and replied:
"The man of humanity does not exceed proper measure in things;
the filial son does not exceed proper measure in things.
Therefore,
the man of humanity serves his parents as he serves Tiān,
and serves Tiān as he serves his parents.
Therefore, the filial son perfects his person."
The Gōng said:
"I have already heard these words,
but I do not know how to handle my future transgressions!"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"That your Lordship has reached this point in your words
is this servant's good fortune."
29.1 Zhòngní was dwelling at leisure,
with Zǐzhāng, Zǐgòng, and Yányóu attending him.
Their conversation turned freely to the subject of Lǐ.
The Master said:
"Sit down!
You three,
I shall speak to you of Lǐ,
so that you may circulate by means of Lǐ
and there be nowhere you do not reach."
Zǐgòng stepped off his mat and replied:
"May I ask what this is like?"
The Master said:
"Respect without hitting the mark of Lǐ
is called coarseness;
reverence without hitting the mark of Lǐ
is called glibness;
bravery without hitting the mark of Lǐ
is called rebelliousness."
The Master said:
"Glibness snatches away compassion and humanity."
29.2 The Master said:
"Shī,
you go too far;
and Shāng
falls short.
Zǐchǎn was like a mother to the people;
he could feed them, but could not teach them."
Zǐgòng stepped off his mat and replied:
"May I ask how one achieves this hitting of the mark?"
The Master said:
"Lǐ! O Lǐ!
It is Lǐ that is used to regulate the mark."
29.3 Zǐgòng withdrew,
and Yányóu stepped forward and said:
"May I ask if Lǐ
is that which restrains evil and preserves the good?"
The Master said:
"It is so."
"Then what is it like?"
The Master said:
"The meaning of the Jiāo and Shè sacrifices
is how one shows humanity toward the ghosts and spirits;
the rituals of the Cháng and Dì sacrifices
are how one shows humanity toward the Zhāomù;
the rituals of food offerings and libations
are how one shows humanity toward the dead and the mourning;
the rituals of archery and the village feasts
are how one shows humanity toward the local community;
the rituals of meals and banquets
are how one shows humanity toward guests."
The Master said:
"One who is clear about the meaning of the Jiāo and Shè sacrifices
and the rituals of the Cháng and Dì sacrifices
would find governing the state as easy as pointing to his palm!
Therefore,
by using them, one's dwelling is in accordance with Lǐ,
and thus elder and younger are distinguished.
By using them, there is Lǐ within the inner gates,
and thus the three degrees of kin are in harmony.
By using them, there is Lǐ in the court,
and thus offices and ranks are in order.
By using them, there is Lǐ in the hunt,
and thus military affairs are well-practiced.
By using them, there is Lǐ in the army,
and thus military achievements are accomplished.
Therefore,
palaces and houses obtain their proper measure,
measures and tripods obtain their proper forms,
flavors obtain their proper seasons,
music obtains its proper rhythm,
carriages obtain their proper style,
ghosts and spirits obtain their proper offerings,
mourning rites obtain their proper grief,
arguments and discussions obtain their proper logic,
officials obtain their proper roles,
and government affairs obtain their proper implementation;
it is applied to the person and arranged before one,
and all the movements of the multitude obtain their propriety."
The Master said:
"What is Lǐ?
It is the order of affairs.
When a Jūnzǐ has an affair,
he must have its order.
To govern a state without Lǐ
is it not like a blind person without a guide?
Faltering and aimless, where would he go?
It is like searching for something in a dark room in the middle of the night;
without a candle, what can one see?
If there is no Lǐ,
then hands and feet have nowhere to be placed,
ears and eyes have nothing to apply themselves to,
and advancing, retreating, bowing, and yielding have no regulation.
Therefore,
by using it in dwelling,
elder and younger lose their distinction;
within the inner gates,
the three degrees of kin lose their harmony;
in the court,
offices and ranks lose their order;
in the hunt,
military affairs lose their strategy;
in the army,
military achievements lose their regulation;
palaces and houses
lose their proper measure;
measures and tripods
lose their proper forms;
flavors
lose their proper seasons;
music
loses its proper rhythm;
carriages
lose their proper style;
ghosts and spirits
lose their proper offerings;
mourning rites
lose their proper grief;
arguments and discussions
lose their proper logic;
officials
lose their proper roles;
government affairs
lose their proper implementation;
it is applied to the person and arranged before one,
and all the movements of the multitude lose their propriety.
In this way,
one has no way to harmonize with the masses."
29.4 The Master said:
"Listen carefully!
You three,
I shall speak to you of
Lǐ, of which there are nine points,
and in the Great Banquet there are four.
If one knows these,
even if one serves in the midst of the fields,
one is a sage.
When two lords meet,
they bow and yield as they enter the gate;
upon entering the gate, the bells and drums are raised.
They bow and yield as they ascend the hall;
upon ascending the hall, the music concludes.
Below, the flutes play the Xiàng and Wǔ,
and the Xià flutes are raised in order.
They arrange the stands and the meat-stands,
ordering the rituals and music,
and providing for all the officials."
In this way,
and only then does the gentleman understand benevolence.
Walking in accordance with the compass,
turning in accordance with the square,
the *hé* and *luán* bells matching the *Cǎiqí*,
the guests departing to the *Yōng*,
and the removal of vessels to the *Zhènyǔ*.
Therefore,
there is nothing for the gentleman that is not within ritual.
Entering the gate as the metal instruments play
is to show emotion.
Ascending to sing the *Qīngmiào*
is to show virtue.
Descending to play the *Xiàng* on flutes
is to show achievements.
Therefore,
the gentlemen of old
did not necessarily need to speak with one another in person;
they communicated through ritual and music alone."
The Master said:
"Ritual
is principle;
music
is regulation.
The gentleman does not move without principle
and does not act without regulation.
If one cannot perform the *Shī*,
one will be confused in ritual;
if one cannot perform music,
one will be plain in ritual;
if one is thin in virtue,
one will be hollow in ritual."
The Master said:
"The systems and regulations reside in ritual;
the cultured actions reside in ritual.
To practice them—
does that not depend on the person?"
*Zǐgòng* stood up from his mat and replied, saying:
"May I ask
if *Kuí* was limited?"
The Master said:
"A man of old?
He was a man of old.
To be proficient in ritual but not in music
is called being plain;
to be proficient in music but not in ritual
is called being one-sided.
As for *Kuí*,
he was proficient in music but not in ritual;
that is why he is known by this reputation;
he was a man of old."
29.5 *Zǐzhāng* asked about governing.
The Master said:
"*Shī*!
Come forward.
Did I not tell you?
If a gentleman is clear about ritual and music,
he simply raises them and applies them."
*Zǐzhāng* asked again.
The Master said:
"*Shī*,
do you think it must be the spreading of small tables and mats,
the ascending and descending, the pouring, offering, pledging, and returning of the toast,
before it can be called ritual?
Do you think it must be the arrangement of the dancers,
the raising of plumes and flutes,
and the playing of bells and drums,
before it can be called music?
To speak and then fulfill it
is ritual.
To act and find joy in it
is music.
If a gentleman exerts himself in these two and stands facing south,
then the world will be at great peace.
The feudal lords will attend court,
all things will submit in form,
and none of the hundred officials will dare not to serve their duties.
What ritual establishes
is the order of the masses;
what ritual discards
is the disorder of the masses.
In a house of skillful design,
there are the *Ào* and *Zuò* positions;
for mats there are upper and lower ends;
for carriages there are left and right sides;
in walking there is a following order;
in standing there is a sequence;
this was the righteousness of old.
A house without the *Ào* and *Zuò*
would result in disorder in the hall and rooms.
A mat without upper and lower ends
would result in disorder upon the mat.
A carriage without left and right sides
would result in disorder in the carriage.
Walking without a following order
would result in disorder on the road.
Standing without a sequence
would result in disorder in positions.
In the past, the Sagely Emperors, Enlightened Kings, and Feudal Lords
distinguished between the noble and the base, the elder and the younger, the distant and the near, men and women, and the internal and external;
none dared to overstep these bounds,
and all proceeded by this path."
After the three disciples
had heard these words from the Master,
it was as clear as if a blindfold had been removed.
30.1 *Kǒngzǐ* was living at leisure,
and *Zǐxià* was attending him.
*Zǐxià* said:
"May I ask
regarding what the *Shī* says:
'The happy and easy gentleman,
the parent of the people,'
in what way can one be called the parent of the people?"
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"Ah, the parent of the people!
One must reach the source of ritual and music
to achieve the five attainments
and practice the three absences,
so as to spread them across the world.
If there is failure in any of the four quarters,
he will surely know it beforehand.
This is what is called being the parent of the people."
*Zǐxià* said:
"Regarding the parent of the people,
I have already heard of that;
may I ask what is meant by the five attainments?"
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"Where the will reaches,
the poetry also reaches.
Where the poetry reaches,
the ritual also reaches.
Where the ritual reaches,
the music also reaches.
Where the music reaches,
sorrow also reaches.
Sorrow and joy produce each other.
Therefore,
though one looks with clear eyes,
it cannot be seen;
though one tilts the ear to listen,
it cannot be heard;
yet the spirit fills heaven and earth.
This is what is called the five attainments."
30.2 *Zǐxià* said:
"The five attainments I have already heard;
may I ask what is meant by the three absences?"
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"Music without sound,
ritual without form,
and mourning without garments—
these are what are called the three absences."
*Zǐxià* said:
"I have heard a summary of the three absences;
may I ask which poems are close to them?"
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"'Day and night he makes the mandate abundant and secret,'
refers to music without sound.
'His dignified demeanor is grand and gentle,
it cannot be measured,'
refers to ritual without form.
'Whenever the common people have a mourning,
he crawls on hands and knees to rescue them,'
refers to mourning without garments."
30.3 *Zǐxià* said:
"These words are great!
They are beautiful!
They are magnificent!
Do these words end here?"
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"How could it be so?
When the gentleman practices them,
there are yet five stages of arousal."
*Zǐxià* said:
"What are they?"
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"In music without sound,
the spirit and will do not conflict;
in ritual without form,
the dignified demeanor is slow and steady;
in mourning without garments,
the internal empathy is extremely sorrowful.
In music without sound,
the spirit and will are attained;
in ritual without form,
the dignified demeanor is grand and reverent;
in mourning without garments,
its influence extends to the four states.
In music without sound,
the spirit and will are followed;
in ritual without form,
those above and those below are in harmony;
in mourning without garments,
it nurtures the ten thousand states.
In music without sound,
it is heard daily throughout the four quarters;"
Rituals without physical form
progress daily and improve monthly;
mourning without mourning clothes
has pure virtue that is extremely bright.
Music without sound
arouses the spirit and will;
rituals without physical form
extend to the four seas;
mourning without mourning clothes
extends to grandchildren."
30.4 Zǐxià said:
"The virtue of the Sān Wáng
matches Heaven and Earth.
I venture to ask:
what must one be like for it to be said that they match Heaven and Earth?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"By upholding the three kinds of selflessness to serve the world."
Zǐxià said:
"I venture to ask what are the three kinds of selflessness?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Heaven covers all without selfishness,
Earth sustains all without selfishness,
the sun and moon shine on all without selfishness.
Upholding these three to serve the world
is what is called the three kinds of selflessness.
As it is said in the Shī:
'The mandate of Dì is not disobeyed,
reaching down to Tāng.
Tāng's descent was not delayed,
his sagely reverence daily uniform.
His brilliance rose slowly,
Shàngdì was revered.
Dì's mandate was a model for the Jiǔ Wéi';
this is the virtue of Tāng."
30.5 "Heaven has four seasons:
spring, autumn, winter, and summer,
wind, rain, frost, and dew;
none are not teachings.
Earth sustains spiritual energy,
spiritual energy produces wind and thunder,
wind and thunder take shape and flow,
and all things are born and manifest;
none are not teachings."
30.6 "When clarity and brightness reside in the person,
the spirit and will are like the divine.
When desires are about to arrive,
there will certainly be a precursor.
Heaven sends down timely rain,
and mountains and rivers emit clouds.
As it is said in the Shī:
'Sōng Gāo is the peak,
its height reaches Heaven.
The peak sent down a spirit,
and gave birth to Fǔ and Shēn.
Shēn and Fǔ
were the supports of Zhōu.
The states on the four sides were a screen,
the four directions were proclaimed to.'
This is the virtue of Wén and Wǔ."
30.7 "When the kings of the Sāndài ruled,
they necessarily had a good reputation first.
The Shī says:
'Brilliant, brilliant is the Tiānzǐ,
his good reputation never ends.'
This is the virtue of the Sāndài.
'Spreading his civil virtue,
harmonizing these four states.'
This was the virtue of Dà Wáng."
Zǐxià rose with a start,
stood against the wall,
and said:
"How could I, your disciple, dare not receive this?"
31.1 The Master said:
"The way of the Jūnzǐ,
is it not like a dike?
It dikes what the people are deficient in.
Even if the dike is made large,
the people still cross over it.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ uses rituals to dike virtue,
punishments to dike depravity,
and mandates to dike desires."
31.2 The Master said:
"A petty person, when poor, becomes desperate,
and when rich, becomes arrogant.
Desperation leads to theft,
and arrogance leads to disorder.
Rituals
follow human emotions and create regulations and patterns for them,
acting as a dike for the people.
Therefore, when the sages instituted wealth and rank,
they made it so that the people's wealth was not enough to make them arrogant,
their poverty did not lead to desperation,
and their rank was not dissatisfied with those above.
Thus, disorder increasingly vanished."
31.3 The Master said:
"To be poor yet love music,
rich yet love rituals,
and numerous yet peaceful,
how few in the world reach this!
The Shī says:
'The people's greed for disorder
would rather be bitter poison.'
Therefore, it was regulated:
a state not exceeding a thousand chariots,
a capital city not exceeding a hundred zhì,
a family's wealth not exceeding a hundred chariots.
Even with these used to dike the people,
among the Zhūhóu there were still those who rebelled."
31.4 The Master said:
"Rituals
are used to clarify doubts and distinguish the subtle,
acting as a dike for the people.
Therefore, when there are ranks for noble and base,
distinctions in clothing,
and positions in court,
then the people have something to defer to."
The Master said:
"Heaven has no two suns,
the land has no two kings,
a family has no two masters,
the honored has no two superiors—
this shows the people the distinction between ruler and minister.
The Chūnqiū does not record the funerals of the kings of Chǔ
or Yuè;
in rituals, a ruler is not called Heaven,
and a grand officer is not called ruler,
for fear of confusing the people.
The Shī says:
'Look at that bird calling for dawn,
even it is still troubled by it.'"
The Master said:
"A ruler does not ride in the same carriage with someone of the same surname;
when riding in the same carriage with someone of a different surname, they do not wear the same clothes;
this shows the people no suspicion of equality.
Even with these used to dike the people,
people still used those of the same surname to assassinate their ruler."
31.5 The Master said:
"When the Jūnzǐ declines the noble and does not decline the base,
and declines the rich and does not decline the poor,
then disorder increasingly vanishes.
Therefore, a Jūnzǐ would rather have his stipend exceed his person
than have his person exceed his stipend."
The Master said:
"With a cup of wine and a bowl of meat,
if one defers and accepts the lesser part,
people still violate seniority;
if on the mat one defers
and sits in a lower place,
people still violate nobility;
if in a court position one defers and takes a lowly one,
people still violate the ruler.
The Shī says:
'When people have no goodness,
they resent each other on one side;
if they receive a rank without deferring,
it leads to their own ruin.'"
The Master said:
"When the Jūnzǐ honors others and humbles himself,
puts others first and himself last,
then the people will practice deference.
Therefore, when addressing another's ruler, he calls him 'ruler';
when addressing his own ruler, he calls him 'Guǎjūn'."
The Master said:
"Regarding benefits and stipends,
if one puts the dead before the living,
then the people will not be unfaithful;
if one puts those who have perished before those who remain,
then the people can be entrusted.
The Shī says:
'Thinking of the former ruler,
to nourish me, the Guǎrén.'
Even with these used to dike the people,
people still turn their backs on the dead and cry out having no one to appeal to."
31.6 The Master said:
"One who possesses a state or a family,
if he honors people and devalues stipends,
then the people will develop deference;
if he values skills and devalues carriages,
then the people will develop arts.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ is sparing with his words,
while the petty person speaks first."
31.7 The Master said:
"If the superior considers the people's words,
then those below will regard the superior as Heaven and the superior will bestow grace;
if the superior does not consider the people's words,
then there will be transgressions;
if those below do not regard the superior as Heaven,
then there will be disorder.
Therefore, if the Jūnzǐ uses sincerity and deference to preside over the people,
then the people's return of rituals will be substantial.
The Shī says:
'The former people had a saying:
"Consult with the grass and firewood cutters."'"
31.8 The Master said:
"If there is good, attribute it to others.
If there is fault, attribute it to oneself,
then the people will not contend.
If there is good, attribute it to others.
If there is fault, attribute it to oneself,
then resentment will increasingly disappear.
The *Shī* says:
'You consult the tortoise-shell and the milfoil stalks;
your actions meet with no words of blame.'"
The Master said:
"If there is good, attribute it to others.
If there is fault, attribute it to oneself,
then the people will yield credit for good deeds.
The *Shī* says:
'The King examined the divination;
he surveyed this *Hào Jīng*;
the tortoise-shell confirmed it;
*Wǔ Wáng* completed it.'"
The Master said:
"If there is good, attribute it to the ruler.
If there is fault, attribute it to oneself,
then the people will practice loyalty.
The *Jūn Chén* says:
'When you have excellent plans or excellent counsels,
enter and inform your ruler within;
then you follow them in public without,
saying:
"This plan and this counsel
derive from the virtue of my ruler."
Ah!
How truly good and illustrious this is!'"
The Master said:
"If there is good, attribute it to one's parents.
If there is fault, attribute it to oneself,
then the people will practice filial piety.
The *Tàishì* says:
'That I conquered *Zhòu*
was not because of my martial prowess,
but because my deceased father *Wén Kǎo* was without fault.
If *Zhòu* had conquered me,
it would not have been because my deceased father *Wén Kǎo* was at fault,
but because I, the little child, was lacking in goodness.'"
31.9 The Master said:
"The superior man glosses over the faults of his parents
and honors their excellence.
The *Lúnyǔ* says:
'If for three years one does not change from the way of his father,
he may be called filial.'
*Gāozōng* said:
'For three years he did not speak;
when he did speak, there was joyous harmony.'"
The Master said:
"To follow commands without indolence,
to offer gentle remonstrance without weariness,
and to labor without resentment,
may be called filial piety.
The *Shī* says:
'The filial son's devotion is inexhaustible.'"
The Master said:
"To be at harmony with the kin of one's parents
may be called filial piety.
Therefore, the superior man uses such harmony to bring the clan together.
The *Shī* says:
'These good brothers
are generous and relaxed;
those who are not good brothers
cause each other distress.'"
The Master said:
"Toward a friend of one's father,
one may ride in his carriage
but should not wear his clothes.
The superior man uses this to broaden the scope of filial piety."
The Master said:
"Even petty men can provide for their parents;
but if the superior man lacks reverence,
how can he be distinguished?"
The Master said:
"Father and son do not hold the same rank,
in order to emphasize reverence.
The *Shū* says:
'If the ruler does not act as a ruler,
he shames his ancestors.'"
The Master said:
"While one's parents are alive,
one does not call oneself old,
one speaks of filial piety but not of being parental;
and within the family gates,
one may jest but not sigh in sorrow.
The superior man uses this as a dike for the people,
yet the people are still deficient in filial piety and excessive in parental affection."
The Master said:
"He who leads the people,
if the court honors the aged,
then the people will practice filial piety."
The Master said:
"In sacrifices, having a personator,
and having a tablet for the ancestral temple,
is to show the people that there are duties to perform.
Maintaining the ancestral temples
and revering the sacrificial rites
is to teach the people to pursue filial piety toward the departed.
Using this as a dike for the people,
the people still forget their parents."
31.10 The Master said:
"Reverence requires the use of sacrificial vessels.
Therefore, the superior man does not discard ritual because of meager offerings,
nor does he let lavishness overwhelm ritual.
Therefore, in the ritual of eating:
if the host personally presents the food,
then the guest performs the sacrifice of the food;
if the host does not personally present it,
then the guest does not sacrifice.
Thus, if it were against ritual,
the superior man would not eat it, however fine it might be.
The *Yì* says:
'The neighbor to the east slaughters an ox,
but it is not equal to the modest summer sacrifice of the neighbor to the west,
who truly receives the blessing.'
The *Shī* says:
'Having been made drunk with wine,
and satiated with virtue.'
Showing this to the people,
they still struggle for profit and forget righteousness."
31.11 The Master said:
"Seven days of vigilance,
and three days of fasting,
followed by supporting one person to be the personator;
those who pass by him walk quickly,
which is to teach reverence.
Sweet wine is in the inner chamber,
reddish wine is in the hall,
and clear wine is below the hall,
showing the people not to be licentious.
The personator drinks three cups,
the various guests drink one,
showing the people that there are higher and lower ranks.
Using the wine and meat,
the clan is gathered together,
to teach the people harmony.
Therefore, those in the hall look toward the inner chamber,
and those below the hall look toward those above.
The *Shī* says:
'The ceremonies and rites are fully according to measure,
and the laughter and talk are perfectly appropriate.'"
31.12 The Master said:
"In the rituals for guests, every advance is made with yielding;
in funeral rituals, every stage increases the distance from the deceased.
Bathing the body in the central atrium,
performing the ritual of putting grain in the mouth under the window,
the lesser dressing inside the door,
the greater dressing on the eastern steps,
placing the coffin in the guest position,
the sacrifice of departure in the courtyard,
and burial in the tomb—
these are to show the increasing distance.
The people of *Yīn* offered condolences at the grave;
the people of *Zhōu* offer condolences at the house;
this is to show the people not to turn their backs on the deceased."
The Master said:
"Death
is the final service of the people;
I follow *Zhōu*.
Using this as a dike for the people,
still some feudal lords
die but are not buried."
31.13 The Master said:
"To ascend by the guest steps
and receive condolences in the guest position
is to teach the people to pursue filial piety.
Not calling the heir 'ruler' until the mourning period is over
is to show the people not to contend.
Therefore, the *Lǔ Chūnqiū* records a funeral in *Jìn* saying:
'They killed the ruler's son *Xīqí* and their ruler *Zhuó*.'
Using this as a dike for the people,
there are still sons who murder their fathers."
31.14 The Master said:
"Filial piety is used to serve the ruler,
and fraternal respect is used to serve elders;
this is to show the people not to be double-hearted.
Therefore, if the superior man has a ruler, he does not seek office elsewhere;
only on the day of divination for a new ruler does one speak of two rulers.
Mourning a father for three years
and mourning a ruler for three years
is to show the people not to have doubts.
While one's parents are alive,
one dares not consider one's body as one's own,
nor dares one treat property as private;
this is to show the people that there are superiors and inferiors.
Therefore, for the Son of Heaven, within the four seas there is no ritual for guests,
as no one dares to act as host to him.
Therefore, when a ruler goes to visit his minister,
he ascends by the eastern steps
and takes his place in the hall,
showing the people that the minister dares not consider the house his own.
While one's parents are alive,
in presenting gifts, one does not include carriages or horses,
showing the people that one dares not act on one's own.
Using this as a dike for the people,
the people still forget their parents and are double-hearted toward their ruler."
31.15 The Master said:
"In rituals, presents of silk and gems come first,
with the desire that the people prioritize service and put emolument second.
If wealth is prioritized and ritual comes after,
then the people will be greedy for profit.
If one acts on feelings without formal expressions,
then the people will contend with each other.
Therefore, when the *Jūnzǐ* has someone offering a gift
whom he cannot see, he does not look at the gift.
The *Yì* says:
'If one does not plow, yet reaps;
if one does not clear the land for one year, yet uses it for three;
it is ominous.'
Even with this as a barrier for the people,
the people still value emolument and disparage conduct."
31.16 The Master said:
"The *Jūnzǐ* does not exhaust all profit, so as to leave some for the people.
The *Shī* says:
'There are handfuls left behind,
there are ungathered sheaves;
they are for the benefit of the widow.'
Therefore, if the *Jūnzǐ* takes office, he does not farm;
if he owns land, he does not fish.
When eating in season, he does not strive for delicacies;
a *Dàfū* does not sit on a sheepskin,
and a *Shì* does not sit on a dogskin.
The *Shī* says:
'Gathering the mustard plant and the radish,
do not reject them because of their lower parts.
Let not your virtuous reputation be violated,
and I will be with you until death.'
Even with this as a barrier for the people,
the people still forget righteousness and struggle for profit,
thus losing their lives."
31.17 The Master said:
"Ritual
is a barrier against the people's excesses,
to clarify the distinctions among the people,
to ensure the people have no suspicions,
and to serve as a regulation for the people.
Therefore, men and women do not interact without a matchmaker,
and do not see each other without a gift,
for fear that there be no distinction between men and women.
Even with this as a barrier for the people,
there are still those who offer themselves.
The *Shī* says:
'How do you cut a handle for an axe?
Without an axe, it cannot be done.
How do you take a wife?
Without a matchmaker, she cannot be obtained.'
'How do you plant hemp?
Crosswise and lengthwise in the acres.
How do you take a wife?
You must inform your father and mother.' "
31.18 The Master said:
"In taking a wife, one does not take one of the same surname,
to emphasize the distinction.
Therefore, when buying a concubine and not knowing her surname,
one consults the tortoise-shell.
Even with this as a barrier for the people,
the *Lǔ Chūnqiū* still removed the surname of the lady from *Wú*,
and at her death recorded it as '*Mèng Zǐ* passed away.' "
31.19 The Master said:
"According to ritual,
except for sacrifices,
men and women do not exchange cups.
Even with this as a barrier for the people,
the Lord of *Yáng* still killed the Lord of *Mù* and stole his wife.
Therefore, at the Great Feast, the ritual for the wife was abolished."
31.20 The Master said:
"The son of a widow,
unless there is something distinguished about him,
one does not befriend him;
the *Jūnzǐ* does this to keep a distance.
Therefore, in the interaction of friends,
if the master is not present,
and there is no great cause,
one does not enter his door.
Even with this as a barrier for the people,
the people still value beauty more than virtue."
The Master said:
"Love virtue as you love beauty.
The feudal lords do not stoop to lust.
Therefore, the *Jūnzǐ* keeps away from lust to serve as a regulation for the people.
Therefore, men and women do not touch when giving or receiving.
When driving a carriage for a woman, one extends the left hand.
Paternal aunts, sisters, and daughters
who have already married and returned,
men do not sit with them on the same mat.
A widow does not wail at night.
When a woman is ill,
in inquiring after her, one does not ask about the nature of the illness.
Even with this as a barrier for the people,
the people still indulge in excess and bring disorder to the clan."
31.21 The Master said:
"In the marriage ritual,
the groom meets the bride in person,
she is presented to the father-in-law and mother-in-law,
and the father-in-law and mother-in-law receive the child to hand her over to the groom,
fearing that the affair might be neglected.
Even with this as a barrier for the people,
there are still wives who do not arrive."
32.1 What Heaven has ordained is called the Nature;
following the Nature is called the Way;
cultivating the Way is called Instruction.
The Way
is something that cannot be departed from for even a moment;
if it could be departed from, it would not be the Way.
Therefore, the *Jūnzǐ* is cautious and vigilant where he is not seen,
and fearful and apprehensive where he is not heard.
Nothing is more manifest than what is hidden,
nothing is more evident than what is subtle.
Therefore, the *Jūnzǐ* is watchful over himself when alone.
When joy, anger, grief, and pleasure have not yet arisen,
it is called the Mean.
When they arise and all reach their proper measure,
it is called Harmony.
The Mean
is the great foundation of the world.
Harmony
is the pervasive Way of the world.
Reaching the states of Mean and Harmony,
Heaven and Earth take their proper places,
and the myriad things are nourished.
32.2 *Zhòngní* said:
"The *Jūnzǐ* embodies the Middle Way;
the *Xiǎorén* acts contrary to the Middle Way.
The *Jūnzǐ*'s embodiment of the Middle Way
is because he is a *Jūnzǐ* and maintains the timely mean;
the *Xiǎorén*'s embodiment of the Middle Way
is because he is a *Xiǎorén* and has no caution or fear."
The Master said:
"The Middle Way is supreme!
Rare is it that the people have been able to keep it for long!"
The Master said:
"That the Way is not practiced,
I know why.
The wise go beyond it,
and the ignorant do not reach it.
That the Way is not understood,
I know why.
The worthy go beyond it,
and the unworthy do not reach it.
Everyone eats and drinks,
yet few can truly know the flavor."
The Master said:
"Alas, the Way is not practiced!"
32.3 The Master said:
"*Shùn* was indeed a man of great wisdom!
*Shùn* loved to ask questions and loved to examine words that were near at hand.
He concealed what was bad and displayed what was good.
He grasped the two extremes
and applied the mean to the people.
Was this not what made him *Shùn*?"
32.4 The Master said:
"Everyone says, 'I am wise,'
yet they are driven and caught in nets, traps, and pitfalls,
and none know how to escape.
Everyone says, 'I am wise,'
yet when they choose the Middle Way,
they cannot remain constant for a full month."
32.5 The Master said:
"As for *Huí*'s character,
he chose the Middle Way,
and when he attained one good thing,
he would hold it fast to his breast
and never lose it."
The Master said:
"The world, the states, and the families could be brought to order,
rank and emolument could be declined,
naked blades could be trodden upon,
but the Middle Way is not easily achieved."
32.6 *Zǐlù* asked about strength.
The Master said:
"Do you mean the strength of the South?
Or the strength of the North?
Or your own strength?
To be broad-minded and gentle in teaching,
and not to retaliate against those who are unprincipled:
this is the strength of the South,
and the *Jūnzǐ* dwells in it.
To sleep on weapons and armor,
and to die without regret:
this is the strength of the North,
and the strong dwell in it.
Therefore, the *Jūnzǐ* is harmonious but does not go with the flow—
how strong and upright!
He stands in the middle and does not lean—
how strong and upright!
When the Way prevails in the state,
he does not change his long-held principles—
how strong and upright!
When the Way does not prevail in the state,
he maintains his course until death—
how strong and upright!"
32.7 Kǒngzǐ said:
“Searching for the obscure and practicing the strange,
later generations might record them;
I will not do so.
The gentleman follows the Way and proceeds,
but stops halfway;
I am unable to stop.
The gentleman relies on the Middle Way,
withdrawing from the world and remaining unknown without regret;
only a Sage can do this.”
The Way of the gentleman is broad yet hidden.
Even the ignorance of common men and women
can participate in the knowledge of it;
but in its ultimate reaching,
even the Sage has something he does not know.
Even the unworthiness of common men and women
can participate in the practice of it;
but in its ultimate reaching,
even the Sage has something he cannot do.
Great as heaven and earth are,
people still find something to regret in them.
Therefore, when the gentleman speaks of greatness,
the world cannot contain it;
when he speaks of smallness,
the world cannot break it.
The *Shī* says:
‘The hawk flies to the height of heaven,
the fish leaps in the deep.’
This says that it is manifest above and below.
The Way of the gentleman
takes its beginning from the relationship of husband and wife;
but in its ultimate reaching,
it is manifest throughout heaven and earth.
32.8 Kǒngzǐ said:
“The Way is not far from people;
if people pursue a way that is far from people,
it cannot be considered the Way.
The *Shī* says:
‘Hewing an axe handle, hewing an axe handle,
the pattern is not far off.’
One grasps an axe handle to hew an axe handle,
yet looking at it askance,
one still considers it far off.
Therefore, the gentleman uses people to govern people,
and stops once they have corrected themselves.
Loyalty and empathy are not far from the Way;
what you do not wish for yourself,
do not do to others.
The Way of the gentleman is fourfold,
and I, Qiū, have not attained even one:
What I require of a son
in serving his father,
I have not been able to do;
what I require of a minister
in serving his ruler,
I have not been able to do;
what I require of a younger brother
in serving his elder brother,
I have not been able to do;
what I require of a friend,
to be the first to bestow,
I have not been able to do.
In the practice of ordinary virtues,
and in the care of ordinary speech;
where there is deficiency,
one dares not but exert oneself;
where there is excess, one dares not exhaust it.
Words correspond to actions,
and actions correspond to words;
how can the gentleman not be earnest!”
The gentleman acts according to his position
and does not desire what is outside of it.
In a position of wealth and honor,
he acts according to wealth and honor.
In a position of poverty and low status,
he acts according to poverty and low status.
In a position among the Yídí,
he acts according to the Yídí.
In a position of trouble and distress,
he acts according to trouble and distress.
There is no situation into which the gentleman enters where he is not at ease with himself.
In a high position, he does not insult those below;
in a low position, he does not cling to those above.
He rectifies himself and seeks nothing from others,
so he has no resentments;
above, he does not resent Heaven,
and below, he does not blame men.
Therefore, the gentleman dwells in ease to await his fate,
while the mean man walks in danger to seek luck.
32.9 Kǒngzǐ said:
“Archery has a resemblance to the gentleman;
when he misses the target,
he seeks the cause within himself.”
The Way of the gentleman
is like traveling far, where one must start from what is near;
it is like climbing high, where one must start from what is low.
The *Shī* says:
‘Loving union with wife and children
is like the playing of lutes and harps.
When brothers are in harmony,
there is joy and delight.
May you bring order to your chamber and home,
and find joy in your wife and children.’
Kǒngzǐ said:
“How pleased the parents must be!”
32.10 Kǒngzǐ said:
“How abundant is the virtue
of the ghosts and spirits!
We look for them and do not see them;
we listen for them and do not hear them;
yet they embody all things and cannot be omitted.
They cause the people of the world
to fast and purify themselves and put on their finest robes
to attend the sacrifices.
Overflowing and vast,
they seem to be above,
and to the left and right.
The *Shī* says:
‘The approach of the spirits
cannot be calculated,
how much less can they be neglected!’
Such is the manifestation of the subtle,
and the impossibility of concealing the sincere!”
32.11 Kǒngzǐ said:
“How great was the filial piety of Shùn!
His virtue was that of a Sage,
his honor was that of the Son of Heaven,
his wealth included all within the four seas;
he is offered sacrifices in the ancestral temple,
and his descendants preserve them.
Therefore, great virtue will surely obtain its position,
surely obtain its wealth,
surely obtain its fame,
and surely obtain its longevity.
Thus, when Heaven produces things,
it surely strengthens them according to their material.
Therefore, the one that is planted is nourished,
and the one that is leaning is overthrown.
The *Shī* says:
‘The admirable and joyous gentleman
has illustrious and excellent virtue.
He is fit for the people and fit for men,
and receives his wealth from Heaven.
It protects, assists, and ordains him,
and from Heaven, it renews its decree.’
Therefore, he who has great virtue will surely receive the Mandate.”
32.12 Kǒngzǐ said:
“The one who had no sorrow
was surely Wén Wáng!
With Wáng Jì as his father
and Wǔ Wáng as his son;
the father founded it,
and the son carried it on.
Wǔ Wáng continued the work of Dà Wáng, Wáng Jì, and Wén Wáng.
Once he donned his armor, he possessed the world,
without losing his illustrious name throughout the world.
His honor was that of the Son of Heaven,
his wealth included all within the four seas;
he is offered sacrifices in the ancestral temple,
and his descendants preserve them.
Wǔ Wáng received the Mandate in his later years.
Zhōu Gōng completed the virtue of Wén and Wǔ,
posthumously titling Dà Wáng and Wáng Jì as Kings,
and sacrificing to the former dukes with the rituals of the Son of Heaven.
This ritual
extended to the feudal lords and the high officials,
and down to the officers and the common people.
If the father was a high official
and the son was an officer,
the burial was as a high official
and the sacrifice was as an officer.
If the father was an officer
and the son was a high official,
the burial was as an officer
and the sacrifice was as a high official.
The one-year mourning period
extended to the high officials.
The three-year mourning period
extended to the Son of Heaven.
In the mourning for parents,
there was no distinction between the noble and the lowly;
it was one and the same.”
32.13 Kǒngzǐ said:
“Wǔ Wáng and Zhōu Gōng
were truly universal in their filial piety!
Now, filial piety
consists in skillfully carrying on the will of others
and skillfully continuing the affairs of others.
In spring and autumn, they repaired their ancestral temples,
displayed their ancestral vessels,
set out their ceremonial robes,
and offered the seasonal foods.
The rituals of the ancestral temple
are for ordering the *Zhāo* and *Mù* generations.
Ordering by rank
is for distinguishing the noble from the base.
Ordering by duty
is for distinguishing the worthy.
In the general toast, the inferiors toast the superiors,
which extends the ceremony to the humble.
Arranging the feast by hair color
is for ordering by age.
Occupying their positions,
performing their rituals,
playing their music,
honoring whom they honored,
and loving whom they loved;
serving the dead as if serving the living,
and serving the departed as if serving the present,
is the height of filial piety.
The rituals of the *Jiāo* and *Shè* sacrifices
are for serving the High Deity.
The rituals of the ancestral temple
are for sacrificing to the ancestors.
To be clear about the rituals of the *Jiāo* and *Shè* sacrifices,
and the meaning of the *Dì* and *Cháng* sacrifices,
would make governing a kingdom as easy as looking at one’s palm.
32.14 Duke *Āi* asked about government.
The Master said:
“The government of King *Wén* and King *Wǔ*
is spread across the tablets and scrolls.
When such men are present,
then their government flourishes.
When such men are gone,
then their government ceases.
The way of man is quick to affect government,
just as the way of the earth is quick to grow trees.
For government
is like the *púlú* reeds.
Therefore, the conduct of government depends on the men;
one attracts such men by means of one’s own character;
one cultivates character by means of the Way;
and one cultivates the Way by means of *Rén*.
*Rén* is being human;
loving one’s kin is its greatest part.
*Yì* is what is appropriate;
honoring the worthy is its greatest part.
The degrees of loving kin
and the grades of honoring the worthy
are what give rise to *Lǐ*.
If those in lower positions do not obtain the confidence of their superiors,
the people cannot be governed.
Therefore, the gentleman must not fail to cultivate his character;
thinking of cultivating his character,
he must not fail to serve his parents;
thinking of serving his parents,
he must not fail to know men;
thinking of knowing men,
he must not fail to know *Tiān*.
There are five universal ways in the world,
and the means by which they are practiced are three.
These are: the relation between ruler and minister,
between father and son,
between husband and wife,
between elder and younger brothers,
and the interaction of friends;
these five are the universal ways of the world.
*Zhì*, *Rén*, and *Yǒng*—these three
are the universal virtues of the world.
The means by which they are practiced is one.
Some are born with the knowledge of them;
some learn them through study;
some learn them through painful effort;
but when it comes to the knowledge of them, they are as one.
Some practice them with natural ease;
some practice them for the sake of benefit;
some practice them with strenuous effort;
but when it comes to their success, they are as one.”
32.15 The Master said:
“To be fond of study is near to *Zhì*;
to practice with vigor is near to *Rén*;
to know shame is near to *Yǒng*.
To know these three
is to know how to cultivate one’s character;
to know how to cultivate one’s character
is to know how to govern men;
to know how to govern men
is to know how to govern the world, the state, and the family.
For all those who govern the world, the state, and the family, there are nine standard rules,
namely:
cultivating the self,
honoring the worthy,
loving one’s kin,
respecting the great ministers,
empathizing with the body of officials,
treating the common people as children,
attracting all kinds of artisans,
being kind to people from afar,
and cherishing the feudal lords.
By cultivating the self, the Way is established;
by honoring the worthy, one is not deluded;
by loving one’s kin, one’s uncles and brothers harbor no resentment;
by respecting the great ministers, one is not confused;
by empathizing with the body of officials, the scholars’ return of ritual is heavy;
by treating the common people as children, the masses are encouraged;
by attracting all kinds of artisans, resources are sufficient;
by being kind to people from afar, people from all quarters flock to him;
and by cherishing the feudal lords, the world stands in awe of him.
32.16 To fast, to purify, and to wear solemn dress,
and to not move against *Lǐ*—
this is how to cultivate the self.
To banish slanderers and distance oneself from sensuality,
to undervalue riches and value virtue—
this is how to encourage the worthy.
To honor their rank,
to make their emoluments heavy,
and to share their likes and dislikes—
this is how to encourage the loving of kin.
To provide a full staff of officials for their use—
this is how to encourage the great ministers.
To be loyal and trustworthy and to provide generous emoluments—
this is how to encourage the scholar-officials.
To employ them at the proper seasons and keep taxes low—
this is how to encourage the common people.
Daily examinations and monthly trials,
and providing rations according to the work—
this is how to encourage the artisans.
To see off those who leave and welcome those who come,
to praise the good and pity the incompetent—
this is how to be kind to people from afar.
To restore broken lines of succession,
to revive fallen states,
to regulate disorder and support those in danger,
to hold audiences and receive envoys at the proper times,
and to give much while receiving little—
this is how to cherish the feudal lords.
32.17 For all those who govern the world, the state, and the family, there are nine standard rules,
but the means by which they are practiced is one.
In all things, preparation leads to success,
and lack of preparation leads to failure.
If words are determined beforehand, there will be no stumbles;
if affairs are determined beforehand, there will be no distress;
if actions are determined beforehand, there will be no regret;
if the Way is determined beforehand, there will be no exhaustion.
32.18 If those in lower positions do not obtain the confidence of their superiors,
the people cannot be governed.
There is a way to obtain the confidence of superiors:
if one is not trusted by friends,
one will not obtain the confidence of superiors.
There is a way to be trusted by friends:
if one is not obedient to parents,
one will not be trusted by friends.
There is a way to be obedient to parents:
if one is not sincere when reflecting on oneself,
one will not be obedient to parents.
There is a way to be sincere in oneself:
if one does not understand what is good,
one will not be sincere in oneself.
32.19 *Chéng*
is the Way of *Tiān*.
Making oneself *chéng*
is the Way of man.
He who is *chéng* hits the mark without effort,
attains without thought,
and naturally follows the Way—
this is the *Shèngrén*.
He who makes himself *chéng*
is one who chooses the good and holds firmly to it.
Study it extensively,
inquire into it accurately,
think over it carefully,
distinguish it clearly,
and practice it earnestly.
If there is something one has not studied,
or having studied it, one cannot do it, one does not give up;
if there is something one has not inquired about,
or having inquired about it, one does not know it, one does not give up;
if there is something one has not thought about,
or having thought about it, one does not understand it, one does not give up;
if there is something one has not distinguished,
or having distinguished it, one does not see it clearly, one does not give up;
if there is something one has not practiced,
or having practiced it, one does not do it earnestly, one does not give up.
Where others succeed in one effort, he will use a hundred;
where others succeed in ten, he will use a thousand.
If one can truly follow this way,
even the dull will become enlightened,
and even the weak will become strong.
32.20 Enlightenment resulting from *chéng*
is called *Xìng*.
*Chéng* resulting from enlightenment
is called *Jiào*.
*Chéng* leads to enlightenment;
enlightenment leads to *chéng*.
Only those in the world who possess utmost sincerity
can fully develop their nature;
being able to fully develop their nature,
they can then fully develop the nature of others;
being able to fully develop the nature of others,
they can then fully develop the nature of things;
being able to fully develop the nature of things,
they can then assist in the transforming and nourishing processes of Heaven and Earth;
being able to assist in the transforming and nourishing processes of Heaven and Earth,
they can then form a triad with Heaven and Earth.
32.21 Next is the cultivation of partial excellence;
in partial excellence, there can be sincerity;
when there is sincerity, it becomes manifest;
when manifest, it becomes apparent;
when apparent, it becomes brilliant;
when brilliant, it moves others;
when it moves others, it changes them;
when it changes them, it transforms them;
only those in the world who possess utmost
sincerity are able to transform.
32.22 It is the way of utmost sincerity
that one can foreknow.
When a nation is about to flourish,
there must be auspicious omens;
when a nation is about to perish,
there must be unlucky omens.
These are seen in the milfoil and tortoise shells
and are moved in the four limbs.
When calamity or fortune is about to arrive,
the good
will surely be known beforehand;
the not good
will also surely be known beforehand.
Therefore, utmost sincerity is like the divine.
32.23 Sincerity is self-completing,
and the Way is its own guide.
Sincerity is the end and the beginning of things;
without sincerity, there would be no things.
For this reason, the *jūnzǐ* prizes sincerity.
Sincerity is not merely for the self-completion of oneself;
it is that by which one completes things.
Completing oneself
is *rén*;
completing things
is *zhì*;
these are the virtues of the nature,
and the Way of uniting the internal and external;
therefore, they are appropriate to be applied at all times.
Thus, utmost sincerity is unceasing;
being unceasing, it is long-lasting;
being long-lasting, it becomes evident;
being evident, it reaches far;
reaching far, it becomes broad and thick;
being broad and thick, it becomes high and brilliant.
Being broad and thick
is how it supports all things;
being high and brilliant
is how it covers all things;
being far-reaching and long-lasting
is how it completes all things.
Breadth and thickness match Earth;
height and brilliance match Heaven;
far-reaching and long-lasting nature is boundless.
Being such,
it becomes manifest without being seen,
it changes without moving,
and it completes without acting.
The Way of Heaven and Earth
can be summarized in one word:
its being is not dual,
and so its production of things is unfathomable.
The Way of Heaven and Earth
is broad,
thick,
high,
brilliant,
far-reaching,
and long-lasting.
32.24 Now, as for Heaven:
it is but this accumulation of small lights;
yet when it comes to its infinity,
the sun, moon, stars, and constellations are suspended in it,
and all things are covered by it.
Now, as for Earth:
it is but a handful of soil;
yet when it comes to its breadth and thickness,
it sustains the *Huá Yuè* without feeling its weight,
and contains the rivers and seas without their leaking,
and all things are supported by it.
Now, as for the mountains:
they are but a fist-sized stone;
yet when it comes to their vastness,
grasses and trees grow upon them,
birds and beasts dwell upon them,
and precious treasures arise within them.
Now, as for the water:
it is but a spoonful;
yet when it comes to its unfathomability,
soft-shell turtles, alligators, iguanas, dragons, fish, and turtles are produced in it,
and wealth and goods multiply there.
The *Shī* says:
"The mandate of Heaven,
how profound and unceasing!"
This refers to what makes Heaven, Heaven.
"Oh, how illustrious
is the purity of *Wén Wáng*'s virtue!"
This refers to what made *Wén Wáng*, *Wén*.
Purity also is unceasing.
32.25 Great is the Way of the Sage!
Overflowing and vast,
it nourishes all things
and rises to the very heavens.
How abundant and great!
There are three hundred rules of ceremony
and three thousand rules of demeanor.
They wait for the right person and then are practiced.
Hence it is said: if there be not the highest virtue,
the highest Way will not be realized.
32.26 Therefore, the *jūnzǐ* honors the virtuous nature and follows the path of inquiry and study,
seeking to reach the greatest breadth while exhausting the most minute,
reaching the highest brilliance while following the *Zhōngyōng*,
reviewing the old to know the new,
and being earnest and generous in his esteem for the rites.
32.27 Thus, in a high position, he is not proud;
in a low position, he is not rebellious.
When the state has the Way, his words are sufficient to bring prosperity;
when the state is without the Way, his silence is sufficient to afford him tolerance.
The *Shī* says:
"Both intelligent and wise,
he protects his person."
This is exactly what is meant!
32.28 The *Zǐ* said:
"To be ignorant and yet like to use one's own judgment;
to be in a low condition and yet like to be self-willed;
to live in the present age
and yet revert to the ways of antiquity—
for those who are like this,
calamities will surely reach their persons."
Unless one is the *Tiānzǐ*,
one does not deliberate on the rites,
does not establish systems,
and does not examine the written characters.
Today, throughout the world, carriages have wheels of the same track,
books use the same characters,
and conduct follows the same principles.
Although one may have the position,
if he does not have the virtue,
he dares not create rites or music.
Although one may have the virtue,
if he does not have the position,
he also dares not create rites or music.
32.29 The *Zǐ* said:
"I can talk about the rites of *Xià*,
but *Qǐ* cannot sufficiently attest to them.
I have studied the rites of *Yīn*,
and they are preserved in *Sòng*.
I have studied the rites of *Zhōu*,
which are used today,
and I follow *Zhōu*."
To rule the world, there are three important things;
by these, one's errors will be few!
As for those in high positions in former times, although they were good, there is no evidence;
without evidence, they are not believed;
if not believed, the people will not follow them.
As for those in low positions,
although they are good, they are not honored;
if not honored, they are not believed;
if not believed, the people will not follow them.
Therefore, the Way of the *jūnzǐ*
is rooted in his own person
and evidenced by the common people.
It is tested against the *Sān Wáng* and found without error,
established before Heaven and Earth and found not to be in conflict with them,
questioned before the *guǐshén* and found without doubt,
and it awaits the Sage of a hundred generations hence without uncertainty.
Being questioned before the *guǐshén* without doubt
shows that he knows Heaven.
Awaiting the Sage of a hundred generations hence without uncertainty
shows that he knows men.
Therefore, the *jūnzǐ* moves and for generations becomes a way for the world;
he acts and for generations becomes a law for the world;
he speaks and for generations becomes a standard for the world.
Those who are far from him look toward him with longing;
those who are near to him never grow weary of him.
The *Shī* says:
"There they have no hatred for him;
here they have no dislike for him.
Thus, from morning to night,
he perpetuates his fame forever."
There has never been a *jūnzǐ* who was not like this
and yet attained early fame throughout the world.
32.30 *Zhòngní* handed down the doctrines of *Yáo* and *Shùn* as his ancestors,
and modeled himself on the regulations of *Wén* and *Wǔ*.
Above, he conformed to the laws of the heavenly seasons,
and below, he conformed to the water and the land.
He may be compared to Heaven and Earth in their supporting and containing all things,
and in their overshadowing and covering all things.
He may be compared to the four seasons in their alternating progress,
and to the sun and moon in their successive shining.
All things are nourished together without harming one another;
ways are practiced together without conflicting.
Small virtues are like flowing rivers;
great virtues transform mightily.
This is why Heaven and Earth are great.
Only the Supreme Sage of the world
possesses the keenness of hearing, clarity of vision, and far-reaching wisdom
sufficient to command others.
Magnanimity, generosity, gentleness, and kindness
are sufficient to show tolerance.
Vigorous strength, firmness, and resolution
are sufficient to maintain control.
Dignity, solemnity, centrality, and uprightness
are sufficient to command respect.
Orderliness, logic, precision, and discernment
are sufficient to make distinctions.
All-embracing, vast, and deep like a spring,
he brings forth these qualities in their season.
All-embracing and vast like Heaven,
deep like a spring and an abyss.
When he appears, the people cannot but respect him;
when he speaks, the people cannot but believe him;
when he acts, the people cannot but be pleased with him.
Therefore, his fame overflows throughout Zhōngguó
and extends to the Mán and Mò;
wherever ships and carriages reach,
wherever human power penetrates,
wherever the heavens overspread,
wherever the earth sustains,
wherever the sun and moon shine,
and wherever the frost and dew fall,
all who have blood and breath
cannot but honor and love him.
Thus it is said, "He is the peer of Heaven."
Only the Supreme Sincerity of the world
can weave the great warp of the world,
establish the great foundation of the world,
and understand the transforming and nourishing work of Heaven and Earth.
How can he depend on anything else?
How earnest is his benevolence!
How deep is his abyss!
How vast is his Heaven!
If one does not truly possess keenness of hearing, clarity of vision, and the sagely wisdom that reaches Heavenly virtue,
who could possibly understand him?
The *Shī* says,
"Over her embroidered robe she puts a plain garment,"
disliking the conspicuousness of its patterns.
Therefore, the Way of the Jūnzǐ
is hidden yet becomes daily more illustrious.
The way of the small man
is conspicuous yet daily fades away.
The Way of the Jūnzǐ
is plain yet one does not tire of it;
it is simple yet refined;
it is warm yet orderly.
He knows that the distant begins from the near;
he knows the source of the wind;
he knows how the subtle becomes manifest.
With this, one may enter into virtue.
The *Shī* says,
"Though the fish dive and remain at the bottom,
they are still quite clearly seen."
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ examines himself inwardly and finds nothing wrong,
having no cause for dissatisfaction with his own will.
That which the Jūnzǐ cannot be equaled in
is precisely that which other people do not see!
The *Shī* says,
"Look into your own room;
be not ashamed even in the secret corner."
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ commands respect without moving
and inspires trust without speaking.
The *Shī* says,
"He makes his offerings in silence,
and at that time there is no contention."
For this reason, the Jūnzǐ does not offer rewards, yet the people are encouraged;
he does not show anger, yet the people are more awed than by axes and halberds.
The *Shī* says,
"What is not manifest is his virtue,
and all the princes imitate it."
For this reason, the Jūnzǐ is earnest and reverent, and the world is at peace.
The *Shī* says,
"I cherish brilliant virtue,
which makes no great noise nor shows a stern countenance."
32.31 The Master said,
"To use sound and countenance to transform the people
is a secondary matter."
The *Shī* says,
"Virtue is as light as a hair."
Yet even a hair has comparisons.
"The workings of High Heaven
have neither sound nor smell."
That is supreme!
33.1 The Master said,
"Return!
The Jūnzǐ is hidden yet manifest,
dignified without being arrogant,
majestic without being severe,
and inspires trust without speaking."
33.2 The Master said,
"The Jūnzǐ does not make a false step before others,
does not lose his composure before others,
and does not speak errantly before others.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ's appearance is sufficient to inspire awe,
his composure is sufficient to inspire respect,
and his words are sufficient to inspire trust.
The *Fǔxíng* says,
'Be reverent and cautious,
and let there be no ill-chosen words in your person.'"
33.3 The Master said,
"To wear an inner and outer garment without following the other's style
is because he wishes the people not to treat one another with familiarity."
The Master said,
"In sacrifice, exercise the utmost reverence,
and do not follow it with music.
At court, exercise the utmost discernment,
and do not follow it with weariness."
33.4 The Master said,
"The Jūnzǐ is cautious in order to avoid calamity,
earnest in order not to be deceptive,
and reverent in order to keep away shame."
33.5 The Master said,
"The Jūnzǐ becomes stronger daily through dignity and reverence,
while he who seeks ease and indulgence becomes more negligent daily.
The Jūnzǐ does not let his person be careless for a single day,
as if he could not finish the day."
The Master said,
"Fast and abstain to serve the ghosts and spirits,
and choose an auspicious day and month to see the ruler,
for fear that the people might lack respect."
The Master said,
"As for disrespectful familiarity,
people would rather die than fear it."
33.6 The Master said,
"Without formal words, people do not interact;
without ritual, people do not meet;
this is to prevent the people from being disrespectful to one another.
The *Yì* says,
'The first divination gives instruction;
the second and third are disrespectful.'
If there is disrespect, no instruction is given."
33.7 The Master said,
"Benevolence
is the standard for the world;
Righteousness
is the regulation for the world;
Reciprocity
is the benefit for the world."
The Master said,
"Repaying virtue with virtue
gives the people something to be encouraged by;
repaying resentment with resentment
gives the people something to be cautioned by.
The *Shī* says,
'No word goes unanswered,
no virtue goes unrequited.'
The *Tàijiǎ* says,
'Without a ruler, the people
would have no one to help them find peace;
without the people, the ruler
would have no one to govern the four quarters.'"
The Master said,
"Repaying resentment with virtue
is the benevolence that eases one's own person;
repaying virtue with resentment
makes one a person fit for punishment."
The Master said,
"Those who love benevolence without desire
and hate unrighteousness without fear
are but one in the whole world.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ discusses the Way based on himself
but establishes laws based on the people."
The Master said,
"There are three kinds of benevolence;
they share the same achievements but differ in sentiment.
Sharing the same achievement of benevolence,
their true benevolence might not yet be known;
but when they share the same faults,
then their benevolence can be known.
The benevolent man finds peace in benevolence;
the wise man finds profit in benevolence;
the man who fears punishment forces himself to benevolence.
Benevolence is the right;
the Way is the left.
Benevolence is being human;
the Way is righteousness.
He who is heavy in benevolence but light in righteousness
is affectionate but not respected;
he who is heavy in righteousness but light in benevolence
is respected but not affectionate.
There is a supreme point to the Way;
there is an examination for righteousness.
With the supreme Way one rules as a King;
with the way of righteousness one rules as a Hegemon;
with the way of examination one ensures there is no error."
33.8 The Master said:
"Benevolence has its measures,
and Righteousness has length, shortness, smallness, and greatness.
Feeling distress and sorrow in the center of one's heart
is the benevolence of loving people;
following the law and forcing oneself to do so
is to rely on benevolence.
The *Shī* says:
'In the waters of the Fēng Shuǐ there are water-lilies,
did Wǔ Wáng not serve?
He bequeathed plans to his grandsons,
to comfort and assist his sons;
how truly great was Wǔ Wáng!'
This is the benevolence of several generations.
The *Guó Fēng* says:
'I now have no time for myself,
how can I worry about those after me?'
This is the benevolence of a single lifetime."
33.9 The Master said:
"As an instrument, Benevolence is heavy,
and its way is long;
those who lift it cannot overcome its weight,
and those who travel it cannot reach its end.
He who takes much of its measure is benevolent;
for those who exert themselves in Benevolence,
is it not difficult?
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ uses Righteousness to measure others,
then it is difficult for people to measure up;
if he uses human standards to look for excellence in others,
then the worthy can be known."
The Master said:
"One whose heart is at peace with Benevolence
is but one person in the world.
The *Dà Yǎ* says:
'Virtue is as light as a hair,
yet few people can lift it;
I have considered and planned for it,
only Zhòng Shān Fǔ can lift it,
I love him but cannot help him.' "
The *Xiǎo Yǎ* says:
'The high mountain is looked up to,
the great path is followed.'
The Master said:
"The *Shī* loves Benevolence like this;
heading toward the Way and proceeding,
failing halfway,
forgetting the old age of one's body,
not knowing the insufficiency of one's years
bending down and striving daily with diligence,
stopping only after death."
The Master said:
"Benevolence has long been difficult to achieve!
Every person loses what they love;
therefore, the faults of a benevolent man are easily excused."
The Master said:
"Respectfulness is close to Ritual,
frugality is close to Benevolence,
trustworthiness is close to genuine feeling,
and acting with reverence and deference;
even if such a one has faults,
they will not be severe.
Respectfulness results in few faults,
genuine feelings can be trusted,
and frugality is easy to accommodate;
those who lose their way because of these,
are they not rare?
The *Shī* says:
'The gentle and respectful person
is the foundation of virtue.' "
The Master said:
"Benevolence has long been difficult to achieve;
only the Jūnzǐ can do it.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ does not distress others with what he is able to do,
nor does he shame others with what they are unable to do.
Therefore, when the Shèng Rén establishes conduct,
he does not establish it based on himself,
but makes the people have reason for encouragement and a sense of shame,
to put his words into practice.
He uses Ritual to regulate them,
trustworthiness to bind them,
appearance and demeanor to adorn them,
robes and garments to differentiate them,
and friends to bring them to the standard,
desiring the people to be unified.
The *Xiǎo Yǎ* says:
'Not feeling ashamed before men,
not fearing Tiān.'
Therefore, when the Jūnzǐ wears his robes,
he adorns them with the demeanor of a Jūnzǐ;
having that demeanor,
he adorns it with the speech of a Jūnzǐ;
having perfected that speech,
he makes it substantial with the virtue of a Jūnzǐ.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ is ashamed to wear the robes without the demeanor,
ashamed to have the demeanor without the speech,
ashamed to have the speech without the virtue,
and ashamed to have the virtue without the conduct.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ wearing mourning garments has a look of sorrow;
wearing the ceremonial cap and robes, he has a look of reverence;
wearing armor and helmet, he has a look that cannot be insulted.
The *Shī* says:
'The pelican is on the dam,
not wetting its wings;
that man there,
is not equal to his robes.' "
33.10 The Master said:
"What the Jūnzǐ calls Righteousness
is that the noble and the humble all have their tasks in the world;
the Tiān Zǐ personally plows,
to provide grain and millet wine for serving Shàng Dì,
therefore the Zhū Hóu are diligent in assisting the Tiān Zǐ."
The Master said:
"In the service of superiors by subordinates,
even if one has the great virtue of protecting the people,
one does not dare to have the heart of a ruler over the people;
this is the depth of Benevolence.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ uses respect and frugality to strive to serve Benevolence,
and trustworthiness and deference to strive to serve Ritual,
not exalting his own tasks,
not honoring his own person,
being frugal regarding his position and having few desires,
deferring to the worthy,
humbling himself and honoring others,
being cautious and fearing Righteousness,
seeking to serve the ruler,
being satisfied with himself whether he succeeds
or does not succeed,
and thus following the mandate of Tiān.
The *Shī* says:
'Thickly grow the creepers,
spreading over the branches and trunks;
the joyous and easy-going Jūnzǐ,
seeks blessings without being devious.'
This refers to Shùn, Yǔ, Wén Wáng,
and Zhōu Gōng!
They had the great virtue of ruling the people,
and the careful caution of serving a ruler.
The *Shī* says:
'This Wén Wáng,
careful and reverent,
brilliantly served Shàng Dì,
thus he enjoyed many blessings,
his virtue was not devious,
and he received the states in all directions.' "
The Master said:
"The former kings used posthumous titles to honor names
and regulations to unify benefits,
feeling ashamed that a name might exceed one's conduct.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ does not magnify his own tasks,
nor does he exalt his own achievements,
in order to remain in the reality of the situation;
he does not boast of extraordinary conduct,
in order to remain in substance;
he displays the goodness of others
and praises the achievements of others,
in order to place himself below the worthy.
Therefore, although the Jūnzǐ humbles himself,
the people respect and honor him."
The Master said:
"Hòu Jì's
achievements for the world,
were they not more than what one hand or one foot could do?
Yet he desired his conduct to exceed his fame,
so he called himself a lowly person."
33.11 The Master said:
"What the Jūnzǐ calls Benevolence,
how difficult it is!
The *Shī* says:
'The joyous and easy-going Jūnzǐ,
the parent of the people.'
Joyous, so he uses strength to teach them;
easy-going, so he uses pleasure to settle them.
Happy but not dissolute;
ritualistic but intimate;
majestic and dignified yet peaceful;
filial and compassionate yet respectful.
He makes the people have the honor of a father
and the intimacy of a mother.
Only after this can one be a parent to the people;
who but those of the highest virtue could be like this?
Now, a father with his own son
is intimate with the worthy and looks down on the incapable;
a mother with her own son,
if he is worthy, she is intimate with him,
but if he is incapable, she pities him.
A mother
is intimate but not honored;
a father
is honored but not intimate.
Water to the people
is intimate but not honored;
fire
is honored but not intimate.
Earth to the people
is intimate but not honored;
Tiān
is honored but not intimate."
The Mandate is to the people:
close but not respected;
ghosts are
respected but not close.
33.12 Zǐ said:
"The Way of Xià honored the Mandate;
they served the ghosts and respected the spirits but kept them at a distance;
they stayed close to the people and were loyal to them;
they put emoluments before awe,
and rewards before punishments.
They were close but not respected.
The flaws of their people:
they were slow-witted and foolish,
arrogant and rustic,
and simple without refinement."
33.13 "The people of Yīn honored spirits;
they led the people to serve spirits;
they put ghosts before ritual,
and punishments before rewards.
