They were respected but not close.
The flaws of their people:
they were unrestrained and not peaceful,
and competitive without shame.
The people of Zhōu honored ritual and valued giving;
they served the ghosts and respected the spirits but kept them at a distance;
they stayed close to the people and were loyal to them;
their rewards and punishments used ranks and grades.
They were close but not respected.
The flaws of their people:
they were profit-seeking and crafty,
refined without shame,
and harmful and deceptive."
33.14 Zǐ said:
"The Way of Xià did not misuse words;
they did not seek perfection;
they did not have great expectations of the people;
thus the people did not tire of their closeness.
The people of Yīn did not misuse ritual,
but they sought perfection from the people.
The people of Zhōu pressed the people;
they did not misuse spirits,
but rewards of rank and punishments were exhausted."
33.15 Zǐ said:
"The Ways of Yú and Xià
caused little resentment among the people.
The Ways of Yīn and Zhōu
could not overcome their flaws."
Zǐ said:
"The substance of Yú and Xià
and the refinement of Yīn and Zhōu
are supreme.
In Yú and Xià, refinement did not exceed substance;
in Yīn and Zhōu, substance did not exceed refinement."
Zǐ spoke of it, saying:
"Though later generations may have creators,
the Yú Dì cannot be equaled.
Ruling the world,
he lived without selfishness
and did not enrich his son upon death.
He treated the people like a father and mother;
he had a compassionate love for them
and gave them loyal and beneficial teachings.
He was close yet respected,
peaceful yet reverent,
majestic yet loving,
wealthy yet ritualistic,
and kind yet able to distribute.
His gentlemen honored benevolence and feared righteousness;
they were ashamed of waste and held material possessions lightly;
they were loyal without offending;
they were righteous and obedient;
refined and quiet;
and broad-minded yet discerning.
The Fǔ Xíng says:
'The majesty of virtue is true majesty;
the clarity of virtue is true clarity.'
Who but the Yú Dì could be like this?"
33.16 Zǐ spoke:
"In serving a ruler, first offer words;
then bow and offer oneself
to establish trust.
Therefore, a ruler has demands of his ministers,
and ministers would die for their words.
Thus they receive emoluments without falsehood,
and their transgressions are few."
33.17 Zǐ said:
"In serving a ruler, if great words are accepted, one expects great benefit;
if small words are accepted, one expects small benefit.
Therefore, a gentleman does not receive large emoluments for small words,
nor small emoluments for great words.
The Yì says:
'Not eating at home
is auspicious.'"
33.18 Zǐ said:
"In serving a ruler, do not communicate low matters,
do not prioritize rhetoric,
and do not follow those who are not the right people.
The Xiǎo Yǎ says:
'Quietly attend to your position,
associating with the upright and honest;
the spirits hear this
and will grant you goodness.'"
33.19 Zǐ said:
"To be distant from the ruler and yet remonstrate
is flattery;
to be close and yet not remonstrate
is to be a mere beneficiary of a position."
Zǐ said:
"Close ministers maintain harmony,
the Prime Minister corrects the hundred officials,
and high ministers deliberate on the four quarters."
Zǐ said:
"In serving a ruler, one desires to remonstrate but not to display his faults.
The Shī says:
'Loving in my heart,
why should I not speak of it?
I keep it in my center;
when shall I ever forget it?'"
33.20 Zǐ said:
"In serving a ruler, if it is difficult to advance and easy to retreat,
then the positions will be in order;
if it is easy to advance and difficult to retreat,
then there is disorder.
Therefore, a gentleman bows thrice to advance
and resigns once to retreat,
so as to avoid disorder."
Zǐ said:
"In serving a ruler, if one is disagreed with three times but does not leave the borders,
then it is for the sake of profit and emolument;
though people say they are not seeking it,
I do not believe them."
Zǐ said:
"In serving a ruler, be cautious at the beginning and respectful at the end."
Zǐ said:
"In serving a ruler, one can be honored or debased,
rich or poor,
allowed to live or be killed,
but one cannot be made to cause disorder."
33.21 Zǐ said:
"In serving a ruler,
in the military one does not avoid danger;
in the court one does not decline low positions.
To occupy a position and not perform its duties
is disorder.
Therefore, when a ruler employs his minister, if the minister's aim is met,
he follows with careful consideration;
if not,
he follows with deep deliberation;
after the task is finished, he retires;
this is the sincerity of a minister.
The Yì says:
'Not serving kings and lords,
he makes his own business lofty.'"
33.22 Zǐ said:
"Only the Son of Heaven receives his mandate from Heaven;
the scholar receives his mandate from the ruler.
Therefore, if the ruler's command is accordant, the minister has accordant commands;
if the ruler's command is contrary, the minister has contrary commands.
The Shī says:
'The magpies are so persistent;
the quails are so ardent.
A man without goodness,
I take as my ruler.'"
33.23 Zǐ said:
"A gentleman does not judge a person solely by their words.
Therefore, when the Way prevails in the world,
then actions have branches and leaves;
when the Way does not prevail in the world,
then words have branches and leaves.
For this reason, when a gentleman is by the side of one in mourning,
if he cannot contribute money,
he does not ask about the expenses;
when by the side of one who is ill,
if he cannot provide food,
he does not ask what they want;
if there is a guest
whom he cannot host,
he does not ask where they are staying.
Therefore, the association of a gentleman is like water;
the association of a petty man is like sweet wine.
The gentleman's is bland but perfects;
the petty man's is sweet but ruins.
The Xiǎo Yǎ says:
'Deceptive words are very sweet;
disorder is thus nourished.'"
33.24 Zǐ said:
"If a gentleman does not praise people with mere words,
then the people will act with loyalty.
Therefore, when a gentleman asks about someone's cold,
he clothes them;
when he asks about someone's hunger,
he feeds them;
when he praises someone's excellence,
he grants them rank.
The Guó Fēng says:
'The sorrow of my heart,
to me it is a refuge.'"
33.25 The Master said:
"Generosity in words while the reality does not arrive
brings calamity and resentment upon one's person.
Therefore, a gentleman, rather than having the burden of a promise,
would rather have the resentment of a refusal.
The 'Guófēng' says:
'Your words and laughter were so cheerful,
Your vows and oaths were so solemn,
You did not think of their reversal;
Since you do not think of that reversal,
then let it be finished!'
33.26 The Master said:
"A gentleman does not use his facial expression to endear himself to others;
if the feelings are distant but the appearance is intimate,
for the petty person, is this not like the crime of boring through a wall?"
The Master said:
"Feelings should be sincere,
and words should be skillful."
33.27 The Master said:
"In the past, the enlightened kings of the Sāndài
all served the spiritual brilliance of Heaven and Earth,
and in all things made use of bǔ and shì,
not daring to use their private
desires to irreverently serve Shàngdì.
For this reason, they did not offend the sun or moon
and did not go against bǔ and shì.
Bǔ and shì were not used repetitively.
For great matters, there were set times and days;
for small matters, there were no set times or days,
but the shì was used.
External affairs used the gāng (strong) days,
and internal affairs used the róu (soft) days.
They did not go against the turtle or the stalks."
The Master said:
"Sacrificial animals of pure color, ritual and music, and the grain offerings being pure,
are the means by which they avoid harming the ghosts and spirits
and avoid resentment from the common people."
33.28 The Master said:
"The sacrifices to Hòujì are easily made abundant;
his words were humble,
his desires were frugal,
and his blessings reached his descendants.
The 'Shī' says:
'Hòujì began the sacrifices,
so that there would be no guilt or regret,
continuing down to the present.'"
33.29 The Master said:
"The vessels of the great man command awe and respect.
The Tiānzǐ has no need of the shì;
the Zhūhóu have official shì diviners.
The Tiānzǐ leads by means of the shì;
the Zhūhóu do not use the shì if not in their own states.
They divine for the site of the residence and the sleeping quarters.
The Tiānzǐ does not divine for the location of the Dàmiào."
The Master said:
"The gentleman uses sacrificial vessels when showing reverence.
Thus, he does not neglect the days and months,
does not go against the turtle or the stalks,
in order to reverently serve his ruler and elders.
In this way, those above do not treat the people with contempt,
and those below do not treat those above with disrespect."
34.1 The Master said:
"When those above are easy to serve,
and those below are easy to know,
then punishments will not be frequent."
34.2 The Master said:
"If one loves the worthy as in 'Zīyī',
and hates evil as in 'Xiàngbó',
then ranks will not be cheapened and the people will become honest,
and punishments will not be tried while the people all submit.
The 'Dàyǎ' says:
'Take Wén Wáng as your model,
and all the states will have confidence.'"
34.3 The Master said:
"As for the people,
if you teach them with virtue
and regulate them with ritual,
then the people will have a sense of dignity;
if you teach them with government
and regulate them with punishment,
then the people will have a mind to evade.
Therefore, for one who rules the people,
if you love them as your children,
the people will feel close to you;
if you bind them with trust,
the people will not rebel;
if you preside over them with respect,
the people will have a compliant mind.
The 'Fǔxíng' says:
'The Miáo people did not obey the orders,
and were controlled with punishments,
creating the five cruel punishments called laws.'
Thus, the people came to have evil character,
and eventually their line was cut off."
34.4 The Master said:
"In serving those above, those below
do not follow what they are ordered,
but follow what they see practiced.
If those above like something,
those below will surely do so to a greater degree.
Therefore, what those above like and dislike
must be handled with caution,
for they are the model for the people."
34.5 The Master said:
"When Yǔ had been established for three years,
the people followed him in benevolence;
was it necessarily that they were all benevolent?
The 'Shī' says:
'Awe-inspiring is Shī Yǐn,
all the people look up to you.'
The 'Fǔxíng' says:
'When the One Man has cause for celebration,
the millions of people rely on it.'
The 'Dàyǎ' says:
'The sincerity of Chéng Wáng
was the model for the land below.'"
34.6 The Master said:
"If those above like benevolence,
then those below will compete to be first in being benevolent.
Therefore, those who lead the people
should make their intentions clear and their teaching upright, honoring benevolence
to love the people as their children;
then the people will exert themselves in their own conduct to please those above.
The 'Shī' says:
'When there is illustrious virtue in conduct,
the four states will follow it.'"
34.7 The Master said:
"The King's words are like silk threads,
but when they come out they are like cords;
the King's words are like cords,
but when they come out they are like ropes.
Therefore, the great man does not initiate idle talk.
If something can be said
but cannot be practiced,
the gentleman does not say it;
if something can be practiced
but cannot be said,
the gentleman does not practice it.
Then the people's words will not contradict their actions,
and their actions will not contradict their words.
The 'Shī' says:
'Be carefully attentive to your behavior,
and do not fail in your demeanor.'"
34.8 The Master said:
"The gentleman guides people with words
and restrains people with his conduct.
Therefore, in speaking, one must consider the end,
and in acting, one must examine the consequences;
then the people will be careful in speech and cautious in action.
The 'Shī' says:
'Be careful in your speech,
and respect your dignified demeanor.'
The 'Dàyǎ' says:
'Solemn and profound was Wén Wáng,
who continuously and brightly remained in reverence.'"
34.9 The Master said:
"Those who lead the people
do not change their clothing haphazardly,
their bearing is constant,
in order to regulate their people;
then the virtue of the people will be unified.
The 'Shī' says:
'Those officers of the capital,
in their yellow fox furs,
their appearance never changes,
their spoken words are orderly,
their conduct returns to Zhōu,
the hope of all the people.'"
34.10 The Master said:
"If the actions of those above can be known by looking at them,
and the duties of those below can be described and recorded,
then the ruler will not doubt his ministers,
and the ministers will not be confused by their ruler.
Yǐn Jí said:
'I, Yǐn, together with Tāng,
both possessed the same single virtue.'
The 'Shī' says:
'The good man, the gentleman,
his demeanor does not err.'"
34.11 The Master said:
"One who possesses a state
makes righteousness clear and conceals evil,
in order to show the people generosity,
then the people's feelings will not be divided.
The 'Shī' says:
'Quietly fulfill the duties of your office,
and love those who are upright.'"
34.12 The Master said:
"If those above are suspicious, then the common people will be confused;
if those below are difficult to know, then the ruler will be burdened.
Therefore, for one who rules the people,
if he makes clear what he likes to show the people the customs to follow,
and is cautious about what he dislikes to restrain the people's excesses,
then the people will not be confused.
If ministers model their conduct,
do not rely on excessive words,
do not reach for what is beyond them,
and do not trouble others with what they do not know,
then the ruler will not be burdened."
The *Shī* says:
"Heaven is reverse and harsh,
and the lower people are all distressed."
The *Xiǎoyǎ* says:
"Not only do they fail to perform their duties,
they are the king's distress."
34.13 The Master said:
"When government is not carried out,
and education is not completed,
then rank and salary are insufficient to encourage,
and punishments and penalties are insufficient to induce shame.
Therefore, those above must not treat punishments with contempt nor treat rank lightly.
The *Kānggào* says:
'Be reverent and clear in your punishments.'
The *Fǔxíng* says:
'To spread punishments that do not follow the proper way.'"
34.14 The Master said:
"When great ministers are not close to the ruler,
and the common people are not at peace,
then loyalty and reverence are insufficient,
while wealth and honor have already become excessive;
when great ministers do not govern, then the near ministers form cliques.
Therefore, great ministers must be treated with respect,
for they are the models for the people;
near ministers must be chosen with caution,
for they are the guides for the people.
If the ruler does not use small matters to scheme against great ones,
does not use distant words to speak of near things,
and does not use internal affairs to plot external ones,
then the great ministers will not resent him,
the near ministers will not be jealous,
and the distant ministers will not be obscured.
The testamentary charge of *Shè Gōng* says:
'Do not let small schemes ruin great works;
do not let favored attendants cause distress to the dignified Queen;
do not let favored officers cause distress to the dignified officers,
the *Dàfū*, *Qīng*, and *Shì*.'"
The Master said:
"When great men are not close to those they should honor as worthy,
but instead trust those they should despise;
the people thereby lose their sense of closeness,
and education thereby becomes burdensome.
The *Shī* says:
'They sought my standards,
as if they could not find me;
they treated me with enmity,
and did not exert strength for me.'
The *Jūnchén* says:
'Before seeing a sage,
it is as if one were unable to see him;
once having seen a sage,
one is still unable to follow the sage.'"
34.15 The Master said:
"The common person drowns in water,
the gentleman drowns in his words,
the great man drowns among the people;
all occur because of that with which they are overly familiar.
Water is close to man yet drowns him;
virtue is easily trifled with but difficult to truly be close to,
making it easy to drown people;
words are profuse and burdensome,
easily uttered but hard to retract,
making it easy to drown people;
the people are isolated from others
and possess rustic minds—
they should be respected and not treated with contempt,
making it easy to drown people.
Therefore, the gentleman must not fail to be cautious.
The *Tàijiǎ* says:
'Do not exceed your mandate so as to overturn yourself.'
'As if preparing a crossbow,
check the notch against its measure before releasing.'
The *Yuèmìng* says:
'Only the mouth causes shame;
only armor and helmets stir up war;
only clothes are kept in the chest;
only shields and spears examine one's person.'
The *Tàijiǎ* says:
'Calamities sent by Heaven
may be avoided;
calamities brought on by oneself
cannot be escaped.'
The *Yǐnjí* says:
'I, *Yǐn*, myself followed Heaven's way,
seeing that in the western city
of *Xià*, although there was a beginning from *Zhōu*, there was an end;
the assistants likewise shared that end.'"
34.16 The Master said:
"The people take the ruler as their heart,
and the ruler takes the people as his body;
if the heart is dignified, the body is at ease;
if the heart is solemn, the appearance is reverent.
If the heart loves something,
the body will surely be settled in it;
if the ruler loves something,
the people will surely desire it.
The heart is made whole by the body,
yet also harmed by the body;
the ruler exists because of the people,
yet also perishes because of the people.
The *Shī* says:
'In the past I had former upright ministers,
whose words were brilliant and clear;
the state was thereby at peace,
the capital and cities were thereby completed,
and the common people were thereby sustained.
Who can now hold the state's completion,
yet does not act uprightly himself,
but instead ultimately toils the common people?'
The *Jūnyá* says:
'In the summer heat and rain,
the common people only complain;
in the bitter cold of winter,
the common people also only complain.'"
34.17 The Master said:
"When those below serve those above,
if their persons are not upright
and their words are not trustworthy,
then their righteousness will not be unified
and their actions will lack consistency."
The Master said:
"When words have substance and actions have standards,
then in life one's will cannot be snatched away,
and in death one's reputation cannot be snatched away.
Therefore, the gentleman hears much,
but grounds it in essentials to keep it;
he remembers much,
but grounds it in essentials to stay close to it;
he knows deeply,
but acts upon the broad outlines.
The *Jūnchén* says:
'In going out and coming in,
follow the deliberations of your multitudes;
then the various words will be in accord.'
The *Shī* says:
'The virtuous person, the gentleman—
his demeanor is one.'"
34.18 The Master said:
"Only the gentleman is able to love what is upright;
the petty person considers what is upright to be a poison.
Therefore, the gentleman's friends have a specific direction,
and his dislikes have a definite principle;
thus, those nearby are not confused,
and those far away do not doubt.
The *Shī* says:
'The gentleman seeks a good match.'"
34.19 The Master said:
"To easily break off with the poor and lowly,
but to find it difficult to break off with the wealthy and noble,
shows that one's love for the worthy is not firm
and one's hatred of evil is not manifest.
Though people say this is not harmful,
I do not believe it.
The *Shī* says:
'Friends should support one another,
supporting each other with dignified demeanor.'"
34.20 The Master said:
"Private favors that do not result in virtue
are not things the gentleman allows himself to keep.
The *Shī* says:
'When people love me,
they show me the great path.'"
34.21 The Master said:
"If there is a carriage,
its crossbar must be seen;
if there are clothes,
their wear must be seen;
if someone speaks,
their voice must be heard;
if someone acts,
their accomplishment must be seen.
The *Gétán* says:
'I wear them without becoming weary.'"
34.22 The Master said:
"If one speaks and then acts upon it,
then the words cannot be artificial;
if one acts and then speaks of it,
then the actions cannot be artificial.
Therefore, the gentleman speaks little
and acts much to fulfill his trustworthiness;
thus, the people cannot exaggerate his beauty nor minimize his faults.
The *Shī* says:
'A flaw in a white jade tablet
can still be polished away;
a flaw in these words
cannot be undone.'
The *Xiǎoyǎ* says:
'Truly is the gentleman;
truly has he great achievement.'
The *Jūnshì* says:
'In the past, *Shàngdì*
surveyed the world to observe the virtue of *Wén Wáng*,
then he gathered the Great Mandate upon his person.'"
34.23 The Master said:
“The Southerners have a saying:
‘If a person lacks constancy,
they cannot be a diviner
or a shaman.’
Is this not an ancient saying?
Even the tortoise shell and yarrow stalks cannot know [the truth of the matter],
how much less so for a person?
The *Shī* says:
‘My tortoise shell is already weary,
it does not tell me the plans.’
The *Yuè Mìng* says:
‘Rank should not be given to those of evil character;
the people will stand firm and affairs will be rectified.’
‘To offer sacrifices with insincerity
is to show disrespect;
if affairs are multifarious, there is disorder;
serving the spirits then becomes difficult.’
The *Yì* says:
‘Not being constant in one’s virtue,
one may meet with shame.’
‘Being constant in one’s virtue is a matter of perseverance;
for a woman it is auspicious,
for a man it is ominous.’”
35.1 The Ritual for Hastening to a Funeral:
When first hearing of a relative's death,
respond to the messenger with weeping,
exhausting one’s grief;
ask for the details,
and weep again, exhausting one’s grief.
35.2 Then depart immediately,
traveling one hundred *lǐ* a day,
and do not travel by night.
Only for the death of a parent,
travel when the stars are visible,
and rest when the stars appear.
If one has not yet been able to depart,
then put on the mourning dress before departing.
When passing through a state and reaching its border,
weep until one’s grief is exhausted and then stop.
Avoid weeping in marketplaces and courts.
Upon seeing the border of one’s own state, weep.
Upon arriving at the house,
enter through the left side of the gate,
ascend by the western steps,
sit to the west of the coffin facing east,
weep until one’s grief is exhausted,
tie up the hair and bare the shoulder,
descend from the hall and take one’s place in the east,
weep facing west,
complete the ritual leaping,
put on the upper garment and the hempen headband in the eastern part of the corridor,
and tie the twisted hempen girdle.
Return to the place,
bow to the guests and complete the ritual leaping,
see off the guests,
and return to the place;
if there are guests who arrive later,
then bow to them,
completing the ritual leaping and seeing off the guests as at the beginning.
The various masters of the house and brothers all exit the gate;
upon exiting the gate, the weeping stops;
close the gate,
and the master of ceremonies announces to take one’s place in the temporary lodging.
At the second weeping,
tie up the hair, bare the shoulder, and complete the ritual leaping;
at the third weeping,
still tie up the hair, bare the shoulder, and complete the ritual leaping.
On the third day,
put on the mourning dress,
and bowing to the guests and seeing them off are both as at the beginning.
35.3 If the one hastening to the funeral is not the chief mourner,
then the chief mourner bows to and sees off the guests for them.
For those hastening to a funeral who wear the *zī cuī* mourning dress or below,
they enter through the left side of the gate, face north in the central courtyard, weep until their grief is exhausted,
put on the *miǎn* and hempen headband in the eastern part of the corridor,
take their place and bare the shoulder,
weep with the chief mourner and complete the ritual leaping.
At the second weeping and the third weeping, they always wear the *miǎn* and bare the shoulder;
if there are guests,
then the chief mourner bows to and sees off the guests.
The way men and women receive them
is entirely according to their positions for the morning and evening weeping,
without change.
35.4 When hastening to a mother’s funeral,
face west and weep until one’s grief is exhausted,
tie up the hair and bare the shoulder,
descend from the hall and take one’s place in the east,
weep facing west,
complete the ritual leaping,
put on the upper garment, the *miǎn*, and the hempen headband in the eastern part of the corridor,
bow to the guests and see off the guests,
all following the ritual for hastening to a father’s funeral,
but at the second weeping, do not tie up the hair.
35.5 When a woman hastens to a funeral,
she ascends by the eastern steps,
sits to the west of the coffin facing east,
and weeps until her grief is exhausted;
she ties her hair in the *zhuā* style in the east,
takes her place,
and performs the ritual leaping in alternation with the chief mourner.
35.6 If the one hastening to a funeral does not arrive before the encoffinment,
they first go to the grave,
sit facing north,
and weep until their grief is exhausted.
The chief mourner receives them
by taking a place to the left of the grave,
while the women are to the right of the grave,
completing the ritual leaping,
exhausting the grief.
Tie up the hair,
take the chief mourner’s place in the east,
put on the headband and twisted hempen girdle,
weep and complete the ritual leaping,
bow to the guests,
return to the place,
complete the ritual leaping,
and the master of ceremonies announces that the matter is finished.
Then put on the cap and return home,
enter through the left side of the gate,
face north and weep until grief is exhausted,
tie up the hair, bare the shoulder, and complete the ritual leaping,
take the place in the east,
and bow to the guests and complete the ritual leaping.
When the guests exit,
the chief mourner bows as he sees them off;
if there are guests who arrive later,
then bow to them and complete the ritual leaping,
seeing off the guests as at the beginning.
The various masters of the house and brothers all exit the gate,
and upon exiting the gate, the weeping stops;
the master of ceremonies announces to take one’s place in the temporary lodging.
At the second weeping,
tie up the hair and complete the ritual leaping;
at the third weeping,
still tie up the hair and complete the ritual leaping.
On the third day, put on the mourning dress;
at the fifth weeping,
the master of ceremonies announces that the matter is finished.
What is different for a mother compared to a father
is that one ties up the hair only once,
and for the rest, one wears the *miǎn* to finish the rites;
other matters are according to the ritual for hastening to a father’s funeral.
35.7 For those wearing the *zī cuī* mourning dress or below who do not arrive before the encoffinment:
first go to the grave,
face west and weep until grief is exhausted,
put on the *miǎn* and hempen headband in the east,
take one’s place,
weep with the chief mourner and complete the ritual leaping,
and put on the upper garment.
If there are guests,
then the chief mourner bows to and sees off the guests;
if there are guests who arrive later,
bow to them as at the beginning.
The master of ceremonies announces that the matter is finished.
Then put on the cap and return home,
enter through the left side of the gate,
face north and weep until grief is exhausted,
put on the *miǎn*, bare the shoulder, and complete the ritual leaping,
take the place in the east,
bow to the guests and complete the ritual leaping,
and when the guests exit,
the chief mourner bows as he sees them off.
At the second weeping,
put on the *miǎn*, bare the shoulder, and complete the ritual leaping;
at the third weeping,
still wear the *miǎn*, bare the shoulder, and complete the ritual leaping.
On the third day, put on the mourning dress;
at the fifth weeping,
the master of ceremonies announces that the matter is finished.
35.8 If one hears of a death but cannot hasten to the funeral,
weep until grief is exhausted;
ask for the details,
and again weep until grief is exhausted.
Then arrange the place,
tie up the hair, bare the shoulder, and complete the ritual leaping,
put on the upper garment, headband, and twisted hempen girdle, and take one’s place;
—bow to the guests, return to the place, and complete the ritual leaping.
When the guests exit,
the chief mourner bows as he sees them off outside the gate,
and returns to his place;
if there are guests who arrive later,
bow to them and complete the ritual leaping,
seeing off the guests as at the beginning.
At the second weeping,
tie up the hair, bare the shoulder, and complete the ritual leaping,
at the third weeping,
still tie up the hair, bare the shoulder, and complete the ritual leaping,
on the third day, put on the mourning dress,
at the fifth weeping,
bow to and see off the guests as at the beginning.
35.9 If one returns after the mourning period has ended,
then he goes to the grave,
wails, and completes the leaping ritual;
to the east he binds his hair, bares his shoulder, and puts on the *zhì* fillet;
he bows to the guests and completes the leaping;
he sees off the guests and returns to his position;
he wails again to the full extent of grief,
and then removes the mourning attire,
and does not wail at home.
The host’s treatment of him
involves no change in dress;
he wails with him,
but does not leap.
35.10 From the *Zīcuī* grade downwards,
that which makes a difference
is the *miǎn* headcloth and the hemp.
35.11 In all cases of setting up a position,
if it is not for a parent’s funeral,
for *Zīcuī* and below,
all take their positions and wail to the full extent of grief,
then to the east they put on the *miǎn* headcloth and *zhì* fillet,
return to their positions,
bare the shoulder, complete the leaping, and put on the upper garment;
they bow to the guests and return to their positions;
wail and complete the leaping;
see off the guests and return to their positions;
and the master of ceremonies announces they should go to their temporary lodging.
On the third day,
after five wailings are finished,
the host goes out to see off the guests;
the other hosts and brothers all go out the door,
and the wailing stops.
The master of ceremonies announces the service is finished.
They put on the mourning dress and bow to the guests.
If the house where the position is set is far,
they put on the mourning dress and go there.
35.12 For *Zīcuī*,
one wails upon seeing the home village;
for *Dàgōng*,
one wails upon seeing the gate;
for *Xiǎogōng*,
one wails upon reaching the gate;
for *Sīmá*,
one wails upon reaching the designated position.
35.13 One wails for the father’s kin in the ancestral temple;
for the mother’s or wife’s kin in the inner chamber;
for a teacher outside the temple gate;
for friends outside the chamber gate;
for acquaintances in the open field under a tent.
In all cases of setting up a position, no offerings are made.
Wailing for the *Tiānzǐ* is nine times,
for the *Zhūhóu* seven,
for the *Qīng* and *Dàfū* five,
and for the *Shì* three.
When a *Dàfū* wails for a *Zhūhóu*,
he does not dare to bow to guests.
When ministers are in another state,
they set up a position and wail
but do not dare to bow to guests.
If one is a brother to a *Zhūhóu*,
he also sets up a position and wails.
In all cases of setting up a position, one bares the shoulder once.
35.14 When an acquaintance offers condolences,
he first wails at the house and then goes to the grave,
and for both he completes the leaping,
following the host and leaping while facing north.
In all mourning,
if the father is alive, the father is the principal mourner;
if the father is deceased,
and brothers live together,
each is principal mourner for the funeral in his own family.
If the kinship is the same,
the eldest is the principal mourner;
if it is not the same,
the one more closely related is the principal mourner.
35.15 Upon hearing of the death of a distant brother,
if the mourning period has already ended when one hears of it,
one puts on the *miǎn* headcloth, bares the shoulder, and completes the leaping ritual,
and when bowing to guests, the left hand is placed on top.
35.16 For those who have no prescribed mourning dress but set up a position,
only for a sister-in-law or brother-in-law, or women who have lowered their grade
but have no dress, they wear hemp.
35.17 In all cases of rushing to a funeral,
if a *Dàfū* arrives,
one bares the shoulder,
bows to him,
and completes the leaping before putting on the upper garment;
for a *Shì*,
one puts on the upper garment and then bows to him.
When a parent first dies,
with hair bound with dark hemp and feet bare,
one tucks in the upper lapel
and wails with hands clasped.
A heart of grief and sorrow,
a feeling of painful distress,
injures the kidneys, dries the liver, and scorches the lungs;
water and congee do not enter the mouth,
and for three days no fire is lit;
therefore neighbors provide thin congee to feed him.
When sorrow and grief are within,
the outward form changes;
when painful distress is in the heart,
the mouth finds no sweetness in flavor,
and the body finds no comfort in beauty.
After three days the encoffining takes place;
on the bed the body is called *Shī*,
in the coffin it is called *Jiù*.
When moving the *Shī* or lifting the *Jiù*,
wailing and leaping are done without count.
A heart of grief and sorrow,
a feeling of painful distress,
when grief is full and the spirit is overwhelmed,
one therefore bares the shoulder and leaps,
as a means to move the body, calm the heart, and settle the breath.
Women should not bare the shoulder,
therefore they open their garments over the breast, strike their hearts, and leap like a sparrow,
with thumping and hollow sounds,
like a wall collapsing—
the extremity of sorrow and painful distress.
Therefore it is said:
“Striking the breast, leaping, wailing, and weeping; with grief one sees them off.
Seeing the physical form depart
and welcoming the spirit back.”
At the departure for burial,
one looks forward with longing and anxiety,
as if chasing someone and being unable to catch up;
on returning and wailing,
one looks about in bewilderment,
as if seeking something and being unable to find it.
Thus the departure is like a child’s yearning for parents,
and the return is like being lost in doubt.
Seeking and finding nothing,
entering the gate and not seeing them,
going up to the hall and still not seeing them,
entering the chamber and still not seeing them.
Gone!
Lost!
They can never be seen again!
Therefore wailing, weeping, striking the breast, and leaping—
one only stops when grief is exhausted.
The heart is disappointed, sorrowful,
bewildered, and full of sighs;
the heart is broken and the mind is sad.
They are sacrificed to in the ancestral temple,
feeding them as spirits,
hoping for their return by some stroke of luck.
After completing the grave and returning,
one does not dare enter the living quarters,
but stays in a lean-to hut,
grieving that the parent is outside;
sleeping on straw and pillowing on a clod of earth,
grieving that the parent is in the soil.
Therefore wailing and weeping occur at no fixed time,
and mourning is diligently observed for three years;
this heart of longing and yearning
is the will of a filial son
and the reality of human feelings.
Someone asked:
“Regarding encoffining only after three days of death—
what is the reason for this?”
The answer was:
“When a parent of a filial son dies,
he is filled with grief and his mind is overwhelmed,
so he crawls and wails for them,
as if they might return to life;
how could he bear to take them away and encoffin them?
Therefore it is said:
encoffining after three days
is to wait for their revival;
if after three days they do not revive,
they will never revive.
The heart of the filial son also gradually weakens;
the arrangements for the household,
and the preparation of mourning garments,
can also be completed;
relatives from afar
can also arrive.
Therefore, the Sages made this decision, establishing three days as the ritual rule.”
Someone asked:
“One who wears a cap does not bare the skin—
why is this?”
The answer was:
“The cap
is most honorable
and should not be on a body with the shoulder bared to the skin;
therefore the *miǎn* headcloth is used to replace it.”
“In that case, those who are bald do not wear the *miǎn*,
the hunchbacked do not bare the shoulder,
and the lame do not leap;
it is not that they are not sorrowful;
but their bodies have chronic ailments,
so they cannot fully perform the rituals.
Therefore it is said:
‘In mourning rituals, grief is the principal thing.’
When women wail, weep, and grieve,
they strike their breasts and are heartbroken;
when men wail, weep, and grieve,
they bow their heads to the ground without regard for appearance;
this is the extremity of grief.”
Someone asked:
"What is the *miǎn* for?"
It was said:
"It is the garment worn by those who do not wear a ceremonial cap.
The *Lǐ* says:
'A youth does not wear the *sī* mourning,
unless he is the head of the household.'
Those in *sī* mourning wear the *miǎn*;
when one is the head of the household, he wears the *miǎn* and carries a staff."
Someone asked:
"What is the staff?"
It was said:
"Bamboo and paulownia are used for the same purpose.
Therefore, for a father, a *jūzhàng* is used;
a *jūzhàng*
is made of bamboo.
For a mother, a *xiāozhàng* is used;
a *xiāozhàng*
is made of paulownia."
Someone asked:
"What is the staff for?"
It was said:
"When a filial son loses a parent,
he wails and cries without limit,
and performs his duties for three years.
His body becomes sick and his limbs emaciated;
he uses the staff to support his illness.
Thus, while his father is alive, he does not dare use the staff,
because an honorable person is present.
He does not use the staff in the hall,
avoiding the place where the honorable person resides.
He does not hurry in the hall,
showing that he is not in haste.
This is the intent of the filial son,
the reality of human emotion,
and the principle of ritual righteousness.
It did not descend from heaven,
nor did it emerge from the earth;
it is simply human emotion."
The *Chuán* says:
"There are cases of moving from light to heavy,"
such as the wife of a *gōngzǐ* mourning for her *huánggū*.
"There are cases of moving from heavy to light,"
such as mourning for the parents of one's wife.
"There are cases of moving from having no mourning dress to having mourning dress,"
such as the wife of a *gōngzǐ* mourning for the maternal brothers of the *gōngzǐ*.
"There are cases of moving from having mourning dress to having none,"
such as a *gōngzǐ* mourning for the parents of his wife.
The *Chuán* says:
"If the mother was divorced,
then one wears mourning dress for the kin of the stepmother;
if the mother died,
then one wears mourning dress for the kin of one's own mother."
If one wears mourning for the kin of one's own mother,
then one does not wear mourning for the kin of the stepmother.
In the three-year mourning,
after the *liàn* sacrifice,
if there is a mourning of one year,
and the burial has already taken place,
then one wears the former kudzu sash,
the *dié* of the one-year mourning,
and wears the *gōngcuī* garment.
For a mourning of *dàgōng*,
it is also like this.
For *xiǎogōng*,
there is no change.
Hemp with its roots
replaces the kudzu of the three-year mourning.
After the *liàn* sacrifice,
if one encounters hemp with its roots cut off,
at the time of the *miǎn*,
one wears the *dié*;
after the *miǎn*,
one removes the *dié*.
Whenever the *dié* can be worn, it must be worn;
after it is worn,
it is removed.
For *xiǎogōng*, one does not change the *liàn* cap of the mourning;
if wearing the *miǎn*,
then one wears the *dié* for *sī* or *xiǎogōng* mourning,
following the original kudzu sash.
The hemp of *sī*
does not change the kudzu of *xiǎogōng*;
the hemp of *xiǎogōng*
does not change the kudzu of *dàgōng*.
The use of roots marks the transition.
For children who die young:
for those of the elder and middle stages,
one changes the kudzu of the three-year mourning.
When the months of mourning for the child who died young are calculated and ended,
one returns to the kudzu of the three-year mourning.
This is not because of double hemp,
but because there is no transition for the end of wailing.
For those of the lower stage, this is not done.
A ruler mourns for the *Tiānzǐ* for three years;
the *fūrén* mourns as the *wàizōng* mourns for the ruler.
The *shìzǐ* does not wear mourning for the *Tiānzǐ*.
Those over whom the ruler presides:
the *fūrén*, other wives, the *dàzǐ*, and the wife of the eldest son.
The eldest son of a *dàfū* mourns for the ruler, the *fūrén*, and the *dàzǐ*
as a *shì* wears mourning.
If the ruler's mother
is not the *fūrén*,
then the various ministers have no mourning.
Only the close ministers, the attendants, and the *cānchéng* follow in mourning;
only what the ruler wears,
do they wear.
A *gōng* wears *xīcuī* when residing among the *qīng* and *dàfū*,
and also when going out.
When attending to affairs, he wears the *biàndié*.
When *dàfū* are with each other,
it is also thus.
For his wife,
he wears it when going to her,
but not when going out.
Generally, when seeing others, one does not wear the *miǎn* or *dié*;
even when attending the court of the ruler,
one does not wear the *miǎn* or *dié*.
Only at the gates of the ruler's palace is there the transition to *qīcuī*.
The *Chuán* says:
"A *jūnzǐ* does not deprive others of their mourning,
nor can his own mourning be deprived."
The *Chuán* says:
"There are many crimes but the punishments are five;
there are many mournings but the garments are five;
attaching to those above and those below,
these are the ranks."
38.1 Why is *jū* hemp worn for *zhǎncuī*?
*Jū*
is of an ugly appearance,
which is used to take the inner state as primary and manifest it on the outside.
The appearance of *zhǎncuī* is like *jū*;
the appearance of *qīcuī* is like *xǐ* hemp;
the appearance of *dàgōng* is like *zhǐ* hemp;
for *xiǎogōng* and *sīmá*, the appearance and manner should be appropriate.
This is sorrow manifesting in the appearance of the body.
The wailing of *zhǎncuī*
is as if departing and not returning;
the wailing of *qīcuī*
is as if departing and returning;
the wailing of *dàgōng*
is three modulations and then a lingering sigh;
for *xiǎogōng* and *sīmá*,
the expression of sorrow should be appropriate.
This is sorrow manifesting in sounds and voice.
For *zhǎncuī*,
one acknowledges but does not respond;
for *qīcuī*,
one responds but does not speak;
for *dàgōng*,
one speaks but does not deliberate;
for *xiǎogōng* and *sīmá*,
one deliberates but does not touch upon music.
This is sorrow manifesting in words and speech.
For *zhǎncuī*,
one does not eat for three days;
for *qīcuī*,
one does not eat for two days;
for *dàgōng*,
one skips three meals;
for *xiǎogōng* and *sīmá*,
one skips two meals.
If a *shì* assists in the enshrouding,
he skips one meal.
Therefore, for the mourning of parents,
after the encoffinment, one eats congee,
one *yì* of rice in the morning,
and one *yì* of rice in the evening.
For the mourning of *qīcuī*,
one eats coarse food and drinks water,
and does not eat vegetables or fruit.
For the mourning of *dàgōng*,
one does not eat vinegar or sauces.
For *xiǎogōng* and *sīmá*,
one does not drink sweet wine.
This is sorrow manifesting in diet.
For the mourning of parents,
after the *yú* and *zúkū* sacrifices,
one eats coarse food and drinks water,
and does not eat vegetables or fruit.
After one year at the *xiǎoxiáng*,
one eats vegetables and fruit.
After another year at the *dàxiáng*,
there may be vinegar and sauces.
In the following month is the *dàn* sacrifice;
after the *dàn*, one drinks sweet wine.
When first drinking wine, one first drinks sweet wine.
When first eating meat, one first eats dried meat.
For the mourning of parents,
one lives in a lean-to hut,
sleeps on straw mats and pillows on a clod of earth,
and does not remove the *dié* or the sash.
For the mourning of *qīcuī*,
one lives in a whitewashed room,
and the mats are trimmed but not woven in.
In the mourning of *Dàgōng*,
one sleeps on a mat;
in *Xiǎogōng* and *Sīmá*,
a bed is permissible.
This is the manifestation of grief in one’s dwelling and rest.
In the mourning for parents,
after the *Yú* sacrifice and the cessation of wailing,
the pillars and lintels are trimmed and a clipped screen is used;
a trimmed sedge mat is used but not tucked in at the edges.
After one year, at the *Xiǎoxiáng* ritual,
one lives in a whitewashed room
and sleeps on a mat.
After another year, at the *Dàxiáng* ritual,
one returns to the regular sleeping quarters.
In the intermediate month, the *Dàn* sacrifice is performed;
after the *Dàn* sacrifice, one may use a bed.
The *Zhǎncuī* cloth is of three *shēng*;
the *Zīcuī* is of four, five, or six *shēng*;
the *Dàgōng* is of seven, eight, or nine *shēng*;
the *Xiǎogōng* is of ten, eleven, or twelve *shēng*;
the *Sīmá* is of fifteen *shēng* with half the threads removed;
when work has been done on the threads but not on the cloth, it is called *Sī*.
This is the manifestation of grief in clothing.
For the *Zhǎncuī* of three *shēng*,
after the *Yú* sacrifice and the cessation of wailing,
it is replaced by a finished cloth of six *shēng* and a cap of seven *shēng*.
For a mother, the *Shūcuī* is of four *shēng*,
and it is replaced by a finished cloth of seven *shēng* and a cap of eight *shēng*.
The hemp is removed and kudzu cloth is worn,
with a kudzu sash of three layers.
After one year, at the *Xiǎoxiáng* ritual,
one wears a boiled-silk cap with light-red borders;
the waist band is not yet removed;
men remove the head band,
while women remove the waist band.
—Why do men remove the head band?
Why do women remove the waist band?
Men place importance on the head;
women place importance on the waist.
When removing mourning garments, one starts with the most important part;
when changing garments, one changes the lighter ones first.
After another year, at the *Dàxiáng* ritual,
one wears plain white silk and a hempen robe.
In the intermediate month, the *Dàn* sacrifice is performed;
after the *Dàn*, one wears fine dark cloth
and there is nothing one may not wear as an ornament.
Why change the garments?
It is to change into lighter ones.
During the mourning of *Zhǎncuī*,
after the *Yú* sacrifice and the cessation of wailing,
if one encounters the mourning of *Zīcuī*,
the lighter mourning is wrapped with the heavier,
while the heavier mourning remains distinct.
After the boiled-silk ritual,
if one encounters the mourning of *Dàgōng*,
the hemp and kudzu are worn together.
38.2 In the mourning of *Zīcuī*,
after the *Yú* sacrifice and the cessation of wailing,
if one encounters the mourning of *Dàgōng*,
the hemp and kudzu are worn together.
38.3 The kudzu of *Zhǎncuī*
is the same as the hemp of *Zīcuī*;
the kudzu of *Zīcuī*
is the same as the hemp of *Dàgōng*;
the kudzu of *Dàgōng*
is the same as the hemp of *Xiǎogōng*;
the kudzu of *Xiǎogōng*
is the same as the hemp of *Sīmá*;
when the hemp is the same, they are worn together.
When wearing them together, if the mourning is for a heavier grade,
then the lighter one is replaced.
39.1 What is the meaning of the three-year mourning period?
It is said:
It establishes formal expressions in proportion to the emotions
and uses them to give order to the multitude,
distinguishing the degrees of closeness and distance, and of nobility and commonness,
such that they cannot be diminished or increased.
Therefore it is said:
"It is a way that does not change."
When a wound is deep, it takes a long time to heal;
when the pain is severe, the recovery is slow.
The three-year mourning
establishes formal expressions in proportion to the emotions;
it is the means to mark the extremity of the greatest pain.
The unhemmed sackcloth, the staff of the female hemp plant,
living in a lean-to hut,
eating congee,
and sleeping on straw with a clod for a pillow—
these are the ornaments of the greatest pain.
The three-year mourning
concludes in twenty-five months.
The sorrow and pain have not yet ended,
and the longing and affection are not forgotten.
Yet the mourning is cut off at this point;
is this not because the sending off of the dead must have an end,
and the return to life must have its regulations?
39.2 Among all things born between heaven and earth,
those belonging to the category of blood and breath
must have consciousness.
Among those with consciousness,
there is none that does not love its own kind.
Now take the large birds and beasts:
when they lose their mates,
after a month or a season has passed,
they will surely return to wander,
passing by their old haunts,
circling around,
crying out,
pacing to and fro,
and hesitating long
before they are able to leave.
Even small ones like swallows and sparrows
will chirp for a moment
before they can leave.
Therefore, among those with blood and breath,
none has more consciousness than man.
Thus, man’s feelings for his parents
are inexhaustible even until death.
39.3 If we followed the way of those who are dissolute and perverse,
they would forget their dead in the evening after they died in the morning.
But if we were to follow them,
then we would be worse than birds and beasts;
how then could we live together in a community without disorder?
39.4 If we followed the way of the refined gentleman who cultivates himself,
then the three-year mourning,
which ends in twenty-five months,
would pass like a team of four horses glimpsed through a crevice;
if he were to follow his feelings to the end,
then it would be unending.
39.5 Therefore, the former kings established a middle course and created regulations;
once they had made it sufficient to fulfill the formal principle,
it was to be set aside.
39.6 In that case, why does the mourning last for one year?
It is said:
For the closest kin, it is cut off at one year.
Why is this?
It is said:
Because heaven and earth have already completed their cycle,
and the four seasons have already changed.
Among all things within heaven and earth,
none does not begin anew;
this is modeled after that.
39.7 In that case, why is it three years?
It is said:
It is to add to its honor.
This is done by doubling it,
thus it is two full years.
39.8 Why are there periods from nine months downward?
It is said:
It is to show that they do not reach the same level.
Therefore, three years is the height of honor,
*Sīmá* and *Xiǎogōng* are the reductions,
while one year and nine months are the intermediate steps.
Above, it takes its model from heaven;
below, it takes its law from earth;
in the middle, it takes its rule from man.
The principle by which people live together in harmony and unity is thus complete.
Therefore, the three-year mourning
is the most refined expression of the Way of Man;
this is called the pinnacle of honor.
This is what all the kings shared,
and what has been uniform from ancient times to the present;
no one knows from whence it first came.
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"A child is three years old
before he leaves his parents' embrace.
The three-year mourning
is the universal mourning for all under heaven."
In ancient times, the *Shēnyī*
had its standard system
to correspond to the compass, the square, the plumb-line, the weights, and the balance.
It was short enough not to show the skin,
and long enough not to drag on the ground.
The side-pieces were joined,
and the edges were curved.
The waist seam was half the width of the bottom hem;
the height of the armpits
allowed for the rotation of the elbow;
the length of the sleeves
was such that they reached the elbow when folded back.
Below the belt, it did not press against the thighs;
above, it did not press against the ribs—
it rested where there are no bones.
Its manufacture:
it used twelve panels to correspond to the twelve months;
the sleeves were rounded to correspond to the compass;
the square collar was like a carpenter’s square to correspond to the square;
the seam down the back reached to the ankles to correspond to the plumb-line;
the bottom hem was as level as the weights and the balance to correspond to equilibrium.
Therefore, for the compass-curve,
the movement of lifting the hand is done for grace;
for those bearing the line and holding the square,
they serve to rectify the government
and square the sense of righteousness.
Thus the *Yì* says:
“The movement of the Six-Two of *Kūn*
is straight and square.”
The lower hem being even like a balance and scale
serves to settle the will and calm the heart.
When these five methods have been applied,
the sages wear it.
Thus, the compass and square are chosen for their impartiality,
the line is chosen for its straightness,
and the balance and scale are chosen for their levelness;
therefore, the former kings valued them.
Thus it can be used for the civil,
it can be used for the military,
it can be used for receiving
or assisting guests,
and it can be used for governing the military;
it is complete yet not wasteful,
the best among garments.
If one has both parents and grandparents,
the borders of the robe are decorated with variegated colors;
if one has parents,
the borders are blue.
For an orphan,
the borders are plain white.
The borders of the sleeves, the edges, and the lower hem
are each an inch and a half wide.
41.1 In the ritual of *Tóuhù*,
the host presents the arrows,
the *Sīshè* presents the *zhōng*,
and someone is instructed to hold the pot.
The host makes a request, saying:
“I have these crooked arrows and an uneven pot,
and I request to entertain the guest with them.”
The guest says:
“You have fine wine and excellent food,
with which I have already been favored;
to add further music to this,
I venture to decline.”
The host says:
“The crooked arrows and uneven pot
are not worth declining;
I venture to persist in my request.”
The guest says:
“I have already been favored,
and to add further music to this,
I venture to firmly decline.”
The host says:
“The crooked arrows and uneven pot
are not worth declining;
I venture to persist in my request.”
The guest says:
“I have firmly declined but have not received your permission;
I venture to respectfully obey.”
41.2 The guest bows twice and receives the arrows;
the host turns and moves away,
saying:
“Avoid.”
The host bows from the top of the eastern steps as the guest departs,
the guest turns and moves away,
saying:
“Avoid.”
41.3 Having bowed,
they receive the arrows,
advance to the space between the two pillars,
and retreat to their positions;
they bow to the guest and proceed to the mats.
41.4 The *Sīshè* advances to measure the distance for the pot,
placing it at a distance of two and a half arrow-lengths;
he returns to his position,
sets up the *zhōng*,
facing east,
and stands up holding eight counters.
41.5 He requests of the guest, saying:
“A direct pitch counts as an entry;
consecutive pitches are not counted separately;
the winners make the losers drink;
after the regular cup has gone around,
I request to set up ‘horses’ for the winner;
one horse follows two horses;
once three horses are established,
I request to celebrate the one with the most horses.”
He makes the same request of the host.
41.6 He commands the musicians, saying:
“Please play *Lí Shǒu*,
keeping the intervals uniform.”
The *Dàshī* says:
“Understood.”
41.7 Those on the left and right report that the arrows are ready
and request to pitch in turn.
If there is an entry,
the *Sīshè* sits and sets down one counter.
The guest’s party is on the right,
and the host’s party is on the left.
41.8 When the pitching is finished,
the *Sīshè* holds the counters and says:
“The left and right have finished pitching;
I request to count.”
Two counters make a *chún*;
they take them by the *chún*,
and a single counter is a *jī*.
Then, using the *jī* counters, he announces:
“Such-and-such person has excelled over such-and-such person by so many *chún*.”
If there is an odd one, he says:
If they are equal, he says:
“The left and right are equal.”
41.9 He orders the pouring of wine, saying:
“Please circulate the cup.”
The pourer says:
“Understood.”
Those who are to drink all kneel and receive the cup,
saying:
“I receive your kind pouring”;
the winner kneels and says:
“I respectfully nourish you.”
41.10 After the regular cup has gone around,
he requests to set up the horses.
Each horse corresponds to its counters.
One horse follows two horses
to celebrate.
The celebratory ritual says:
“The three horses are complete;
I request to celebrate the one with the most horses.”
Both the guest and the host say:
“Understood.”
After the regular cup has gone around,
he requests to remove the horses.
41.11 The number of counters is determined by their seats.
As for the arrows:
inside a room, they are five *fú* long;
on the hall, seven *fú*;
in the courtyard, nine *fú*.
The counters are one foot and two inches long.
The pot:
its neck is seven inches long,
its belly is five inches long,
and the mouth diameter is two and a half inches;
it holds one *dǒu* and five *shēng*.
The pot is filled with small beans
to prevent the arrows from bouncing out.
The pot is two and a half arrow-lengths away from the mats.
The arrows are made of wild mulberry or thornwood,
and their bark is not removed.
41.12 The Lǔ instruction to the disciples says:
“Do not be disrespectful,
do not be arrogant,
do not stand with your back turned,
do not speak across others;
for standing with the back turned or speaking across others,
there is a regular penalty cup.”
The Xuē instruction to the disciples says:
“Do not be disrespectful,
do not be arrogant,
do not stand with your back turned,
do not speak across others;
those who do such things shall be penalized.”
41.13 Drumming: half is Lǔ drumming;
half is Xuē drumming.
Using half or less constitutes the ritual of *Tóuhù*;
using it in its entirety constitutes the ritual of archery.
The *Sīshè*,
the *Tíngzhǎng*,
and the capped gentlemen standing there
all belong to the guest’s party;
the musicians, the attendants, and the youths
all belong to the host’s party.
Lǔ drumming:
half;
Xuē drumming:
half.
42.1 *Lǔ Āi Gōng* asked *Kǒngzǐ*, saying:
“Is your attire, Master,
the attire of a scholar?”
*Kǒngzǐ* replied, saying:
“When I, *Qiū*, was young and lived in Lǔ,
I wore robes with wide sleeves;
when I lived in Sòng,
I wore the *Zhāngfǔ* cap.
I, *Qiū*, have heard:
A gentleman’s learning is broad,
but his attire follows local custom;
I do not know of any specific scholar’s attire.”
*Lǔ Āi Gōng* said:
“May I venture to ask about the conduct of a scholar?”
*Kǒngzǐ* replied:
“If I were to enumerate them quickly,
I could not finish the list of items;
if I were to enumerate them in detail, it would take a long time,
even changing attendants would not be enough to finish.”
*Lǔ Āi Gōng* ordered a mat to be set.
*Kǒngzǐ* sat in attendance.
He said:
"A Rú possesses treasures on a mat while awaiting an invitation;
he studies diligently day and night while awaiting questions;
he harbors loyalty and trustworthiness while awaiting recommendation;
he acts with effort while awaiting selection.
Such is his self-establishment.
"A Rú is proper in his cap and gown;
he is cautious in his movements and actions.
His great deference seems like negligence;
his small deference seems like pretense.
In great matters, he seems awe-inspiring;
in small matters, he seems ashamed.
He is difficult to advance but easy to withdraw;
he appears humble as if he lacks ability.
Such is his appearance.
"A Rú remains composed and serious in his dwelling;
his sitting and rising are respectful.
In speech, he prioritizes trustworthiness;
in action, he must be upright and balanced.
On the road, he does not compete for the advantage of easy or difficult paths;
in winter and summer, he does not compete for the comfort of shade or warmth.
He cherishes his life to await his purpose;
he cultivates his body to accomplish things.
Such is his preparation and caution.
"A Rú does not treasure gold or jade,
but regards loyalty and trustworthiness as his treasures.
He does not pray for land,
but establishes righteousness as his land.
He does not pray for great accumulation of wealth,
but regards much learning as his wealth.
He is hard to obtain but easy to provide with a salary;
he is easy to provide with a salary but hard to keep as a retainer.
If it is not the right time, he is not seen;
is he not indeed hard to obtain?
If it is not righteous, he does not join;
is he not indeed hard to keep?
He works first and receives a salary later;
is he not indeed easy to provide with a salary?
Such is his way of approaching others.
"If a Rú is entrusted with goods and wealth,
or immersed in pleasures and hobbies,
he sees gain but does not compromise his righteousness.
If he is threatened by a crowd
or intimidated by weapons,
he sees death but does not change his principles.
Faced with predatory beasts' pouncing and striking, he does not measure his courage;
pulling a heavy tripod, he does not measure his strength.
He does not regret the past;
he does not worry about the future.
He does not repeat a mistaken word;
he does not trace rumors to their source.
He does not break his dignity;
he does not practice deceitful schemes.
Such is his independent standing."
42.2 "A Rú can be befriended but not coerced;
he can be approached but not pressured;
he can be killed but not insulted.
His dwelling is not extravagant;
his food and drink are not rich;
his faults may be gently pointed out but not enumerated to his face.
Such is his fortitude."
42.3 "A Rú takes loyalty and trustworthiness as his armor,
and ritual and righteousness as his shield.
He walks carrying Rén on his head;
he dwells embracing righteousness.
Even if there is tyrannical government,
he does not change his stance.
Such is his self-establishment."
42.4 "A Rú may have a dwelling of one mǔ,
a room of surrounding walls,
a wicker gate and a small opening in the wall,
or a door of mugwort and a window from a broken jar.
He exchanges clothes to go out;
he eats only one meal for two days.
If the superior responds to him, he does not dare to doubt;
if the superior does not respond, he does not dare to flatter.
Such is his service in office."
42.5 "A Rú lives with the people of today,
but consults with the people of antiquity.
He practices it in the present age
to be a model for future generations.
If he happens not to encounter a favorable age,
if the superiors do not support him,
and the subordinates do not promote him,
and if slanderous and flattering people
form cliques to endanger him,
his person may be endangered,
but his will cannot be taken away.
Although endangered, in his daily life
he ultimately realizes his will,
and he still will not forget the sufferings of the common people.
Such is his concern."
42.6 "A Rú is broad in learning and never exhausted,
and earnest in practice and never weary.
He dwells in seclusion without excess;
he communicates with the high without being constrained.
In ritual, he values harmony;
he appreciates the beauty of loyalty and trustworthiness.
He follows the way of being leisurely and composed;
he promotes the worthy and tolerates the multitude;
he rounds off sharp corners and fits in like tiles.
Such is his magnanimity."
42.7 "In recommending internally, a Rú does not avoid relatives;
in recommending externally, he does not avoid enemies.
He measures merit and accumulates deeds;
he promotes the worthy and advances them,
without expecting a reward.
If the ruler achieves his purpose,
and if it benefits the state,
he does not seek wealth or honor.
Such is his promotion of the worthy and support of the capable."
42.8 "If a Rú hears of something good, he tells others;
if he sees something good, he shows others.
In rank and position, they yield to each other;
in times of trouble and danger, they die for each other.
They wait for each other for a long time;
from afar, they reach out to each other.
Such is his recommendation and employment."
42.9 "A Rú bathes his body and washes in virtue.
He sets forth his words and then remains humble.
He is quiet and corrects himself;
the superiors do not know of him.
He is plain yet stands tall,
and he is not in a hurry to act.
He does not stand over a depth to appear high;
he does not add to a little to make it much.
When the world is well-governed, he does not act lightly;
when the world is in chaos, he is not discouraged.
He does not join those who are the same in cliques;
he does not condemn those who are different.
Such is his independent standing and solitary action."
42.10 "A Rú, above, does not serve the Son of Heaven as a mere subject;
below, he does not serve the feudal lords.
He is cautious, quiet, and values magnanimity.
He is firm and resolute in dealing with people;
he is broad in learning to know what to submit to.
He studies literature to sharpen his integrity.
Even if a state were divided for him, he would see it as a trifle;
he does not act as a subject or serve in office under wrong conditions.
Such is his conduct and planning."
42.11 "A Rú shares his will and follows the same direction with others;
he pursues the Dào with the same methods.
Standing together, they rejoice;
yielding to each other, they never tire.
Even if they have not seen each other for a long time,
hearing rumors, they do not believe them.
Their actions are based on integrity and establish righteousness.
If they agree, they advance together;
if they disagree, they withdraw.
Such is his friendship."
42.12 "Mildness and goodness
are the roots of Rén;
respect and caution
are the ground of Rén;
magnanimity and generosity
are the manifestation of Rén;
humility in dealing with others
is the ability of Rén;
ritual and moderation
are the appearance of Rén;
speech and conversation
are the refinement of Rén;
song and music
are the harmony of Rén;
distributing and sharing
are the application of Rén.
A Rú possesses all of these,
yet he still does not dare to claim to be Rén.
Such is his respect and deference."
42.13 "A Rú is not dejected in poverty and low status,
nor is he arrogant in wealth and honor.
He does not offend the ruler,
nor does he burden his superiors,
nor does he cause trouble for the officials.
Therefore, he is called a Rú.
Today, the common people use the term Rú recklessly,
and they often use Rú as a term of abuse and criticism."
Kǒngzǐ returned to his lodging,
and Āigōng provided him with quarters.
Having heard these words,
his speech became more trustworthy
and his actions became more righteous.
"For the rest of my life," he said,
"I shall not dare to make fun of the Rú."
43.1 The Way of the Dàxué
consists in manifesting illustrious virtue,
in loving the people,
and in resting in the highest excellence.
Knowing where to rest, the mind becomes settled;
being settled, the mind can be calm;
being calm, the mind can be at peace;
being at peace, one can deliberate;
deliberating, one can attain.
Things have their roots and branches;
affairs have their ends and beginnings.
To know what comes first and what comes last
is to be near the Dào.
Ancient ones who wished to manifest clear virtue throughout the world
first governed their states;
those who wished to govern their states
first regulated their families;
those who wished to regulate their families
first cultivated their persons;
those who wished to cultivate their persons
first rectified their minds;
those who wished to rectify their minds
first made their intentions sincere;
those who wished to make their intentions sincere
first extended their knowledge;
extending knowledge lies in the investigation of things.
When things are investigated, knowledge becomes complete;
when knowledge is complete, intentions become sincere;
when intentions are sincere, the mind becomes rectified;
when the mind is rectified, the person is cultivated;
when the person is cultivated, the family is regulated;
when the family is regulated, the state is governed;
when the state is governed, the world is at peace.
From the Tiānzǐ down to the common people,
all must take the cultivation of the person as the root.
That the root be in disorder and the branches be well-ordered is impossible;
to treat what is important as trivial
and what is trivial as important—
that has never been!
This is called knowing the root,
this is called the perfection of knowledge.
What is meant by "making the intentions sincere":
it is to allow no self-deception,
as in hating a foul smell,
or as in loving a beautiful color;
this is called self-satisfaction.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ must be watchful over himself when alone!
The Xiǎorén, in retirement, practices what is not good,
leaving nothing undone;
but when he sees a Jūnzǐ, he attempts to conceal himself,
hiding his evil
and showing off his good.
But others see him
as if looking at his lungs and liver;
then what is the use?
This is called being sincere within,
taking form on the outside.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ must be watchful over himself when alone.
Zēngzǐ said:
"What ten eyes behold,
what ten hands point to—
how formidable it is!"
Wealth enriches the house,
virtue enriches the person;
the mind is expansive and the body is at ease.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ must make his intentions sincere.
The Shī says:
"Look at that bend in the Qí River,
the green bamboos are so lush.
There is the elegant Jūnzǐ,
as if cut, as if filed,
as if carved, as if polished.
How majestic, how imposing!
How brilliant, how distinguished!
There is the elegant Jūnzǐ,
never to be forgotten!"
"As if cut, as if filed" refers to
the way of learning;
"as if carved, as if polished" refers to
self-cultivation;
"how majestic, how imposing" refers to
reverent awe;
"how brilliant, how distinguished" refers to
dignified bearing;
and "the elegant Jūnzǐ
never to be forgotten" refers to
the fact that his abundant virtue and supreme goodness
cannot be forgotten by the people.
The Shī says:
"Alas!
The former kings are not forgotten!"
The Jūnzǐ honors those whom they honored and loves those whom they loved;
the Xiǎorén enjoy what they enjoyed and benefit from what they benefited from;
this is why they are not forgotten even after their passing.
The Kāng Gào says:
"He was able to manifest clear virtue."
The Tài Jiǎ says:
"He kept in view the bright mandate of Heaven."
The Dì Diǎn says:
"He was able to manifest lofty virtue."
All these speak of manifesting one's own virtue.
The basin inscription of Tāng says:
"If you can renovate yourself one day,
renovate yourself every day,
and again renovate yourself day after day."
The Kāng Gào says:
"Make a new people."
The Shī says:
"Though Zhōu is an old state,
its mandate is ever new."
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ leaves nothing unused to reach the ultimate.
The Shī says:
"The royal domain is a thousand lǐ,
it is where the people rest."
The Shī says:
"The twittering yellow bird
rests on the corner of the hill."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In resting,
it knows where to rest.
Can a human being be less than a bird?"
The Shī says:
"Profound was Wén Wáng,
ah, how he continued to shine and was reverent in his resting!"
As a ruler,
he rested in benevolence;
as a minister,
he rested in reverence;
as a son,
he rested in filial piety;
as a father,
he rested in kindness;
in dealing with the people of the state,
he rested in good faith.
43.2 Kǒngzǐ said:
"In hearing litigation,
I am like others.
What is necessary is to cause there to be no litigation!"
Those who are without sincerity cannot finish their speeches.
Having great awe for the will of the people—
this is called knowing the root.
What is meant by "the cultivation of the person lies in the rectification of the mind":
if one is under the influence of anger,
one will not achieve its rectification;
under the influence of fear,
one will not achieve its rectification;
under the influence of fond pleasures,
one will not achieve its rectification;
under the influence of sorrow and distress,
one will not achieve its rectification.
When the mind is not present,
one looks but does not see,
one listens but does not hear,
one eats but does not know the flavor.
This is what is meant by "the cultivation of the person lies in the rectification of the mind."
What is meant by "the regulation of the family lies in the cultivation of the person":
people are biased toward those whom they love and are close to,
biased toward those whom they despise and dislike,
biased toward those whom they fear and respect,
biased toward those whom they pity and feel compassion for,
and biased toward those whom they are arrogant and indifferent to.
Therefore, to love someone yet know their faults,
or to dislike someone yet recognize their beauty—
those are rare in the world!
Thus, there is a proverb that says:
"No one knows the faults of his own child;
no one knows the greatness of his own sprouts."
This is meant by "if the person is not cultivated, one cannot regulate the family."
What is meant by "governing the state must first involve regulating the family":
one who cannot teach their own family yet can teach others—
such a person does not exist.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ, without leaving his home, completes the instruction for the state:
filial piety
is that with which one serves the ruler;
fraternal respect
is that with which one serves elders;
kindness
is that with which one directs the multitude.
The Kāng Gào says:
"As if protecting a newborn baby."
If one sincerely seeks it in the mind,
though one may not hit the mark exactly, one will not be far off.
There has never been one who first studied how to raise a child and then got married!
When one family is benevolent,
the whole state will rise to benevolence;
when one family is courteous,
the whole state will rise to courtesy;
when one man is greedy and perverse,
the whole state will descend into disorder.
Such is the mechanism.
This is what is meant by "one word ruins an affair"
and "one man stabilizes the state."
Yáo and Shùn led the world with benevolence,
and the people followed them;
Jié and Zhòu led the world with violence,
and the people followed them.
If what they commanded was contrary to what they loved,
the people would not follow.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ must have it in himself
before he seeks it in others,
and must be without it in himself
before he condemns it in others.
What is stored in one's person without reciprocity,
yet to be able to make others understand—
that has never been.
Therefore, governing the state lies in regulating the family.
The Shī says:
"The peach tree is young and elegant,
its leaves are luxuriant;
this lady is going to her home,
she will be suitable for her family."
Only after one is suitable for their family
can one instruct the people of the state.
The *Shī* says:
"Harmonious with elder and younger brothers."
When one is harmonious with elder and younger brothers,
then one can instruct the people of the state.
The *Shī* says:
"His demeanor is without error,
thus rectifying the four states."
When his conduct as father, son, and brother is sufficient for imitation,
then the people will imitate it.
This is what is meant by saying that governing the state lies in regulating the family.
What is meant by saying that bringing peace to the world lies in governing one's state is this:
when those above treat the elderly as elderly, the people are inspired to filial piety;
when those above treat seniors as seniors, the people are inspired to fraternal respect;
when those above show compassion to the orphaned, the people do not act contrary;
therefore the *Jūnzǐ* has the Way of the Measuring Square.
What you dislike in your superiors,
do not employ in treating your subordinates;
what you dislike in your subordinates,
do not employ in serving your superiors;
what you dislike in those before you,
do not employ in leading those behind you;
what you dislike in those behind you,
do not employ in following those before you;
what you dislike in those on your right,
do not employ in your dealings with those on your left;
what you dislike in those on your left,
do not employ in your dealings with those on your right:
this is called the Way of the Measuring Square.
The *Shī* says:
"Pleasant is the *Jūnzǐ*,
the parent of the people."
What the people like, he likes;
what the people dislike, he dislikes;
this is called being the parent of the people.
The *Shī* says:
"Lofty is that Southern Mountain,
with its rocks so craggy;
majestic is *Shī Yǐn*,
all the people look up to you."
Those who possess states must be cautious;
if they are biased, they will be disgraced before the world.
The *Shī* says:
"Before the *Yīn* had lost the multitude,
they were able to be companions to *Shàng Dì*;
look at the *Yīn* as a mirror,
the great mandate is not easy to keep."
This means that by gaining the multitude, one gains the state;
by losing the multitude, one loses the state.
Therefore, the *Jūnzǐ* is first cautious about virtue.
Having virtue, there will be the people;
having the people, there will be the land;
having the land, there will be wealth;
having wealth, there will be utility.
Virtue is the root;
wealth is the branch.
If one makes the root external and the branch internal,
one will struggle with the people and teach them plunder.
Therefore, when wealth is concentrated, the people are scattered;
when wealth is scattered, the people are gathered.
Therefore, words spoken in violation of right
will return in violation of right;
goods acquired in violation of right
will be lost in violation of right.
The *Kāng Gào* says:
"The Mandate is not constant!"
This means that by being good one gains it,
and by not being good one loses it.
The *Chǔ Shū* says:
"The state of *Chǔ* considers nothing else to be treasure,
it considers only goodness to be treasure."
*Jiù Fàn* said:
"An exile has nothing to consider as treasure,
humanity and kinship are what he considers treasure."
The *Qín Shì* says:
"If there were a single minister,
sincere and upright, though having no other skills,
yet his heart were generous
and as if it could contain all things.
When others have skills,
he regards them as if they were his own;
when others are talented and sagely,
his heart loves them,
not merely expressing it with his mouth,
but truly being able to tolerate them.
Such a man can protect my descendants and the black-haired people;
surely he would be beneficial!
But if when others have skills,
he is jealous and dislikes them;
or when others are talented and sagely,
he opposes them and prevents them from being known;
truly he cannot tolerate them.
Such a man cannot protect my descendants and the black-haired people;
indeed, he is a danger!"
Only the humane man can banish such a person,
driving him out to the *Sì Yí*,
not allowing him to dwell together with the *Zhōngguó*.
This is why it is said: only the humane man is able to love others
and able to hate others.
To see the worthy and not be able to promote them,
or to promote them but not be able to give them precedence,
is a slight;
to see the bad and not be able to remove them,
or to remove them but not be able to distance them,
is a fault.
To love what people hate
and to hate what people love
is called acting against human nature;
disaster will surely reach his person.
Therefore, the *Jūnzǐ* has a great Way:
he must be loyal and trustworthy to gain it,
and he will lose it through pride and extravagance.
There is a great Way to generate wealth:
let those who produce it be many,
and those who consume it be few;
