let those who work at it be diligent,
and those who use it be economical;
then wealth will always be sufficient.
The humane man uses wealth to develop his character;
the inhumane man uses his person to accumulate wealth.
Never has there been a case where those above loved humanity
and those below did not love righteousness;
never has there been a case where people loved righteousness
and their tasks were not completed;
and never has there been a case where the wealth in the treasuries
was not the ruler's wealth.
*Mèng Xiàn Zǐ* said:
"He who keeps a carriage and horses
does not concern himself with chickens and pigs;
the family that cuts ice
does not keep cattle and sheep;
a house of a hundred carriages
does not keep a minister who gathers heavy taxes;
rather than having a tax-gathering minister,
it is better to have a thieving minister."
This means that a state does not consider profit as profit,
but considers righteousness as profit.
When those who lead a state or family make wealth their primary concern,
they must be following petty men.
If they think these men are good
and employ petty men to run the state and family,
calamities and injuries will arrive together.
Even if there are good men,
they will be unable to do anything
about it!
This means that a state does not consider profit as profit,
but considers righteousness as profit.
That by which a person is human
is ritual and righteousness.
The beginning of ritual and righteousness
lies in rectifying one's demeanor, standardizing one's expression, and making one's speech compliant.
When the demeanor is rectified,
the expression standardized,
and the speech compliant,
then ritual and righteousness are complete.
By these, one rectifies the relationship between ruler and subject, brings intimacy to father and son, and harmony to elder and younger.
When ruler and subject are rectified,
father and son are intimate,
and elder and younger are in harmony,
then ritual and righteousness are established.
Therefore, after the capping ceremony, the full attire is complete;
after the attire is complete, the demeanor is rectified, the expression standardized, and the speech made compliant.
Therefore it is said:
"Capping
is the beginning of ritual."
For this reason, the ancient sage kings held the capping ceremony in high esteem.
In ancient times, for the capping ceremony, they would divine the day and divine the guests,
as a way of showing respect for the capping;
showing respect for the capping
was a way of honoring ritual;
and honoring ritual was the way to establish the root of the state.
Therefore, the capping takes place at the *Zuò* steps,
to signify the succession;
the toast is made at the guest's position;
and the three additions of the cap become progressively more honorable,
signifying the completion of growth;
once capped, the person is given a courtesy name,
which is the way of an adult.
He appears before his mother,
and his mother bows to him;
he appears before his brothers,
and his brothers bow to him;
this is because he is now an adult and ritual is performed with him.
Wearing the dark cap and the dark formal robe,
he presents his ritual gift to the ruler,
and then with the ritual gift, he appears before the district officials and the district elders;
he appears as an adult.
To treat him as an adult
means that adult ritual responsibilities will be expected of him.
To expect adult ritual responsibilities of him
means that he will be expected to perform the rituals of being a son,
being a younger brother, being a subject,
and being a junior.
When the conduct of these four roles is to be demanded of a person,
how can the ritual not be held in high esteem?
Therefore, when the practices of filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, and obedience are established,
only then can one be considered a human being;
once one can be considered a human being,
only then can one govern others.
Therefore, the sage kings valued ritual.
Therefore it is said:
“The capping ceremony
is the beginning of the rituals
and the most important of the auspicious ceremonies.”
For this reason, the ancients valued capping;
valuing capping, they performed it in the ancestral temple;
performing it in the ancestral temple
was to show respect for this important matter;
respecting the important matter, they did not dare to handle it presumptuously;
not daring to handle it presumptuously
was how they humbled themselves and honored their ancestors.
45.1 The marriage ceremony
is intended to join the bonds of two surnames,
above to serve the ancestral temple,
and below to continue the future generations.
Therefore, the superior person values it.
Hence, in the marriage ceremony, the *Nàcǎi*,
*Wènmíng*,
*Nàjí*,
*Nàzhēng*,
and *Qǐngqī*
all involve the host arranging mats and stands in the temple,
bowing and greeting outside the gate,
entering,
bowing and yielding before ascending,
and receiving the message in the temple;
this is to treat the marriage ceremony with reverence, caution, importance, and correctness.
45.2 The father gives a celebratory drink to the son
and commands him to go and meet the bride,
for the male takes precedence over the female.
The son receives the command to meet her;
the host arranges mats and stands in the temple
and bows and greets him outside the gate.
The groom enters holding a wild goose,
bows and yields before ascending the hall,
bows twice and places the goose on the ground;
this is for him to receive her personally from her parents.
He descends,
exits,
and drives the bride’s carriage;
the groom hands her the mounting cord
and drives the wheels for three rotations.
He waits first outside his gate;
when the bride arrives,
the groom bows to her and enters;
they eat together from the same animal sacrifice
and drink from the joined gourds to rinse their mouths;
this is to unite their bodies
and to equalize their status to create intimacy between them.
45.3 Reverence, caution, importance, and correctness are established before intimacy follows;
this is the general principle of ritual,
by which the distinction between male and female is established
and the righteousness of husband and wife is established.
When there is a distinction between male and female,
then there is righteousness between husband and wife;
when there is righteousness between husband and wife,
then there is affection between father and son;
when there is affection between father and son,
then there is correctness between ruler and subject.
Therefore it is said:
“The marriage ceremony
is the root of ritual.”
45.4 Now, ritual begins with capping,
is rooted in marriage,
is most serious in mourning and sacrifice,
is most dignified in audiences and missions,
and is made harmonious in archery
and the district drinking ceremony; these are the general principles of ritual.
45.5 Rising early,
the bride bathes to wait for the interview;
at dawn,
the assistant introduces her to her father-in-law and mother-in-law;
she carries a basket with dates, chestnuts, and sliced dried meat for the interview.
The assistant serves sweet wine to the bride;
the bride offers dried meat and sauce,
and offers the wine,
completing the ritual of the bride.
The father-in-law and mother-in-law enter the inner room,
and the bride serves them with a single young pig,
manifesting her obedience.
The next morning,
the father-in-law and mother-in-law host the bride with a single-offering banquet
and set down the pledge-cup.
The father-in-law and mother-in-law first descend from the western steps,
and the bride descends from the eastern steps,
to manifest the succession.
45.6 Completing the bride’s ritual,
manifesting her obedience,
and further emphasizing it by manifesting the succession
are ways to place heavy responsibility on the bride’s obedience.
The bride’s obedience
means being obedient to her father-in-law and mother-in-law and
harmonious with the members of the household;
then she will be acceptable to her husband,
to complete the work of silk, hemp, and textiles,
and to carefully manage the stores and granaries.
Therefore, when the bride’s obedience is complete, the internal affairs will be harmonious and orderly;
when the internal affairs are harmonious and orderly, the family can long endure;
therefore, the sage kings valued it.
45.7 Thus, in ancient times, three months before a woman was married,
if the shrines of her ancestors were not yet removed,
she was taught in the public palace;
if the shrines had been removed,
she was taught in the clan hall;
she was taught in womanly virtue, womanly speech, womanly appearance, and womanly work.
When the teaching was completed, a sacrifice was offered,
using fish as the victim
and seasoning it with duckweed and pondweed;
this was to perfect the bride’s obedience.
45.8 In ancient times, the Empress of the Son of Heaven established six palaces,
three *Fūrén*, nine *Pín*, twenty-seven *Shìfù*,
and eighty-one *Yùqī*,
to direct the internal governance of the world
and to clearly manifest womanly obedience;
thus the internal world was harmonious and families were orderly.
The Son of Heaven established six ministries,
three *Gōng*, nine *Qīng*, twenty-seven *Dàfū*,
and eighty-one *Yuánshì*,
to direct the external governance of the world
and to clearly manifest the male instruction of the world;
thus the external world was harmonious and the state was well-governed.
Therefore it is said:
“The Son of Heaven directs male instruction,
the Empress directs female obedience;
the Son of Heaven manages the Way of *Yáng*,
the Empress governs the Virtue of *Yīn*;
the Son of Heaven directs external governance,
the Empress directs internal duties.
When instruction and obedience become custom,
and external and internal affairs are harmonious and obedient,
the state and the house are well-governed;
this is what is called Abundant Virtue.”
45.9 Therefore, if male instruction is not cultivated,
the affairs of *Yáng* go wrong,
this is shown in the heavens,
and the sun is eclipsed;
if female obedience is not cultivated,
the affairs of *Yīn* go wrong,
this is shown in the heavens,
and the moon is eclipsed.
Hence, when a solar eclipse occurs, the Son of Heaven wears plain white robes and cultivates the duties of the six ministries,
purifying the *Yáng* affairs of the world;
when a lunar eclipse occurs, the Empress wears plain white robes and cultivates the duties of the six palaces,
purifying the *Yīn* affairs of the world.
Thus the relation between the Son of Heaven and the Empress
is like that between the sun and the moon
and between *Yīn* and *Yáng*,
depending on each other for completion.
The Son of Heaven cultivating male instruction
is the Way of the Father;
the Empress cultivating female obedience
is the Way of the Mother.
Therefore it is said:
“The relation between the Son of Heaven and the Empress
is like that between a father and a mother.”
Therefore, for the *Tiānwáng*, one wears the *zhǎncuī* mourning garment,
representing the duty to a father;
for the Empress, one wears the *zīcuī* mourning garment,
representing the duty to a mother.
46.1 The meaning of the District Drinking Ceremony:
The host bows and greets the guests outside the gate of the *Xiáng* school;
they enter,
making three salutations before reaching the steps,
and yielding three times before ascending;
this is to express honor and yielding.
Washing hands and rinsing the cup, and raising the *zhì* cup
is to express purity.
Bowing upon arrival,
bowing when the cup is rinsed,
bowing when receiving,
bowing when offering,
and bowing when finished
are to express reverence.
Honor, yielding, purity, and reverence
are the means by which the superior person interacts with others.
When the superior person practices honor and yielding, there is no contention;
when there is purity and reverence, there is no disrespect;
without disrespect or contention,
one is far from fighting and disputing;
without fighting
and disputing, there is no disaster of violence or disorder;
this is how the superior person avoids human calamity;
therefore the sages regulated these through the Way.
46.2 The district people, officers, and superior persons
placed the wine jars in the space between the rooms,
where guests and host shared them.
In the jars, there was dark water,
to value its simplicity.
The delicacies came out from the eastern room,
provided by the host.
The basin was placed under the eastern eave,
as the means for the host to purify himself
in order to serve the guests.
46.3 The guest and host represent Heaven and Earth;
the Jiè and Zhuàn represent Yīn and Yáng;
the three guests represent the Three Lights;
the three yieldings
represent the three days it takes for the moon to form its crescent;
the seating on four sides
represents the four seasons.
The stern and freezing breath of Heaven and Earth
begins in the southwest
and reaches its fullness in the northwest;
this is the majestic and solemn breath of Heaven and Earth;
this is the breath of Righteousness (Yì) of Heaven and Earth.
The warm and generous breath of Heaven and Earth
begins in the northeast
and reaches its fullness in the southeast;
this is the breath of abundant Virtue (Dé) of Heaven and Earth;
this is the breath of Benevolence (Rén) of Heaven and Earth.
The host honors the guest,
therefore he seats the guest in the northwest
and seats the Jiè in the southwest to support the guest.
The guest
is one who interacts with others through Righteousness (Yì),
therefore he is seated in the northwest.
The host
is one who interacts with others through the abundance of Virtue (Dé),
therefore he is seated in the southeast,
and the Zhuàn is seated in the northeast
to support the host.
When Benevolence (Rén) and Righteousness (Yì) meet,
and the guest and host conduct their business,
if the number of stands and platters is appropriate, it is called Sagacity (Shèng).
When Sagacity is established and carried out with respect, it is called Ritual (Lǐ).
When Ritual is used to embody the order of elders and juniors, it is called Virtue (Dé).
As for Virtue (Dé),
it is what is obtained within oneself.
Therefore it is said:
"Those of old who studied the arts and the Way
intended to obtain it within themselves.
Therefore, the Sages devoted themselves to it."
46.4 The food offering
and the libation of wine
are acts of respectful Ritual (Lǐ).
Tasting the lung
is a ritual of tasting.
Sipping the wine
is the completion of the Ritual (Lǐ).
Doing so at the edge of the mat
signifies that the proper purpose of this mat
is not solely for eating and drinking,
but for performing the Ritual (Lǐ);
this is why Ritual (Lǐ) is valued and material goods are undervalued.
Finishing the cup (zhì)
and placing it on the western steps
signifies that at this seat,
it is not solely for eating and drinking;
this is the principle of putting Ritual (Lǐ) first and material goods second.
Putting Ritual (Lǐ) first and material goods second,
then the people will act with respect and yielding and will not struggle.
46.5 In the District Drinking Ritual (Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ Lǐ),
those who are sixty years old sit,
while those who are fifty stand and wait
to hear of administrative duties;
this is to make clear the honoring of elders.
Those who are sixty have three platters,
those who are seventy have four platters,
those who are eighty have five platters,
and those who are ninety have six platters;
this is to make clear the care for the aged.
When the people know to honor elders and care for the aged,
only then can they be filial and fraternal at home.
When the people are filial and fraternal at home
and honor elders and care for the aged abroad,
only then is education completed;
when education is completed, then the state can be at peace.
What the superior man calls filiality
is not just visiting every house to see it daily;
by gathering them for the district archery
and teaching them the District Drinking Ritual (Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ Lǐ),
the practice of filiality and fraternity is established.
46.6 Kǒngzǐ said:
"When I observe the district rituals,
I know how very easy the Kingly Way (Wáng Dào) is."
46.7 The host personally invites the guest and the Jiè,
and the other guests follow of their own accord.
Arriving outside the gate,
the host bows to the guest and the Jiè,
and the other guests enter on their own;
the distinction between the noble and the humble is thus differentiated.
46.8 With three salutations (yī) they arrive at the steps,
and with three yieldings the guest ascends.
The bows of arrival, the offering, and the pledge-cup—
the steps of declining and yielding are numerous.
For the Jiè, these are abbreviated.
As for the other guests, they ascend and receive,
sit to offer the sacrifice,
and stand to drink;
they do not return the pledge (cuò) before descending;
the distinction between full and reduced rituals is thus differentiated.
46.9 The musicians (gōng) enter.
They ascend and sing three pieces to completion,
and the host makes an offering to them.
The sheng-pipes enter and play three pieces to completion,
and the host makes an offering to them.
Alternating songs are performed three times,
and the ensemble music is performed three times.
The musicians announce that the music is complete
and then depart.
One person raises the cup (zhì),
and then the Master of Ceremonies (Sīzhèng) is established,
showing they can be harmonious and joyful without becoming dissolute.
46.10 The guest pledges the host,
the host pledges the Jiè,
and the Jiè pledges the other guests,
younger and elder according to age,
ending with those who provide the water for washing.
This shows they can treat the younger and elder properly without omission.
46.11 They descend,
remove their shoes, ascend, and sit,
passing the cups without a fixed number.
The moderation of drinking wine:
the morning session does not interfere with the morning duties,
and the evening session does not interfere with the evening duties.
The guest departs,
the host bows to see him off,
and the measured steps and cultural forms are followed to the end.
This shows they can be at ease in a banquet without becoming disorderly.
46.12 When noble and humble are clear,
full and reduced rituals are distinguished,
there is harmony and joy without dissolution,
the younger and elder are treated properly without omission,
and they are at ease in the banquet without disorder—
these five practices
are sufficient to rectify the person and bring peace to the state.
When the state is at peace, the world (Tiānxià) is at peace.
Therefore it is said:
"When I observe the district rituals,
I know how very easy the Kingly Way (Wáng Dào) is."
46.13 The meaning of the District Drinking Ritual (Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ Yì):
establishing the guest represents Heaven,
establishing the host represents Earth,
setting the Jiè and Zhuàn represents the Sun and Moon,
and establishing the three guests represents the Three Lights.
In ancient times, when Rituals (Lǐ) were formulated,
they were grounded in Heaven and Earth,
ordered by the Sun and Moon,
and aligned with the Three Lights.
This is the foundation of governance and education.
46.14 Boiling the dog in the east
follows the model of the Yáng breath arising in the east.
The washing basin (xǐ) is at the eastern steps,
and the water is to the east of the basin,
following the model of the sea being to the left of the world.
The wine vessels contain the dark water (xuán jiǔ)
to teach the people not to forget their origins.
46.15 The guest must face south.
The east is Spring (Chūn);
"Chūn" means "to stir" (chǔn).
He who produces the myriad things is sagacious (Shèng).
The south is Summer (Xià);
"Xià" means "to be great" (jiǎ).
To nourish them, grow them, and bestow upon them
is Benevolence (Rén).
The west is Autumn (Qiū);
"Qiū" means "to gather" (chóu).
To gather them according to the season
is to be an observer of Righteousness (Yì).
The north is Winter (Dōng);
"Dōng" means "to be within" (zhōng).
"Within" means "to store" (cáng).
Therefore, when the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) stands,
he has sagacity on his left and faces benevolence,
while having righteousness on his right and storage behind him.
The Jiè must face east,
for he mediates between guest and host.
The host must reside in the east.
The east is Spring (Chūn);
"Chūn" means "to stir" (chǔn).
It is that which produces the myriad things.
The host is the one who initiates;
he is the one who produces the myriad things.
The moon forms its crescent in three days,
and three months form a season.
Therefore, Ritual (Lǐ) has three yieldings,
and in establishing a state, one must appoint Three High Ministers (Sān Qīng).
The three guests
are the foundation of governance and education
and the great triads of Ritual (Lǐ).
47.1 In ancient times, when the Feudal Lords (Zhūhóu) held archery contests,
they first performed the Banquet Ritual (Yàn Lǐ).
When the High Ministers (Qīng), Grand Masters (Dàfū),
and Officers (Shì) held archery contests,
they first performed the District Drinking Ritual (Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ Lǐ).
Thus, the Banquet Ritual (Yàn Lǐ)
is how the Righteousness (Yì) between ruler and minister is made clear.
The District Drinking Ritual (Xiāng Yǐn Jiǔ Lǐ)
is how the order of elders and juniors is made clear.
47.2 Therefore, the archer,
in advancing, retreating, and turning around, must necessarily conform to ritual.
Internally, his intent is upright;
externally, his body is straight.
Only then can he hold the bow and arrow with scrutiny and firmness.
Holding the bow and arrow with scrutiny and firmness,
only then can one speak of hitting the mark.
Through this, one can observe moral conduct.
47.3 Its rhythm:
The *Tiānzǐ* uses "Zōu Yú" as the rhythm;
the *Zhūhóu* use "Lí Shǒu" as the rhythm;
the *Qīng* and *Dàfū* use "Cǎi Píng" as the rhythm;
the *Shì* use "Cǎi Fán" as the rhythm.
"Zōu Yú"
expresses the completeness of the official ranks;
"Lí Shǒu"
expresses the timeliness of the assembly;
"Cǎi Píng"
expresses the following of the law;
"Cǎi Fán"
expresses not failing in one's duties.
Therefore, the *Tiānzǐ* takes the completeness of officials as his rhythm;
the *Zhūhóu* take the timely assembly with the *Tiānzǐ* as their rhythm;
the *Qīng* and *Dàfū* take the following of laws as their rhythm;
the *Shì* take not failing in their duties as their rhythm.
Therefore, by clarifying the intent of the rhythm
so as not to fail in their affairs,
merit is achieved and moral conduct is established.
When moral conduct is established, there will be no calamity of violent rebellion.
When merit is achieved, the state is at peace.
Therefore it is said:
"Archery
is that by which one observes abundant virtue."
47.4 For this reason, in ancient times, the *Tiānzǐ* used archery to select the *Zhūhóu*, *Qīng*, *Dàfū*, and *Shì*.
Archery
is an affair for men;
thus it is adorned with ritual and music.
Therefore, for an affair to fully embody ritual and music
and be frequently performed
to establish moral conduct,
there is nothing like archery.
Thus the Sagely Kings made it a primary concern.
47.5 Therefore, the system of the ancient *Tiānzǐ*:
The *Zhūhóu* would annually present recommended *Shì* to the *Tiānzǐ*;
the *Tiānzǐ* would test them at the *Shè Gōng*.
Those whose appearance and posture accorded with ritual,
whose rhythm accorded with music,
and who hit the mark many times,
were permitted to participate in the sacrifices.
Those whose appearance and posture did not accord with ritual,
whose rhythm did not accord with music,
and who hit the mark few times,
were not permitted to participate in the sacrifices.
When one was frequently permitted to participate in sacrifices, the ruler received congratulations;
when one was frequently not permitted to participate in sacrifices, the ruler received reprimands.
After frequent congratulations, land was increased;
after frequent reprimands, land was reduced.
Therefore it is said:
"Archery
is archery for the sake of being a *Zhūhóu*."
Consequently, the rulers and ministers of the *Zhūhóu* devoted their full intent to archery
to practice ritual and music.
For a ruler and minister who practice ritual and music to end up in exile or ruin—
such a thing has never occurred.
47.6 Therefore the *Shī* says:
"The great-grandson, the *Hóu Shì*,
the four upright ones are all raised;
the *Dàfū* and gentlemen,
together with all the officers,
small and great, none remain idle,
they attend at the ruler's place,
to feast and to shoot;
then there is feasting, then there is praise."
This speaks of ruler and minister together devoting their full intent to archery
to practice ritual and music;
then there is peace and there is praise.
Therefore the *Tiānzǐ* instituted it,
and the *Zhūhóu* strove for it.
This was the means by which the *Tiānzǐ* cultivated the *Zhūhóu*
without using weapons;
it was the tool by which the *Zhūhóu* rectified themselves.
47.7 *Kǒngzǐ* was practicing archery at the garden of *Jué Xiāng*;
the spectators were like a wall.
When the archery reached the stage of the *Sīmǎ*,
he had *Zǐlù* hold his bow and arrows
and come out to invite the archers, saying:
"Generals of a defeated army,
*Dàfū* of a fallen state,
and those who have become heirs to others are not to enter;
the rest may all enter."
About half left,
and half entered.
He then had *Gōngwǎng Zhīqiú* and *Xù Diǎn*
raise the *zhì* and speak.
*Gōngwǎng Zhīqiú* raised the *zhì* and spoke, saying:
"Have you been filial and fraternal in youth and maturity,
loved the rites in old age,
not followed common customs,
and cultivated your person while awaiting death?
Have you or have you not?
Stay in this position."
About half left,
and half remained.
*Xù Diǎn* then raised the *zhì* and spoke, saying:
"Have you been fond of learning without weariness,
fond of ritual without changing,
and in extreme old age still followed the Way without confusion?
Have you or have you not?
Stay in this position."
Only a few remained.
47.8 The meaning of the word *shè* is drawing out;
some say it means releasing.
Drawing out
means each person draws out his own intent.
Therefore, with the mind calm and the body upright,
holding the bow and arrow with scrutiny and firmness,
holding the bow and arrow with scrutiny and firmness,
then the shot will hit the mark.
Therefore it is said:
"He who is a father
takes the father's target;
he who is a son
takes the son's target;
he who is a ruler
takes the ruler's target;
he who is a minister
takes the minister's target."
Thus, each archer shoots at his own target.
Therefore, the Great Archery of the *Tiānzǐ*
is called Shooting at the *Hóu*;
Shooting at the *Hóu*
means archery for the sake of being a *Zhūhóu*.
If the shot hits the mark, one may become a *Zhūhóu*;
if the shot does not hit the mark, one may not become a *Zhūhóu*.
47.9 When the *Tiānzǐ* was about to sacrifice,
he first had to practice archery at the *Zé*.
The *Zé*
was the place to select officers.
Having shot at the *Zé*,
they then shot at the *Shè Gōng*.
Those who hit the mark were permitted to participate in the sacrifices;
those who did not hit the mark were not permitted to participate in the sacrifices.
Those not permitted to participate in the sacrifices were reprimanded
and had their land reduced;
those permitted to participate in the sacrifices were congratulated
and had their land increased.
This is what is meant by promoting rank or reducing land.
47.10 Therefore, when a male child is born,
a mulberry bow and six artemisia arrows are used
to shoot at Heaven, Earth, and the four directions.
Heaven, Earth, and the four directions
are the domains where a man has affairs to attend to.
Thus, he must first have his intent set upon the affairs he will have,
and only then dare to use grain.
This refers to eating.
47.11 Archery
is the way of benevolence.
In archery, one seeks correctness within oneself.
Having made oneself upright, one then releases.
If one releases and does not hit the mark,
one does not resent the one who defeated them,
but simply seeks the cause within oneself.
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"The *Jūnzǐ* has nothing to contend for,
but if he must, let it be in archery!
Bowing and yielding, they ascend,
and descending, they drink;
such a contention is that of a *Jūnzǐ*."
47.12 *Kǒngzǐ* said:
"How does the archer shoot? How does he listen?
Releasing in accordance with the sound,
and releasing without missing the target—
is this not only for the worthy?
As for the unworthy,
how could they be able to hit the mark?"
The *Shī* says:
"He shoots at that target,
to pray for your cup."
Praying
means seeking;
one seeks to hit the mark to decline the cup.
Wine
is used to nourish the aged
and to nourish the sick;
seeking to hit the mark to decline the cup
means declining nourishment.
48.1 In ancient times, among the officials of the *Zhōu Tiānzǐ*,
there was the office of the *Shùzǐ*.
The *Shùzǐ* official was in charge of the cadets of the *Zhūhóu*,
*Qīng*, *Dàfū*,
and *Shì*.
He managed their warnings and orders,
oversaw their instruction and governance,
distinguished their ranks,
and corrected their positions.
When the state has a major affair,
then it leads the *Guózǐ* and presents them to the *Tàizǐ*,
to be used as he sees fit.
If there is an affair of armor and weapons,
then it provides them with chariots and armor,
organizes their companies and squads,
appoints their officers,
and governs them with military law;
the *Sīmǎ* does not tax them.
In all the administrative affairs of the state,
the *Guózǐ* remain as reserve troops,
causing them to cultivate virtue and study the Way.
In spring, they assemble at the various schools,
and in autumn, they assemble for the various archery rites,
in order to examine their skills and promote or demote them.
48.2 The meaning of the *Yànlǐ* for the *Zhūhóu*:
The ruler stands to the southeast of the eastern steps,
facing south toward the *Qīng*
and *Dàfū*, who all advance slightly,
which is to establish their positions;
the ruler’s mat is at the top of the eastern steps,
occupying the position of the host;
the ruler alone ascends to stand upon the mat,
facing west and standing uniquely,
signifying the principle that no one dares to be his equal.
48.3 Establishing guest and host
is the ritual of drinking wine;
making the *Zǎifū* the host for the offerings
means that no subject dares to compete in ritual with the ruler;
not taking a *Qīng* or *Gōng* as the guest,
but taking a *Dàfū* as the guest,
is because of potential doubt,
and to clarify the principle of avoiding suspicion;
when the guest enters the central courtyard,
the ruler descends one level and bows to him,
which is to treat him with ritual.
48.4 When the ruler offers a general toast to the guest,
and when the guest receives the cup bestowed by the ruler,
they both descend, bow twice, and kowtow,
then ascend to complete the bow,
clarifying the ritual of a subject;
the ruler returns the bow;
in ritual, there is nothing that goes unreturned,
clarifying the ritual of the ruler above.
When subjects below exhaust their strength and fulfill their abilities to establish merit for the state,
the ruler must repay them with rank and salary;
therefore, all subjects strive to exhaust their strength and fulfill their abilities to establish merit,
and thus the state is secure and the ruler is at peace.
In ritual, there is nothing that goes unreturned;
this means that the superior does not take from those below in vain.
The superior must clarify the correct Way to lead the people;
the people follow the Way and achieve merit,
and only then does he take a tithe of one-tenth;
therefore, the superior has sufficient resources and those below are not impoverished;
thus, those above and below are in harmony and close, not resenting one another.
Harmony and peace
are the use of ritual;
this is the great righteousness between ruler and subject, superior and inferior.
Therefore it is said:
“The *Yànlǐ*
is that by which the righteousness of ruler and subject is clarified.”
48.5 Regarding the mats:
The lower *Qīng* follow the upper *Qīng*,
the *Dàfū* follow the lower *Qīng*,
and the *Shì* and *Shùzǐ* take their positions below in sequence.
To toast the ruler,
the ruler raises the cup for a general toast;
afterwards, toast the *Qīng*,
and the *Qīng* raises the cup for a general toast;
afterwards, toast the *Dàfū*,
and the *Dàfū* raises the cup for a general toast;
afterwards, toast the *Shì*,
and the *Shì* raises the cup for a general toast;
and afterwards, toast the *Shùzǐ*.
The meat stands, the vessels, the sacrificial animals, the offerings, and the delicacies
all have grades and differences,
which is how the noble and the lowly are clarified.
49.1 In the *Pìnlǐ*,
a *Shànggōng* has seven attendants,
a *Hóu* or *Bó* has five attendants,
and a *Zǐ* or *Nán* has three attendants,
which is how the noble and the lowly are clarified.
Using attendants to convey commands
means the *Jūnzǐ* does not dare to approach those he honors directly,
which is the utmost respect.
49.2 Yielding three times and then conveying the command,
yielding three times and then entering the temple gate,
bowing three times and then reaching the steps,
and yielding three times and then ascending,
are how respect and yielding are expressed.
49.3 The ruler sends a *Shì* to welcome them at the border,
a *Dàfū* offers greetings at the outskirts,
and the ruler personally bows and welcomes them within the great gate and receives them in the temple,
bowing to the north while receiving gifts
and bowing for the honor of the ruler’s command,
which is how respect is expressed.
49.4 Respect and yielding
are that by which the *Jūnzǐ* interact with one another.
Therefore, if the *Zhūhóu* interact with respect and yielding,
they will not infringe upon or oppress one another.
49.5 A *Qīng* serves as the primary usher,
a *Dàfū* serves as the assisting usher,
and a *Shì* serves as the minor usher.
The ruler personally treats the guest with ritual,
and the guest has private interviews,
private audiences,
presents offerings of food and livestock,
returns the *Guī* and *Zhāng*,
provides gifts and donations,
and holds banquets, meals, and feasts,
which are how the righteousness of guest and host, and ruler and subject, are clarified.
49.6 Therefore, the Son of Heaven regulates the *Zhūhóu*:
every year there is a small mission,
and every three years there is a large mission,
encouraging one another through ritual.
If an envoy on a mission makes an error,
the host ruler does not personally host the feast or meal,
which is how to shame and encourage them.
If the *Zhūhóu* encourage one another through ritual,
then externally they do not invade one another,
and internally they do not oppress one another.
This is how the Son of Heaven nurtures the *Zhūhóu*;
weapons are not used,
and it is the means by which the *Zhūhóu* rectify themselves.
49.7 Conducting missions with the *Guī* and *Zhāng*
is a heavy ritual;
returning the *Guī* and *Zhāng* after the mission
is the principle of treating wealth lightly and ritual heavily.
When the *Zhūhóu* encourage one another to treat wealth lightly and ritual heavily,
then the people will practice yielding.
49.8 When the host state treats a guest,
they provide three stores for arrival and departure,
provide livestock for the guest at his lodging,
the requirements for five sacrificial animals are displayed within,
thirty carts of rice,
thirty carts of grain,
and fodder and firewood double the amount of grain,
all displayed without.
Five pairs of birds are provided daily,
and all the attendants are provided with livestock.
There is one meal and two banquets,
and feasts and occasional gifts are without number,
which is how the ritual is made generous and heavy.
49.9 In ancient times, the use of wealth was not always equal to this;
however, the reason for using wealth so generously
is to say that one exhausts oneself in the ritual.
If one exhausts oneself in the ritual,
then internally ruler and subject do not oppress one another,
and externally they do not invade one another.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven regulates it,
and the *Zhūhóu* strive for it.
49.10 The rituals of mission and archery
are the greatest rituals.
They begin the proceedings at first light,
and the ritual is completed only when the sun is nearly at its zenith;
none but those who are strong and powerful can perform them.
Therefore, the strong and powerful
shall use their strength to perform ritual.
Though the wine is clear,
a person is thirsty but dares not drink;
though the meat is dry-cured,
a person is hungry but dares not eat.
When the day ends and people are weary,
they remain solemn,
upright, and composed,
and dare not become lax or indolent.
By this, they complete the measures of ritual,
rectify ruler and subject,
bring closeness to father and son,
and harmonize old and young.
This is what the multitude finds difficult,
but the *Jūnzǐ* performs it;
therefore, it is said he has “conduct”;
having conduct is called having righteousness;
having righteousness is called being brave and bold.
Therefore, what is valued in being brave and bold
is the ability to establish righteousness;
what is valued in establishing righteousness
is having conduct;
what is valued in having conduct
is the performance of ritual.
Therefore, what is valued in being brave and bold
is the daring to perform ritual and righteousness.
Thus, those who are brave, bold, strong, and powerful,
when the world is at peace,
are used for ritual and righteousness;
when the world has troubles,
they are used for victory in battle.
Used for victory in battle, they are peerless;
used for ritual and righteousness, there is submissive order;
with no peer externally
and submissive order internally,
this is called abundant virtue.
This is why the sage kings valued bravery and physical strength
in this way.
Bravery and physical strength,
if not used for ritual, righteousness, and victory in war,
but instead used for fighting and brawling,
are then called the qualities of a person of disorder.
When punishments are carried out in the state,
those who are executed are these people of disorder.
In this way,
the people follow governance and the state is at peace.
49.11 Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"I venture to ask why a superior man values jade and slights *mín*?
Is it because jade is scarce and *mín* is abundant?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It is not because *mín* is abundant
that it is slighted,
nor because jade is scarce
that it is valued.
In ancient times, the superior man compared virtue to jade.
Being warm, moist, and glossy,
it represents benevolence;
being fine, compact, and strong,
it represents wisdom;
being sharp-edged but not cutting,
it represents righteousness;
hanging down as if to drop,
it represents ritual;
when struck, its sound is clear, ringing, and long,
and at its end stops abruptly,
it represents music;
its flaws do not hide its beauty, and its beauty does not hide its flaws,
it represents loyalty;
its brilliance shining through to the outside,
it represents trustworthiness;
its spirit like a white rainbow,
it represents Heaven;
its essence appearing in the mountains and rivers,
it represents Earth;
the *guī* and *zhāng* scepters communicating independently,
it represents virtue.
That there is no one in the world who does not value it,
it represents the Way.
The *Shī* says:
'I think of the superior man,
he is mild as jade.'
Therefore, the superior man values it."
50.1 In general, the great substance of ritual
embodies Heaven and Earth,
follows the four seasons,
models itself on the *yīn* and *yáng*,
and accords with human feelings;
therefore it is called ritual.
Those who criticize it
do not know from whence ritual arises.
50.2 Ritual:
the ways of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness are different
and must not interfere with each other;
this is taken from *yīn* and *yáng*.
There are four systems for mourning,
changing to follow what is appropriate;
this is taken from the four seasons.
There is kindness and principle,
moderation and discretion;
this is taken from human feelings.
Kindness is benevolence,
principle is righteousness,
moderation is ritual,
and discretion is wisdom.
Benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and wisdom:
the Way of Man is complete in these.
50.3 For those whose kindness is thick,
their mourning dress is heavy;
therefore for a father one wears the *zhǎncuī* for three years;
this is established by kindness.
50.4 In the governance of the household,
kindness hides righteousness;
in the governance outside the household,
righteousness severs kindness.
Drawing on the service to a father to serve the ruler,
the respect is the same;
honoring the noble and respecting the honorable
is the greatest form of righteousness.
Therefore for a ruler one also wears the *zhǎncuī* for three years;
this is established by righteousness.
50.5 Eating after three days,
bathing after three months,
changing to the *liàn* dress after a full year;
being emaciated but not to the point of destroying one's nature,
not using the dead to harm the living.
Mourning does not exceed three years;
the coarse hemp dress is not patched,
and the burial mound is not built up;
on the day of the *xiáng* sacrifice,
the plain zither is played,
to announce to the people that there is an end;
this is established by moderation.
Drawing on the service to a father to serve the mother,
the love is the same.
Heaven does not have two suns,
the earth does not have two kings,
the state does not have two rulers,
the family does not have two honored heads;
it is governed by unity.
Therefore when the father is alive,
for the mother one wears the *qící* for one year;
this shows there are not two honored heads.
50.6 Why use a staff?
It is for rank.
On the third day the staff is given to the son,
on the fifth day the staff is given to the *dàfū*,
on the seventh day the staff is given to the *shì*.
Some say it "supports the master";
some say it "assists the sick."
Women and children do not use a staff,
because they cannot be "sick" in this way.
When all the officials are present,
and all the materials are prepared,
and affairs are carried out without speaking,
one rises being supported;
when affairs are carried out only after speaking,
one rises using a staff;
when one personally manages affairs and then they are carried out,
one merely has a begrimed face.
The bald do not wear the *guā* hair-band,
the hunchbacked do not bare the shoulder,
the lame do not leap,
and the old or sick do not abstain from wine and meat.
These eight things
are established by discretion.
50.7 From the beginning of the death,
for three days there is no negligence,
for three months no remissness,
for one year there is grief and sorrow,
for three years there is melancholy;
this is the diminishing of kindness.
The sages followed this diminishing to establish moderation;
this is why mourning lasts for three years.
The worthy must not exceed it,
and the unworthy must not fall short of it;
this is the Middle Way of mourning;
it is what kings constantly practice.
The *Shū* says:
"Gāozōng lived in the mourning hut,
for three years he did not speak,"
which praises him;
no king fails to practice this ritual.
Why then is he alone praised?
It is said:
Gāozōng is Wǔ Dīng.
Wǔ Dīng
was a worthy king of Yīn.
Having succeeded to the throne, he was compassionate and good in his mourning;
at that time,
Yīn had declined and was rising again,
ritual had been abandoned and was being restored;
therefore he was praised.
Because he was praised,
it was recorded in the *Shū* and he was highly regarded;
therefore he was called Gāozōng.
In the three years of mourning,
the ruler does not speak.
The *Shū* says:
"Gāozōng lived in the mourning hut,
for three years he did not speak,"
which refers to this.
However, regarding the saying:
"speech is not refined,"
it refers to the ministers and subordinates.
In ritual:
during the *zhǎncuī* mourning,
one acknowledges but does not answer back;
during the *qící* mourning,
one answers back but does not initiate speech;
during the *dàgōng* mourning,
one speaks but does not deliberate;
during the *sī* and *xiǎogōng* mourning,
one deliberates but does not touch upon music.
In mourning for parents,
one wears the mourning dress and cap, the hemp rope hat-string, and the grass shoes;
for three days one eats only gruel;
after three months one bathes;
in the thirteenth month one wears the *liàn* cap;
and in the third year the *xiáng* sacrifice is performed.
50.8 By following through these three stages,
through the benevolent person one can observe their love,
through the wise person one can observe their reasoning,
and through the strong person one can observe their will.
Ritual is used to govern them,
righteousness is used to rectify them;
filial sons, respectful younger brothers, and chaste wives
can all be observed through this.
